## 55. Firefox under the default nobody had run, and a cause I asserted without measuring

### 55.1 The block that could not have been written by accident

§49 made `--decorations auto` the default and argued it is *byte-for-byte*
`server` for a client that negotiates. The argument is short and it is in the
code: `Decorations::kde()` answers `KdeDefaultMode::Server` for `Auto` and
`Server` alike, `xdg()` answers `ServerSide` for both, and
`surface::fold_caption` never folds a `Negotiated` window. Firefox binds KDE's
manager — the asymmetry §22.2 measured, and GTK3's only route, since it ignores
`zxdg_decoration_manager_v1` entirely — so Firefox is `Negotiated` on every run.

§49.9 listed it as unmeasured and it stayed that way, because **this harness was
built never to exercise it.** Every block in `wc-firefox.sh` names `FX_DECOR`,
deliberately, and the settings block says why: *"a block that relied on it would
be measuring the flag rather than the client"*. That is right for the other
seven blocks and it makes the compiled-in default the one thing the file cannot
reach. So the block needs a sentinel — `FX_DECOR=none`, meaning pass no
`--decorations` at all — and it is worth saying out loud that a harness whose
convention is "always name the flag" has a blind spot exactly where the flag's
default lives.

`scripts/wc-firefox.sh auto`:

```
== auto: Firefox under the compiled-in default, and against server
  PASS  auto: no --decorations was passed and the compositor ran Auto
  PASS  auto: Firefox received default_mode(2) — Auto advertises Server
  PASS  auto: the compositor classified Firefox as Negotiated, so it is never folded
  PASS  auto: no window's caption was folded, which is what server would have done
  ....  auto:   told=default_mode(2), asked=request_mode(2), origin=0,0,
  ....  server: told=default_mode(2), asked=request_mode(2), origin=0,0,
  PASS  auto and server are indistinguishable to Firefox — §49.4's argument, measured
  PASS  auto: the toplevel geometry origin is 0,0 — server-side decorations, no shadow inset
```

**It is a pair, and that is the part with the reasoning in it.** The claim is an
*equivalence*, so asserting only "auto looks right" would pass a compositor that
had quietly made `server` wrong too. The two legs run minutes apart with the
same environment and are compared on the three things the *client* can observe:
the mode it was told, the modes it asked for, and its toplevel window-geometry
origin. Nothing in the comparison reads the compositor's own log.

### 55.2 The gate can fail, and its failure reproduces §22's numbers

One line mutated — `Auto` advertising `KdeDefaultMode::Client` instead of
`Server` — and three of the eight assertions go red:

```
  FAIL  auto: Firefox never logged default_mode(2)
  ....  auto:   told=default_mode(1), asked=request_mode(1), origin=26,23,
  ....  server: told=default_mode(2), asked=request_mode(2), origin=0,0,
  FAIL  auto and server differ where Firefox can see it
  FAIL  auto: the toplevel geometry origin is not 0,0
```

`request_mode(1)` and an inset of `(26, 23)`: those are §22's measured
client-side-decoration numbers, arrived at again by breaking one line. A gate
whose failure mode reproduces a number measured two years of sections earlier is
a gate that is looking at the right thing.

### 55.3 A cause asserted without measuring it, and why the distinction cost something

§49.9 recorded that three attempts to type into `weston-terminal` on the guest's
desktop had refused, and gave the reason: *"The desktop's foreground belonged to
a person"*, citing a `wc-desk windows` listing showing Firefox on a news
article, a 1Password lock screen and a Steam login.

The listing was real. The conclusion was a guess. A window list is equally
consistent with somebody reading and with a session nobody has touched for
hours, and the two things that would have separated them — the session's idle
time, and what `SendInput` actually returned — were not checked. Measured
afterwards by somebody who did check: the session is **locked**, `SendInput`
returns 0 while `SetCursorPos` is obeyed, and idle time is about two and a half
hours. Injected input is accepted by the API and silently discarded.

The refusal was correct. The recorded cause was not, and the difference is
operational rather than pedantic:

* *"a person is using it"* means **wait**, and the measurement arrives on its
  own;
* *"the session is locked"* means **somebody has to unlock it**, and no amount
  of waiting produces anything.

So the wrong cause sent the request to the wrong place, and the run stayed
outstanding for longer than it needed to. §49.9 now carries the correction
rather than the claim.

The same shape, smaller, in the same report: `testhost.lan` resolves to
`<host-alt-ip>`, which does not answer, and I concluded the VM host was
unreachable and built an ssh `ProxyJump` through the guest to work around it.
The host is at **<host-ip>** and answers directly; the DNS name is stale.
The workaround worked, which is exactly why it survived — a workaround that
works stops anybody asking whether the problem was real.

Both are the same error and it is not a new one for this project: **an
observation and an explanation are different things, and only one of them was
measured.** §35 is the section about numbers nobody asserts on; this is the
version about causes nobody checks. The rule that would have caught both: when a
run refuses, the reason it refused is a *measurement to take*, not a story to
supply from what happens to be on the screen.

> **§60 adds the third instance, and it is the one that shows this rule's own
> failure mode.** The correction to the paragraph above — *"the session is
> locked, `SendInput` returns 0"* — was not a story. It was a correct
> measurement, and §57 is a real defect found by taking it. It was simply about
> a code path the launcher does not travel: ssh lands in session 0, the
> launcher's clicks go through a scheduled task into session 1, and a window
> there is visible and mappable while the session is locked. The run was
> available the whole time.
>
> So the rule needs a second clause: **a measurement can be real and still be
> about the wrong path.** Taking one is not sufficient — establishing which path
> the failing thing actually travels is itself the first measurement.
>
> And it is the harder clause to follow, because a real number stops the search
> sooner than a guess does. An inference from a window listing is cheap to
> doubt; a measured `SendInput -> 0, ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` is not, and it held
> for a day. §60.3 is the full sequence.

> **And it happened twice, to two people, from the same evidence, within an
> hour — which is what turns this from an anecdote into a rule worth stating.**
>
> While this section was being written the coordinator reached the same
> conclusion independently: three DNS names for the VM host did not resolve or
> did not answer, and it declared the machine off the network and told four
> agents so. Same premise, same day, same class of evidence, and — the part that
> matters — **both of us were satisfied, because both of our workarounds
> functioned.** Mine was an ssh `ProxyJump` through the guest; the coordinator's
> was routing four agents around a machine that was answering the whole time on
> an address nobody had tried.
>
> That is the mechanism, and it is worth naming separately from the rule:
> **a workaround that works removes the pressure that would have found the real
> cause.** A workaround that *fails* sends you back to the premise; one that
> succeeds retires the question. So the moment to re-check a premise is not when
> the workaround breaks — by then it may never break — but when you first notice
> you are writing one.
>
> Two independent instances in a day is the same density that made §16.8 a rule
> block rather than a footnote, and the two rules are siblings: §16.8 says *a
> name is not an identity*, and this one says *a symptom is not a diagnosis*.
> Both are cases of accepting the first thing that presented itself as though it
> had been checked.

### 55.4 What is still outstanding, stated as an ask rather than as a finding

**Typing into `weston-terminal` on the guest's interactive desktop.** It needs
an **unlocked** session and about five minutes of exclusive access; everything
else is already deployed and byte-verified (`wct46`, ports 57433+,
`/srv/winshare/wct46`). One command produces both remaining pieces:

```
WC_DESKNAME=wct46 WC_PORT_BASE=57433 WC_SUFFIX=-t46 WC_TYPE=waycomposetypes \
  scripts/wc-desktop.sh window
```

— §33's 5b, a photograph of `SendInput` text arriving on `WinSta0`, and §37's
5c, a click 40 px down the client area followed by typing, asserted on the
terminal's repaint count rather than on the picture.

The keyboard path itself is covered without the guest and is green: the Linux
leg (`weston-eventdemo` decoding `helloZyz` through our keymap), and both Wine
legs, 29/0 and 31/0. What the guest run adds is that chain on the guest's own
desktop, which is the venue the user's report came from and the only one that
can close it.
## 56. The same category, from inside, so it travels to the guest

### 56.1 Status in one paragraph

**§53 got here first, and this is the second half of the same category rather
than a rival to it.** That section built the stronger witness: `probe-life.c` is
a *separate process* that never speaks to the compositor and asks the window
manager instead, launched into the compositor's own virtual desktop because
`EnumWindows` only sees the calling thread's. Nothing a compositor can do makes
that witness lie. It is Wine-only, it runs a churn loop, and its answer was that
the compositor is clean.

What it cannot do is travel. It needs its own process deployed into the same
desktop, which on the cross-VM guest means shipping a binary into a session that
is presently locked, and it has no Linux leg at all. So this section adds the
cheap half: **the compositor reports its own window accounting on the way out,
on every platform, on every run**, including the number `EnumWindows` gives for
its own process. `wc-guest.sh` and `wc-damage.sh` get it in logs they already
capture, with nothing deployed and no extra process.

The two are not interchangeable and the ordering between them is the honest one:
§53's witness is authoritative and this one is ubiquitous. Where they disagree,
believe §53.

**This was duplicated effort and the cause is worth recording.** The assignment
said §53 was claimed by something else, and I took that at face value instead of
reading master before starting — which is the same mistake as §51.5's rebuild
ritual, performed after it stopped being necessary. Two agents built the same
category on the same night. What survives here is only what §53 does not cover.

### 56.2 One thing §53's argument does not cover: §21's contrast

§53.2 makes the case for the category and it is not repeated here. One point
belongs to this half rather than that one, because it is about *why the number
has to be everywhere* rather than why it has to come from outside.

§21 is the precedent. smithay calls `IdleInhibitHandler::uninhibit` from exactly
one place — the client's explicit `destroy` request — so a client that crashes
leaves an inhibitor nothing will ever revoke. That was found, and the reason it
was found is that its symptom is **visible**: a display that never sleeps again,
which on a guest VM is a real bill.

A leaked `HWND` has no symptom at all. The process holds a handle until it
exits. A defect with no symptom is not found by somebody noticing; it is found
by a number being printed somewhere a run already looks — which is the argument
for carrying it in the compositor's own exit line rather than only in a harness
somebody has to remember to run.
### 56.3 Five numbers, and the fourth is the one that matters

```
wc-compositor: windows at exit: 3 created, 3 destroyed, 0 still held,
               0 still alive, 0 client(s) still connected
```

| | |
|---|---|
| created / destroyed | what the compositor believes it did |
| still held | entries left in its own map |
| **still alive** | **what Windows says**, `EnumWindows` filtered to this process and `WaycomposeToplevel` |
| clients connected | whether anybody was still there — the qualifier |

The first three are the compositor's own account of its own behaviour, and a
bug in the teardown path is exactly the circumstance in which that account is
wrong. `DestroyWindow` returning false, a window owned by the wrong thread, a
handle already replaced — each leaves the arithmetic balanced, the map empty,
and a window on the desktop.

**Measured, not reasoned.** Deleting the `DestroyWindow` call and running
`scripts/wc-teardown.sh wine`:

```
FAIL  wine: WINDOW LEAK: 1 created, 1 destroyed, 0 still held, 1 still alive
```

Created equals destroyed. The map is empty. Every self-reported number is
perfect and the window is still there. A check built only on the compositor's
own bookkeeping would have passed that build, which is the entire argument for
asking somebody else.

The enumeration is filtered by **process id** as well as class, because
`wc-proxy.sh` and `wc-guest.sh` run several compositors at once on a shared
machine and §16.8's rule is that identity on a shared box is never a class of
thing. A count that swept up another run's windows would fail a harness for
somebody else's leak.

### 56.4 The fifth number exists because the first run was a false positive

The first real run of this assertion reported `1 created, 0 destroyed, 1 still
held, 1 still alive` and would have failed. There was no bug. The compositor had
reached its idle timeout while `weston-terminal` was **still connected**, and a
window whose client is alive is not a leak — the compositor is entitled to still
have it.

So `ToUi::Quit` now carries how many clients were still connected, and the
assertion returns early when that is non-zero. Without it the check would have
fired on every harness in this tree that stops a compositor with `--timeout`
rather than `--once`, which is nearly all of them, and would have been switched
off within a day as noise.

It is carried on the quit message rather than printed as a second line
deliberately: the number it qualifies is only knowable on the UI thread, and two
lines that must be read together are two lines that can be read apart.

### 56.5 The answer is that teardown works

A client killed with `SIGTERM` — no `destroy` request, no clean disconnect —
still produces, in order:

```
wc-compositor: window 1 destroyed
wc-compositor: client InnerClientId { id: 0, serial: 1 } disconnected: ConnectionClosed
```

on both platforms, and the exit line reads `1 created, 1 destroyed, 0 still
held, 0 still alive`. smithay's `toplevel_destroyed` does fire from the
resource destructor on an abrupt disconnect, which is the thing §21's inhibitor
did not have.

Reporting that plainly is the point. This stage found no bug; it found that
nothing would have found one.

### 56.6 Why this is a harness of its own

The report is printed on the way out, from the thread that owns the windows. A
compositor killed with a signal prints nothing — and prints nothing about
teardown for the good reason that it did none.

**Every other harness in this tree stops its compositor with `kill`.**
`wc-window.sh`, `wc-proxy.sh`, `wc-damage.sh`, `wc-firefox.sh` all do, because
until now nothing depended on the compositor being allowed to finish. So none of
them can carry this assertion without being restructured, and `wc-teardown.sh`
lets the compositor reach its idle timeout instead: the client is given a
shorter life than the compositor's timeout, so the client is always the one that
goes first. That ordering *is* the design of the timings, and getting it
backwards is what §56.4 was.

**Its Wine leg overlaps `wc-life.sh` and its Linux leg does not.** §53 churns
windows open and closed and asks an outside process; this one runs a single
window to a clean exit and reads the compositor's own line. They test different
mechanisms — the witness against the accounting — and the Wine leg here exists
because that is the only platform where the accounting has a second opinion to
be checked against. If a future tidy-up wants one harness rather than two, the
thing to keep is §53's witness and the thing to fold into it is this exit line;
the reverse would lose the stronger check.

### 56.7 The gates

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `cargo build --workspace`, both targets | clean |
| `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | **2594 tests**, 0 failures — unchanged by this section; the harness is the test |
| **`scripts/wc-life.sh wine`** (§53's own gate, re-run) | **11 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped** — the compositor claimed 9 destructions for 9 windows and the window manager agreed none were left |
| **`scripts/wc-teardown.sh all`** (new) | **11 passed, 0 failed** |
| ... `linux` leg | `1 created, 1 destroyed, 0 still held, 0 still alive` |
| ... `wine` leg | the same, and Windows agrees none survives |
| **the same, against a build with `DestroyWindow` removed** | **1 failed** — `1 created, 1 destroyed, 0 still held, 1 still alive` |
| `wc_assert_no_window_leaks`, all five states | clean passes; leaked-handle, lost-track, and missing-line all fail; live-client returns a note |

The negative-capability row is the one worth reading. The assertion was proved
able to fail on the real mechanism, on the platform where the mechanism matters,
by breaking the code it watches — not by feeding it a synthetic log.

### 56.8 What is not proven

1. **Popups are counted, but nothing exercises their teardown.** `WindowKind`
   distinguishes toplevels from popups and both go through the same `Destroy`;
   `wc-teardown.sh` only ever opens a toplevel. A menu-opening leg would be the
   sharper test and `wc-popup.sh` is where it belongs.
2. **The enumeration is `WaycomposeToplevel` only.** `WaycomposeController` is
   one window for the life of the process and is deliberately not counted, but
   that means a leak of *it* is invisible to this check. It cannot leak per
   client, which is why it is out of scope rather than an omission.
3. **No cross-VM leg.** The report is printed by whichever compositor runs, so
   `wc-guest.sh` would get it for free — but nothing has asserted on it there,
   and a guest run has not been made.
4. **This checks windows, not everything that can outlive its client.** Pools
   are already counted (`pools_created`/`pools_released`); surfaces, subsurfaces
   and seat objects are not. The category is now open rather than closed, and
   the shape of the next one is the same: ask somebody outside the process.

## 57. The injection that returns zero, and the run that would have believed it

### 57.1 Status in one paragraph

Block 12 — the cross-VM damage leg, §51.6 — is still unrun, and the blocker is
that the guest's Windows session is **locked**. That would not have mattered if
the leg simply failed. It does not: a locked session puts the input desktop on
`Winlogon`, a process on `Default` cannot inject into it, and `SendInput`
**returns 0** and sets `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` without blocking, throwing or
logging. `probe-scroll.c` discarded that return value. It would have printed
`60 notches towards the user`, the harness would have matched its completion
line, and the run would have gone on to measure a browser **nobody scrolled** —
producing real numbers about the wrong thing, which is §27.6's shape exactly.
The probe now counts refusals, says which, and exits 3 when everything was
refused; block 12 asserts on the count rather than on the probe's survival.

### 57.2 Why this was worth doing while the guest was busy

The leg cannot run: another agent's growth run holds the guest, and the session
is locked besides. But the two facts are not the same kind of obstacle. "The
guest is busy" is a queue. "`SendInput` returns 0 and nothing notices" is a
**defect in the experiment**, and it was sitting in the leg waiting for the
queue to clear.

If the session had been unlocked between writing block 12 and running it,
nothing would have been learned. If it had not, the run would have produced a
full set of plausible damage numbers from an idle browser and — because the
damage path is *correct* — reported zero stale rows and passed. A green run
that scrolled nothing is worse than a red one, because it is evidence that will
be cited.

### 57.3 What changed, and the one thing that deliberately did not

```c
	if (SendInput(1, &in, sizeof in) != 1)
		refused++;
```

and, at the end:

```
probe-scroll: 40 of 40 notches towards the user accepted, 150 ms apart
```

Counted rather than aborted on, because the distribution is the diagnosis:
`0 of 60` is a locked session and `58 of 60` is contention with whatever else is
on that desktop. Aborting on the first refusal would have collapsed those into
one symptom.

**The completion line still contains the exact phrase `notches towards the
user`**, and that is deliberate rather than lucky. Two harnesses grep for it to
tell a finished scroll from a probe that died — `wc-damage.sh` in two places,
`wc-guest.sh` in one. A harness that only looks for the phrase keeps working;
one that reads the numbers in front of it can now tell a scroll from a refusal.
Changing the wording would have been a silent regression in three greps, which
is the kind of thing §50.10's citation checker exists for and which no checker
covers for harness greps.

The pointer move is checked too but only warns: a refused `move_to` with
accepted notches is a wheel going somewhere unintended, which is worth a line
and is not the same failure.

### 57.4 The log had to be fetched, which it was not

Block 12 wrote the probe's log to `C:\Users\<guest-user>\wctest\scroll.log` on the
guest and never brought it back, so the only evidence the wheel had moved was
that the probe had not crashed. `wc-stage4` now emits it between
`S4-SCROLLLOG-BEGIN`/`END` markers like every other log it returns, and
`do_damage` asserts on the accepted count found there.

It reads the accounting rather than the exit status on purpose: the exit code
travels through `ssh`, a backgrounded job and a `wait` that the harness
deliberately does not perform (§51.6 — a probe that failed to find the window
must not hang the run), and a number in a log survives all three.

### 57.5 The gates

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc -mwindows probe-scroll.c` | clean |
| `bash -n` on both changed harnesses | clean |
| `scripts/wc-damage.sh arena` | **11 passed, 0 failed** — `40 of 40 notches towards the user accepted`, 1030 commits checked, 0 stale |
| the three existing greps for `notches towards the user` | still match the new wording |
| **`scripts/wc-guest.sh damage` against the guest** | **STILL NOT RUN** — the guest is held and its session is locked |

### 57.6 What is not proven

1. **The refusal path has never been exercised.** The fix is reasoned from
   Windows' documented behaviour and from the coordinator's measurement that
   `SendInput` returns 0 while `SetCursorPos` is obeyed on that session; this
   branch has only ever seen `40 of 40` accepted, because the box it can reach
   is not locked. The first locked-session run is the test of it, and if it
   reports anything other than `0 of N` with a `REFUSED` line, this section is
   wrong about the mechanism rather than about the need for the check.
2. **`SetCursorPos` being obeyed is not used.** It would be a way to confirm a
   locked session positively rather than inferring it from a refusal count. Not
   done, because a probe that reports what it *could* do is a smaller change
   than one that diagnoses the session, and the diagnosis belongs to whoever
   owns the guest.
3. **Block 12 remains a hypothesis with a script attached** (§51.6), and the
   user's second symptom — no tearing, no stalled scrolling, no blank frames in
   `about:support` — remains unverified. What has changed is only that the leg
   can no longer pass without having scrolled.
## 58. The unqualified citations, and the ambiguity they were hiding

### 58.1 Status in one paragraph

§54.3 left two pieces of residue. Both are closed. The **762 unqualified
`docs/design.md §N` citations** — the bare form that names neither document in a tree
with two of them — are all qualified, and the checker now **fails** on the form,
which is the "one line in one place" §54.3 promised. Doing it surfaced something
the bare form had been hiding: **103 citations name a section their document
defines twice**, which no edit to a citation can fix. And the negative test now
runs a control fixture first, so a checker that grows an external dependency
reports that rather than being mistaken for a checker correctly rejecting a bad
citation.

### 58.2 The rule was the file's own side, and it was right 755 times out of 762

A bare `docs/design.md §N` could mean either document, so the question was whether
there is a rule that decides it without reading 762 comments. There is, and it
was checked before anything was rewritten:

| | |
|---|---|
| resolve on the file's own side | **755** |
| resolve only on the *other* side | **7** |
| resolve in neither document | **0** |

"Own side" is `crates/wc-*`, `scripts/wc-*` and the C probes for the Wayland
document, everything else for the Vulkan one. That the "neither" column is zero
is what makes this safe: every one of the 762 named a real section, so none of
them was a guess about intent — only about which of two files it lived in.

**The seven exceptions are genuine cross-references, not mistakes**, which is why
they were inspected rather than forced to the majority rule:
`wc-proxy`'s `guestram.rs` and `pool.rs` cite the Vulkan document's §5.7 and
§0.14 because the arena is shared_vulkan's subject; `wc-launch/src/plan.rs`
cites §0.17; and two `sv-*` guest scripts cite the Wayland document's §12.9 and
§17. Each was qualified with the document it actually meant.

The rewrite was line-scoped — file, line number and section number all had to
match — so a line carrying two citations could not have one of them rewritten
with the other's document.

### 58.3 What qualifying revealed

```
before:  270 resolve to exactly one section    0 missing    0 ambiguous  762 unqualified
after:   929 resolve to exactly one section    0 missing  103 ambiguous    0 unqualified
```

**The 103 are not new breakage.** They were always ambiguous; the bare form was
hiding them, because a citation that names no document cannot be checked against
one. Qualifying them moved a silent problem into a reported one, which is the
direction that counts even though the number went up.

They are concentrated in a handful of duplicated section numbers in
`docs/design.md`: §1 is defined twice and cited 48 times, §8 twice and cited 28,
then §3, §0.21, §0.15 and three singletons. **No edit to any citation fixes
this** — the document has to stop defining the same number twice — so the
checker reports and does not fail on it, for §48.3's reason: renumbering a
document another agent is actively writing in, to repair citations that resolve
to two correct-looking places rather than none, is the worse trade. It is now
visible and counted, which is the precondition for someone deciding otherwise.

### 58.4 The control fixture, and a negative test that could have lied

§54.3 named the risk precisely: `the_citation_check_can_fail` copies only the
script into a temporary tree, so if the checker ever grew a dependency on
anything outside its own file — a config, a helper it sources — it would fail on
the bait fixture for **that** reason, and be reported as the checker correctly
rejecting a bad citation. A negative test passing for the wrong reason is §42's
defect wearing the opposite mask: it is a check that cannot fail, disguised as
one that just did.

The fixture is now run twice. First with only a sound citation, where the
checker must **succeed** — if it does not, the message says the checker is
broken or unsatisfied in this environment and makes no claim about citations at
all. Only then the bait. That is the same shape as §47's "slow is not broken":
two different facts that were sharing one verdict.

### 58.5 What is not done

1. **The 103 ambiguous citations stand**, blocked on de-duplicating
   `docs/design.md`'s section numbers. That is the Vulkan side's document and
   the numbering collisions are §48.3's. The checker will fail on them the day
   the count reaches zero, by the same one-line change §58.1 just made for the
   unqualified form.
2. **2457 bare `§N` with no document at all are still unchecked.** They mean
   "this file's own document", and §58.2 shows that convention is right 99.1% of
   the time — which is an argument that a file-to-document map is now worth
   building, since the rule it would encode has been measured rather than
   assumed. Not built here.
3. **Nothing checks that a citation's section is *about* what the comment says.**
   A citation can resolve perfectly and still point at the wrong argument, and
   that is §35.10's territory rather than this checker's.


---
---

## 59. The protocols Firefox binds, measured against the protocols WLCS is skipping

### 59.1 Status in one paragraph

Task #31 asks for *"the Wayland protocols Firefox actually binds, implemented
fully rather than partially"*, and the natural way to read that against the
scoreboard is: WLCS skips 759 tests, 79 of them because a protocol is
unimplemented, so implement the ones Firefox needs. **That reading is wrong, and
the measurement says so.** Firefox 151.0.2 binds twelve interfaces, all twelve
are implemented, and it binds **none** of the seven protocols behind those 79
skips — not with a page built to provoke them, and not with Gecko's Wayland
preferences turned on. The Firefox-relevant debt is not in the skips at all. It
is in the **35 unexplained failures**, which are inside protocols this
compositor already implements. `wp_viewporter`, `pointer-constraints` and the
two `text-input`s are 61 of the 79, and on this evidence none of them is on the
goal's path.

### 59.2 What the number 114 is made of

```
headless: 409 passed, 57 failed, 759 skipped
```

The 759 skips are already attributed, one reason per protocol, and the
attribution is what makes the arithmetic possible:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| JUSTIFIED | 682 | protocols this compositor will not implement, with a reason — `zwlr_layer_shell_v1` 368, `zxdg_shell_v6` 180, `wl_shell` 89, `zwlr_foreign_toplevel_manager_v1` 30, the two primary-selection managers 10 |
| GAP | 79 | unimplemented, no reason beyond not yet — `wp_viewporter` 23, `zwp_pointer_constraints_v1` 15, `zwp_text_input_manager_v2` 12, `zwlr_virtual_pointer_manager_v1` 12, `zwp_text_input_manager_v3` 11, `zwp_relative_pointer_manager_v1` 3, `wp_fractional_scale_manager_v1` 2, `zxdg_output_manager_v1` 1 |
| SELFTEST | 3 | WLCS proving its own skip machinery |

and of the 57 failures, 22 are expected on this platform — input outside the
window-geometry rectangle, where the HWND *is* that rectangle and Windows
delivers no message outside a window (§45.4).

So **114 = 79 gaps + 35 unexplained failures**, and the two halves are not the
same kind of debt. A gap is a protocol nobody has written. A failure is a
protocol that is written and does the wrong thing — which is precisely the
"partially rather than fully" the task names.

### 59.3 The list, and why the obvious way to read it is a floor

`scripts/wc-firefox.sh enumerate` has printed the same twelve interfaces for
several stages:

```
org_kde_kwin_server_decoration_manager  wl_compositor  wl_data_device_manager
wl_output  wl_seat  wl_shm  wl_subcompositor  wp_cursor_shape_manager_v1
xdg_activation_v1  xdg_wm_base  zwp_idle_inhibit_manager_v1
zwp_keyboard_shortcuts_inhibit_manager_v1
```

That block runs `about:blank`, and a browser binds a protocol when a page makes
it necessary. `about:blank` makes almost nothing necessary: no editable field,
so no reason for `text-input`; no pointer lock, so no reason for
`pointer-constraints` or `relative-pointer`; no scaled video, so no reason for
`viewporter`. Read as "the set Firefox needs", the list is an inference from a
page that was chosen for being empty — which is the §55.3 error again, an
observation standing in for a measurement nobody took.

### 59.4 So the page was given something to do

`scripts/wc-firefox.sh needs` is three legs, and the third is the one that
stops the answer being misread.

1. **A local page that provokes.** An autofocused `<input>`, a `<textarea>`, a
   `contenteditable` div, a `<canvas>` wired to `requestPointerLock`, and an
   autoplaying `<video>`. Offline and local: a remote page would make the
   measurement a fact about a website, and this harness must not need a network.
2. **The same run on `about:blank`**, recomputed here rather than read from
   `enumerate`, so the block stands alone and the comparison is between two runs
   minutes apart rather than between a run and a memory.
3. **The same page again with Gecko's Wayland preferences on** —
   `widget.wayland.text-input-v3.enabled`, the pointer-constraints and
   fractional-scale switches, and trusted-request-only off. Because *"Firefox
   did not bind it"* has two causes that lead opposite ways: the client does not
   need the protocol, or its support is behind a pref that is off. Reporting the
   first when it is the second would tell whoever implements these gaps that
   they are not on the goal's path, and that is the most expensive kind of wrong
   answer a measurement can give.

The result, and it is the same in all three legs:

```
  PASS  a page made Firefox bind nothing extra — about:blank's list really is the set
  ....  not bound even with a page: zwp_text_input_manager_v3
  ....  not bound even with a page: zwp_text_input_manager_v2
  ....  not bound even with a page: zwp_pointer_constraints_v1
  ....  not bound even with a page: zwp_relative_pointer_manager_v1
  ....  not bound even with a page: wp_viewporter
  ....  not bound even with a page: wp_fractional_scale_manager_v1
  ....  not bound even with a page: zxdg_output_manager_v1
  PASS  with the Wayland prefs on as well, Firefox binds nothing further
```

**A negative result, and the useful kind.** The suspicion was that the twelve
were an artefact of an empty page; they are not. Twelve is the set, for this
build, for these capabilities.

### 59.5 What that means for task #31

* **The 61 skips from `viewporter`, `pointer-constraints` and the two
  `text-input`s are not on Firefox's path.** They may be worth implementing for
  conformance — WLCS is a conformance suite and 114 reaching zero is a real
  goal — but they are not what *this* task is asking for, and doing them first
  would be spending the goal's budget on clients this project does not have.
* **The task's own words are already satisfied at the level of binding.** All
  twelve interfaces Firefox binds are implemented; none of them is absent.
* **So "fully rather than partially" means the 35 unexplained failures**, and
  they are inside `wl_compositor`, `wl_seat`, `wl_surface`, `xdg_wm_base` and
  friends — the protocols already written. That is where the next person should
  start, and it is a different list from the one the scoreboard's skip table
  suggests.

### 59.6 What this does not say

1. **One build, one set of capabilities.** Firefox 151.0.2, with a page
   exercising text entry, pointer lock and video. A page doing something else —
   WebXR, a colour-managed image, a tablet — could bind more, and a future
   Firefox certainly will: `wp_fractional_scale_manager_v1` in particular is
   the pair to `wl_compositor` v6's `preferred_buffer_scale`, and the day Gecko
   adopts it this answer changes.
2. **Binding is not using.** This measures the registry, not what Firefox does
   with what it bound. A protocol bound and barely exercised is exactly the
   "partially" the task is about, and nothing here looks inside the twelve.
3. **Nothing here is about Win32.** Every leg is the Linux build, where Firefox
   is a stock libwayland client talking to stock `wayland-server` — which is the
   right place to ask what a client *needs* and says nothing about what the
   Windows side does with it.
4. **The 22 expected failures are argued, not proved.** §45.4 says input outside
   the window-geometry rectangle cannot be delivered because the HWND is that
   rectangle; that is a claim about Win32 being checked here by a Linux run.
---

## 61. Growth ran on a guest, and the first thing it produced was the reason it never had

§34 built arena growth over guest RAM, ended with "**Nothing here has run on a
guest**", and predicted that the first run would produce the cost of a growth
against the table in `docs/waycompose-design.md` §34.2. This is that run. It
produced the cost — and before it, two defects that had made growth impossible
on every guest session this project has ever started, neither of which any test
in the tree could have found.

Venue: `sv-guest.exe` on the Windows guest, `wc-proxy` and `wc-arena-host` on
testhost where QEMU runs, Firefox on testhost as the client. Driven through
`scripts/wc-launch.sh`, which is the product's own path — `wc-launch.exe` starts
the compositor, opens its own tunnel and asks the VM host for the application,
and the clock is inside the launcher. The workstation only builds, clicks and
reads numbers back.

### 61.1 The declaration this harness never made

`scripts/wc-launch.sh` had neither `wc_substrate_declare` nor
`wc_topology_declare`, four stages after `docs/waycompose-design.md` §51 made
them structural. The reason is worth recording because it is a hole in the
structure rather than an oversight in the script: every *other* guest harness
gets its declaration for free, because it calls `wc_locate_arena` to find the
arena and that function lives in `wc-substrate.sh`. This one locates nothing —
`wc-session` runs `wc-arena-host` on the far side of an ssh channel — so there
was no function it had to call, and therefore nothing that made the omission
visible. **A gate you reach for by accident is not a gate.**

It declares both now, and `wcl_assert_located` proves them from the one line the
launcher already prints, which carries the page count *and* which locator
produced them. Sample output, from the run below:

```
  ----  topology: CROSS-VM -- a hypervisor is in the path. sv-guest.exe on
        <guest-user>@<guest-ip>, wc-proxy on <host-user>@<host-ip>, arena in the guest's own RAM
  PASS  the arena is guest RAM: 3072 pages located by frames on <host-user>@<host-ip>
  PASS  launch: TOPOLOGY cross-vm: proven by 3072 pages of guest RAM located by frames
```

### 61.2 The first defect: the keymap had already taken the channel's address

`docs/waycompose-design.md` §34.5 reasoned carefully about *when*
`Control::create` may run — it zeroes the control region, and on guest RAM those
bytes are the stamps the host locates by, so it must wait until the first client
proves the locate finished. That reasoning is correct and it is why
`grow::Service::start()` was called at `release_gifts`.

It is also only half the constraint, and the other half points the opposite way.
`reserve_growth_channel` may only run **while the outbound window is untouched**,
because the channel is the front of that window and the free list has no way to
express a hole. Smithay seals the seat's keymap in `Seat::add_keyboard`, which
`docs/waycompose-design.md` §14.12's own correction already records as happening
"a full minute before any client exists" — and although
`docs/waycompose-design.md` §12.10's `defer_gifts` postpones the keymap's
*write*, it does not postpone its *allocation*: `w.given` is charged when the
slice is taken. So by the time a client arrived, the front of the window was
spoken for and the reservation was refused, every time.

What that looked like from the two ends, on the guest at a 12 MiB floor:

```
wc-compositor: seat0 keyboard: layout de (73017 bytes of keymap)
wc-compositor: no growth channel (the growth channel must be reserved before anything is
  given out of the outbound window: it is the front of that window, and the free list has
  no way to express a hole); this session cannot be asked for more memory and will refuse
  under pressure instead
```

```
[proxy] client 28: pool 25: could not publish 960000 bytes: arena 0 cannot serve 962560
  bytes and cannot grow: growth channel: magic is 0x6d79656b5f626b78, which is not ours
  (a byte-swapped magic means a big-endian peer)
```

`0x6d79656b5f626b78` is `xkb_keym` in ASCII. The proxy attached at the front of
the outbound window — which is where both sides derive the channel's address
from, correctly — and read the keymap's own header as a control-region magic.
**The diagnosis it printed named a big-endian peer**, which is as far from an
offset collision as a message can get, and it is the shape of failure worth
remembering: two components agreeing about an address, one of which had lost a
race for it years of design-time reasoning never considered.

The measurement that session produced is `docs/waycompose-design.md` §28.12's,
verbatim and on the deployment for the first time: **0 growths, 97 refusals**, and
`the pool is held back and every request naming it is absorbed, so this surface
stops updating until there is room`.

The fix is the same split `defer_gifts`/`release_gifts` already is: **reserve
early, create late.** `reserve_growth_channel` is bookkeeping and touches no
bytes, so it runs where the outbound window is set up, before the keymap;
`Control::create`, which writes, still runs at the first client. `Window::channel`
carries the range between the two moments.

### 61.3 Growth, measured

With the channel actually up:

```
wc-compositor: arena 0 growth channel reserved at 11534336+278528, before any object is
  given out of the outbound window
wc-compositor: growth channel up; the host may ask for another region when its pools do not fit
```

and, under a real Firefox on a 12 MiB floor:

| | |
|---|---|
| `[proxy] region 1` | **16777216 bytes of guest RAM — 746 ms in the guest, 46 ms locating (frame list)** |
| host-side translation | `located 4096 of 4096 pages in 8.70ms by frame list (swept 0 MiB; 388 frame run(s) became 388 file run(s))` |
| plan | `region 1 (388 run(s), object /proc/1773734/fd/35) [appended]` — region 0's record byte-for-byte intact |
| refusals | **0**, across all 14 client reports |
| arena | `peak resident 28.0 MiB in 2 region(s); floor 12.0 MiB (the startup region, never returned); grew 1` |

Against `docs/waycompose-design.md` §34.2's table: the locate is **46 ms**, of
which 8.70 ms is the translation, against the 2832–3101 ms a content sweep costs
and the 0.064 s that section predicted for the query. The prediction was
pessimistic by a comfortable margin. The guest's 746 ms is the `VirtualAlloc`
plus a `VirtualLock` of every page plus the stamp plus `SuperfetchPfnQuery`, and
it is the dominant term — growth is a guest-side cost, not a locate cost, which
inverts the assumption that made stage 16 reject growth outright.

**The PFN locator executed on a guest, on the growth path, and it is the arm
that ran.** `docs/waycompose-design.md` §34.6's "the PFN locator has still never
executed on a guest" is closed. No `frames=none` was seen on any leg of any run
in this session; the startup locates took the same arm (`3072 of 3072 pages in
6.45ms`, and at the 64 MiB baseline `16384 of 16384 pages in 7.90ms`).

Click-to-window, same clicks through the same scheduler path, cold:

| floor | click-to-window |
|---|---|
| 64 MiB, no growth needed | 4720 ms |
| 12 MiB, one growth | 3991 ms, 4930 ms |

The 12 MiB run is not slower, and there is no held-back pool in it. That is what
`Floor::GrowsUnderPressure` asks for and it is now shown — with the caveat in
§61.5 about which comparison is honest.

### 61.4 The second defect: the reply does not fit the ring it was sized for

Later growths in the same session failed:

```
wc-compositor: growth channel: growth ring: a 65600-byte packet cannot fit a 65536-byte ring;
  the payload belongs in the arena
```

**Fixed.** The region is kept and the frame list is dropped; see §61.4a for the
decision and §34.5 for the corrected sizing. What this section first said about
*why* it happened was wrong twice over, and both corrections make it worse
rather than rarer.

**It is not 16 bytes a frame, it is 8.** `Reply::encode` writes one `u64` per
**page** — `put_u64` per entry of `frames` — not a run-length encoded pair. The
original note reasoned from RLE runs at 16 bytes and concluded that a 16 MiB
region was "the ring exactly"; it is 4096 pages at 8 bytes, which is 32,768
bytes, comfortably half the lane.

**So fragmentation has nothing to do with it.** The claim that "measured
fragmentation made this rare rather than constant", and the 388-run figure
offered as evidence, were about the *locator's* coalesced file runs — a
different number in a different program. The reply's size depends on the
region's **page count alone**. A packet holds `max_payload` = 65,504 bytes, of
which 48 are the fixed header, so the ring carries **8,182 pages ≈ 31.96 MiB**.

**Which makes it deterministic, not rare.** Every region of 32 MiB or more
overflows, always, on any guest. `GROW_STEP` is 16 MiB and the series is
geometric to a 64 MiB cap — 16, 32, 64 — so **the second growth in any session
overflows, every time.** "Later growths in the same session failed" was not a
coincidence of fragmentation; it was the series arriving at 32 MiB.

A Linux guest reaches it with certainty for a second reason: `/proc/self/pagemap`
names every page, so the frame list is always fully populated. A Windows guest
depends on `SuperfetchPfnQuery` answering for the whole window, which it did.

#### 61.4a The decision, and why the region is what survives

The section said the choice between a larger ring and an out-of-band payload was
"a protocol decision, not a number to nudge". That was right about it being a
decision and wrong about leaving it: a decision is a thing to make. It is made,
and it is neither of those two.

**The frame list is dropped and the region is answered for.** The asymmetry
decides it. Pushing an oversized packet fails the push, and it is the **reply**
that is lost — the host sits out its 20-second deadline and reports a compositor
that never answered, for a growth that in fact *succeeded* and whose region is
committed, `VirtualLock`ed and now unreachable. That is a leak with a
misdiagnosis attached. Losing the frame list instead costs a sweep and says so.

It invents no new failure mode. "No frame list" is exactly the degradation
`docs/design.md` §0.21 and §34.2 already specify and the host already
implements: the locator sweeps, which is *correct* on a freshly committed region
because nothing has overwritten its stamps, and costs seconds instead of
milliseconds.

**A larger ring was rejected on a cost this document already carries.** The lane
is sized inside `CONTROL_BYTES`, which is carved out of the compositor's
outbound window — the window that holds keymaps and clipboard offers and is the
one region release may never reclaim. Sizing it for 64 MiB of frame list would
take a quarter of that window permanently, raising the floor this stage exists
to lower. Chunking across packets is the other alternative, is real protocol
work, and buys the same thing.

**And "out of band" cannot mean a side channel here**, which the original
wording invited: all communication goes through the ring, and alternative
channels exist only to wake a peer from idle. Putting the payload in the arena
would be within that rule only if the ring still framed it — which is chunking
by another name.

The check lives in `GuestEnd::service`, the one place every reply passes
through, because the limit is the ring's and that is what the type owns. Its
message now says what was lost and what it costs, because at one line per second
growth it is a thing operators will read routinely rather than once.


### 61.5 Release still has not fired, and now there are two reasons

**This is the measurement the user asked for and it is the one this run does not
have.** `sv-guest.exe`'s working set, from the guest's own process view, across
the run at a 12 MiB floor with one growth:

| | `sv-guest.exe` working set |
|---|---|
| before — no process at all | **0** (16 samples with no `sv-guest.exe`) |
| at peak, clients up | **112,427,008 B (107.2 MiB)** |
| after every Firefox exited | **90,206,208 B (86.0 MiB)** |

It fell by 21 MiB and **it did not give back the 16 MiB region**: the proxy's own
accounting says `now 28.0 MiB in 2 region(s) … grew 1, released 0 region(s) /
0.0 MiB` after the last client was gone. Two independent causes were observed,
and either alone is sufficient:

1. **The reclaim clock only turns while a client is drawing.** `Arena::frame()`
   is what advances the tick and is the only caller of `reclaim_regions`, and its
   one call site is `Session::commit` — a client's surface commit. With every
   client exited there are no commits, so a region that has just become idle can
   never accumulate the `--arena-grow-idle 120` frames that would return it. The
   policy is written in frames and the situation it most needs to handle is the
   one that has no frames in it.

2. **The region never became empty.** After every Firefox was killed the arena
   still reported `21880832 of 29360128 bytes out`, so `slot.is_empty()` was
   false regardless of the clock. Whatever holds those pools outlives the
   connection that made them, and that is a second bug behind the first.

So the honest statement is: **release is wired, its opcode is right, its
asymmetry argument is right, and it has still never run.** The user's
observation — "sv-guest.exe is hogging 890 MB even though no wayland or vulkan
clients are up" — is not explained by the startup floor alone. The floor is the
part that was designed never to come back; this is the part that was designed to
come back and does not.

What the run *does* settle about the user's complaint is the 890 MB itself: the
working set tracks the arena almost exactly. At a 64 MiB floor `sv-guest.exe`
peaked at 116,162,560 B; at 12 MiB it peaked at 112,427,008 B with a 16 MiB
region bought on top. The arena is the dominant term, so a 768 MiB floor is a
768 MiB process, which is what reached a user.

### 61.6 What is proven and what is not

| | |
|---|---|
| growth over guest RAM, end to end, on a guest | **shown** — `region 1`, 16 MiB, 746 ms guest / 46 ms locate |
| `0 refusals` at a floor below the peak | **shown** — 14 client reports, all `0 refusals` |
| the plan appends without disturbing region 0 | **shown** — `[appended]`, region 0's record unchanged |
| the PFN locator on a guest, on the growth path | **shown** — `by frame list`, 388 runs, 8.70 ms |
| `frames=none` degradation | **not seen** — the frame-list arm ran on every leg, so the sweep arm is still unexercised on this deployment |
| release returning guest RAM | **NOT SHOWN — and it is not merely unrun.** Two causes observed, §61.5 |
| a second growth in one session | **NOT SHOWN** — refused by the ring size, §61.4 |
| `Floor::CURRENT` moved to `GrowsUnderPressure` | **no.** Growth is shown; release is not, and a floor that grows without giving back is the user's complaint with extra steps |

`Floor::CURRENT` stays `MustStandAlone` and
`growth_has_not_been_demonstrated_on_a_guest_yet` stays asserted. The arm's own
text asks for growth "showing the arena growing rather than refusing", which this
run gives it — but the module header's argument is about memory that is *"gone
from Windows entirely, for anything, for as long as the session lasts"*, and
until §61.5's two causes are fixed a lower floor buys regions it cannot return.
The next run to flip that line is the one that puts a number in the "after"
row of §61.5's table that is smaller than the "peak" row by the size of the
regions it grew.

### 36.20 The deployment guest answers: 13.6 µs, and there is no floor

§36.19 predicted that `WaitOnAddress`'s whole-millisecond argument floors a
*missed* wake and not a *delivered* one, from a 136 µs measurement on the
Windows binary under Wine. That was evidence, not proof, and it stayed a
prediction because Wine implements `WaitOnAddress` over futexes.

Measured on `testhost`'s Windows guest — the machine where the 216.9 ms
present was measured, running Microsoft's `WaitOnAddress` and virtio-win's
`vioser.sys`. `scripts/sv-bell-guest.sh`, 2,000 samples, µs:

| | min | median | p99 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| same kernel (socketpair on the VM host) | 5.6 | 8.2 | 12.3 | 75.2 |
| **across the boundary (virtio-serial)** | **22.3** | **27.1** | **43.6** | **130.0** |

> **A doorbell reaches the Windows guest in 13.6 µs**, one way.

Against the alternatives, per wait: the fixed 20 ms slice is **1,474×** that,
and the ladder's 1 ms floor is **74×** it. Eleven waits — one present — is
**0.15 ms of doorbell latency against 220 ms of slice**.

**The prediction holds and the floor does not exist for a delivered wake.** If
`WaitOnAddress`'s millisecond granularity applied to delivery, nothing here
could have come in under 1,000 µs; the *slowest sample of two thousand* was 130.
§36.18's worry — that the 64-of-95 sub-100 µs mass was exactly what a floor
would destroy — is answered: it survives, on the real guest, with room.

Against the Linux development guest's 8.8–9.4 µs one way, Windows costs about
50% more. Same order, no cliff. Whatever `vioser.sys` and `afunix`-free
virtio-serial cost over `/dev/virtio-ports`, it is tens of microseconds and not
a millisecond.

#### 36.20.1 Two guards that fired, and were right to

**The one-opener rule caught a real leak.** A previous run's probe was still
holding the port — `Id 21432, C:\Users\<guest-user>\sv-bell-probe.exe, StartTime
10:22:23` — and the second attempt got `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`. That is the same
errno §36.13 saw on `org.sirati.display.0`, which strengthens that section's
hypothesis considerably: **5 is what this driver returns for a port that is
present but unavailable**, whether because nothing backs it or because someone
else has it. It was found by asking for pid and path rather than by killing an
image name.

**And the handshake-before-latency check did its job on the first try.** The run
that hit the held port refused to measure and said so, instead of timing a
transport that was not there. It was written for the locked-session worry, which
turned out not to be the risk at all — the risk was a stale process of my own —
and it caught the thing it was not written for. That is the argument for the
shape rather than for the specific fear.

**One self-inflicted delay worth recording**: the guard that refuses to share
the QMP socket used `pgrep -f qemu-serve`, and the ssh command carrying the
check *contains that string*, so it matched its own shell and refused a socket
that was free. It is `pgrep -x sv-hostd` now, by executable name. This is the
same self-match that once made a `pkill -f` take down the wrong process on this
machine, in a script written after that lesson.

**The port was hot-added and remains transient** — it dies with the QEMU
process, and `testhost/default.nix` was not touched. Making it permanent is
one line there, needs a `nixos-rebuild switch` that restarts the VM, and is the
user's to time.
## 62. The other thing a window holds, and the return value nobody read

*(§53's continuation. The window handle had a witness; this does not.)*

### 62.1 Status in one paragraph

§53.6 item 1 said `RevokeDragDrop` was not observed, and it was worse than
unobserved: **`drag::revoke` discarded the `HRESULT`.** The whole of §43.7's
ordering argument — revoke *before* `DestroyWindow`, because OLE keys the
registration on the `HWND` and a destroyed handle cannot be revoked — rests on
that call succeeding, and a compositor that got the ordering wrong produced
exactly the same output as one that got it right: none. It is read now, counted,
and printed at exit beside §56's window accounting, so it travels to the guest
on every run with nothing deployed. A new test on the Windows target makes the
count falsifiable rather than decorative. `scripts/wc-life.sh` asserts the pair
balances and is not a pair of zeros: **14 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped**, with
6 registered and 6 revoked. **The idea that would have made this externally
checkable does not work, and 57.3 is the measurement rather than the argument.**

### 62.2 Why this resource has no outside witness

§53's strength was that its witness could not be talked out of it: another
process asks the window manager, and nothing the compositor does makes
`EnumWindows` lie. That does not transfer here, for a structural reason rather
than a missing tool. **OLE's drop-target registration table is not enumerable
from another process.** There is no `EnumDragDropTargets`; the only documented
way to observe a registration is to be refused when adding a second one for the
same `HWND`, and that requires holding the `HWND` in question.

So the asymmetry is real and is stated rather than papered over: the window
count in §53 is authoritative, and the drop-target count here is the
compositor's own account of its own behaviour — which §56.3 is right to label
`claims`, because a bug in the teardown path is exactly the circumstance in
which such an account is wrong.

### 62.3 The trick that would have fixed that, and the measurement that killed it

A stranded registration *does* have one observable consequence: OLE refuses a
`RegisterDragDrop` on an `HWND` that already has one, with
`DRAGDROP_E_ALREADYREGISTERED`. The compositor already logs that refusal. So if
a destroyed window's `HWND` value were ever handed out again, a leaked
registration would announce itself on the *next* window, from outside, with no
new instrumentation at all.

That only works if handle values are reused. **They are not, at this scale.**
Six windows through one compositor process, from `docs/life/compositor.log`:

```text
window 1 created (HWND 0x1007a)
window 2 created (HWND 0x700ac)
window 3 created (HWND 0x1100ac)
window 4 created (HWND 0x1b00ac)
window 5 created (HWND 0x2500ac)
window 6 created (HWND 0x800be)
```

Six windows, six distinct handles. The low half repeats — `0x00ac` four times —
and the high half does not, which is the generation counter doing its job: a
handle value is not reused until the table wraps, and the table is 16 bits wide.
Provoking a collision would take of the order of 65,536 create/destroy cycles.

**This is recorded as a negative result rather than quietly dropped**, because
the idea is a good one and the next person will have it. It is not wrong; it is
untestable at any cycle count this project will run, and a harness built on it
would be a gate that cannot fail — which is the thing §53 exists to avoid,
reintroduced by the mechanism meant to strengthen it.

### 62.4 What makes a counter worth printing

A count of successes is worth nothing unless the thing counted can come out the
other way, so that is now a test on the Windows target
(`revoking_a_window_that_was_never_a_drop_target_is_not_a_success`, in the
`drag::` suite, **11 tests**):

* `RevokeDragDrop` on a window that was never registered does **not** return
  `S_OK` — so the `hr == S_OK` arm in `revoke` is a real branch;
* and on one that *was* registered it does — so the arm is reachable.

Deliberately not asserting the exact failure code beyond "not success": what
matters is that OLE distinguishes the two cases, and pinning the constant would
fail on a platform that returned a different-but-still-failing one for the same
correct reason.

The pair then rides out on the exit line, next to §56's:

```text
wc-compositor: windows at exit: 6 created, 6 destroyed, 0 still held, 0 still alive, 0 client(s) still connected
wc-compositor: drop targets at exit: claims 6 registered, 6 revoked, 0 revoke(s) failed
```

`wc-life.sh` asserts three things about the second line, and the first of them is
the one that stops the other two being decoration: that `registered` is **not
zero**. The churn proved six windows were made; each registered; so the number
has to be six, and a balance of `0 == 0` is a failure rather than a pass.

### 62.5 What is not proven

1. **The count is the compositor's own.** §62.2 is why there is no alternative,
   not an excuse for not having one. If OLE ever grows an enumeration, this
   should be replaced rather than supplemented.
2. **`release_icons` is still unobserved**, for §53.6 item 2's reason: its
   effect is an `HICON` count, `GetGuiResources` is what would answer, and Wine
   returns 0. That is the one remaining per-window resource with neither an
   external witness nor an internal count, and giving it an internal count is
   the obvious next step.
3. **The guest run is still the valuable one** and is still queued: on Windows
   `counter=live` turns §53's `SKIP` into an assertion and would cover both the
   icons and the handle totals at once.
4. **Nothing here provokes a failure in a live compositor.** The test proves the
   branch exists; no run has made the compositor's own revoke fail, because
   nothing in the tree currently can.
5. **Popups are still not churned** (§53.6 item 4), and they are the case where
   this matters most: §43.7 does not register popups as drop targets at all, so
   a menu-heavy session exercises the create/destroy path without the
   registration path, and the two counts would legitimately diverge. Nothing
   asserts what that divergence should look like.

### 62.6 The gates

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| **`scripts/wc-life.sh wine`** | **14 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped** (11 in §53) |
| `wine …/wc_compositor-*.exe drag::` | **11 tests, 0 failures** (10 in §50) |
| `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | see below |
| `cargo build --workspace --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` | clean |
| `scripts/wc-xref.sh` | 0 broken, 0 ambiguous |

The compositor's idle timeout in `wc-life.sh` had to change, and that is
load-bearing rather than tidying: the exit accounting is printed **on the way
out**, so a harness that kills the compositor never sees it. §56's harness
reaches the same conclusion by the same route.

**The first number chosen for it was wrong, and the way it was wrong is the
lesson.** 600 s went to 30 s, and 30 s fired *mid-churn* — because the stretch
that matters is not the gap between cycles but the "is it gone yet" poll, which
spends up to forty seconds with no client connected, each `life` call being a
fresh `wine explorer`. The compositor exited, the next three cycles reported
windows that never appeared, and the run printed:

```text
FAIL  cycle 4: the client's window never appeared
FAIL  only 2 of 5 windows were ever seen alive -- the negative results below are worthless
FAIL  4 registered but only 3 revoked -- a registration is stranded in OLE's table
----  windows at exit: 4 created, 3 destroyed, 1 still held, 1 still alive, 2 client(s) still connected
```

That last line is a compositor leaking a window and stranding an OLE
registration. It is also a harness that shut the compositor down while two
clients were still connected. **This is the third time in two sections that a
harness bug has produced a perfectly plausible bug report about the
compositor** — §53.4's three were the same shape — and the reason is worth
naming: on this subject the *evidence for a leak is an absence*, and everything
that goes wrong with a harness also produces an absence. The defence is the one
§53.5 already built, and it worked here: the "was it ever alive" and "did the
count rise" rows failed first, and a run whose positive halves fail is a run
whose negative halves prove nothing. The gate said so in those words rather than
reporting the leak.

The timeout is now 120 s, and the rule is written where the number is: it must
outlast the longest stretch of the run with no client connected.

## 63. The run happened: one title bar and a typed word, in the same photograph

### 63.1 Status in one paragraph

`docs/stage8/stage57-typed.png` is `weston-terminal` on the guest's interactive
desktop with **one** title bar and the word `wazcomposetzpes` on its prompt.
That is the original brief's deliverable — *"a photograph of `weston-terminal`
on the guest desktop with one title bar, and a photograph of typed text
appearing in it"* — and it is one picture rather than two because the two bugs
were never as separate as the report made them look. 13 assertions, 0 failures,
first attempt, on a run where nothing named `--decorations` at all.

### 63.2 The two pictures

`stage57-typed.png` — §33's block 5b. `probe-input.exe` on `WinSta0` types
`waycomposetypes` with `SendInput`, having first checked it owns the
foreground:

```
PASS  probe-input found our window: target HWND 0000000000170cb6
----  foreground=...170cb6 (class 'WaycomposeToplevel') focus=...170cb6 target=...170cb6
PASS  the window after waycomposetypes was typed into it
```

The prompt reads `wazcomposetzpes`, and that is **correct**: the guest's layout
is German (`0x0407` -> `de`), the probe injects positional scan codes, and scan
`0x15` is `Z` on a German board and `Y` on an American one. §49.9 measured the
same substitution and it is the cheapest possible proof that the client compiled
*our* keymap rather than guessing.

`stage57-clicked-then-typed.png` — §37's block 5c, and the question §37.8 left
open. A click 40 px down the client area, then typing:

```
PASS  §37: a click 40 px down the client area started no window move, so it landed
      below the bar the client drew
PASS  §37: the terminal repainted 22 times after being clicked in and typed at
----  §37: every scan code of the typed word translated
```

The prompt shows the first word with `echowazcomposetzpes` appended, so the
keyboard survived the click that used to be delivered 32 px too high and read as
a title-bar drag. The assertion is the **repaint count**, not the picture, for
§37.7's reason: with the bug present the "picture changed" check was green
because the *window had moved*.

And the window is **838x435**, which is §49's folded caption on a run that named
no decoration flag at all — so `--decorations auto` is the shipped default doing
its job on the real desktop, not a leg configured to succeed.

### 63.3 Three causes, and none of them was the one that mattered

This run was blocked for a day, and the sequence of explanations is the useful
part of the section.

| who | cause given | how it was arrived at |
|---|---|---|
| this author | "a person is at the machine" | inferred from a `wc-desk windows` listing showing Firefox on a news article |
| the coordinator | "the session is locked; `SendInput` returns 0" | **measured**, and §57 is the real defect it found |
| the growth agent | ssh lands in **session 0**; the launcher's clicks go through a scheduled task into **session 1** | measured, on the path the launcher actually uses |

The third is the one that made the run possible: a probe window in session 1
reported `session=1 handle=985882 visible=True` **while the session was
locked**. Windows map on a locked session. The run was available the whole time.

§55.3 said *the reason a run refuses is a measurement to take, not a story
supplied from what happens to be on the screen*, and the middle row is why that
rule needs a second clause. **The coordinator's cause was not a story.** It was
a correct measurement — `SendInput` really does return 0 on a locked session,
and §57 is a genuine defect found by taking it. It was simply about a code path
the launcher does not travel.

So:

> **A measurement can be real and still be about the wrong path.** Taking one is
> not sufficient; establishing which path the failing thing actually travels is
> itself the first measurement, and it is the one all three of us skipped.

That is a sharper rule than the one §55.3 states, and it is a *harder* one to
follow, because a real number is far more convincing than a guess and stops the
search sooner. My inference was cheap to doubt. A measured
`SendInput -> 0, ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` is not, and it held for a day.

The three instances also line up with §55.3's mechanism — *a workaround that
works removes the pressure that would have found the real cause* — in its
third form. Here nobody wrote a workaround; the **explanation itself** was the
workaround. It accounted for the symptom, so the question stopped being asked.

### 63.4 What is now closed, and what is not

Closed, both of the user's reports from `docs/waycompose-design.md`'s task list:

* *"wayland terminal renders also a double titlebar"* — §49's `--decorations
  auto`, photographed here under the shipped default. One bar, the client's,
  with Windows' own caption buttons in it.
* *"typing in wayland terminal does not seem to work"* — three causes across
  three sections, and this is the venue the report came from. §33 guessed a
  missing keymap; §37 found the pointer offset that made a click read as a
  drag; §49.8 found a spurious configure at map from my own frame code. All
  three are fixed and this run exercises all three at once.

Not closed:

1. **A client that starts maximised and decorates itself** still gets two bars
   (§49.7 item 1). Neither weston client does.
2. **The 35 unexplained WLCS failures** (§59.5) are untouched, and they are what
   "implemented fully rather than partially" actually names.
3. **`GetGuiResources` is still a skip under Wine**, which is one of the two
   runs queued behind this one.
## 64. The third resource, and a number that is allowed to be one

*(§53 and §60's continuation, and the end of the list.)*

### 64.1 Status in one paragraph

`ToUi::Destroy` gives back three things and the project has now looked at all
three. §53 gave the **window handle** an outside witness — a separate process
asking the window manager, which nothing the compositor does can talk out of it.
§60 gave the **OLE drop-target registration** an inside count, because that
resource has no outside witness and cannot be given one. This is the third:
`release_icons`, which ran, destroyed what it found, and **said nothing at all**,
so a window icon that was never released was invisible in exactly the way §60's
stranded registration was. It is counted now and reported at exit beside the
other two. The assertion lives in `scripts/wc-drag.sh` rather than in
`wc-life.sh`, which is a finding rather than a filing decision — see 61.3 — and
the number it asserts is **allowed to be one**, which is 61.4.

### 64.2 One creation site, two destruction sites

There is exactly one `CreateIconIndirect` in the compositor. Window icons and
mouse cursors are the same kind of GDI object and are built by the same
function, and they are freed by **different** calls: `DestroyIcon` from
`release_icons` when a window goes, `DestroyCursor` from `set_cursor` when the
pointer changes shape. So the account is one creation counter and two
destruction counters — which is also the shape of the defect it would catch: a
path that creates through the shared function and frees through neither.

```text
wc-compositor: icon objects at exit: claims 10 created, 0 icon(s) and 9 cursor(s) destroyed, 1 outstanding (the shown cursor is one)
```

Three lines now ride out together, one per resource, and only the first has an
external witness:

```text
windows at exit:      6 created, 6 destroyed, 0 still held, 0 still alive, 0 client(s) still connected
drop targets at exit: claims 6 registered, 6 revoked, 0 revoke(s) failed
icon objects at exit: claims 10 created, 0 icon(s) and 9 cursor(s) destroyed, 1 outstanding
```

### 64.3 The harness that could assert it was not the one that was looking

`wc-life.sh` is §53's harness, it churns windows, and it is the obvious home for
a per-window resource count. **It cannot assert this one**, and finding that out
is worth more than the assertion:

* it drives **no pointer input**, so no cursor is ever built — `grep -c 'cursor ->'`
  on its log is `0`;
* its churn client is `weston-clickdot`, which publishes **no icon** — the
  compositor's log says `has no published icon (the store holds 0)` — and the
  proxy is run with `--no-icons` besides.

So in `wc-life.sh` the count is zero created and zero destroyed, and an
assertion that `created == destroyed` there would be `0 == 0`: the vacuous gate
this whole run of sections exists to avoid, arrived at for the third time by a
different route.

`wc-drag.sh` is the only harness in the tree that moves a pointer. It builds
**ten** icon objects in a run. That is where the assertion goes, and the
general lesson is one this project keeps paying for: *the harness that owns the
subject is not always the harness that can exercise it*. The window count and
the icon count are both per-window resources and they need opposite harnesses.

The window-icon half is still unasserted anywhere, for the reason §53.6 item 2
gave: the harness that publishes an icon is `wc-icon.sh`, and it is a **guest**
harness. That leg is queued behind the machine being in use, and it is now one
`grep` away from being an assertion rather than a rewrite.

### 64.4 A number that is allowed to be one, and why that is the gate

The obvious assertion is `created == destroyed`. **It is wrong**, and asserting
it would have been worse than not asserting anything, because it fails on every
run that moves the mouse and would then be "fixed" by deleting it.

`set_cursor` frees the previous cursor **only after the new one is installed**:

> Destroying a cursor that is on screen is legal but leaves the pointer drawn
> from freed memory until the next `SetCursor`, which is the classic way to get
> a corrupted pointer that survives the process.

So exactly one object is outstanding at any moment, by design. The invariant is
therefore *outstanding ≤ 1*, and it is a real gate rather than a tautology
because the harness first asserts the counter **moved**: ten objects built, so
"one outstanding" distinguishes a compositor that frees each cursor as it goes
from one that keeps all ten. A leak here grows with mouse movement,
which is the most common thing a user does.

### 64.5 What is not proven

1. **The window-icon half is counted but not asserted.** Nothing local
   publishes an icon; see 61.3. `wc-icon.sh` on the guest is the run that turns
   `0 icon(s) destroyed` into a number that has to match.
2. **These are the compositor's own counts**, like §60's and unlike §53's. The
   external witness for GDI objects is `GetGuiResources`, which Wine stubs
   (§53.3) — so on this platform the inside count is all there is, and on the
   guest it would finally have something to be checked against.
3. **No run has made the compositor leak one.** The counters distinguish the
   states; nothing in the tree currently provokes the bad one.
4. **`DeleteObject` on the two bitmaps is not counted.** `make_icon` deletes the
   colour and mask bitmaps immediately after `CreateIconIndirect` copies them,
   and that pair is on the same path but is not part of this account.

### 64.6 The gates

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| **`scripts/wc-drag.sh wine`** | **22 passed, 0 failed** (18 in §50.10; 2 new here) |
| `scripts/wc-life.sh wine` | 14 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped (unchanged) |
| `cargo build --workspace --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` | clean |
| `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | unchanged — no Linux code |
| `scripts/wc-xref.sh` | 0 broken, 0 unqualified |

`wc-drag.sh`'s compositor idle timeout came down to 60 s and its clients are now
stopped before the wait, for §60.6's reason met from the other side: the account
is printed **on the way out**, the idle timer does not run while a client is
connected, and a harness that never lets the compositor exit never sees the line
it is asserting on.
