## 65. The debt number was wrong, and the expected-failure table could not say why

### 65.1 Status in one paragraph

§59 said task #31's real content is *"the 35 unexplained WLCS failures"*. It is
**23**, and the difference is two separate corrections: eight the tree fixed
while this was waiting for a guest, and four that were never debts — WLCS drives
`xdg_toplevel.move`/`.resize` and asserts the window moved, and the headless
platform has no window manager to move it with. Reclassifying those four needed
the expected-failure table to learn which **leg** it is describing, because the
same four are entitled to pass under Wine, where §22.7 wires them to `SC_MOVE`
and `SC_SIZE`. A table that excused them on both legs would have been a false
green on the only leg that can observe them.

```
headless: 413 passed, 53 failed, 759 skipped
EXPECTED    26  input outside the window geometry rectangle …(§45.4)
EXPECTED     4  interactive move and resize: the headless platform has no window
                manager … the Wine leg is where these must pass
headless: 30 of the failures are expected on this platform, and the rest are debts
```

### 65.2 Why the table needed a leg, and why that is not a loosening

`justified_failure_patterns` emitted one list for every caller. Adding the four
interactive-move tests to it would have excused them on the Wine leg too, and
the Wine leg is precisely where they are *not* excused: on Win32 the request
reaches a real window manager, so a failure there is a real failure. The
function now takes the leg and the new block is guarded by
`[ "$leg" = headless ] || return 0`.

That is a **tightening**, and the distinction is worth keeping straight because
"add a leg parameter to the excuse table" reads like the opposite. Before: one
list, applied everywhere, so any entry that was leg-specific was either omitted
(and its tests counted as debts forever) or added (and its tests excused on a
leg that could have caught them). After: an entry can say which leg it is about,
and the Wine leg's list is *shorter* than the headless one by exactly these
four.

The existing self-check does the rest, and it is why this could be added at all
without taking anything on trust: a listed test that **passes** is an error, and
a listed pattern that matches **nothing** is an error. Both fired during this
work — the second on every filtered run, which is a real wrinkle worth knowing:

> `wc-wlcs.sh headless 'XdgToplevelStableTest.*'` reports 26 stale entries,
> because the filter means the other 26 patterns match no test **in that run**.
> The guard is right and the report is noise. Validating a change to this table
> needs an unfiltered run; a filtered one can confirm the new entry matched and
> nothing more.

### 65.3 What the 23 are, and they are all on Firefox's path

Deduplicated and grouped, with the parametrised instantiations folded together:

| group | ~n | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `SubsurfaceTest`, `SubsurfaceMultilevelTest` | 7 | sync/desync commit semantics and `place_above`/`place_below` — when a subsurface moves relative to its parent's and grandparent's commits |
| `XdgPopupTest` (both instantiations) | 6 | reactive popups following a moved parent, grab semantics, keyboard focus for a grabbed popup, `popup_done` ordering |
| `XdgToplevelStableConfigurationTest` | 4 | `defaults`, `activated_state_follows_pointer`, fullscreen and unfullscreen initiated by the client |
| `XdgSurfaceStableTest` | 1 | attaching a buffer to an unconfigured `xdg_surface` must be a protocol error |
| `XdgDecorationV1Test` | 1 | destroying a toplevel before its decoration must throw `orphaned` |
| `CopyCutPaste` | 1 | a focused sink must see the offer a source makes |
| `ClientSurfaceEventsTest` | 1 | `surface_resizes_under_pointer` |
| `BadBufferTest` | 1 | a truncated shm file must be a protocol error |

**Every group is inside an interface Firefox binds**, and the two largest are
the two §59 predicted would matter:

* **Subsurfaces.** `wc-firefox.sh enumerate` measures Firefox creating a
  `wl_subsurface` for its content, and it binds `wl_subcompositor`. Seven
  failures about *when* a subsurface moves are seven failures on the path the
  browser's content takes.
* **Popups.** §15 established that every Firefox menu, dropdown, autocomplete
  and tooltip is an `xdg_popup`. Six failures about grabs, focus and
  `popup_done` ordering are six failures in the machinery §15 built.

So §59's conclusion survives its own arithmetic being wrong: the Firefox-relevant
debt is entirely in protocols already written, none of it is in the 79 gap
protocols, and the work has a shape — subsurface commit semantics first, popup
grab semantics second, five singletons after.

### 65.4 What this section did not do

1. **None of the 23 is fixed.** This is a corrected number and a grouped work
   list; the largest group is subsurface commit ordering and it is real work.
2. **The four reclassified tests are unproven on the leg that matters.** The
   claim is that they pass under Wine because §22.7 wires the requests to
   `SC_MOVE`/`SC_SIZE`. Nothing here ran the Wine leg — it is a claim about
   where they *should* be measured, and the table now makes that claim
   explicitly instead of silently counting them as debts. Running
   `wc-wlcs.sh wine 'XdgToplevelStableTest.*'` would settle it and is one
   command on this workstation.
3. **Eight of the twelve-test improvement is not mine.** 409/57 became 413/53
   across a master merge; only the four reclassifications are this section's,
   and the other eight were fixed by whoever moved the tree in between.


### 36.21 A present, not a wake: the last link, on topology 1

Everything before this measured a **wait**. §36.15 got 18.96 ms per wait against
a 20 ms slice; §36.20 got a 13.6 µs wake to the Windows guest. But the figure
that started all of it — 216.9 ms — was a **present**, and a present had never
been measured across a boundary with the fix in place.

**Venue, stated because §51 exists for this reason: topology 1, Linux host →
Linux VM** (`nix build .#svGuest`, lavapipe in the guest). Not Wine, not
testhost. The Windows numbers in §36.20 are a different venue and do not
transfer to this table, nor this one to them.

`scripts/sv-guest-e2e.sh` now takes `SV_E2E_APP`, so the application can be
something that *presents* rather than something that enumerates.
`vk-present-probe`, 60 frames at 256×256, 256 MiB arena:

| condition | ring waits | parked | **mean per wait** | shape |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fixed 20 ms slice | 281 | 5664.9 ms | **20.160 ms** | `<100ms=281` |
| slice ladder | 281 | 631.1 ms | **2.246 ms** | `<10us=38 <100us=8 <1ms=137 <10ms=83 <100ms=15` |
| **ladder + doorbell** | 281 | 116.4 ms | **0.414 ms** | `<10us=108 <100us=33 <1ms=121 <10ms=17 <100ms=2` |

**281 ring waits in every condition**, as with the enumeration workload: the
same presents, differing only in what a wait costs. **48.7× on the mean**, and
the top row is again the whole story of the defect — every one of 281 waits in
the 10–100 ms bucket, which is what "the number *was* the slice, once per wait"
looks like for a present.

And the probe's own per-frame timing, from the doorbell run:

```
timing 256x256 over 60 frames: 0.66 ms/frame total,
  0.54 ms/frame in vkQueuePresentKHR,
  0.009 ms/frame in vkAcquireNextImageKHR (0.2 MB/frame, 462 MB/s presented)
PASS: 60 frames presented
```

> **A cross-VM present costs 0.54 ms in `vkQueuePresentKHR`.**

That is the last link. 216.9 ms per present → diagnosed as a 20 ms slice once
per wait → confirmed at 18.96 ms per wait → fixed by a hypervisor-carried wake
→ **and now a present measured end to end at sub-millisecond across a real
hypervisor.** Parking for the whole 60-frame run fell from 5.66 s to 116 ms.

Two honest limits. The presents here are 256×256, not 1080p, so this is the
*latency* of a present and not its bandwidth — `vk-present-probe`'s header asks
for a 1080p run and that is still owed. And 281 waits over 60 frames is 4.7 per
frame, which includes setup; the per-wait figure is the transferable one.

#### 36.21.1 Two guards caught this run's mistakes, one of them mine

The first attempt died with **R13's protocol-hash detector**: guest
`0xc2ddabe30ce597a2` against host `0x3522313e5c823788`. That is the
`sv_icd.json` trap `sv-present.sh` documents — a reflink-seeded worktree's
manifest is a generated file holding an *absolute path*, and mine still named
the base tree. The detector did exactly its job: refused to load rather than
answering locally, and said which two hashes disagreed.

The second was found by pointing §36's own freshness helper at the two halves,
and it was **a bug in that helper**: `libsv_icd.so` reported stale and blamed
`crates/wc-compositor/src/platform/drag.rs`, a file it cannot depend on. Cargo
names the depfile after the *crate* — `libsv_icd.d`, not `libsv_icd.so.d` — and
the helper stripped only `.exe`, so every `.so` fell down the whole-tree
fallback and got blamed on whatever that walk reached first. Fixed to strip
`.so` and `.dylib` too.

Worth recording because it is the same defect the helper was written to remove,
surviving in the helper: **a check whose scope is wrong reports a real-looking
failure against an innocent file**, and the only reason it was caught is that
the fallback path *says* it is the weaker check.

---
---

## 66. The subsurface group is not the work §65 said it was

### 66.1 Status in one paragraph

§65 grouped seven WLCS failures as *"subsurface sync/desync commit semantics
and `place_above`/`place_below`"* and called it the largest coherent piece of
task #31. Read properly, **none of the seven is commit plumbing.** Every one is
an assertion about *pointer focus*, made by moving or restacking a subsurface
and then asking which surface the pointer is over — so the group is a scene
lookup group, which is §40's territory, not a double-buffering group. Nothing is
fixed here: this section is the diagnosis, and it changes what the next person
should open.

### 66.2 What the seven actually assert

The failure messages, which are the thing §65 never read:

```
Subsurface did not move after parent commit                  Actual: (7680, 7680)
Subsurface moved to new location without parent being committed  Actual: (2560, 2560)
Subsurface moved without parent being committed              Actual: (2560, 2560)
Subsurface moved when hierarchy commits were in the wrong order  Actual: (2560, 2560)
wrong surface/subsurface on top                              Actual: 0x…f0160
wrong surface/subsurface on top                              Actual: 0x…e15f0
C++ exception "bad optional access" thrown in the test body
```

`2560` and `7680` are `wl_fixed`: 10.0 and 30.0. They are **pointer positions**,
not subsurface positions. The four "did/did not move" tests never look at the
subsurface's geometry at all — they park a pointer, commit, and infer where the
subsurface went from the surface-local coordinates the client is told. So a
compositor with perfect commit semantics and a wrong hit test fails all four,
and that is the shape to check first.

### 66.3 What is already right, which is why the diagnosis moved

Two things §40 built are correct and were the obvious suspects:

* **`placed_tree` reads the double-buffered state.** It takes
  `SubsurfaceCachedState::current().location`, not `pending()`, so a subsurface
  position applied on the parent's commit is what the walk sees.
* **`surface_under` descends into subsurfaces** and hit-tests them top-down
  against their own input regions, with the ancestor-mapped rule. Pointer input
  reaching a subsurface at all is implemented; §37.8 item 2's "every pointer
  event goes to the toplevel's surface" is out of date.

So the group is not "subsurfaces do not receive input". It is narrower, and the
narrowing is the useful part.

### 66.4 Two of the seven may not be ours, and saying which needs a reference run

`place_above_simple` and `place_below_simple` both end with two assertions, and
read together they appear unsatisfiable. Taking `place_below_simple`, with the
fixture's `subsurface` at (0,0) 50x50 and `subsurface_moving_down` created after
it at the same place:

```c
wl_subsurface_place_below(subsurface_moving_down, subsurface);   // moving_down goes under
…
ASSERT_THAT(focused_window(), Ne(subsurface_moving_down)) << "place_below() did not have an effect";
ASSERT_THAT(focused_window(), Ne(subsurface))             << "wrong surface/subsurface on top";
```

After the restack `subsurface` is the topmost surface under the pointer, so the
first assertion is satisfied *because* the second cannot be. `place_above_simple`
is the mirror image with the same pair. Our run fails the second in both.

**That is a hypothesis and it is deliberately not written up as a finding.**
This session has spent three sections on causes asserted from strong-looking
evidence and found to be about the wrong thing (§55.3, §60.3), and "the
conformance suite is wrong" is exactly the conclusion that should be trusted
least. What would settle it is one run of these two tests against a reference
compositor — Weston or Mir, which is what WLCS is developed against. If they
pass there, the reading above is wrong and the fault is ours; if they fail there
too, these two are upstream and the subsurface debt is five, not seven.

Until that run happens they stay counted as ours.

### 66.5 What the next person should open

1. **The four position tests**, and the question is not "when is the location
   applied" but "what surface-local coordinate does a client under a stationary
   pointer receive after the scene beneath it changes". Note that all four move
   the pointer *before* the change, not after — so whether a commit that moves a
   subsurface must produce a fresh `wl_pointer.motion` is the protocol question
   to answer first, and `pointer_motion` is currently called only from real
   input events.
2. **`subsurface_extends_parent_input_region`**, which throws rather than
   failing an assertion — a `bad optional access` on `focused_window()` means
   the pointer entered nothing at all, so this one is about a surface that
   should have accepted input and did not.
3. **The two restacking tests**, after the reference run in §66.4.

### 66.6 What this section did not do

Nothing is fixed, no test moved from failing to passing, and the debt number is
unchanged at 23. What changed is the description of seven of them, from a
double-buffering problem to a pointer-focus problem — which matters because the
two live in different files and only one of them was on the list anybody was
about to read.

## 67. Wine becomes first class, and four of the six known quirks were not Wine

The Wayland server runs on Windows. It also has to run under Wine, because a
Wine box is the venue that is *always* available and a Windows guest is the one
that has to be arranged — so nearly every gate in `scripts/` is a Wine gate, and
Wine has been carrying evidence about Windows for thirteen stages without ever
having been asked to say who it was.

The requirement, in the user's words:

> the wayland server rn runs on windows. thats cool and all, but we also need to
> be able to test against a vm running only wine and wine does have some quirks
> and obviously there is no windows kernel there to talk to. so wine becomes
> first class supported. for stuff where we know wine is just broken and
> requires a workaround, we impl a workaround. on wayland server start you
> detect if we are running under wine, based on that OnceCell all other code
> paths that need it choose between windows and wine. **important: only if
> something is truly broken under wine, it gets a wine path, the wine test
> should still be a stand-in test for windows so this is only minimal fixes**

The last sentence is the design. Every `if under_wine()` is one more thing the
Wine run stops testing about the Windows run, so the interesting number in this
stage is not how many branches were added but how many were *refused*.

**Six known quirks went in and none of them came out as a Wine branch.** Four
were not Wine at all — two of those four because of a bug in this project's own
harness that had been written up as a fact about Wine and quoted as such for two
stages — and the other two are real Wine behaviour that nothing depends on. The
two branches that do exist were both found while checking something else, which
is the honest way round: the quirks somebody remembers are not the ones still
biting.

### 67.1 What was built

`crates/wc-compositor/src/wine.rs`. A `OnceLock<Win32>` with three values —
`Windows`, `Wine { version, host }`, and `None` for the Linux build — decided
once and never re-asked.

The probe is the one Wine documents: `GetModuleHandleW("ntdll.dll")` and then
`GetProcAddress` for `wine_get_version`, whose presence is the whole answer.
`wine_get_host_version` gives the kernel underneath, and both are kept rather
than reduced to a boolean, because every claim in §67.4 is a claim about a
*particular* Wine and the first question asked of a quirk that stops
reproducing is which one it was measured on. Measured here:

```
wine_get_version       -> "11.14"
wine_get_host_version  -> "Linux 6.18.33"
```

`ntdll` is resolved with `GetModuleHandleW` rather than `LoadLibraryW` because
it is mapped into every Windows process before `main` runs — there is nothing
to load and nothing to release. On the Linux build `probe()` returns `None`
rather than a plausible `Windows`, which is §13.6's lesson applied to this
module's own construction: an answer taken where the question is meaningless is
not an answer.

**The line, first in every log.**

```
wc-compositor: win32 is wine 11.14 (host Linux 6.18.33)
wc-compositor: win32 is windows
wc-compositor: win32 is none -- this is the Linux build and nothing here is evidence about Windows
```

It is printed from `run_from` immediately after `--log` has been redirected and
**before `platform::start`**. That ordering is load-bearing rather than tidy:
what platform a run is on must not depend on the platform having come up, or
the one run that most needs attributing — the one that failed to start — is
exactly the one that cannot be. It is also why the guest leg in §67.6 works at
all on a VM with no X.

`None` is a variant rather than an absence for the same reason. A harness that
meant to run the `.exe` and got the Linux build has measured nothing about
Windows, and §35 is a whole section about gates that reported success while
something was wrong.

### 67.2 The override, and why a stale assumption has to be falsifiable

`WC_WIN32=windows|wine` replaces the probe's answer, in the compositor and in
`scripts/probe-cursor.c` alike. Two uses, both of which were needed within
hours of it existing:

* **Force the Windows path under Wine**, to check that a branch is still
  earning its place. Every entry in §67.4 is a claim about wine-11.14; this is
  how the next person tests whether it has been fixed upstream without booting
  anything.
* **Force the Wine path on Windows**, so a workaround is not code that has only
  ever run where it does not matter.

An unrecognised value is a **startup failure**, not a warning — the same
treatment `--decorations` gets. A typo that quietly falls back to the probe is a
run that was told to exercise one path, measured the other, and passed.

`WC_WIN32=windows` is what settled §67.5, and it settled it in one run. That is
the argument for the flag in a sentence: the tool built to falsify a Wine claim
falsified three of them the first afternoon it existed.

### 67.3 Harnesses can no longer be wrong about which platform they measured

`scripts/wc-cursor.sh` gained `win32_of()`, which reads the line out of a
compositor log, and both legs now **assert** on it: the `wine` leg fails if the
answer is not `wine`, and the `linux` leg fails if it is anything but `none`.

This is cheap and it is the half of "first class" that pays for itself. §33
records a photograph of "this compositor ignoring input" that was another
worktree's `weston-terminal`, written into `docs/` as evidence before anybody
noticed. A leg that cannot say what it ran on can be wrong in that direction
silently, and this stage's own §67.5 is a second example of the same failure
wearing different clothes.

### 67.4 The Wine paths, and there are two

**Neither changes a pixel.** Both correct a claim that was false under Wine.

**1. `dwmapi` answers `S_OK` for things it does not implement.**
`platform::win32::apply_frame`.

§31.7 named this hole precisely and left it open, because the `HRESULT` cannot
close it:

> A run that extends the frame and finds `dwmapi` stubbed would look exactly
> like `noglass.png` and would report success. That is the one failure mode of
> this arrangement with no diagnostic.

Measured, wine-11.14 staging, on a plain `WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW` with nothing else
in the process:

| call | Wine's answer |
|---|---|
| `DwmIsCompositionEnabled` | `S_OK`, `enabled = 1` |
| `DwmExtendFrameIntoClientArea` | `S_OK` |
| `DwmGetWindowAttribute(DWMWA_CAPTION_BUTTON_BOUNDS)` | **`0x80004001` — `E_NOTIMPL`**, `RECT` untouched |

The two calls that only have to return a status return success; the one that has
to return *data* admits it is a stub. So there is no composition behind that
frame and `S_OK` says there is. The compositor's log said
`DwmExtendFrameIntoClientArea ok`, which under Wine is a false statement about
the one arrangement in this tree whose failure has no other symptom.

The branch replaces that log line under Wine and does nothing else. It does not
need to: `caption_button_rect` already returns `None` when DWM will not answer,
and the fallback that produces is exactly what `--caption-buttons off` asks for
on purpose. **What was broken was the evidence, not the window.**

**2. Wine's stock `HCURSOR`s are per-process, so a cursor cannot be named across
one.** `scripts/probe-cursor.c` and `scripts/wc-cursor.sh`.

`probe-cursor.c`'s header states the property its whole method rests on: "Stock
cursors are shared per-session handles, so an exact match is proof of identity
rather than resemblance". That is true on Windows. Measured on wine-11.14, the
sixteen `LoadCursorW(NULL, IDC_*)` handles in one process are stable across
calls and are `0x1004e, 0x10050 … 0x1006c` — a dense run from a per-process
base, which a second process allocates from again. The probe reads the cursor
off the **compositor's** input queue, so the two numbers come from two
namespaces; the comparison can both miss a match and manufacture one.

Everything therefore reads `cursor=custom` under Wine whatever it really is. The
probe now prints `stock-identity=unavailable` so that word cannot be mistaken
for a measurement, and `wc-cursor.sh` substitutes the weaker test the guard is
actually about — **the frame's handle must differ from the client area's** —
while Windows keeps the assertion by name, where the name means something:

```
PASS  the border's cursor is not the client's (handle=…100b0 vs handle=…20090);
      Wine cannot say which system cursor it is (§67.4)
```

Weaker, and stated as weaker. It proves the compositor did not claim the resize
border; it says nothing about which system cursor is there.

### 67.5 The six that were refused, and two of them were this project's own bug

This is the more useful half of the stage.

**`GetCursorInfo` kills the probe (§23.7 item 1) — not Wine.**
It reproduced, three runs out of three, exactly as recorded: a fatal
`X Error of failed request: BadWindow (invalid Window parameter), Major opcode
38 (X_QueryPointer)` in Wine's X11 driver, killing `probe-cursor.exe` mid-line.
A Wine path was written for it.

Then the isolated control: a binary that does `SendInput` and then
`GetCursorInfo`, with no compositor and no `AttachThreadInput`, returns a clean
`1` and the injected position. So it was the *combination*, and the combination
included `wc-cursor.sh` killing the compositor **one second after the launcher
returned, while the probe was still in its `--settle` sleep** — because
`wine explorer /desktop=NAME` attaches to a desktop that already exists and
returns at once. `wc-damage.sh` documents that exact trap at length; this
harness had never hit it because the probe used to die a second in, so
everything it was ever going to write was already written.

With the harness waiting for `probe-cursor: done`, the call is clean and returns
every reading. **The Wine path was deleted.**

**And the race is still live on master, at about one run in three.** Master's own
`wc-cursor.sh wine` was run three times unmodified while this section was being
written: 10 passed / 0 failed, 10 passed / 0 failed, then **5 passed / 3
failed** — "the compositor never turned a cursor surface into pixels", "no
reading of the compositor's queue: missing", and the three notes. So this was
never a stable "Wine limitation" being tolerated; it was a flaky harness whose
*good* outcome was three notes and whose bad outcome was three failures, and
both were being read as facts about Wine. A reproducible wrong diagnosis is more
durable than an intermittent one, and this one was both by turns.

**§63.3's rule is this finding seen from the other side, and the pair is worth
stating together.** §63.3 settles on:

> A measurement can be real and still be about the wrong path. Taking one is not
> sufficient; establishing which path the failing thing actually travels is
> itself the first measurement.

There, a *correct* measurement — `SendInput` returns 0 on a locked session —
attributed a blockage to a path the launcher does not travel, and held a run up
for a day. Here, a *correct* observation — `GetCursorInfo` dies with
`BadWindow (X_QueryPointer)`, three runs out of three — was attributed to Wine
when it belonged to the harness. Both are the same error: the evidence was
sound and the *subject* of the sentence was wrong. Neither would have been
caught by repeating the measurement, which is the instinct both cases invite;
both needed the control that varies the suspected cause and holds the rest
still — an isolated `SendInput`-then-`GetCursorInfo` binary here, a session-1
probe window there.

The asymmetry that makes §63.3's version harder is worth keeping in view: its
wrong attribution came with a real number attached, and a real number stops the
search. Mine came with a 3-of-3 reproduction, which is the same thing wearing
different clothes. **Reproducibility is evidence that a phenomenon is real, and
no evidence at all about what causes it** — and this section spent its first
afternoon writing a Wine path on the strength of exactly that confusion.

**Cross-process `SendMessageW(WM_SETCURSOR)` is not delivered (§23.7 item 2) —
not Wine.** Same cause, and it falls out of the same fix. §23.7 recorded `0` for
both hit-test codes, with "the cursor on the queue does not change for `HTRIGHT`
either" as the tell that the message never reached the window procedure. Both
`SendMessageW`s were being sent to a window that had already been destroyed, and
`SendMessageW` to a dead window returns 0. With the wait in place, the same
wine-11.14 returns:

```
client-area-msg WM_SETCURSOR(hittest=1)  returned 1
frame-msg       WM_SETCURSOR(hittest=11) returned 0
```

— the two sharp assertions §23.7 said only a real guest could make, and the
frame's cursor handle differs from the client area's, which is the tell it was
looking for. **The allowance was withdrawn rather than made conditional**, which
matters: a Wine path here would have frozen a harness bug into the design as a
property of Wine, and the guest leg was paying for it too. The guard was, in
§23.7's own words, "defended by reading and not by measurement" — on *both*
platforms.

**A signal-killed client does not flush stdio (§11.7 item 3) — not Wine, and not
even Windows.** Full buffering plus `SIGKILL` loses the buffer on any platform;
the client in question is a Linux `weston-eventdemo` writing to a file. It is
filed under "what Wine got wrong" and it is a harness fact. Already fixed twice
over with `stdbuf -oL` and an ordered shutdown. No branch.

**`FindWindowW` enumerates one desktop (§11.7 item 1) — topology, not a defect.**
`wine explorer /desktop=` makes a second desktop; that is what it is for. Already
solved by running the probe inside the same desktop, and by `--pid` plus
`EnumWindows` in `probe-input.c`. A real guest has no `wine explorer` at all, so
a branch here would be a branch on the *harness's* arrangement wearing a
platform's name. No branch.

Two more were checked and left alone:

* **`SetThreadExecutionState` returns `0x7` (§25.8).** Wine's stub reports
  `ES_SYSTEM_REQUIRED | ES_DISPLAY_REQUIRED | ES_USER_PRESENT` as a previous
  state, which no real thread returns. The code tests only for the documented
  failure — a return of `0` — so nothing depends on it. §25.8 already called it
  "a curiosity rather than a dependency" and it still is. No branch.
* **Two `SendInput` moves arrive out of order (§37).** `probe-input.exe` prints
  both points it visited and accepts either, which costs nothing on Windows and
  asserts an order neither platform guarantees. Left as it is; tightening it to
  "the click came from the last move" on Windows only is a real option and is
  §67.8's list, not this one.

**And the ones §13.6 and §26.5 already settled, which stay settled.**
`SetProcessDpiAwarenessContext` was a session-0 window station with no display
and Wine was right — §13.6 withdrew the claim and this stage does not reopen it.
Nothing about `afunix.sys`, named sections across sessions or `Local\`
namespaces gets a branch: those are real Windows behaviours Wine models
differently *because there is no hypervisor and no second session in the test*,
which is §26.5's correction and is about the topology.

**On the tally.** §13.6 is the authority: four recorded discrepancies, one of
which was withdrawn. This stage removes two more from the folklore — §23.7's
pair were never Wine — and adds one that is: `dwmapi` reporting success it
cannot deliver. Cite the document, not a number somebody remembers.

### 67.6 A VM running only Wine

`scripts/wc-wine-guest.sh`, and it is the venue the requirement asked for.

`nix build .#svGuest` boots a NixOS VM on this workstation with a
`memory-backend-memfd` and a QMP socket. It has no Wine of its own and does not
need one: `/nix/store` is shared into it over 9p, so the same
`wine-wow64-staging-11.14` the dev shell uses runs there by absolute path,
unbuilt and unchanged. **`nix/guest.nix` is not modified**, which is the point —
the guest stays the minimal disposable thing it was designed to be.

The compositor runs as a Windows binary under Wine *inside the VM*, and the
assertion is one sentence: it says which Win32 it is on, and it is the guest's
Wine and not this workstation's.

```
  PASS  the guest ran the payload: guest-kernel: Linux 6.18.44
        wc-compositor: win32 is wine 11.14 (host Linux 6.18.44)
        …
  PASS  inside the VM the compositor says: win32 is wine 11.14 (host Linux 6.18.44)
[09:31:53] on this workstation the same binary says: win32 is wine 11.14 (host Linux 6.18.33)
  PASS  and it is the guest's Wine, not this workstation's: 'Linux 6.18.44' inside, 'Linux 6.18.33' out
```

`wine_get_host_version` reports the kernel Wine sits on, so the two lines name
two kernels and a run cannot claim to have measured the VM while having measured
the host. That is what turns the platform line from decoration into evidence,
and it is the first Wine leg in this document that is not one machine with no
boundary in it (§26.5).

**So it is also the only Wine harness in the tree that declares `cross-vm`**
(§51, §52). Every other one declares `same-box` and is right to. Two things
about that declaration are worth stating, because `wc_topology_declare` refuses
a `cross-vm` claim that cannot back itself:

* `WC_HOST` and `WC_GUEST_CONFIGURED` are set *by* this script rather than
  expected from the environment. The other cross-VM harnesses **reach** a guest
  somebody else configured and are refused when there is none; this one **is**
  the VM host — it starts QEMU itself a few lines later — so the two facts the
  guard checks are facts it establishes. That is stating the arrangement, not
  evading the guard, and §67.6's two kernels are the run's own proof of it.
* **No substrate is declared, and that is the answer rather than an omission.**
  `wc_substrate_declare` offers `guest-ram` and `wine-fixture` and this leg uses
  neither: with no client there is no `wl_shm` pool and no arena, so nothing
  crosses. Declaring `guest-ram` would name a mechanism the leg never touches.
  `wc_latency_claim` is unavailable to it in consequence, which is correct — it
  makes no timing claim and must not grow one without a locate behind it.

**Further than expected, and worth writing down.** With no X in the guest at all
(`graphics = false`) the whole platform still comes up:
`SetProcessDpiAwarenessContext` succeeds, the clipboard listener starts, the
keyboard layout compiles to a 71,249-byte keymap, the message pump runs, the
socket binds, the high-resolution waitable timer is used, and the process exits
cleanly on its idle timeout. Wine's null display driver is enough for everything
short of a real `HWND` with pixels in it — which is more than `flake.nix`'s note
about needing Xvfb implies for this particular use, and that note is about
`CreateWindowExW` succeeding, which is not exercised here.

**What it does not do**, said plainly: no client, so no toplevel, no window and
no pixel. A rendering leg in the guest needs an X server and a client in there
too. §67.8.

### 67.7 The gates

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `cargo build --workspace` | clean |
| `cargo build --workspace --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` | clean |
| `cargo clippy -p wc-compositor --all-targets` (Linux) | no warnings from this branch |
| `cargo clippy -p wc-compositor --all-targets --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` | no warnings from this branch |
| `design_citations` (the §54 gate, tightened by §55) | `every_design_document_citation_resolves` passes; every citation this branch added names its document |
| `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | **86 binaries, 2627 tests**, 0 failures; seven are this branch's `wine::tests`, and the figure held across the last two merges |
| `scripts/wc-cursor.sh linux` | **8 passed, 0 failed** |
| `scripts/wc-cursor.sh wine` | **17 passed, 0 failed** (master: 10, and see below) |
| `scripts/wc-cursor.sh all` | **25 passed, 0 failed** |
| `scripts/wc-wine-guest.sh` (new) — arrangement 2 | **3 passed, 0 failed**, re-measured on the merged tree |
| `scripts/wc-vm-client.sh linux` (new) — arrangement 1 | **9 passed, 0 failed** |
| `scripts/wc-vm-client.sh wine` (new) — arrangement 3 | **10 passed, 0 failed** |

The seven new tests are `wine::tests`, and they are over `decide()` — the pure
function that applies `WC_WIN32` to the probe — which is why they run on the
machine that builds them. The same argument `wc-handle`'s Unix build makes for
itself. They pin the override in both directions, that a forced Wine does not
invent a version number the log would then carry, that forcing what the probe
already said is still *reported* as forced, that a typo is refused rather than
ignored, and that the three tags are the strings the harnesses grep for.

`cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` and not `cargo test`, for the reason
that has now misled several people: plain `cargo test` stops at the first
failing binary and under-reports the total.

**On the wine leg's `+7`, and the run that measured master to check it.** Master's
own `wc-cursor.sh wine` was run three times on this tree, unmodified, with only
the compositor changed: **10 passed / 0 failed, 10 passed / 0 failed, and 5
passed / 3 failed.** The third is §67.5's race caught in the act — "the
compositor never turned a cursor surface into pixels", "no reading of the
compositor's queue: missing", and the three notes — and it is roughly one run in
three. So the honest comparison is not 10 against 17 but *an intermittently
failing 10* against 17. The seven: `WM_SETCURSOR`'s pair, the platform line, the
three that were notes, and `SendInput`'s refusal count below.

That the baseline had to be *measured* rather than quoted is the point. The
number in the previous draft of this table was 8, taken on `e5e5963` before the
merge, and it was neither wrong nor comparable.

**The seventh came from §57, which landed on master while this branch was being
merged.** §57 found `probe-scroll.c` discarding `SendInput`'s return value, and
`SendInput` returns 0 with `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` on a locked session without
blocking, throwing or logging — so the leg would have measured a browser nobody
scrolled. `probe-cursor.c` had exactly the same hole in `move_to`, and it is
worse-shaped here: **every** reading in this harness that names a position is a
claim about where the pointer is, so a refused move does not fail them, it makes
them describe wherever the pointer already was. On Xvfb they would have found
the compositor's cursor and passed. The probe now counts refusals, prints
`moves-refused N of M` whether or not any were, and exits 3 when all were; the
harness asserts the count is zero and reads `refused 0 of 4`.

Worth naming as a pattern rather than a fix: §57 and §67.5 are the same failure
one level apart — a probe that cannot tell "I measured this" from "I measured
whatever was already there". §67.5's version was the harness outliving the
probe; §57's is the window server refusing the probe. Both produce readings that
look exactly like measurements.

**The clippy gate is `-p wc-compositor` rather than `--workspace`**, because the
workspace run has pre-existing warnings in crates this branch does not touch
(`wc-launch`, `sv-transport`, `sv-proto`, `wc-handle`). Within `wc-compositor`
the only two warning sites on either target are `lib.rs`'s `file_arena_tests`
and `platform/drag.rs`, both master's and both unmoved by this branch; nothing
in `wine.rs` produces one.

**A correction to an earlier draft of this section**, kept because it is the
same mistake this stage is about. It claimed
`cargo clippy --workspace --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` "does not build at
all", on `sv-hostd`'s `std::os::unix`. That was true of `e5e5963` and was fixed
on master while this branch was being written — the gate now builds clean and
`cargo build --workspace --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` is a standing gate. A
stale claim about a gate is exactly as misleading as a stale claim about a
platform, and this one survived from a measurement taken hours earlier on a tree
that had moved. The underlying point is unaffected and still worth keeping:
**`cargo clippy --target` builds metadata, not an executable**, so it cannot
catch a link failure and is not a substitute for `cargo build --target`.

**The guest leg's three assertions were measured on `e5e5963`, not on the merge.**
**The guest row was carried undated for four merges and is now measured.** For
several revisions of this table it read *"measured on `e5e5963`, not re-run"*,
because the development guest was held by another run. The argument for
believing it in the meantime was that nothing in those merges touches what it
measures — the platform line, printed before `platform::start`, and
`wine_get_host_version`. That argument was correct and it was still an argument.
It has now been run on the merged tree and reports the same two kernels, so the
row is a measurement again; the point of having labelled it is that a reader
could tell the difference while it was not.

The Windows laptop remains unavailable, which is what §67.8 item 1 is about and
is unchanged by any of this: all three arrangements above are Linux and Wine.

### 67.8 What is not done

1. **No real Windows guest ran this.** Everything above is Wine, on this
   workstation and in the VM. The `windows` branch of every assertion in
   `wc-cursor.sh` has been exercised only by `WC_WIN32=windows` under Wine,
   which tests the *branch* and not the platform. The `dwmapi` entry in §67.4
   in particular predicts that a real guest logs
   `DwmExtendFrameIntoClientArea ok` with no Wine caveat, and §31.7 says it
   does — but that was a different run on a different day.
2. **A rendering leg in the guest.** §67.6 has no client. An X server and a
   `weston-eventdemo` inside the VM would make `wc-cursor.sh wine` runnable
   there, which is the first Wine cursor run that would not share a wineserver,
   an X server and a machine with ten other worktrees.
3. **The other harnesses do not assert the platform line yet.** `wc-cursor.sh`
   does; `wc-input.sh`, `wc-clip.sh`, `wc-damage.sh`, `wc-inhibit.sh` and
   `wc-wlcs-wine.sh` all read a compositor log and none of them check who wrote
   it. `win32_of()` is six lines and should be shared rather than copied.
4. **`wc-damage.sh`'s wait, everywhere else.** §67.5's cause — the harness
   outliving the thing it was measuring — is a shape, not an incident.
   `wc-cursor.sh` has the fix now and `wc-damage.sh` had it already; the others
   should be read with it in mind, because the symptom is a *missing* reading
   and a missing reading has been printed as a note in more than one file.
5. **§37's `SendInput` ordering**, tightened to an assertion on Windows only.
   Refused above for being a difference rather than a defect, which is the right
   call for a Wine branch and the wrong call for leaving the Windows leg
   untested.


### 67.9 All three arrangements, and the client is in another kernel

The user asked for three, and they are the three combinations of *which side is
Wine* that exist while the Windows laptop is unavailable:

| | arrangement | harness | result *as first run* |
|---|---|---|---:|
| 1 | linux → linux vm | `wc-vm-client.sh linux` | 9 passed, 0 failed |
| 2 | linux → wine linux vm | `wc-wine-guest.sh` | **3 passed, 0 failed** |
| 3 | wine linux → linux vm | `wc-vm-client.sh wine` | 10 passed, 0 failed |

> **Read §67.10 before this table.** Two of these three rows have since been
> withdrawn as transport results and one of them no longer passes. The legs
> carry the wire on a channel the user's rule forbids, so they are demoted to
> venue evidence; and their assertions stopped before the session broke, so the
> zeros in rows 1 and 3 were measuring less than they appear to. The leg names
> are now `linux-relay` and `wine-relay`, and `ring` is the leg that asks the
> transport question properly. Row 2 is unaffected — it moves no Wayland traffic
> across the boundary at all.

Arrangement 3 is the one §26.5 specified as "leg 3" and nobody had run: *"Wine
plays the Windows side, and a Linux VM guest runs the client."* Arrangement 1 is
its control, which is why the two live in one file with one word between them —
§13.8 is the record of comparing two numbers taken on two trees with two
instruments and being wrong, and leg 1's whole value is that it differs from
leg 3 in exactly one thing.

**What is new here is not Wine, it is the boundary.** §26.5's correction is that
every Wine run in this document before it was one machine with no VM in it, and
several consequences of *having no hypervisor* were written up as "Wine lied".
In arrangements 1 and 3 the client is in another kernel: it cannot see the
host's filesystem except where 9p says so, it cannot open a host Unix socket,
and its `SCM_RIGHTS` cannot cross. Those are the real deployment's constraints
and the local Wine legs do not have them.

#### How the bytes cross, and why it is not a socket

The guest has no network at all — `nix/guest.nix` sets `networkingOptions = []`
— and a Unix socket node exported over 9p is a host kernel object a guest
`connect()` cannot reach. What the guest does have is the virtio-serial cold
path, whose host end is a Unix socket QEMU listens on:

```text
  client ── wc-proxy ── /tmp/up.sock            (guest)
                            │ socat
             /dev/virtio-ports/org.sirati.svcold.0
        ═════════════ the hypervisor boundary ═════════════
                    $SV_RUNDIR/cold.sock          (host)
                            │ socat
              the compositor's AF_UNIX socket
```

Two `socat`s and one virtio-serial port, forwarding the byte stream unaltered —
which is `probe-relay.c`'s argument for the same move on the real guest, and
here it is *more* honest than the local legs, where the "boundary" was two
processes on one kernel.

`wl_shm` pools and the keymap are the two things not on the wire, and both use
9p rather than the port: the client's pools are written into `/sv/pools` in the
guest, which is `$SV_RUNDIR/pools` on the host, which the compositor opens by
the path `--peer-prefix` gives it — a `winepath -w` of the host directory on
leg 3, the host directory itself on leg 1. The keymap goes the other way.
**That is a file transport and therefore a fixture, not the deployment**, whose
answer is the arena in guest RAM (§12); the harness declares the absence
explicitly rather than declaring a substrate it does not use.

#### Two measurements the first run produced

**`--no-icons`, and it is the port's arithmetic rather than a preference.**
`wc-proxy` opens a *second* upstream connection to resolve app ids to icon
pixels. A virtio-serial port is one stream, so two connections interleave into
it; the compositor sees a corrupt second message flow and closes, and the first
connection dies of a broken pipe. That is exactly what the first run printed —
`icon: the compositor closed the icon connection` followed by
`client 1 failed: Broken pipe (os error 32)`, with `2 client msgs` already
across, so the relay itself was working. The icon feed is not what this leg
tests and the honest fix is to not open the second connection rather than to
multiplex a port that cannot carry it.

**`cold.sock` does not exist until QEMU makes it.** The first version connected
the host relay before booting the guest and got a `socat` that exited
immediately, producing a leg that failed two steps away from where it went
wrong. The relay now starts after the socket appears.

#### The kernel check, in both directions

§67.6's assertion has a mirror image here, and the pair is the part worth
keeping:

* `wc-wine-guest.sh` asserts the compositor's `wine_get_host_version` is the
  **guest's** kernel, because there the compositor is inside the VM.
* `wc-vm-client.sh wine` asserts it is the **host's**, and that it differs from
  the kernel the payload reported from inside.

```
  arrangement 2:  compositor 'Linux 6.18.44'  (inside)   client on the host
  arrangement 3:  compositor 'Linux 6.18.33'  (host)     client 'Linux 6.18.44'
```

Neither can be satisfied by a run that put both halves in the same place, which
is the failure both are guarding against — and it is the failure this project
actually has a history of: §26.5's whole correction is that runs believed to
have a boundary did not. Between them the two assertions say *which side of the
boundary each half was on* rather than asserting that there was one.

#### What these legs do not do

`wayland-info` is the client, so this is the registry and not a pixel. No
window is mapped, nothing is committed, and the `wl_shm` path is advertised
rather than exercised — the pool directory is configured and stays empty. A leg
that maps a window needs a drawing client in the guest and is the obvious next
step now that the transport underneath it is known to work. It is also the leg
that would first exercise the 9p pool path in anger, which is the part of this
arrangement most likely to be wrong.

---
---


### 67.10 The relay is withdrawn, the ring is blocked, and the file pool cannot cross 9p

§67.9's two `*-relay` legs carried the Wayland wire over
`/dev/virtio-ports/org.sirati.svcold.0` through two `socat`s. The user's rule:

> all communication is to go through the ring. alternative channels are
> permitted only for wakeup from idle

**That forbids them.** The doorbell is the sanctioned use of virtio-serial
(§36.6) because ringing a bell to wake a parked consumer *is* wakeup; a byte
relay carrying `wl_shm`, `wl_surface` and every commit is the conversation. §70.5
withdrew `--upstream-cold` for exactly this and observed that withdrawing only
the flag would leave this harness standing, "because what the rule forbids is
the channel, not the flag that names it". That is correct and this section
accepts it.

The legs are **kept and demoted**, not deleted. What they establish is about the
*venue* and none of it is a transport claim: the guest has no network, a Unix
socket node exported over 9p is a host kernel object a guest `connect()` cannot
reach, and both halves really are in different kernels — which the kernel
assertion proves in both directions. Each leg now prints a banner saying it is
not a sanctioned transport before it prints anything else.

#### The ring, attempted, and two measured refusals

`scripts/wc-vm-client.sh ring` is the leg that tries to obey the rule. For this
arrangement — compositor on the host, client in the guest — the control region
has to be memory *both kernels can map*, which on this rig means the guest's RAM
through the memfd backend. The compositor offers a control region two ways and
neither reaches that:

```text
--wayland-cold  →  exit 2: "publishes a control region out of guest RAM, which
                   needs the Linux guest-RAM provider (sv_arena::guestram) …
                   no compositor has been taught to do it yet"
--wayland-ring  →  accepted: "accepting Wayland rings in Local\wc-vm-ring"
```

The second *works*, and being a **named section** is exactly why it does not
help: a section is a same-machine object, and the compositor's own startup says
so about the neighbouring keymap in the very next line — *"unopenable by one
across the boundary"*. The ring section is the same kind of object.

**And the obvious fallback does not exist either, which is the third
measurement.** If a section cannot cross, the next idea is a *file*-backed
control region on the one filesystem both sides can see: `--wayland-ring
$RUNDIR/ring` on the host, `--upstream-ring /sv/ring` in the guest. The Linux
compositor creates it happily. The guest's proxy then says:

```text
wc-proxy: mmap failed: errno 22
```

`SharedRegion::map_fd` is an `mmap(MAP_SHARED)`, and that is the same EINVAL the
pool publish gets, for the same reason, on the same mount. So **one measurement
rules out both fallbacks at once** — the file pool *and* the file control
region — and the only substrate that crosses this boundary is guest RAM through
the memfd backend. Which is the deployment's answer, and the ring's, and the
thing `--wayland-cold` does for Linux only. The circle closes on the missing
function rather than on a missing idea.

So there is no combination that puts a **Windows-build** compositor's control
region into a form the far side of a hypervisor can map, and the missing piece
is one function. `RingLink::publish` is `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]`; the
compositor already commits and stamps guest RAM on Windows for an *arena*
(`--arena-guest-ram`, through `awe-probe`), and ringlink has simply never been
wired to it. Both refusals are measured here rather than read out of the source,
because a blocker asserted from reading is what §67.5 is about.

#### The harness passed over a session that had already died

§70.5's run reported **9 passed / 0 failed** while the session broke immediately
after the window appeared, because every assertion stopped at
`window … created`. **This harness had the same defect and it is worth being
plain about that**: its assertions stopped at the registry walk, and
`wayland-info` disconnects cleanly, so a leg could pass with the interesting
part untouched.

`assert_session_survived` is the fix, and it is three sources because each
failure was visible in only one of them:

* the **client's** own log — a `wl_display` protocol error ends the session, and
  libwayland prints it and carries on;
* the **proxy's** log — a failed client, a refused pool, a keymap the far side
  cannot open;
* the **compositor's** log, so this is not one end agreeing with itself.

The third is not decoration. Run with `WC_VM_POOLTEST=1`, which swaps the
registry walk for `wc-pooltest` — the smallest client that sends an `h` —
**both legs break, and `wc-pooltest` prints `4 pools created and destroyed` and
exits 0 anyway**:

```text
FAIL  the client hit a protocol error, so the session died:
      wl_display#1: error 0: Invalid new_id: 6.
FAIL  the proxy reports the session did not survive:
      pool 3: could not publish 1228800 bytes: Invalid argument (os error 22)
....  the h-sending client: wc-pooltest: 4 pools created and destroyed
....  and its own exit status was 0
```

A client's exit status is not a session check. That is a sharper form of §70.5's
lesson: there the *harness* stopped at the first good news, here the **client
itself** reported success over a dead connection, and a harness that trusted its
exit code would have agreed with it.

#### Two failures, and the control separates them cleanly

The two legs differ in exactly one thing — whether the compositor is the Linux
build or the Windows one under Wine — which is the pairing the dialect question
turns on (§70.2, §72). That is what leg 1 was built to be, and with the session
check in place it pays for itself immediately: **one of the two failures moves
when the dialect moves and the other does not.**

| symptom | linux leg | wine leg | so it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pool 3: could not publish 1228800 bytes: EINVAL` | yes | yes | **not** the dialect |
| `wl_keyboard.keymap (event): argument 1 claims 35572 bytes, 0 available` | yes | no | **the dialect** |

The second is the interesting one and it arrives on the *plain* run, with
`wayland-info` and no pool in sight. It is `wc-proxy` reading the compositor's
**server-to-client** `wl_keyboard.keymap`: against the Windows build the
descriptor is in band (§2.3) and the proxy finds it; against a Linux compositor
the fd came as `SCM_RIGHTS` and the in-band read finds `0 available`. §72 reports
the same mismatch in the client-to-server direction on `create_pool`; this is the
other direction of the same fact, and between them the dialect is wrong both
ways round rather than only on the path a pool takes.

It also means §67.9's original claim — that the legs "walked the registry only,
so the in-band path is advertised and not exercised" — was too generous to
itself. The registry walk *does* reach the dialect, through the keymap the seat
sends unprompted. The old harness did not notice because nothing was looking.

#### The `EINVAL` is 9p, and it is not the dialect

Measured directly, in the guest, with a five-line probe:

```text
/sv mount: 9p rw,relatime,access=client,msize=16384,trans=virtio
  mmap MAP_SHARED  on /sv    → FAILED, Invalid argument (errno 22)
  mmap MAP_PRIVATE on /sv    → ok
  mmap MAP_SHARED  on /tmp   → ok            (tmpfs, the control)
```

`SharedFile::create` ends in `Handle::map_mut`, an `mmap(MAP_SHARED)` on the
pool file, and the share is mounted with **no cache mode**, where 9p refuses
shared mappings. So `could not publish … os error 22` is the mount, not Wine,
not the compositor and not the translator. It also explains §70.5's six
identical refusals, which were on the same share.

**The consequence is larger than one harness.** The file pool transport is not
merely "a fixture rather than the deployment" across this boundary — it is
**non-functional** across it. Nothing can publish a pool into a 9p share this
way. The only substrate that crosses is the arena in guest RAM, which is the
deployment's answer and the ring's, and §71 is the section building it. A
`cache=loose` mount would probably make the fixture work and is deliberately
**not** proposed here: it would restore a path the rule says should not carry
this traffic anyway.

One thing is left unattributed on purpose: `Invalid new_id: 6` arrives on both
legs alongside the refusals, and whether it is downstream of the held-back pool
or independent has not been established. Naming a cause for it here would be
§63.3's error with a fresh coat of paint.

#### The ring probe made §63.3's mistake twice before it worked

Worth recording because the section is about exactly this and the instances are
mine, in one function, minutes apart:

1. The leg used `$RUNDIR/ring` as its scratch **directory** and then passed the
   same path to `--wayland-ring`. The compositor could not create a region at a
   path that was already a directory, and the harness reported *"the Linux
   compositor did not create a file-backed ring"* — true, and about the wrong
   step.
2. Fixed, the proxy then exited on argument validation (`--peer-prefix is
   required for --transport shared-file`) before it had touched the region at
   all, and the check — which matched *any* error — read that as the mapping
   being refused. It would have recorded a correct conclusion supported by
   evidence for something else entirely.

Both were caught only by reading the log rather than the verdict. The check now
keys on what the log says **about the region**, and the inconclusive case is a
third outcome rather than being folded into either of the other two. A probe
that cannot say "I did not get far enough to tell you" will eventually tell you
something else instead.

#### Where this leaves §67.9

| leg | what it is now | result |
|---|---|---:|
| `ring` | the transport question, answered: blocked, with all three refusals measured | 3 passed, 0 failed |
| `linux-relay`, `wine-relay` | venue evidence only, banner-labelled, **not** a transport result | see above |
| `wc-wine-guest.sh` | unaffected — it runs one process under Wine in the guest and moves no Wayland traffic across the boundary at all | 3 passed, 0 failed |

**And the leg is written so that it starts working rather than needing to be
written again.** Two things have to land before this arrangement can carry the
wire, and neither is in this section:

* **A guest-RAM publish for the Windows build.** `RingLink::publish` is
  `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]`; the compositor already commits and stamps guest
  RAM on Windows for an *arena* through `awe-probe`. When ringlink is wired to
  it, `--wayland-cold` stops exiting 2 and the first assertion in `run_ring`
  inverts — which is the shape a blocked leg should have, because the day it
  unblocks is the day the harness says so instead of somebody remembering to
  check.
* **The dialect.** `wc-proxy` writes the in-band form upstream unconditionally,
  which is why the `linux-relay` leg's keymap fails and why §72's `create_pool`
  desynchronises. `ProtoFd` step 1 is on master; when the per-connection flag
  follows, the `linux-relay` leg's session check should go green without the
  harness changing, and that will be evidence rather than an expectation.

Until then the honest summary is short: the arrangement is viable, the venue is
real and measured, and **no sanctioned transport reaches it yet**.

The arrangement is viable — §70.5 got a mapped `HWND` out of it and this section
got a registry walk — and the thing that makes it *shippable* is not a channel
but the two pieces named above: a guest-RAM publish for the Windows build, and
the negotiated format §72 is for. Neither belongs to this section.

### 67.11 The day it unblocked, and what a leg written to announce it actually said

§67.10 said the legs were written "to start working rather than to need
rewriting", and named two things that had to land. One of them did:
`ProtoFd`/`WireFd` chose the `h` encoding **per connection from the transport**
instead of by platform, and `scripts/wc-pool.sh` is its acceptance test — four
pools through the proxy to a Linux compositor, client exit 0, with a control leg
proving that removing one flag brings the original hang back. It passes on this
tree.

So the legs were re-run. **Three things moved and one of them was mine.**

#### The keymap failure moved, and it needed the flag §79 added

The first re-run reported the failure **byte-identical** to before:

```text
FAIL  client 1 failed: compositor: wl_keyboard.keymap (event):
      argument 1 claims 35572 bytes, 0 available
```

Which was correct, and the reason is in `--in-band`'s own doc comment: *"A ring
slot needs no flag — a connection that arrives as one **is** the proxy, by
construction. A socket cannot say who is on the far end, and the relay legs put
the proxy on one (`wc-vm-client.sh --upstream`), so the operator that arranged
the relay declares it here."* §79 anticipated this harness by name. The leg was
putting the proxy on a socket and never declaring it, so the compositor treated
it as a stock libwayland client and wrote the keymap descriptor out of band.

With `--in-band` on the Linux compositor:

```text
wc-compositor: client 1 accepted, h in band
wc-compositor: client InnerClientId { .. } disconnected: ConnectionClosed
[proxy] client 1 ... 8 client msgs, 30 server msgs
```

No keymap complaint, orderly close. **The dialect half of §67.10's two-cause
split is closed.**

#### The other half did not move, which is the point of having split them

Run with `WC_VM_POOLTEST=1`, the `h`-sending client still fails — and now with
*only* the one failure left:

```text
FAIL  pool 3: could not publish 1228800 bytes: Invalid argument (os error 22)
....  the EINVAL is 9p: mmap(MAP_SHARED) on /sv returns errno 22
```

That is the split holding up under the fix, which is the strongest evidence it
was drawn in the right place. §67.10 predicted that one of the two failures would
move when the dialect moved and the other would not; the dialect landed, the
keymap went, the `EINVAL` stayed exactly where it was. A two-cause diagnosis that
survives one of its causes being fixed is worth more than the reasoning that
produced it.

#### `assert_session_survived` reported it — and had a false positive of its own

It did report the change without a harness edit, which was the point. But once
the session actually *worked*, it kept failing the leg on:

```text
FAIL  client 1 stopped: the compositor closed the connection
```

`run.rs` prints `client N stopped: {why}` for `Ok(why)` and `client N failed:
{e}` for `Err(e)` — an orderly end against an error — and the check was matching
both. So a clean `wayland-info` disconnect read as the session not surviving.
Fixed by keying on `failed`.

**That is the failure mode after the one it was written for**, and it is worth
naming because it is the more dangerous of the two. A check that cries wolf gets
switched off, and this one is now load-bearing in four harnesses across three
agents. It was caught the same way everything else in this section was caught:
by reading the log rather than the verdict.

#### What was *not* shown, said plainly

`SealedFile` — the keymap as a `memfd` rather than a file in `--shared-dir` — is
the next piece of the dialect work, and `WC_VM_SEALED=1` drops `--shared-dir` so
this leg can reach it. It passed, and that was **not** evidence the path works:
the proxy reported `0 fds in, 0 out`, so nothing appeared to have crossed.

**That reasoning was wrong, and §80 is what corrected it.** Two mistakes, both
mine, and both the same shape as everything else this section keeps finding:

* *"`wayland-info` never binds a `wl_keyboard`"* — it does. §80 chose it for
  exactly that property. What it does not do is print anything about the keymap,
  so reading its output for the word was the wrong instrument.
* *"`0 fds in, 0 out`, so nothing crossed"* — an in-band `h` **is not an fd**, so
  that counter reads zero whether or not the keymap crossed and cannot separate
  the two cases. A real number, about the wrong question. §63.3 again, in my own
  log.

§80's assertion is the right one and this harness now makes it:
`wl_keyboard.repeat_info` follows the keymap immediately, so its absence is the
symptom in a run whose exit code says everything is fine.

#### And with a real assertion, the `SealedFile` path fails — differently than predicted

| | keymap crosses? |
|---|---|
| `--shared-dir` (a file both sides can name) | **yes** — 1 `repeat_info` line |
| `WC_VM_SEALED=1` (a `SealedFile` memfd) | **no** — no `repeat_info` |

And the reason is not the dialect:

```text
[proxy] client 1 failed: compositor: wl_keyboard.keymap names
  Section { name: "/tmp/nix-shell.U3jLqN/wc-270a9ffb…", size: 35572 },
  which this side cannot open: No such file or directory (os error 2)
```

**The name is a path on the host, and the proxy is in the guest.** It is not a
`WrongDialect` refusal — the dialect is agreed and the descriptor is read
correctly — it is a named object whose name means nothing on the other side of
the boundary. That is §11.2's problem arriving in the Linux-to-Linux-VM
direction, the same shape §70.5 hit from the Windows side with a
`Local\wc-…` section, and it is **invisible on one machine**, where the path
resolves and the leg passes.

This leg is the only one in the tree that can show it, because it is the only
one with a hypervisor between the proxy and the compositor. Recorded here for
whoever owns `SealedFile`: making the keymap a `memfd` is necessary and not
sufficient; the *name* has to be one the far side can resolve, and a cross-VM
leg is the only place that distinction is testable.

`Invalid new_id: 6` still arrives beside the pool refusal and is still
unattributed.

#### Where the arrangement stands

| | |
|---|---|
| `wc-vm-client.sh all` | **24 passed, 0 failed** (was 22/1) |
| `wc-vm-client.sh ring` | 3 passed, 0 failed — all three refusals still stand |
| with `WC_VM_POOLTEST=1` | the 9p `EINVAL` alone, dialect no longer implicated |

The transport conclusion is unchanged and none of the above touches it: the
relay legs still carry the wire on a channel the rule forbids, and they are still
venue evidence rather than a transport result. What moved is that the venue is
now known to be sound for everything the file substrate does not block — which
makes the remaining blocker exactly one thing, a guest-RAM publish for the
Windows build, rather than two.

## 68. Subsurface state that belongs to the parent's commit is applied on the child's

### 68.1 Status in one paragraph

§66 narrowed the seven subsurface failures from "commit semantics" to "the scene
lookup", and that narrowing was half right. The lookup is fine. What is wrong is
one thing, in `vendor/smithay`, which this project owns outright: **`set_position`
and `place_above`/`place_below` are double-buffered on the *parent* surface, and
smithay applies them on the child's commit and on the bare request
respectively.** Two sentences of protocol text say so, and they are the whole
argument. Nothing is fixed here — the change is delicate and belongs to its own
session — but the group is no longer seven puzzles; it is one deviation with a
citation.

### 68.2 The two sentences

From `vendor/wayland-server/wayland.xml`, `wl_subsurface`:

> **`set_position`** — "Position is double-buffered state **on the parent
> surface**, see wl_subsurface and wl_surface.commit for more information."
>
> **`place_above`** / **`place_below`** — "Z-order is double-buffered state **on
> the parent surface**, see wl_subsurface and wl_surface.commit for more
> information."

"On the parent surface" is the operative phrase in both, and it is not the same
as "double-buffered". Sync and desync change when the *subsurface's own* state is
applied; they do not move position or z-order off the parent's commit, because
those never belonged to the child in the first place.

### 68.3 What smithay does instead

**Position.** `set_position` writes `SubsurfaceCachedState.pending().location`,
and that cache hangs off the **subsurface's own** surface:

```rust
impl Cacheable for SubsurfaceCachedState {
    fn commit(&mut self, _dh: &DisplayHandle) -> Self { Self { location: self.location } }
```

so it is promoted on the *subsurface's* commit. In sync mode that is invisible,
because the child's cache is applied when the parent commits anyway. In **desync**
mode the child's commit applies immediately, and the position moves with no
parent commit at all.

That is exactly what WLCS reports. `subsurface_does_not_move_when_parent_not_committed`
sets desync, sets position (20, 20), commits **only the subsurface**, and then
asks where the pointer at (30, 30) landed:

```
Expected: (30, 30)      the subsurface has not moved, so the pointer is at (30,30) in it
  Actual: (10, 10)      it moved: 30 - 20
```

`(2560, 2560)` in the raw log is `wl_fixed` for `(10.0, 10.0)`.

**Z-order.** Worse, and simpler: it is not buffered at all.

```rust
wl_subsurface::Request::PlaceAbove { sibling } => {
    if let Err(()) = PrivateSurfaceData::reorder(&data.surface, Location::After, &sibling) {
```

`reorder` runs on the request. The parent's commit is not involved.

### 68.4 What this does to §66.4's hypothesis

§66.4 recorded that `place_above_simple` and `place_below_simple` look
unsatisfiable — each asserts that neither the moved subsurface nor the fixture's
is focused, when after the restack one of them must be — and refused to conclude
the suite was wrong without a reference run.

That refusal now looks better than it did. With z-order applied on the request
rather than on the parent's commit, **the stack these tests are asserting about
is not the stack we build**, and reasoning about which surface "should" be on top
from the request order was reasoning about a sequence the spec does not describe.
The hypothesis is not disproved and it is not needed: fix the deviation first,
and re-read the assertions against what the parent's commit actually produces.

The reference run in §66.4 is still the way to settle it, and it is still one
command. But it is no longer the *first* thing to do.

### 68.5 Why this is ours to fix, and the shape of it

`Cargo.toml` is explicit: *"Nothing in `vendor/` is upstream code any more; treat
it as ours."* `vendor/PATCHES.md` is the index of what has been changed and why,
and this would be another entry.

The shape, and the reason it is not done here:

* **Position** wants moving from a `Cacheable` on the child to state applied when
  the parent commits. smithay's cache machinery has the hook — sync children are
  already committed from the parent — but "apply the child's location on the
  parent's commit while leaving the rest of the child's state alone" is a
  different split from the one the type currently expresses.
* **Z-order** wants the reorder staged and applied at the parent's commit, which
  means a pending stacking list per parent where today there is one live list.
* Both are changes to the traversal every other part of this compositor reads
  through — `placed_tree` feeds both the blit and the hit test (§40), so an error
  here is an error in two places that must stay each other's inverse.

That is a session's work with its own measurements, not a change to append to
this one.

### 68.6 What is claimed and what is not

Claimed: the two spec sentences, the two pieces of smithay that contradict them,
and that `subsurface_does_not_move_when_parent_not_committed`'s numbers are the
predicted consequence of the first.

**Not claimed: that fixing this fixes six tests.** Four are position tests and
the mechanism accounts for them directly; two are restacking tests and §68.4
says only that they cannot be judged until the stack is built at the right time.
The seventh, `subsurface_extends_parent_input_region`, throws `bad optional
access` — the pointer entered nothing at all — and nothing here explains it.

Also not claimed: that this is a *bug* in upstream smithay as shipped. This is
what `vendor/smithay` does at the revision this tree carries, read from the
source in the tree. Whether upstream has since changed it was not checked.
## 69. Wine inside the Linux VM, and a skip that has nowhere to go

*(Topology 2 of the three the user asked for. §64's continuation.)*

### 69.1 Status in one paragraph

The user asked for three arrangements with a real hypervisor in the path, and
this is the second: **a Windows binary under Wine, inside the Linux VM guest**.
`scripts/wc-ring-vm.sh` was the first and runs the *Linux* compositor in the
guest; nothing before this ran a Windows binary in one. The question it was
built to settle is §53.3's: `GetGuiResources` returns 0 under Wine on this
workstation, the USER/GDI leak assertion was skipped for that reason, and the
skip could not say whether the zero was a fact about **Wine** or a fact about
the **venue**. It is the first. Inside the guest, on the guest's own kernel,
with the probe owning five windows, Wine answers `user=0 gdi=0` exactly as it
does on the host. **No arrangement of Linux virtual machines can turn §53's SKIP
into an assertion; only a real Windows kernel can** — which is worth knowing
before the user's machine is spent on it, and which leaves the queued testhost
run as the only thing that can settle it rather than one option among several.

### 69.2 What the guest ran, and how it got a `.exe` without one being installed

`nix/guest.nix` shares the host's `/nix/store` over 9p and says why: *"the guest
half is handed in from the host's store, which the guest can see because
/nix/store is shared. So there is nothing to install: the harness runs an
absolute path."* Wine and Xvfb are store paths, so the guest runs them without
the image growing a package; `probe-life.exe` is not in the store, so it is
copied into the shared run directory the guest sees as `/sv`. The existing
`sv-payload` rendezvous — a `guest-cmd.sh` appearing in that directory — is what
starts it, unchanged.

```text
GUEST-UNAME: Linux nixos 6.18.44 #1-NixOS SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC …
GUEST-WINE-VERSION: wine-11.14 (Staging)
before user=0 gdi=0
after  user=0 gdi=0
windows=5
counter=stub
```

against this host's `Linux devhost 6.18.33`. The harness **fails
if those two unames match**, because a run that measured the host would
otherwise be indistinguishable from a run that measured the guest — §51's
mistake in a new place, and the reason that check is an assertion rather than a
printed line.

### 69.3 Why the verdict is `stub` and not an absence

`user=0` is the same string a process with no windows would print, so the probe
does not print it alone. `probe-life.exe selftest` creates four windows of its
own, samples `GetGuiResources` before and after, and reports the enumerated
window count beside both numbers. Five windows and `user=0` is a stub; no
windows and `user=0` is an absence, and the harness refuses to draw a conclusion
below four windows. That is the same discipline §64.4 needed for a different
reason: a number is only evidence once something has been shown to move.

### 69.4 What this does and does not establish

**It establishes** that this Wine build does not implement `GetGuiResources`,
measured on a second kernel behind a real hypervisor rather than argued.

**It does not establish that a different Wine would stub**, and the reason is
the venue's own construction: the guest runs the host's `/nix/store` over 9p, so
the Wine inside the VM is byte-for-byte the Wine outside it. The hypervisor is
real and the kernel is not the host's, but the *binary under test is the same
binary*. For the question actually asked — "is the zero about Wine or about the
venue" — that is exactly right, because holding the binary constant while
changing the venue is what isolates the variable. For any question about Wine
versions it is no evidence at all.

**The corollary is the useful part.** §53.6 item 3 and §64.5 item 2 both name
the guest run as the one that would turn the SKIP into an assertion. That is now
narrowed: it must be the **Windows** guest, not a Linux one, and no amount of
local virtualisation substitutes. The three topologies the user asked for are
worth running for what they *do* test — a real boundary for the transport, the
proxy and the descriptor rule — and this particular assertion is not among them.

### 69.5 What is not proven

1. **The compositor was not run in the guest**, only the probe. This answers one
   question cheaply; running `wc-compositor.exe` under Wine in the VM is the
   rest of topology 2 and is not done here.
2. **Topologies 1 and 3 are untouched by this section.** `wc-ring-vm.sh` is 1;
   3 (Wine-Linux host driving a Linux VM guest) has no harness yet.
3. **One Wine build, one guest kernel.** See 66.4.
4. **`release_icons` is still unasserted anywhere** (§64.5 item 1), and this
   section removes the hope that a local VM would fix it.

### 69.6 The gates

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| **`scripts/wc-wine-vm.sh`** (new) | **3 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped** — the skip *is* the finding |
| `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | unchanged — no Rust outside `probe-life.c` |
| `scripts/wc-xref.sh` | 0 broken, 0 unqualified |

It declares `cross-vm` — the first harness in this tree to do so and mean this
box. `wc_topology_declare` refuses that unless a VM host and a guest are
configured, a guard written when the hypervisor was always somebody else's; here
the harness *starts* the hypervisor, so it points both at this machine rather
than weakening the guard.

**Two harness bugs paid for on the way, both of the same family as §53.4's.**
The `sv-payload` unit echoes the script it is about to run into the same log the
harness greps, so an unanchored `grep "GUEST-SELFTEST-END"` matched the *source
line* and the first two runs "finished" in seconds having measured nothing. And
the verdict came back as `stub\r`: mingw's stdio turns every `\n` into CRLF, so
`case "$counter" in stub)` did not match and the harness reported *"unexpected
verdict 'stub'"* about a verdict it had just printed. That is the **third** time
this session — `probe-drag`'s window list in §50, `probe-life`'s `gone` in §53,
this — and it is always the same bug wearing a different symptom.

## 70. Topology 3 cannot mean what it sounds like, and what it does mean needs one flag

*(§69's continuation. A feasibility finding, not a run.)*

> **AMENDED. The title is wrong and §70.5 is the correction.** The flag this
> section proposed — `--upstream-cold` on `wc-proxy` — was written, run
> successfully, and then **withdrawn**, because the user restated the
> architectural rule: *"all communication is to go through the ring.
> alternative channels are permitted only for wakeup from idle."* A
> virtio-serial port carrying the protocol stream is not a wakeup, it is the
> whole conversation on an alternative channel. The reasoning below about *why
> the arrangement needs a channel at all* still stands; only the choice of
> channel was wrong.

### 70.1 Status in one paragraph

The third of the user's three arrangements — *"wine linux to linux vm"* — was
handed to me as "a client under Wine on this host against a compositor in a VM".
**That arrangement cannot be built, and the reason is a `cfg`, not a
difficulty.** The Windows build of the vendored `wayland-backend` encodes an `h`
argument *in band* and the Linux build passes it out of band as `SCM_RIGHTS`;
the two are selected by `#[cfg(windows)]` / `#[cfg(unix)]` in
`vendor/wayland-backend/src/rs/wire.rs`, so a Windows client and a Linux
compositor do not speak the same protocol and no transport between them changes
that. §29.7 made exactly this argument for why the clipboard leg could not be
split into two, and it applies here unchanged. **The coherent reading of
topology 3 is the other one** — Wine on this workstation as the *Windows side*
and the Linux VM as the *client* side, which is the arrangement §29.8 named in
so many words — and that one is buildable, is the closest thing to the
deployment that exists without the user's laptop, and is **one missing flag**
away. This section names the flag rather than writing it, because writing it is
