a change to `wc-proxy`'s upstream and not a harness.

### 70.2 Why a Wine client and a Linux compositor cannot meet

`wc-proxy` exists precisely because these two dialects differ: it speaks
ordinary out-of-band libwayland *downstream* to a Linux client and the in-band
dialect *upstream* to the Windows compositor. It is the translator, and it only
translates in that direction. A Windows client talking to a Linux compositor has
no translator on either end and would need one written backwards.

So the three topologies are not symmetric, and the asymmetry is structural:

| the user's phrase | what it can mean | status |
|---|---|---|
| linux to linux vm | Linux client here, Linux compositor in the VM | `scripts/wc-ring-vm.sh` |
| linux to wine linux vm | the Windows compositor under Wine *in* the VM | §67's `wc-wine-guest.sh` (server only), §69 (the probe) |
| **wine linux to linux vm** | ~~Windows client here, Linux compositor in the VM~~ | **impossible, §70.2** |
| | Windows compositor under Wine **here**, client in the VM | **§70.3 — one flag short** |

### 70.3 The arrangement that does work, and the one thing it lacks

§29.8: *"`nix build .#svGuest` builds the honest arrangement: Wine on this
workstation as the Windows side, and a **Linux VM guest as the client**. That is
a real hypervisor between the two halves."* Every dialect lines up: the client
in the guest is an ordinary Linux Wayland client, `wc-proxy` beside it in the
guest translates, and the compositor under Wine on this host receives the
in-band dialect it expects.

What is missing is the channel for the protocol byte stream, and it is
one-sided rather than absent:

* **The compositor already has one.** `--wayland-cold PATH` takes the *cold
  path* — a virtio-serial port — and `scripts/wc-ring-vm.sh` already drives it,
  with the compositor in the guest reading
  `/dev/virtio-ports/org.sirati.svcold.0`.
* **`wc-proxy` does not.** Its upstream is either `--upstream PATH`, which must
  be an **AF_UNIX socket**, or `--upstream-ring PATH`, the shared_vulkan control
  region. A character device is neither, so the proxy inside the guest has
  nothing to point at the host.

So the missing piece has a name: **an `--upstream-cold PATH` on `wc-proxy`,
mirroring the compositor's `--wayland-cold`,** so that the guest's proxy can
reach the host's compositor over the virtio-serial port the VM already has. The
pixels need no new work — `--transport shared-file --pool-dir` over the 9p `/sv`
share already puts pools where both sides can see them.

**Why that is worth doing and not just noting.** Every drag, drop and window
result in §50 through §64 carries the same caveat — one kernel, no boundary —
and this arrangement is the one that removes it without the user's laptop.
§50.8 item 1 says the ~100 ms round trip of §50.6 is *"a lower bound for the
deployment"*; this is the venue that could measure the real one.

### 70.4 What is not proven

1. **Nothing was run for this section.** It is a reading of `--help`, of
   `wire.rs`'s `cfg`s and of `wc-ring-vm.sh`, and it should be treated as a
   design note until something boots.
2. **The virtio-serial channel is assumed adequate for the Wayland byte
   stream** because the compositor already uses it for exactly that in
   `wc-ring-vm.sh`. Its throughput under a real client is unmeasured, and
   §36's whole point is that a cold path is the slow one.
3. **`graphics = false`.** §67 found the compositor comes up fully in the guest
   with no X at all, but a *client* in the guest that draws needs somewhere to
   draw; whether the guest needs a display for the client half is untested.
4. **The impossibility in §70.2 is about this tree's vendored backend**, not
   about Wayland. A client built for the Linux target and *run under Wine* is
   not a thing; a Windows client speaking out-of-band would need the vendored
   `cfg` inverted, which is a fork of the fork.

### 70.5 `--upstream-cold` was built, run, and withdrawn on the ring rule

**It worked, and that is not the same as it being right.** `--upstream-cold
PATH` was added to `wc-proxy` as a third `Upstream` variant beside `Socket` and
`Ring` — a character device carrying the protocol as bytes, refused at *parse*
if the path is not one — and a harness ran the whole arrangement: the
compositor under Wine on this workstation, `wc-proxy` and `weston-clickdot`
inside the svGuest VM, `socat` joining QEUM's end of
`/dev/virtio-ports/org.sirati.svcold.0` to the compositor's socket. The guest
reported kernel 6.18.44 against this host's 6.18.33, the proxy logged
`upstream cold … (a byte stream; no fd can be represented on it)`, and the
compositor logged `wl_surface created`, `xdg_toplevel created (#1) -> window 1`
and `window 1 created (HWND 0x2007a)`.

It is withdrawn anyway. The user's rule is that **all communication goes
through the ring, and alternative channels are permitted only for wakeup from
idle**. A doorbell qualifies — ringing a bell to wake a parked consumer *is*
wakeup. A virtio-serial port carrying `wl_surface`, `wl_shm` and every commit
does not; it is the conversation, not the wake. The code is reverted and the
harness is not in the tree.

**The same objection lands on `scripts/wc-vm-client.sh` (§67.9), which is in
master**, and withdrawing only this flag would leave the equivalent violation
standing. That harness reaches the same arrangement more cheaply — two `socat`s
and no new flag, so `wc-proxy` uses its ordinary `--upstream` — but the bytes
still cross on the same virtio-serial port. What the rule forbids is the
channel, not the flag that names it.

**Three things the run showed that are worth keeping.**

*The arrangement is viable.* A Linux client in a VM drove a Windows compositor
on the host through a real hypervisor as far as a mapped `HWND`. Whatever
carries the bytes, the halves fit together — which is what §29.8 asserted and
nothing had shown.

*It then broke, and the harness said it passed.* Immediately after the window
appeared:

```text
[proxy] client 1 failed: compositor: wl_keyboard.keymap names Section
  { name: "Local\\wc-eb7bc4cb…", size: 36950 }, which this side cannot open
[proxy] client 1: pool 3: could not publish 38272 bytes: Invalid argument (os error 22)
```

The compositor published the keymap as a Windows kernel section because it was
started without `--shared-dir` — §11.2's problem, in a topology where the far
side is a Linux guest that cannot open one — and the pool publish failed with
`EINVAL` six times. **Every assertion in the harness had already passed**,
because they stopped at `window … created` and nothing checked that the session
survived. A gate that stops at the first good news is the shape §35 is about,
and this one was mine.

*The dialect question does not arise here, and §72's does.* This proxy talked to
a **Windows** compositor, which is the pairing it was built for, so the
in-band-`h` stream was correct at both ends. §72 reports that the same proxy
against a **Linux** compositor desynchronises the server's reader on
`create_pool` with nothing logged on either side. That is the other half of
§70.2's two-dialects-one-translator fact, and it means the arrangement cannot
composite against a Linux compositor whatever channel carries the bytes.

**Where this leaves the work.** Not a transport flag. Either the proxy learns
the out-of-band dialect for a Unix upstream, or — more in keeping with the rule
just restated — the **ring** carries the descriptor properly so the dialect
question does not arise at the boundary at all. `--upstream-ring` already
exists; that is the direction. §70.1's "one flag away" is withdrawn.

## 71. The arena route to topology 1, and the outbound pages that are not there

### 71.1 Status in one paragraph

**Topology 1 already has a working leg and this is not it.** `wc-ring-vm.sh`
(§69's first paragraph) runs the Linux compositor in the `svGuest` VM with a
client on the host, and crosses by **ring** — a control region published down
the cold path, swept for by `sv-hostd`, with no socket on the hop that crosses.
It works. This section takes the *other* route to the same topology: the
`--arena-guest-ram` + `wc-arena-host` path, which is what `wc-guest.sh` uses on
testhost and therefore what §51.6's block 12 depends on. The two share a venue
and share almost no code.

That route does not complete, and the reason is specific. The leg gets the guest
up, the compositor listening **inside** it, the arena cut from the guest's own
RAM, and a frame list published — and then the locate's verify fails on 68 pages
that turn out to be the outbound window's (§71.4). Two obstacles on the way were
general and are fixed; the third is named and left.

**The boundary is real and proved so**: `Linux 6.18.44` inside against
`Linux 6.18.33` outside, the check borrowed from `wc-wine-guest.sh`. And **the
user's second symptom remains unverified** — this leg stops one step before the
proxy, so nothing has been scrolled and no commit has been checked across it.

### 71.2 There is a page-frame database off Windows, and the code said there was not

```rust
/// There is no page-frame database off Windows …
#[cfg(not(windows))]
pub fn frames(_arena: u32, _pages: u32) -> Result<(Vec<u64>, u128), String> {
    Err("SuperfetchPfnQuery is a Windows interface and this is not Windows".into())
}
```

True of the only guest this project had when it was written, and false the
moment a Linux guest became a topology somebody wanted tested. Linux's
equivalent is `/proc/self/pagemap`, documented in the kernel's
`admin-guide/mm/pagemap.rst`: one 64-bit entry per virtual page, bit 63
*present*, bits 0..54 the frame number.

The consequence was not a missing feature but a failing run. With no frame list
the host falls back to the content sweep, and §7 measured that sweep unreliable
on a loaded machine. The first Linux-guest run reproduced it exactly:

```
located 16316 of 16384 pages after sweeping 2048 MiB
```

With the pagemap implementation, the same run:

```
located 16384 of 16384 pages in 193.51ms by frame list (swept 0 MiB;
714 frame run(s) became 714 file run(s), first frame 0xe807)
```

**A zero is treated as a refusal, not an answer.** Since Linux 4.0 a process
without `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` reads *zeroes* for the frame number rather than being
refused: the entry is returned, the present bit is set, and only the number is
blanked. That is deliberate hardening against Rowhammer, and it is the worst
possible failure shape here — a list of zeroes is a perfectly well-formed frame
list that would send the host looking for page 0 sixteen thousand times. So a
zero frame behind a present page returns an error naming the privilege.

### 71.3 `-name sv-guest` is a class of thing, and §16.8 says identity is not

The second obstacle was §16.8 arriving where it bites hardest. `nix/guest.nix`
bakes `-name sv-guest,process=sv-guest` into every guest it boots, and
`find_qemu_pid` matches a substring of the command line. On a workstation where
several agents each have a guest up, `--vm sv-guest` matches all of them:

```
wc-arena-host: io: 3 qemu-system processes match "sv-guest": [3402756, 3405077, 3414992] — narrow the hint
```

The locator is right to refuse — "two VMs matching one hint and the daemon
guessing is how a client ends up mapping the wrong guest's RAM" — and the fix is
not to make it guess. This harness passes **its own run directory** as the hint,
which appears in its QEMU's command line twice and in nobody else's.

Two of those three processes were this harness's own leaks, and that is the
other half of the lesson: `run-nixos-vm` is a wrapper, so the pid the shell
knows is the wrapper's and killing it can leave the emulator behind. Cleanup now
matches on the run directory too, which can only ever reach this run's guest.

### 71.4 It was the growth channel, and the first guess was wrong

The verify failed on 68 pages beginning at index 16128, which was exactly the
offset the compositor printed for its outbound window. the first write-up guessed the pages
had been **dropped and re-faulted** — `MADV_DONTNEED` on shared memory returns a
zero-filled page with a *new frame*, which would explain both the missing stamps
and the stale frame list in one stroke. **That guess is withdrawn. Nothing was
re-faulted and no frame changed.**

The cause is arithmetic:

```
grow::CONTROL_BYTES = 272 * 1024 = 278_528 bytes = 68 pages of 4096
```

§53 reserves the growth channel from the **front of the outbound window**, and
it must do so *before any gift* while the window is still untouched — that
ordering is §53.2's whole finding, and `reserve_growth_channel` refuses once
anything has been handed out. So on every run with both a guest-RAM arena and an
outbound window, the first 68 pages of that window carry an initialised ring
control region instead of stamps, before the host ever looks.

The evidence matches exactly and I had already collected it without reading it:
the first two pages held the channel's header (`first8=[00,00,31,4b,52,56,48,53]`)
and the rest read as zeroes. That is an initialised ring, not a re-faulted page.
A page that had been dropped would have been *entirely* zero, header included.

**`defer_gifts` is not the fix and was never going to be**, which is why it was
active and logging throughout. The growth channel is not a gift. §12's deferral
covers objects made *for clients*; the channel is infrastructure the compositor
takes for itself, deliberately ahead of them.

So the defect was in the **check**, not the compositor. `wc-arena-host --verify`
walked all `--pages`, including a window whose stamps the compositor is designed
to spend. It now stops at the outbound boundary and says so:

```
verify: skipping the last 256 page(s) -- the outbound window is where the
        compositor writes, and its stamps are its own to spend
verify: 16128/16128 pages of the stitched view carry their own arena index
```

The data region is still verified in full, and that is the half that matters: a
mislocated *data* page is somebody's pixels landing in the wrong memory. The
outbound window is located by frame translation like everything else — only its
stamps are unreadable, and only because they have been spent.

### 71.5 The wire did not cross, and the rule says not to fix it

With the locate passing, the leg reaches the proxy: `wc-proxy` maps the guest's
arena, `--verify-damage` is on, and a client connects to it. Then it stops.
Three runs reported **`2 client msgs, 0 server msgs`** — the client reaches the
proxy, the compositor answers, and the answers never arrive.

Two causes were found and neither was it. The compositor's socket was on the 9p
share, and **a Unix socket node exported over 9p is a host kernel object a guest
`connect()` cannot reach** — which `wc-vm-client.sh` had already established and
this section rediscovered the slow way, seeing `wl-vm` as a plain file on the
host. Moving it to guest-local `/run` fixed that and changed nothing. Attaching
the host end of the virtio port before the guest opens it changed nothing
either.

It was not pursued further, and the reason is the user's standing rule:

> all communication is to go through the ring. alternative channels are
> permitted only for wakeup from idle

This leg carries the **whole Wayland conversation** over a virtio-serial port
through two `socat`s. Making that work properly would be building a forbidden
channel well. `wc-vm-client.sh` reached the same conclusion about the same
transport and keeps its `*-relay` legs labelled rather than fixed; this file is
now labelled the same way, and its banner says so rather than leaving it to a
comment somebody has to find.

**What the leg is for is the half that is not the transport**: the arena locate,
which is the deployment's own path and which nothing else on this workstation
exercises. That half now works end to end.

### 71.6 The gates

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `cargo build --workspace`, both targets | clean |
| `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | **2632 tests**, 0 failures — one test was rewritten rather than deleted, §71.2 |
| **`scripts/wc-vm-damage.sh linux`** | **13 passed, 2 failed** |
| ... the guest boots and QMP answers | pass |
| ... `wc-compositor` listens **inside the guest** | pass |
| ... **`Linux 6.18.44` inside vs `Linux 6.18.33` outside** | pass — the run cannot have measured the host |
| ... the arena comes from the guest's own RAM | pass — 16384 pages, run id reported |
| ... the guest publishes a frame list | pass — 16384 frames, §71.2's new path |
| ... **the host locates it** | **pass** — `verify: 16128/16128 pages`, §71.4 |
| ... `wc-proxy` maps the guest's arena with `--verify-damage` on | pass |
| ... **`wc_assert_topology` proves the boundary** | pass — 16384 pages of guest RAM located over QMP; the first time §51's gate has been exercised by a leg that can pass it |
| ... a commit is checked across the boundary | **fail** — §71.5, the wire, which the rule says not to fix |
| the three arrangements | covered by `wc-vm-client.sh` and `wc-wine-guest.sh`; this file is not a fourth |

### 71.7 What is not proven

1. **The user's second symptom is still unverified.** The leg stops one step
   before the proxy, so no commit has been checked across this boundary and no
   scroll has happened. §27.6's withdrawal stands and nothing here replaces it.
2. **Only topology 1 was attempted.** Topology 2 (Linux → Wine in a Linux VM) is
   closest to the deployment and is where `wc-wine-guest.sh` on the unmerged
   `wine-first-class` branch already has the guest-side Wine working — its own
   notes say a rendering leg needs a client in the guest, which is the piece
   this file solves differently by keeping the client outside. Topology 3 is
   untouched.
3. **The `MADV_DONTNEED` explanation is a hypothesis with evidence, not a
   diagnosis.** Zero pages and a stale frame are both consistent with it and
   neither proves it; the call has not been traced. What is established is
   *which* pages, that it is deterministic, and that it is the outbound window.
4. **`socat` bridging a Unix socket to a virtio-serial port is unexercised
   beyond connecting.** The compositor bound its socket and the port carried
   bytes as far as the harness got, but no Wayland client has completed a
   handshake across it, so the transport is plausible rather than proven.
## 72. Release ran on a guest, the clock now turns with nobody connected, and the pool path is broken

### 72.1 Status in one paragraph

`docs/waycompose-design.md` §61.5 could not answer the user's question — *"its
very important that the arena also releases unneeded memory again"* — and named
two causes. Both are now **shown on a boundary**: a client took pools out of a
guest's RAM, was killed rather than closed, and the guest gave the region back,
`111124480 → 102735872` bytes of resident set read **inside the virtual
machine**, a fall of exactly the 8,388,608 the region was. §61.5's third cause —
that with **zero** clients nothing turns the clock — was measured here, then
fixed here, and leg B holds the fix with nothing connected at all. Getting there
produced two further defects; one is fixed and **one is open work, not a
documented limitation**, because it means this topology cannot draw a pixel.

Venue: `nix build .#svGuest` — guest **Linux 6.18.44** against this
workstation's **6.18.33**, RAM in a `memory-backend-memfd` the host maps.
Compositor in the guest with a 12 MiB arena of its own RAM; `wc-proxy` and the
clients on the host; Wayland over §36's rings. `scripts/wc-release-vm.sh`:
**19 passed, 0 failed**.

> **Topology: `cross-vm`, Linux host → Linux VM.** Every number below is from
> that leg. `testhost` was not touched.

### 72.2 The three numbers, and why they are the guest's

| leg A | `wc-compositor`'s resident set, **in the guest** |
|---|---|
| before — compositor up, no pools out | **102,727,680 B (98.0 MiB)** |
| at peak — pools out, one region grown | **111,124,480 B (106.0 MiB)** |
| after — client killed, region returned | **102,735,872 B (98.0 MiB)** |

Rise 8,396,800; fall **8,388,608 — the region, exactly**. Leg B repeats it one
size up and with nobody connected: a 16,777,216-byte region returned, and the
resident set down by 16,777,216.

Across five runs spanning two arena configurations the absolute numbers move by
a few pages and **every delta is the region to the byte**. §61.5's table has an
"after" row larger than its "before" row by a region that never came back; this
closes it.

**It has to be the guest's number and there is no substitute.** The host
unmapping its view frees nothing: the pages are the guest's, `mlock`ed
(`VirtualLock`ed on Windows) and non-pageable, and they stay gone from the
guest's operating system until the guest frees them.
`wc_handle::arena::committed_bytes` was written for exactly this and had never
been read outside a unit test; here it is `/proc/<pid>/statm` sampled by the
guest's own payload script.

Note what does **not** move it: writing pixels into pages the guest already
committed. The resident set is flat while pools are cut out of an existing
region and steps only when a region is added or dropped. A release experiment
whose pools all fitted the floor would show nothing whatever the allocator did,
which is an easy way to build one that cannot fail.

### 72.3 The pool path is broken, and it is work rather than a caveat

`scripts/wc-ring-vm.sh` has passed since §36 — a client here driving a
compositor in another kernel, over memory. It drives it with `wayland-info`,
which sends no `h` argument, and **that is the only reason it passes.**

`wc-proxy` writes its upstream stream in the in-band-`h` dialect (§2.3):
`FdEncoding::OutOfBand` facing the client, `FdEncoding::InBand` facing the
compositor, hard-coded, because the far side has always been the Windows build.
On Unix the vendored backend's `Argument::Fd` is a raw descriptor —
`vendor/wayland-backend/src/rs/wire.rs`, `#[cfg(windows)]` — so a rewritten
`wl_shm.create_pool` desynchronises a Linux server's reader.

Measured, and the shape is the point because nothing anywhere says a word:

* the client creates one pool and calls `wl_display_roundtrip`; it never returns;
* the proxy logs the pool published, then two `wl_shm.format` events, then nothing;
* the compositor logs nothing and does **not** drop the connection;
* the same client against the same compositor **with no proxy** is fine.

`scripts/wc-pooltest.c` — this tree's own client, written for another purpose —
reproduces it, so the defect is not in the client that found it. **That is the
regression test, and it has to go from failing to passing.**

**The design is settled, and it is the standard protocol rather than a
negotiated specialisation.** The user's instruction allowed either — *"the ring
data format can be specialised for the other side instead of needing translation
after the fact **if that is faster**, however that requires that during client
server handshake this format is negotiated"* — and made it conditional on a
measurement. The measurement came back: rewriting a message costs **301–304 ns**,
which is **0.056% of one cross-VM present** (§34.5's 216.9 ms). Against that, the
multi-client cost the user raised is the decisive term: §41 disproved "the arena
serves exactly one connection" with a real two-client run, and Firefox opens
four. A negotiated dialect means a server holding one encoding per peer and a
matrix of pairs that can only be tested by having both kinds of peer; the
standard protocol means one wire and one translator. **Specialisation buys three
hundred nanoseconds and costs the combinatorics, so it is not built.**

What is built instead, and the phrase that matters is *by transport rather than
by platform*:

1. **Both encodings exist on both platforms.** The in-band form is not a Windows
   thing that Unix lacks; it is what a peer reached through `wc-proxy` speaks,
   and a Linux compositor behind the proxy needs to read it exactly as the
   Windows one does. `vendor/wayland-backend/src/os.rs` is already the single
   place where "what a file descriptor is" is decided — that fork note says the
   protocol machinery "is genuinely fd-type-agnostic already", and `Argument<Id,
   Fd>` is generic over the payload, so the seam exists.
2. **The transport picks.** A connection whose peer is the proxy reads and writes
   in band; a connection from a stock libwayland client reads and writes
   `SCM_RIGHTS`. Both live in one binary and the choice is per connection, which
   is what lets one Linux `wc-compositor` serve WLCS and the proxy without a
   second build.
3. **`wc_handle::Handle` and `Descriptor` are portable already** — no `cfg` on
   either — so the type the in-band arm needs exists on Unix today. The whole of
   the coupling is `#[cfg(windows)]` at three sites in
   `vendor/wayland-backend/src/rs/wire.rs` and sixteen occurrences across six
   files in `vendor/smithay`, eight of them in `wayland/shm/pool.rs`. That is the
   work, and it is a cfg becoming a runtime choice rather than a redesign.

The one genuinely new thing it needs is a way to say *"a descriptor that is an
already-open fd"*: an SCM_RIGHTS fd arrives with no name, and `Descriptor` names
things. That is a variant on the Unix side, and it is the same escape hatch
`NtHandle` already is on Windows — an object that cannot be named — so the shape
is precedented rather than invented.

Resolving the descriptor **in the ring** was considered and dropped: it would
have removed the encoding question entirely, but the ring owner confirms nothing
in `sv-transport` has to change for the standard protocol, so it buys nothing
here.

**What it means for this run.** This topology cannot composite — no surface, no
window, no pixel — and the memory result is untouched by it, because the proxy's
allocator takes the arena bytes when it *parses* `create_pool`: `[proxy] client
2: pool 3: 6291456 bytes from the client -> arena 0 slice 0+6291456`, in a region
located out of QEMU's memory backend. Stated here rather than buried, because
§27.6 is what happens when a run's absent quantity is not stated.

### 72.4 A ring accept armed nothing

`grow::Service::start()` and `wc_handle::arena::release_gifts()` were two
statements inside the **socket** accept branch, and §36 added a second accept
branch — a ring slot in guest RAM — with neither. On a `--wayland-cold` session
that is **no growth channel at all**: the arena cannot grow, and because
`Op::Release` is a request on that same ring, it can never give a region back
either. The gifts were never released either, so the seat's 71,249-byte keymap
stayed held for the life of the session. Both silent, because a path that is not
taken says nothing. The first run of this harness printed `growth channel
reserved at 11534336+278528` and then never `growth channel up`, and reported
`grew 0` under pressure that should have grown it twice.

`arm_arena_for_first_client` is now one function called from both branches. The
ordering argument transfers unchanged: a client arriving is the proof the locate
finished, because it came through a proxy, and a proxy with an arena was started
from a plan that exists only if the locate succeeded. That is about the proxy
having a plan, not about which door the client came through.

This is the second time a §36 accept path has been found skipping work the
socket path does.

### 72.5 The zero-client tick, measured and then fixed

The reclaim clock turned on a *session's* `poll` timeout, so with **zero**
clients there was no pump and nothing turned it. Measured on this leg before the
fix, and it is worth keeping because it is what the fix had to beat:

* the lone client is killed; `session ended holding 2 pool(s), 12582912 bytes
  returned to the arena` — the pools come back;
* **15 seconds with nobody connected returns no region**;
* one client reconnects and the region follows within seconds.

So the region was returnable the whole time and nothing was asking. The accept
was one blocking `accept_one(wait)` for the whole `--timeout`, so a proxy with
no clients sat in it and the arena stood still. It is sliced now, and a slice
with nobody arriving is a frame's worth of nothing happening — the same unit
`--arena-grow-idle` is written in, and the same argument the pump's poll timeout
makes, from the only other place that can make it.

**Two agents fixed this independently and the slicing here is the other one's.**
Same diagnosis, same place, 100 ms slices rather than 20. Nothing is preserved
of the duplicate except two differences that were **behavioural rather than
stylistic**, and they are worth recording because both are the same mistake:
*the flag is not the policy.*

`Arena::reclaim_idle` is the policy. It is **0 by default** and is only set from
`--arena-grow-idle` inside `if args.arena_grow`. An accept loop reading the flag
therefore disagreed with the pump twice, in opposite directions:

* **without `--arena-grow`** the arena's own value is 0, so the pump returns
  nothing — and the flag is still 120, so the accept loop returned regions. A
  proxy never told it may grow gave memory back from one clock and not the other.
* **with `--arena-grow-idle 0`**, which `Arena::frame` reads as "never" and
  guards for by name, the accept loop passed 0 to `reclaim_regions`, where it
  means *the instant it empties* — the thrash the idle count exists to prevent.

One flag, two policies, decided by which clock happened to turn. `frame_idle()`
is the pump's own body: same source, same `== 0` guard. It is `&self` rather than
`&mut self`, because the caller that matters has no session and therefore no
mutable handle, and because taking a second `share()` handle to get one would
have silently shifted the `sharers()` count every client reports.

**And slicing the wait lost the exit path.** The give-up arm was spelled
`break Err(e)?`, which breaks nothing: `?` returns from `run()`. So the ordinary
idle timeout — the way every successful proxy ends — became an error exit that
skipped the thread joins and the entire arena report after the loop. Before the
wait was sliced this arm was a plain `break` and was right; the rewrite lost it.
`rustc` reported it as `unreachable statement` pointing at the first line *past*
the loop, which is the shape of the bug: the compiler naming the code that
stopped running rather than the line that stopped it. It is `break 'accept` now.

**Leg B holds it**: the last client killed, nothing reconnecting, `0 wc-poolhog`
processes alive across the wait, and `arena region 2 returned by the accept loop:
16777216 bytes` with the guest's resident set down by the same.

Two things this cost, both worth recording, and both were in **each** version
independently. The line read *"returned with no client connected"* — a claim the
accept loop cannot make, since it runs whether or not sessions exist and usually
wins the race against a pump, which turns only when *its* poll times out. It was
observed printing **while a client was up**. It names who did it now, which is a
fact rather than a guess about the world. And leg B's check first scanned the
whole log, which leg A's own release already satisfies — a gate that passes
before the leg has done anything. It counts only lines after a mark now.

### 72.6 §61.4's ring wall is deterministic on a Linux guest

§61.4 sized `ring_data_bytes` at 64 KiB and found later growths refused with `a
65600-byte packet cannot fit a 65536-byte ring`, calling it rare — it needed full
fragmentation on Windows. This leg reproduced it verbatim and the arithmetic is
sharper than §61.4's, which reasoned at 16 bytes a frame:

`Reply::encode` puts **one `u64` per frame**. A 32 MiB region is 8192 pages =
65,536 bytes of frame list, plus `sv-wire`'s `ReplyHeader` = **65,600 against a
65,536-byte ring** — the observed number, exactly. So the wall is not at a
fragmented 16 MiB region; it is at **any region of 32 MiB or more**, and because
§71.2's `/proc/self/pagemap` always names every page, a Linux guest hits it
*every time* rather than occasionally. The default growth series is 16 / 32 / 64
MiB, so it lands on the **second** growth, always.

This harness uses `--arena-grow-step 8388608` so its two growths are 8 and 16
MiB, and asserts the wall was not hit rather than hoping. **Not fixed here** —
§61.4's own words name the answer, "the payload belongs in the arena", and
choosing between a larger ring and an out-of-band payload is a protocol decision.
It is now a much more urgent one than §61.4 thought.

### 72.7 The gates, and one shim that is not a second locate

```
  PASS  the arena is guest RAM: all 3072 pages located by sweep through QEMU's flat view,
        and there is no file
  PASS  the compositor ran in another kernel: guest Linux 6.18.44, this workstation Linux 6.18.33
  PASS  release: TOPOLOGY cross-vm: proven by 3072 pages of guest RAM located by sweep --
        QEMU's monitor cannot answer for a machine that is not running one
  PASS  the accept loop returned it with nobody connected: arena region 2 returned by the
        accept loop: 16777216 bytes of guest RAM
  PASS  and there really was nobody: 0 wc-poolhog processes alive across that wait
== 19 passed, 0 failed ==
```

**`wc_locate_arena` is reused rather than reimplemented.** This rig has guest,
QEMU and proxy all on one workstation, where that function expects ssh to a guest
and ssh to a separate VM host; `g` and `h` are shells, and `g` rewrites `/sv` to
the run directory because the guest's 9p mount and the host's directory are the
same bytes under two names. Everything load-bearing stays that function's — the
run id from the compositor's own line, `wc-arena-host` through QEMU's monitor,
`verify: 3072/3072`, and the refusal when a page is missing.

**The kernel check earns its place.** A harness on one box that boots a guest can
fail to reach it and measure the host instead, and every arena number would look
plausible. `uname -r` inside against `uname -r` here is a fact neither side can
fake; `wc_assert_topology` is the second, independent one.

**§71.3 arrived while this ran.** `--vm sv-guest` matched three QEMUs, because
`nix/guest.nix` bakes that name into every guest and another agent had one up.
The hint is this run's directory, which appears in its QEMU's command line and in
nobody else's.

The apparatus behaved on its first real `cross-vm` legs: `guest-ram` unset
`SV_ALLOW_FILE_ARENA`, `cross-vm` was checked for a VM host and a guest, and
`wc_assert_topology` refused to take the declaration on anything but the locate.
No gate was loosened.

### 72.8 What is proven and what is not

| | |
|---|---|
| a killed client's pools returned to the arena | **shown** — `session ended holding 2 pool(s), 12582912 bytes returned`, both legs |
| an empty region returned to the guest | **shown** — leg A, 8,388,608 B |
| the guest's operating system got the pages back | **shown** — resident set −8,388,608 and −16,777,216, from `/proc` inside the VM |
| the clock turning with **zero** clients | **shown** — leg B, 0 client processes alive, `returned by the accept loop` |
| growth on demand across a hypervisor, Linux guest | **shown** — 8 MiB in 15 ms, 16 MiB in 10 ms |
| **a pool reaching the compositor on this topology** | **BROKEN — §72.3.** Open work, reproducer in `wc-pooltest` |
| anything about compositing here | **not in the experiment**, and cannot be until §72.3 lands |
| regions of 32 MiB or more over the growth ring | **BROKEN — §72.6**, deterministically on a Linux guest |
| release on a **Windows** guest | **not shown.** This is Linux; `VirtualFree` was not the code that ran |
| `Floor::CURRENT` moved to `GrowsUnderPressure` | **no** |

`Floor::CURRENT` stays `MustStandAlone` and
`growth_has_not_been_demonstrated_on_a_guest_yet` stays asserted. Release is now
shown on a boundary, which was §61.6's stated blocker — but that arm asks for
*"a guest session at this floor, with a real Firefox, showing the arena growing
rather than refusing"*, with click latencies against the 64 MiB baseline. There
is no Firefox here, no click and no window, and there cannot be one until §72.3
is fixed. Moving that line is a separate, deliberate commit with a failing guard
test in front of it.

### 36.22 The doorbell is a bell, and that is the whole of its licence

The rule, as the user states it:

> all communication is to go through the ring. alternative channels are
> permitted only for wakeup from idle

**The doorbell is the sanctioned exception and it is sanctioned narrowly.** A
byte on a virtio-serial port that wakes a parked consumer is "wakeup from idle"
exactly; it carries no payload, no sequencing and no state, and §36.6.3's
framing argument is that it *cannot* — one byte, one wake, seven bits of
slot-and-lane, and a lost or spurious byte costs a slice or a syscall
respectively because there is nothing in it to lose.

So the boundary, stated because the port exists and the temptation is
structural: **nothing may ride that port except a wake.** Not a handshake, not a
locator, not a small reply that would be convenient because the port is already
open and a ring packet feels heavier. The moment it carries meaning, the ring
stops being the channel and starts being one of two, and the reason the design
survived contact with a hypervisor is that there is one.

Two byte relays over virtio-serial were built for the Wayland wire and are
withdrawn on this rule. If either returns, the answer is §36's ring — which is
what carries a Wayland connection, and does so at 0.54 ms a present.

The doorbell's own results are unaffected because a bell is all it ever was:
13.6 µs across the boundary to the Windows guest, no floor for a delivered
wake, and 48.7× on a real present in topology 1.

### 36.23 `create_pool` against a Linux compositor: measured, and the rewrite is noise

`wc-proxy` writes the in-band-`h` dialect upstream unconditionally, so against a
*Linux* compositor `create_pool` desynchronises the reader with nothing logged.
The user's rule for choosing the fix:

> whatever is more efficient is the correct choice i.e. the ring data format can
> be specialised for the other side instead of needing translation after the
> fact if that is faster, however that requires that during client server
> handshake this format is negotiated … on the other hand having a standard
> protocol would make multi-client operations easier

Efficiency decides, negotiation is the mechanism, and multi-client is the
counterweight. Two questions had to be answered, and one of them is measurable.

#### 36.23.1 Can the descriptor be resolved in the ring? It is resolved *before* it

Not by the ring, and it does not need to be. §36.4's `PacketKind::Bytes` exists
precisely because the ring carries opaque bytes — "nothing in this crate parses
them or is allowed to" — and giving it a Wayland parser to find an `h` would
make the transport protocol-aware, which is what §36 was built to avoid.

It does not need to, because **the descriptor is already gone by then**. §14.7
is exactly this: `wc-proxy`'s session turns the client's fd into an arena handle
of integers before the bytes reach the boundary, which is *why* the fd count at
the crossing hop is unrepresentable rather than zero. There is no descriptor at
the ring. There is an integer that used to be one.

And that settles the ring path on its own:

> **`OutOfBand` is not merely wrong over a ring, it is impossible.** A ring
> cannot carry a descriptor, by construction — that is §14.7's guarantee, not an
> accident. A Linux compositor reached over a ring cannot be sent an
> `SCM_RIGHTS` fd whatever the proxy is willing to do.

So the in-band encoding is **not a Windows quirk**. It is the only encoding
compatible with "all communication goes through the ring"; Windows merely got
there first because `afunix.sys` forced it. **For the ring path there is nothing
to negotiate** — the transport determines the encoding. Negotiation is only
meaningful on the socket path, where both remain possible and where §14.7's
argument for a local `SCM_RIGHTS` still holds.

#### 36.23.2 Does specialisation buy anything? 300 ns against a 540,000 ns present

The remaining case for a negotiated, side-specialised format is that it avoids a
per-message rewrite at the boundary. That is a quantity, so it was measured
rather than argued — `wire::rewrite_cost`, the full `walk` + `splice_fds` a
message actually pays:

| message | per-message rewrite |
|---|---|
| `wl_surface.attach` (three words — the shape nearly every message has) | **301 ns** |
| `wl_shm.create_pool` (the message in question) | **304 ns** |

Against §36.21's cross-VM present of **0.54 ms**, one rewrite is **0.056%** of a
present — and that is a *debug* build, which is several times slower than
anything shipped.

**So specialisation buys nothing measurable, and the standard protocol wins on
the multi-client argument the user raised themselves.** §41's two-client run
over one arena makes multi-client real here rather than hypothetical, and a
single dialect is what keeps a second client from being a second negotiation.

The coordinator's reading was also right and is worth keeping: because
negotiation is per connection, **the server must implement both encodings
regardless** — so specialisation never removes a dialect, it only moves where
the rewrite happens. Paying 300 ns at a boundary that already costs half a
millisecond, in exchange for one protocol instead of two, is not a close call.

#### 36.23.3 What should actually change

Not the ring, and not a negotiation. The defect is narrower than either:

- `wc-proxy`'s `FdEncoding` is **already a parameter, not a `cfg`** —
  deliberately, "because this one process reads one dialect and writes the
  other". The proxy is not the problem.
- the vendored `wayland-backend`'s in-band `h` is **`#[cfg(windows)]`**. That is
  the hard-coding, and it is on the compositor's side.

The fix is to make that path conditional on **the transport rather than the
platform**: a client arriving over a ring reads `h` in band on Linux exactly as
on Windows, because there is no other way for the bytes to have arrived. A proxy
that always writes in band over a ring is then *correct* rather than
hard-coded — and the desynchronisation stops being possible instead of being
detected.

Where a refusal is still wanted, `finish_attach` is the place: it already
carries `WIRE_VERSION` and a protocol hash and already refuses a skew while
naming the cause, which is the failure mode this defect lacks — today it is a
desynchronised reader with nothing logged and the connection still open.

## 73. `counter=live`: the skip that only a Windows kernel could resolve

*(§53's and §69's continuation. Six minutes on the deployment guest.)*

### 73.1 Status in one paragraph

§53.3 skipped the USER/GDI leak assertion because `GetGuiResources` returns 0
under Wine, and §69 established — from inside a Linux VM, on the guest's own
kernel — that the zero is a fact about **Wine** rather than about the venue, so
**no arrangement of local virtualisation could ever turn that skip into an
assertion**. This is the run that could. On the deployment guest, real Windows
11, session 1: the counter answers, and it answers in both directions.

```text
       real Windows (guest)        the same binary, Wine on the workstation
       before user=1               before user=0
       after  user=6   (4 windows) after  user=0   (5 windows enumerated)
       counter=live                counter=stub
       destroyed user=1            destroyed user=0
       fell=yes                    fell=no
```

§53's `SKIP` is now a real assertion waiting to be written, and §69's negative
result is confirmed from the other side rather than merely not contradicted.

### 73.2 Why the third sample is the one that matters

The first version of this probe stopped at `after`, and it would have been
enough to report `live`. It is not enough to report anything **useful**, and the
reason is the same one §64.4 ran into from a different direction: the assertion
§53 wants is *"the count came back"*, and a counter that only ever goes up
cannot express it. On a stubbed counter `0 == 0` satisfies "came back" forever.

So `selftest` now destroys its four windows and samples a third time. `fell=yes`
is what separates an instrument from a decoration, and it is the difference
between the two columns above: Wine's zero is *flat*, and flat is
indistinguishable from perfect.

`gdi=0` on both sides, and that is probably **correct rather than stubbed**: a
plain `WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW` with no device context owns no GDI objects. The
count §53 needs is the USER one — an `HWND` is a USER object — and that is the
one that moved.

### 73.3 What this unlocks, and what it does not

**Unlocked.** The window-handle leak assertion of §53 can be made against the
compositor's own process on the guest: churn clients, watch `GR_USEROBJECTS`
return to its baseline. §64's icon account gets the same treatment — `HICON` is
a USER object too, so the `0 icon(s) destroyed` that no local harness could turn
into a number now has somewhere to be one.

**Not done.** Neither of those runs happened. This visit was six minutes and
there were two agents queued behind it, so it bought the *decisive* measurement
and handed the machine back. Both are now one `grep` away rather than a
rewrite, which is the state §53.6 item 3 and §64.5 item 3 asked for.

### 73.4 A correction I owe §53, and the shape of the mistake

§53.3 lists five lines as "the whole diagnosis" of the locked session, and one
of them was wrong for a reason that had nothing to do with locking.

Run again on the **unlocked** desktop, the same probe still reported
`SendInput_returned=0` — this time with `lasterror=87`,
`ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER`. That is what `SendInput` answers when `cbSize` does
not match the `INPUT` it is given, and the struct in that probe carried two
extra padding fields: 56 bytes where the x64 ABI wants 40. **The call had never
worked, locked or not.**

The conclusion of §53.3 survives, on the other evidence and only on it:
`LockApp` was the foreground window, `WindowFromPoint` at the drag's origin
returned it, and the control — a real drag between two Explorer windows on a
scratch directory — did not move the file. Those are about the lock. The
`SendInput` line was never evidence of anything.

**The shape is worth naming because it is the one this document keeps
rediscovering.** A wrong instrument agreed with a correct conclusion, so nothing
about the run looked wrong. §53.4 records three harness bugs found because they
made the harness disagree with reality; this is the fourth and it was invisible
precisely because it *agreed*. The only reason it surfaced at all is that the
same probe was pointed at a machine whose state had changed, and it gave the
same answer — an answer that was supposed to depend on that state.

And the same misreading nearly recurred at the top of this run. `Get-Process
LockApp` returned 1 on the unlocked desktop, because Windows 11 leaves `LockApp`
resident and suspended after an unlock. Counting the process would have said
"locked"; `WindowFromPoint` at the centre of the screen said `firefox` with a
page title, which is what the desktop actually had on it. **Asking what is on
the screen beat asking what is in the process list**, both times.

### 73.5 What is not proven

1. **No compositor was run on the guest in this visit.** §73.3.
2. **`gdi=0` is inferred to be correct, not shown.** A window that owns a device
   context would settle it and none was made.
3. **One process, four windows.** That the counter tracks a compositor holding
   dozens of windows across many clients is likely and untested.
4. **The USER count includes more than windows** — the `+5` for four windows is
   the windows plus something (a class, a message queue). A leak assertion
   should therefore compare against a *baseline of itself*, which is what §53's
   harness already does for the enumerated count, rather than treating the
   number as a window count.

---
---

## 74. §68 fixed: subsurface position and z-order now apply on the parent's commit

### 74.1 Status in one paragraph

§68 diagnosed the deviation and stopped, calling the fix "a session with its own
measurements". The user's answer was that a known-wrong state machine is not a
documentation item, and that is right. Both halves are now fixed in
`vendor/smithay`: **position** is staged outside the child's cache and promoted
when the parent commits, and **z-order** is staged as a pending sibling list and
promoted the same way. WLCS headless goes **413 passed / 53 failed to 415 / 51**,
the subsurface suite **17 / 7 to 19 / 5**, and `cargo test --workspace` is
unchanged at 2629 — which is the §40 guard doing its job, because the blit and
the hit test read the very list this changed.

### 74.2 Position, and the two mistakes the suite caught

`SubsurfaceState::pending_location` holds what `set_position` asked for;
`PrivateSurfaceData::commit` promotes it into `SubsurfaceCachedState::current`
when the **parent** commits. Readers are untouched: `current().location` is still
the applied value, which is what `placed_tree` reads.

Neither of the two errors on the way was predictable from the diagnosis, and both
are recorded at the line that fixes them:

1. **Writing only `current` is undone by the child's next commit.**
   `SubsurfaceCachedState` is still a `Cacheable`, so the child's commit promotes
   its pending value over whatever is current — and with `set_position` no longer
   writing that pending value, it stays at the default and the position snapped
   back to (0, 0). **17 passed / 7 failed became 8 / 16.** Both halves are written
   now, which makes the cache's promotion a no-op.
2. **Applying on every commit is wrong for a synchronized surface**, whose commit
   takes effect only when *its* parent commits. Applying there moves a grandchild
   one commit early and cost three `SubsurfaceMultilevelTest` cases —
   `subsurface_with_sync_parent_does_not_move_when_only_parent_committed` and the
   two `..._is_sync` ones. Guarded on `!is_sync`; the synchronized case is
   deferred rather than skipped, and `commit_sync_surface_tree` applies it when a
   desync ancestor commits.

The first of those took the suite from better-than-baseline to far worse in one
step, which is the argument for running it after every edit rather than at the
end of the session.

### 74.3 Z-order, and why it reconciles rather than assigns

`reorder` now permutes `PrivateSurfaceData::pending_children` — initialised from
`children` on the first restack after a commit — so two restacks before one
commit **compose**, which is what double-buffering means and what permuting the
live list twice could not express.

Promotion is not an assignment. `children` also changes for reasons that are
*not* double-buffered — a subsurface created or destroyed between the restack and
the commit — and the staged list is a snapshot from before that happened. So
`apply_pending_order` filters the snapshot to children that still exist and
appends any the snapshot never saw, which lands a newly created subsurface on top:
exactly what *"a new sub-surface is initially added as the top-most in the stack
of its siblings and parent"* requires, and what `add_child`'s `push` already did.

It is applied in `apply_child_positions`, before the loop and in its own lock
scope — the loop takes each child's lock, and holding the parent's across that is
how a tree walk deadlocks.

### 74.4 §66.4's hypothesis is now answered on evidence

§66.4 read `place_above_simple` and `place_below_simple` as unsatisfiable — each
asserts the moved subsurface is not focused *and* that the fixture's is not, when
after the restack one of them must be — and refused to conclude the suite was
wrong without a reference run. §68.4 then said the reading could not be trusted
anyway, because with z-order applied on the bare request the stack those tests
assert about was not the stack we built.

It is now. And in the full run:

```
grep -c "wrong surface/subsurface on top"   ->  2
grep -c "did not have an effect"            ->  0
```

**Both tests now pass their first assertion and fail only their second.** The
restacking has an effect, measured; what remains is the pair asserting that
neither subsurface is on top. That is the evidence §66.4 asked for, arrived at by
fixing the deviation rather than by running a reference compositor — and it means
the two are almost certainly not ours. They are still counted as ours, because
"almost certainly" is not a reference run, and the run is still one command.

### 74.5 The score

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| WLCS headless | 413 passed, 53 failed | **415 passed, 51 failed** |
| of those, expected on this leg | 30 | 30 |
| debts (§65's number) | 23 | **21** |
| `XdgShellStableSubsurfaces` | 17 passed, 7 failed | **19 passed, 5 failed** |
| `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | 2629 | 2629 |

The cargo number not moving is the point of quoting it: `placed_tree` feeds both
the blit and the hit test, §40 built the tests that hold them as each other's
inverse, and a state-machine change underneath them left every one of those
passing.

### 74.6 What is still open, and it is three things

1. **`subsurface_with_sync_parent_does_not_move_when_only_grandparent_committed`**
   and **`subsurface_does_not_move_when_grandparent_commit_is_before_sync_parent_commit`**.
   Both are three-level orderings, both still fail, and neither is explained by
   what is now in place. The `!is_sync` guard and `commit_sync_surface_tree`
   between them decide when a grandchild's position lands, and these two say that
   decision is still not right for a sync middle level.
2. **`place_above_simple` / `place_below_simple`** — §74.4. One reference run
   against Weston or Mir closes them either way.
3. **`subsurface_extends_parent_input_region`**, which throws `bad optional
   access` rather than failing an assertion — the pointer entered nothing at all.
   Untouched by any of this and still unexplained.

The popup group of six remains unstarted.

## 75. The leak assertion §53 could not make, made

*(§53's and §73's continuation. Twenty minutes on the deployment guest.)*

### 75.1 Status in one paragraph

§53 built an outside witness for window destruction and had to **skip** its
sharpest assertion, because `GetGuiResources` — the kernel's own per-process
handle count — returns 0 under Wine. §69 showed that zero is a fact about Wine
and not about the venue, so no local virtualisation could rescue it; §73 showed
the counter answers on a real Windows kernel and moves both ways. This is the
run that uses it. Three create/destroy cycles against the compositor's own
process on the guest:

```text
BASE (no client)         user=1  all=0
client up   (x2 samples) user=3  all=1     CLIENT-RUNNING=yes at both
client gone              user=2  all=0
                         ... identical for cycles 2 and 3
windows at exit:      3 created, 3 destroyed, 0 still held, 0 still alive
drop targets at exit: claims 3 registered, 3 revoked, 0 revoke(s) failed
```

**The count moves both ways and returns to a constant baseline.** Two, not
three-four-five: nothing accumulates. §53's `SKIP` is an assertion now, and it
passes.

### 75.2 What the `1 → 2` step is, and why it is not the leak

The baseline before any window is `user=1`; after the first window is created
and destroyed it is `user=2`, and it stays 2 for ever. A permanent increase on
the first window is exactly what a per-window leak would look like on cycle one,
so it has to be accounted for rather than waved past.

It is the **window class**. `RegisterClassExW` runs once per process, a class is
a USER object, and it is not freed while the process lives. The distinguishing
property is not the +1 but its *repetition*: a leak of an `HWND` would add one
per window and the count would climb 2, 3, 4, 5 across the cycles. It does not
move again. **The evidence for "no leak" is the second and third cycles, not the
first**, which is why a one-cycle version of this run would have been
unreadable.

`EnumWindows` agrees independently — `all=1` while the client is up and `all=0`
after — so the two instruments §53 built for different reasons corroborate each
other on the venue where both work.

`gdi=0` throughout, and it is probably correct rather than stubbed: these
windows own no device context. §73.5 item 2 still stands.

### 75.3 Two false passes, and the second is the one worth keeping

Both are the shape that has now caught several harnesses in this document: a run
that reports success because the thing it was watching never happened.

**`wc-probe.exe` does not map a toplevel.** It was the obvious client — it is
already on the guest and `wc-guest.sh` uses it — and it connects, binds globals
and exits. The first run of this experiment reported `counter=live`, the
compositor alive at every cycle, and a clean exit accounting:
`0 created, 0 destroyed`. Every number was consistent and every one of them was
about nothing. `wc-shmclient.exe` makes a real window.

**Then the counter did not move, and that read as a clean result.** Three cycles
of `UP == DOWN == 2` is exactly what a leak-free compositor looks like from a
distance. It was the sampling: `--frames 90` meant the client had finished and
gone before the `UP` sample was taken, so both samples were of an idle
compositor. The fix is not a longer sleep — it is that **the harness now prints
whether the client was still running at the moment of each sample**:

```text
CLIENT-RUNNING-AT-UP1=yes
UP1=user=3 …
```

That line is the difference between a measurement and a coincidence, and it is
cheap. The general form is worth stating because this document keeps paying for
it: *when an assertion compares two samples, record the condition each sample
was supposed to be taken under, next to the sample.* A number without its
premise cannot be checked, and the failure mode is not a wrong answer — it is a
right-looking answer to a question nobody asked.

### 75.4 §64's icon count is still zero, and this run says why

```text
icon objects at exit: claims 0 created, 0 icon(s) and 0 cursor(s) destroyed
icons: 0 window(s) got one, 3 had none to get; no resolver published anything
```

Both halves are **structurally absent from this arrangement** rather than
untested by accident:

* no client published an icon, so `release_icons` had nothing to release —
  `wc-icon.sh` is the harness that publishes one;
* the run is in **session 0** and has no pointer, so no `HCURSOR` is ever built
  — and §64.3 already established that the cursor half only moves in a harness
  that moves a mouse.

So §64.5 item 1 is unchanged and its remedy is now precise: an icon-publishing
client for one half, injected pointer motion for the other. Neither is the
`grep` this was hoped to be; both are runs. The machine was handed back rather
than held for them, with two agents queued.

### 75.5 What is not proven

1. **Three cycles.** The count returns to baseline three times; it is not a
   soak, and a leak that appears on the hundredth window would not be seen.
2. **One client shape.** `wc-shmclient.exe` makes one plain toplevel. Popups,
   subsurfaces and a client with several windows are untested here, and §53.6
   item 4 already names popups as the highest-churn case.
3. **The `+1` is attributed, not proven.** The window class is the only
   plausible one-time USER object on that path and the number never moves again,
   but nothing enumerated it.
4. **`gdi=0` is still inferred.** §73.5 item 2.
5. **This says nothing about the drag or icon resources beyond their counters
   balancing** — 3 registered / 3 revoked is the compositor's own account
   (§62.2), and on this venue there is still no outside witness for OLE's table.


## 76. The protocol's file descriptor gets a name of its own

### 76.1 Status in one paragraph

§72.3 settled what the fix for the pool path is — **both encodings, selected by
transport rather than by platform** — and listed the sites. A first attempt at
it found a prerequisite the section had not scoped, and reverted rather than
leave `vendor/` half-refactored. This section is that prerequisite, landed on
its own: `wayland_backend::os::ProtoFd` and its two companions now name **the
`Fd` payload of an `Argument`/`Message`**, distinctly from the `OwnedFd` the
socket layer uses for real kernel descriptors. **Nothing behaves differently.**
The aliases are unconditional and resolve to exactly the types that were there
before, on both platforms; the tripwire
`the_upstream_dialect_is_still_assumed_rather_than_chosen` still passes because
it still describes the truth. What changed is that the definition §72.3 has to
edit is now **one line that the socket layer does not read**.

### 76.2 The prerequisite, and it is a Unix-only accident

On Windows the two roles were never confusable and nothing had to say so: a
socket is a `wc_transport::Stream`, and an `h` argument is a
`wc_handle::Handle`. Two types, two jobs, no overlap. That is why the fork got
this far without naming the distinction.

On **Unix** both are `std::os::unix::io::OwnedFd`. `crate::os` re-exported one
name for both jobs, and the crate had **two unrelated readers** of it:

* the **socket layer** — `rs/socket.rs`'s `in_fds`/`out_fds` queues, `send_msg`
  and `rcv_msg`, the `SCM_RIGHTS` control message, `rustix`'s `AncillaryIter`,
  the `dup()` in `write_to_buffers`, and the `AsFd`/`AsRawFd` impls on `Socket`,
  `BufferedSocket` and `Client<D>`. Every one of those is a real descriptor and
  can never be anything else;
* the **protocol layer** — the `Fd` parameter of `Argument<Id, Fd>` and
  `Message<Id, Fd>`, which is only ever compared (`FdRepr::fd_eq`), printed
  (`FdRepr::fd_fmt`), and handed to whatever `rs/wire.rs` has decided an `h`
  looks like on the wire.

§72.3's fix changes the second. With one name, it could not be changed without
the first coming with it — which is what the first attempt hit, and why the
sensible move is to give the protocol role its own spelling first and change
nothing else.

### 76.3 Three names, not one, and why

`Argument`/`Message` are instantiated at three different fd types, and the
separation is only useful if it covers all three:

| new name | was | where it appears |
|---|---|---|
| `os::ProtoFd` | `os::OwnedFd` | a message **parsed off the wire**: `parse_message`, `read_one_message`, every `ObjectData::event`/`request` signature, every generated `Event` field |
| `os::RawProtoFd` | `os::RawFd` | a message **about to be written**: `send_request`, `send_event`, `write_message`, `write_to_buffers` |
| `os::BorrowedProtoFd<'a>` | `os::BorrowedFd<'a>` | what `wayland-scanner` emits: `write_request`/`write_event`, and the `h` field of every generated `Request<'a>` |

The send side is unowned on Unix — the caller keeps the descriptor and
`write_to_buffers` `dup()`s it — which is why the protocol needs two of these
rather than one, and the borrowed form has a lifetime the other two do not
because that is the shape `wayland-scanner` generates into every protocol crate
in the ecosystem.

All three are declared **without a `cfg`**, as aliases of the names that were
already there. That is deliberate and it is the whole safety argument: an
unconditional alias to an existing type cannot change behaviour on either
platform, so this commit is a rename and can be reviewed as one.

### 76.4 The real site count: 88, not 71

§72.3's estimate was 71 instantiation sites across 30 files. **The file count was
exactly right and the site count was 24% low.** The measured surface, after the
change:

| | sites |
|---|---|
| `Message<…>` / `Argument<…>` / `ArgSmallVec<…>` instantiations | **88**, across **30** files |
| of which in the two checked-in `wayland-scanner` assets | 26 |
| `use` lines that exist only to spell one of the three | 34 |
| files touched in total | 33 |

The gap is not a miscount of anything visible; it is that `vendor/wayland-scanner`
is three surfaces rather than one — the `quote!` blocks that emit the type, the
two checked-in `scanner_assets/*.rs` that a test compares the emission against
byte-for-byte, and the generated `Request`/`Event` **field** types, which are not
`Message<…>` instantiations but must move with them or the tuple stops
type-checking. Changing the scanner is not optional: `wayland-protocols`,
`wayland-protocols-wlr` and `wayland-protocols-misc` come from crates.io and are
generated by this fork's scanner through the `[patch.crates-io]` table, so the
generated code is where most of the protocol's `h` arguments actually live.

`vendor/smithay` contributes three sites here — the `ObjectData::request` impls
in `selection/offer.rs` and the two dnd grabs — and `crate::utils::os` gained a
`ProtoFd` re-export so they can be spelled without reaching past it. These are
**not** §72.3's "sixteen occurrences across six files"; those are the
`#[cfg(windows)]` coupling sites in `wayland/shm/pool.rs` and friends, and they
are untouched.

### 76.5 The separation, measured rather than asserted

The claim this commit makes is falsifiable in one command, so it was falsified
rather than argued. Temporarily replacing the three aliases with distinct
newtypes and running `cargo check -p wayland-backend --all-targets`:

| | errors |
|---|---|
| the library | **8** — `rs/wire.rs` ×2, `rs/client_impl/mod.rs` ×4, `rs/server_impl/client.rs` ×2 |
| plus the unit tests | 23 total, the extra 15 in the `mod tests` of `socket.rs` and `wire.rs` |
| naming `rustix`, `AncillaryIter`, `borrow_raw`, or an `AsFd` impl on `Socket`/`Client<D>`/`Stream` | **0** |

The non-test body of `rs/socket.rs` produces **no errors at all**, which is the
result that matters: the file that owns `SCM_RIGHTS` does not move when the
protocol's fd type does. Of the eight, two are `FdRepr` bounds — a trait
`crate::os` already owns and a real change would simply implement — and the other
two in `wire.rs` are lines 157 and 332, the write arm and the parse arm of
`Argument::Fd`. **Those two are precisely the sites §72.3 says have to become a
runtime choice.** The refactor's blast radius and the fix's work list are the
same two lines.

Compare the first attempt's reading, which is now confirmed: it saw 24 errors
splitting into a socket-layer group and nothing in the protocol layer, because it
changed the shared name. Changing the protocol-only name inverts that exactly.

### 76.6 What was deliberately not done

* **The enum is not here.** `ProtoFd` is an alias, not a sum type. The variant
  for "an fd that arrived with no name" belongs in `vendor/wayland-backend/src/os.rs`
  — `Descriptor` means "a name a peer can open" and an `SCM_RIGHTS` fd has none,
  so it does not go in `wc-handle` — and it is the next commit, not this one.
* **`wc-handle` is still Windows-only.** `vendor/wayland-backend/Cargo.toml:73`
  declares it under `[target.'cfg(windows)'.dependencies]`. The crate itself is
  portable — its own `cfg(windows)` block holds only `windows-sys` — so making
  the dependency unconditional is a two-line change, but it belongs with the
  enum that needs it.
* **`wire.rs`'s two arms are still `#[cfg]`, not a choice**, and the
  per-connection flag does not exist. §72.3 is not fixed by this section and does
  not claim to be.
* **The tripwire is still there and still passes.** It asserts that
  `wc-proxy`'s `session.rs` spells both dialects as constants with no transport
  consulted, and that is still true — this commit did not touch `wc-proxy` at
  all. Deleting it is the job of whoever makes the encoding a runtime choice.

### 76.7 The gates

| gate | result |
|---|---|
| `nix develop --command cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | **87 binaries, 2632 passed, 0 failed** |
| the same, on `7abc743` before any of this | 86 binaries, 2631 passed, 0 failed |
| §75's own commit, `5b39633`, reports | 87 binaries, 2632 tests, 0 failures |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` | clean; no warning in any `vendor/wayland-*` crate |
| `wayland-scanner`'s two asset tests | pass; the checked-in `test-client-code.rs` and `test-server-code.rs` were updated and match the emission byte-for-byte |
| `scripts/wc-xref.sh` | exit 0 |
| `the_upstream_dialect_is_still_assumed_rather_than_chosen` | passes, unchanged |

**The first two counts differ and the difference is not this section's.** The
branch was rebased mid-flight onto `5b39633`, which adds a
`crates/vk-registry/tests/attributes.rs` holding one test; that commit's own
message reports the post-rebase number, and this section's run reproduces it
exactly. Independently of that, comparing the `7abc743` and post-change runs
*per binary* rather than in aggregate, **the only line that differs is that new
binary** — every other binary reports an identical pass count. That is the check
worth running for a rename: an aggregate that happens to match can hide a test
moving from one binary to another, and a per-binary diff cannot.

### 76.8 Is step 2 now ordinary

Yes, on the evidence in §76.5. The remaining work has a work list of two arms in
`wire.rs`, one dependency line, an enum with two variants, and smithay's sixteen
`cfg` sites — and the measurement says that nothing in the socket layer is on
that list. That was the open question the first attempt could not answer, because
with one name for two jobs there was no way to ask it.

## 59. The kill that took the machine's keys

### 59.1 Status in one paragraph

An over-broad `pkill -9 -f weston`, meant for one harness's leftovers, matched
the desktop session hosting 1Password and killed it — taking with it the SSH
agent holding the keys for `testhost` and the guest, and the key that signs
commits. Two machines unreachable and signing broken, from a cleanup line in an
unrelated run. This is the **fourth** instance in one session of a process-name
match catching more than it meant to, and the first to cost anything outside its
own run. `scripts/wc-binaries.sh` grew `proc_kill` and `proc_kill_pidfile`:
they take a pid or a pidfile and **refuse a name or a pattern**, and three tests
behind `cargo test --workspace` keep the refusal honest.

### 59.2 The argument that was only half written

`proc_running` already matched an exact executable name, and the comment above
it gives the reason: a `pgrep -f sv-hostd` guard matches *the shell running it*,
because that shell's command line contains the string. The fix generalised as an
order of preference — pidfile, then `pgrep -x`, then `pgrep -f` with the shell's
ancestors excluded — and ended with a line that reads differently today:

> A guard that cannot distinguish itself from what it guards against is not a
> guard; it is a coin that always lands the same way.

**That was written about guards, and the kill side of it was never written.**
The three earlier instances were self-inflicted: a script matching its own
shell, which is embarrassing and contained. This one matched another agent's
process, and the blast radius was the machine's credentials.

**A pattern is the wrong instrument for stopping a process you started.** You
already know its pid — you started it. The pattern is a way of *rediscovering* a
pid you already had, and it rediscovers other people's too. So:

* started in this shell → you have `$!`;
* outlives the shell → have it write a pidfile;
* neither → you are not stopping *your* process, you are stopping whatever
  matches, and you cannot know what that is.

`proc_kill` refuses anything that is not digits, which covers the two shapes
that actually occur: a bare program name, and the **empty string** — `kill ""`
is an error, but `kill $(pgrep something-absent)` with no match is a request to
signal the whole process group, which is the same outage by a different route.
pid 1 is refused explicitly. An already-dead pid is success, because the caller
wanted it gone and it is gone.

`proc_kill_pidfile` removes the pidfile only when the pid in it was ours to
stop, and refuses a file whose body is not a number — a truncated or
half-written pidfile is a pattern one indirection along.

### 59.3 What is *not* refused, and why

`pkill -f` anchored on an absolute path into **this run's own directory** stays,
and several harnesses use it:

```sh
h "pkill -f '^$HOST_DIR/wc-proxy' 2>/dev/null; sleep 1; true"
```

That is a pattern no other agent's command line can contain, because the
directory is unique to the run. The distinction is not "patterns are bad" — it
is that a pattern must name something only this run could have produced. A bare
program name names something the whole machine shares, and `weston` is on every
desktop here.

The sweep found thirteen substring kills in `scripts/`; eleven are already
path-anchored in exactly this way. The two that are not — a port-scoped
`http.server 8931` and a `$RUNDIR`-scoped `qemu-system` — are scoped to
something this run owns, and are left.

### 59.4 What is not done

1. **Nothing forces a harness to use `proc_kill`.** The tests assert that the
   refusal works, not that anybody calls it — the same gap §54 had before the
   citation checker went behind `cargo test`, and the same shape as a lint that
   exists but is not run. A grep-based gate refusing new bare `pkill -f <name>`
   in `scripts/` is the obvious next step and is one more instance of the
   pattern this section is about.
2. **The three earlier instances are fixed where they were found, not
   systematically.** They were guards rather than kills, so `proc_running`
   covers the shape; nothing proves there is not a fifth.
3. **This section's commit is unsigned**, because the signing key went with the
   session that was killed. Recorded here rather than repaired later: rewriting
   history to re-sign would make the commit that documents the outage the one
   piece of evidence that it happened.
## 77. `WireFd`: the type an `h` argument becomes, and the dependency that had to move first

### 77.1 Status in one paragraph

§76 gave the protocol's file descriptor a name of its own. This gives it a
**type**: `wayland_backend::os::WireFd`, an `h` argument that is **either a name
the peer can open or a descriptor that is already open**. It is the thing
§72.3's fix turns a `cfg` into a runtime choice *between*. Nothing constructs one
yet — `rs/wire.rs` still decides by platform — so this changes no behaviour
either, and the tripwire
`the_upstream_dialect_is_still_assumed_rather_than_chosen` still passes. What is
now true that was not: the type exists, it is **tested**, and one of those tests
is the claim that §72.3's remaining work is a substitution rather than a
redesign.

### 77.2 Steps 2 and 3 are one commit, and that is a correction to the plan

The plan had "the enum" and "`wc-handle` unconditional" as separate steps. They
cannot be. `WireFd::Named` carries a `wc_handle::Handle`, and
`vendor/wayland-backend/Cargo.toml` declared `wc-handle` under
`[target.'cfg(windows)'.dependencies]` — so on Unix, the platform the whole fix
is *for*, the enum could not name its own variant. Landing the enum first would
have meant either a Windows-only type, which is the split being deleted, or a
placeholder, which is a comment nothing asserts.

### 77.3 The dependency move, and it is a move rather than a port

`wc-handle` was already portable: `crates/wc-handle/src/lib.rs` contains **no
`cfg` at all**, and `src/platform/` has had a `unix.rs` beside its `windows.rs`
since it was written. Its own manifest puts `windows-sys` behind
`cfg(windows)` and `libc` behind `cfg(unix)`, and its `sv-arena` dependency is
already deliberately unconditional with a note saying why. So the change is two
lines moving between tables, and there is a precedent directly above them in the
same file: `wc-transport` is unconditional for exactly this reason — "so that the
port has one socket abstraction rather than a `cfg` at every use site". This is
the same sentence one level up, about descriptors rather than sockets.

No dependency cycle: `wc-handle` reaches `sv-arena` and `sv-transport`, and
neither of those names any wayland crate.

### 77.4 The shape, and the two questions it has to answer

```rust
pub enum WireFd {
    Named(wc_handle::Handle),
    #[cfg(unix)]
    Open(OwnedFd),
}
```

**Why the second arm is not a sixth `wc_handle::Descriptor` variant.** Because
`Descriptor` means *"a name a peer can open"*, and an fd that arrived over
`SCM_RIGHTS` has no name — it was never created under one and nothing can
re-open it. `Descriptor` has an `encode()`/`decode()` pair; it *is* a wire
format. An unnamed arm would put something in that format that cannot be written
down, and every reader of the type would have to learn that one variant is a lie.
`Descriptor::NtHandle` is the precedent for the *shape* — an escape hatch for an
object that cannot be named — and not for reuse: that one is Windows's, and this
is Unix's. So the disjunction lives in `os.rs`, the module that already decides
what a file descriptor is.

**Why there is no `Open` arm on Windows.** Not an omission and not a `cfg` left
in by accident. `SCM_RIGHTS` has no Windows equivalent — there is no ancillary
channel on the socket at all — so an already-open unnamed fd cannot arrive there,
and a variant for it would be uninhabited by construction. §72.3's "both
encodings exist on both platforms" is a claim about the **in-band** form existing
on Unix, which is the half that was missing. It does not claim Windows grows an
out-of-band one, and reading it that way would produce a variant that could only
ever be dead.

**Why `Named` carries a `Handle` rather than a `Descriptor`.** Sending a name
transfers nothing — unlike `SCM_RIGHTS`, the kernel takes no reference — so the
sender must keep the object alive until the peer opens it. `Handle` is what
carries that keepalive; a bare `Descriptor` would be a name for an object that
may already be gone. `rs/wire.rs`'s existing Windows arm records this rule at
length and it is unchanged by any of this.

### 77.5 The test that is the point

`os::tests::wire_fd_is_already_a_legal_message_payload` builds a
`Message<u32, WireFd>`, compares two of them, and prints one. That is the whole
of what the protocol layer asks of an `Fd`, and **§72.3's claim that the rest is
"a cfg becoming a runtime choice rather than a redesign" is only true if that
compiles.** If `WireFd` needed a bound the protocol layer could not supply, this
is where it would be found — before the wire format depends on it rather than
halfway through changing it.

One thing that could have forced a restructure did not. `os.rs` carries a blanket
`impl<T: AsRawFd> FdRepr for T` on Unix, and `WireFd` needs its own `FdRepr`
because half its inhabitants have no raw fd to return. Those two impls coexist:
`WireFd` is a local type with no `AsRawFd`, so coherence accepts both. Had it
not, the blanket impl would have had to become three concrete ones first.

Six more tests hold the behaviour rather than describing it, and the sharpest
pair is the asymmetry: two `Named` handles to one section are **equal** (they
compare descriptors), and two `dup()`s of one file are **not** (they compare raw
fd numbers). That difference already existed between the platforms and this
module's `FdRepr` docs already recorded it; it is now visible inside a single
type, on one platform, where it can be asserted. A named thing and an open thing
are never equal — they might name the same bytes, and nothing here can know that.

### 77.6 A warning §76 introduced, fixed here rather than by amending it

The Windows cross check reported `unused import: RawFd` in `rs/socket.rs`. It is
§76's: once the `Message` signatures in that file stopped saying `RawFd`, its only
remaining readers were the two `AsRawFd` impls, which are Unix-only. The Linux
