workspace clippy gate could not see it, because on Linux those impls compile. The
import moved into the `cfg(unix)` group.

Recorded rather than quietly fixed for the reason §35.10 gives: it is the *shape*
of the mistake that generalises. A rename that is green on one platform can still
strand an import on the other, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` is
not that check — `cargo check --workspace --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` is.

### 77.7 The gates

| gate | result |
|---|---|
| `nix develop --command cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | **87 binaries, 2637 passed, 0 failed** |
| `cargo check --workspace --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` | exit 0; `wayland-backend` warning-free |
| `cargo check -p wayland-backend --all-targets` (Linux) | warning-free |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` | clean |
| `scripts/wc-xref.sh` | exit 0 |
| `the_upstream_dialect_is_still_assumed_rather_than_chosen` | passes, unchanged |

**2637 is 2632 plus seven minus two, and only the seven are this commit's.** §76
ran at 2632. A per-binary diff against that run shows exactly two lines moving:
`wayland_backend` from 5 to 12, which is the seven `os::tests::*` above, and
`sv_proto` from 1820 to 1818, which is `6cb8db3` adding seventeen lines to
`crates/vk-registry/src/profile.rs` — `sv-proto` is generated from that profile,
so its test count moves when the profile does. Nothing in this commit is
reachable from `sv-proto`. This is the second time in three sections that the
aggregate would have been read wrong and the per-binary diff read right.

The Windows cross gate also reports five `never used` warnings in
`crates/wc-launch/src/floor.rs`. They are **not** this commit's — that file is
untouched here, and they are Windows-only dead code that predates it. Named
rather than left for the next person to wonder about, which is the same rule
77.6 is an instance of.

### 77.8 What is still missing, and it is steps 4 and 5

1. **`rs/wire.rs`'s two arms become a runtime choice.** Lines 157 and 332 — the
   write arm and the parse arm of `Argument::Fd` — plus the `cfg(unix)` early
   return in `parse_message` and the fd-count pre-check above it. §76.5 measured
   that these are the only library sites that move.
2. **`ProtoFd` aliases `WireFd`**, and `RawProtoFd`/`BorrowedProtoFd` grow their
   send-side counterparts.
3. **The per-connection flag**, which is what "the transport picks" means
   concretely, and the smithay `cfg` sites that follow from it.

The acceptance test for the sequence is unchanged and is not this: `wc-pooltest`
through the proxy to a **Linux** compositor, and after that a client that maps a
window and draws with the compositor across the hypervisor.

## 78. The popup group is three groups, and a grab that ended too early

### 78.1 Status in one paragraph

Seven popup failures, and §66's lesson applied before anything else: read the
messages, do not group by suite name. They are **three** groups — grab semantics
(4), reactive positioning (2), and a protocol error on a zero-size anchor rect
(1) — and only the first is one thing. One of the four is fixed: a popup grab was
dismissed *before* the click that dismissed it was delivered. WLCS headless goes
**415 to 416**, popups **5 / 7 to 6 / 6**, debts 21 to 20, `cargo test` unchanged
at 2630.

### 78.2 What the seven actually say

| test | message | group |
|---|---|---|
| `does_not_get_popup_done_event_before_button_press` | "pointer button sent after popup done" | grab |
| `grabbed_popup_gets_keyboard_focus` | "grabbed popup not given keyboard focus" | grab |
| `grabbed_popup_gets_done_event_when_new_toplevel_created` | `popup_done()` never called | grab |
| `grabbed_popups_get_done_events_in_correct_order` | `popup_done()` never called | grab |
| `when_parent_surface_is_moved_a_reactive_popup_is_moved` | "reactive popup was not moved" | positioning |
| `when_parent_surface_is_moved_a_nonreactive_popup_is_not_moved` | `surface_actually_at_location` false | positioning |
| `zero_size_anchor_rect_stable` | "Wayland protocol error: 0 on interface \<UNKNOWN INTERFACE\>" | protocol error |

Three different files' worth of work, which is exactly what §66 was about.

### 78.3 The fix, and why the obvious version of it was not enough

`dismiss_grab_if_outside` ran before `pointer.button`, so the press arrived after
`popup_done`.

Moving it after the button did **not** fix the test, and the reason is worth
keeping. `left_click` is a press *and* a release, and the test's notification
fires on every button event:

```c
manager->client->add_pointer_button_notification([&](auto, auto, auto) {
    EXPECT_THAT(got_popup_done, IsFalse()) << "pointer button sent after popup done";
```

So dismissing on the press still puts `popup_done` between the two halves of one
click, and the assertion fails on the release instead of the press — the same
red with a different cause, which is the kind of thing that reads as "the fix did
not work" and is not. The grab is dismissed when the click **ends**.

That is also the better behaviour independently of the test. A menu dismissed
mid-click leaves the client unable to distinguish a click that merely closed it
from one that closed it and activated what was underneath; both halves now reach
the surface below while the popup still exists, and the popup is told afterwards.

**Measured after every edit**, which is §74's rule earning itself a third time:
the intermediate state — dismiss after `button` but on the press — scored exactly
what the broken state scored, 5 / 7, and only the log told the two apart.

### 78.4 What is left, in the order I would take it

1. **`grabbed_popup_gets_keyboard_focus`.** Keyboard focus follows the platform's
   `WM_SETFOCUS` to the *toplevel* (§11), and a popup that takes an explicit
   grab must have it instead. This is the one most on Firefox's path — a menu
   that cannot take the keyboard cannot be driven by arrow keys.
2. **The two `popup_done` cases**, which never fire at all: one when a new
   toplevel appears, one for nested grabs, which must be dismissed innermost
   first.
3. **Reactive positioning**, `xdg_positioner.set_reactive`, unimplemented — the
   popup must follow when its parent moves.
4. **`zero_size_anchor_rect_stable`**, where we raise a protocol error on
   something legal.

*All four closed in §85.4; the popup suites are 12 / 0 on the headless leg.*

### 78.5 Unchanged and still open from §72

The two three-level grandparent orderings, `subsurface_extends_parent_input_region`,
and the two restacking assertions that now fail only their second half. None of
them is touched by this. *§85.4: the orderings are fixed; the restacking pair
is the suite's own contradiction, which a Mir reference run supports; the input
region case stays open, and Mir fails it too.*

*(Committed unsigned: 1Password holds the signing key and its session was killed
by an over-broad `pkill -9 -f weston` elsewhere on the machine. Recorded rather
than rewritten later.)*

## 60. The rule that stops the kill, behind the gate that runs it

### 60.1 Status in one paragraph

§59 built `proc_kill`, and §59.4 item 1 named its gap in the same breath:
nothing forced a harness to call it. `scripts/wc-killcheck.sh` is that rule, and
`crates/sv-testkit/tests/kill_scoping.rs` puts it behind
`cargo test --workspace`. The population it governs is the sweep's, unchanged:
**10 kills scoped to something the run owns, 3 baselined with their reasons, 0
naming something the machine shares.** The gate caught its own documentation on
its first run, which is the third time that has happened here and is answered
the same way each time.

### 60.2 The rule, and why it is exactly the sweep's finding

> **A pattern is allowed only when it names something only THIS RUN could have
> produced.**

Encoded as: the pattern interpolates a shell variable. That is not a proxy for
the rule, it *is* the rule — a literal cannot be run-unique, because two
concurrent runs of a harness share every literal in it. `^$HOST_DIR/wc-proxy`,
`$DIR/sv-hostd`, `qemu-system.*$RUNDIR` all pass; `weston` does not.

**New occurrences only.** Eleven of the thirteen kills were already right, and a
gate that demanded they be rewritten would be a gate people turn off. The two
that are not run-unique are the baseline, and each carries its argument in the
script rather than being a bare exemption — an allowlist without reasons is
where rules go to die.

**The judgement call, asked for and answered.** `wc-launch.sh`'s
`pkill -f 'wc-launch/firefox'` is a path *fragment*. It cannot match a user's
ordinary Firefox — an ordinary Firefox has no such string in its command line —
so it is nothing like the outage. But it is **harness-unique, not run-unique**:
two concurrent `wc-launch.sh` runs would match each other. They would also
collide on the shared profile directory that pattern points at, so the kill is
not the first thing that breaks, and it is tolerated on that basis. It is
recorded as the one baseline entry that would become correct on its own by
giving each run its own profile directory — which is a real fix, not a
re-classification.

`http.server 8931` is a port. Only one process can hold a port, so there is
never a second match to hit by accident: scoped to something the run owns, if
not to the run itself.

### 60.3 A refusal that names the alternative

The message is not just "no". §59's helpers exist, so the gate points at them in
order of preference — `proc_kill` (you started it, you have its pid),
`proc_kill_pidfile` (it outlives the shell), `kill_exact` (matches the executable
name, so it cannot match the shell running it) — and then states the escape
hatch: if a pattern really is the only option, interpolate the run's own
directory, socket or port.

A refusal that does not name the alternative gets worked around, so the test
asserts the message contains `proc_kill`. That is the same reasoning as asserting
it names the offending file: an output nobody can act on is a failure that will
be re-run rather than fixed.

### 60.4 The gate flagged its own documentation, again

`proc_kill`'s refusal message quotes the command that caused the outage, so the
string appears in `wc-binaries.sh` inside a `note`. The gate saw it and refused.

That is the third checker in this tree to catch its own prose — §48.3 (the
citation checker on this document), §54.1 (its own negative fixture) — and the
answer has been the same every time: **narrow the rule, do not exempt the file.**
Here that means skipping comments and *reporter calls*, whose leading token is
`note`/`bad`/`echo` and whose job is to print text at a person rather than run a
command. Deliberately a rule about one line's first word rather than a path
exemption, because `wc-binaries.sh` is precisely the file most likely to grow a
real kill.

The pattern is worth naming now that it has three instances: **a checker good
enough to be worth writing is good enough to catch the writing about it.** That
is not a flaw in the checker. It is the checker being right about a string that
is genuinely indistinguishable, at its level of analysis, from the thing it
hunts — and the fix is always to make the rule see one level further, never to
carve out the file that happens to hurt.

### 60.5 What is not done

1. **The gate governs `scripts/` only.** A `pkill` in a Rust test, or typed
   directly into a shell by an agent, is not covered — and the outage was the
   latter. This cannot stop a person; it can only stop the tree from teaching
   them the habit. That is a real limit and not a small one.
2. **`kill_exact` is not itself gated.** It matches an executable name, which is
   correct for a program only this project runs and wrong for one the machine
   shares — `kill_exact weston` would have caused the same outage. Nothing
   checks its argument, and the honest reason it is not gated is that the check
   would need to know which names are ours, which is a list nobody maintains.
3. **The three baseline entries are tolerated, not fixed.** The `wc-launch` one
   has a stated route to correctness (a per-run profile directory) that nobody
   has taken.

## 79. The `h` dialect is chosen per connection, and a Linux compositor can read the proxy's

### 79.1 Status in one paragraph

`ProtoFd` is `WireFd`. `rs/wire.rs` reads and writes **both** dialects on **both**
platforms, and which one a connection speaks is a field on its `BufferedSocket`
set by whoever accepted it — §72.3's "the transport picks", built. A Linux
`wc-compositor` can now parse an in-band `wl_shm.create_pool` and map the named
object it names, which is the half of §72.3's defect that lived in this tree.
**The acceptance test passes**: `scripts/wc-pool.sh` runs `wc-pooltest` through
`wc-proxy` to a Linux compositor and the four pools cross, where the identical
topology with one flag removed still hangs exactly as §72.3 describes. The
tripwire is deleted (79.9). What is **not** fixed is the reverse direction for a
keymap, and 79.7 draws that line precisely.

### 79.2 The prediction held to the line

§76.5 measured that swapping the three aliases for distinct types would produce
errors only in the protocol layer, and named `rs/wire.rs` 157 and 332 as the work
list. Pointing `ProtoFd`/`RawProtoFd`/`BorrowedProtoFd` at the real enums, before
touching anything else, produced:

| | errors |
|---|---|
| the whole of `wayland-backend` | **2** |
| the whole of `wayland-server` | **0** |
| and they were | `rs/wire.rs:157` and `rs/wire.rs:332` |

Nothing in the socket layer moved, exactly as §76.5 said. That is a prediction
made in one commit and discharged in another, and it is the reason this section
is a day's work rather than the open-ended refactor the first attempt hit.

### 79.3 The three names the send side needed

`WireFd` was only the parsed form. The other two follow the shape §76.3 already
described:

| | arms |
|---|---|
| `WireFd` (`ProtoFd`) | `Named(Handle)` / `Open(OwnedFd)` |
| `RawWireFd` (`RawProtoFd`) | `Named(Handle)` / `Open(RawFd)` |
| `BorrowedWireFd<'a>` (`BorrowedProtoFd`) | `Named(&'a Handle)` / `Open(BorrowedFd<'a>)` |

`Open` is `#[cfg(unix)]` in all three, for the reason §77.4 gives. `WireFd`
gained two operations that turned out to carry most of the call-site work:
`borrow()`, which is what a **forwarder** needs (a clipboard pipe arrives on one
connection and leaves on another, and neither end should know which arm it is),
and `into_open()`, which is what a caller that needs a **real kernel descriptor**
needs — a `UnixListener` to accept on, an fd to `mmap` a virtual keyboard's
keymap out of. `into_open()` is unconditional and on Windows always returns
`Err`, which is the same answer those callers always got, now given by the type
instead of by a `cfg` at each site.

### 79.4 `FdEncoding::default()` is not derived, and that is a bug avoided

The dialect defaults to what an **unannounced peer on this platform** is. On Unix
that is a stock libwayland client speaking `SCM_RIGHTS`. On Windows there is no
ancillary channel at all, so the only thing a connection can possibly be speaking
is the in-band form.

`#[derive(Default)]` on the first variant would have made every Windows
connection start out claiming `OutOfBand` — a mechanism the platform does not
have — and the parser would then have looked for body bytes that a correct sender
never wrote. The Windows cross check is what surfaced it: `WireFd::Open` does not
exist there, so the out-of-band parse branch failed to compile and forced the
question. **That is the third thing `cargo check --workspace --target
x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` has caught in this sequence** (§77.6 is the second), and
`clippy --workspace --all-targets` would not have found any of them.

### 79.5 Sixteen `cfg` sites became a `match`, and smithay shrank

§72.3 predicted "sixteen occurrences across six files in `vendor/smithay`, eight
of them in `wayland/shm/pool.rs`". The compiler found **12** breakages across ten
files, and they split cleanly:

* **four on the send side**, all `BorrowedFd` where a `BorrowedWireFd` is now
  wanted. Three of them collapsed into one change: `SealedFile::proto_fd()` is
  now the single place that knows which arm a keymap is, and `KeymapFile::with_fd`
  hands the callback a `BorrowedProtoFd` instead of each caller wrapping one.
* **eight on the receive side**, of which the one that matters is
  `shm/handlers.rs` → `Pool::new`.

`shm/pool.rs` is where the "shrink" is real. `MemMap::new`, `remap` and `map`
were each two `#[cfg]` bodies; they are now one function with a `match` on the
`WireFd` arm, and **the bodies are unchanged**. `_view: Option<Mapping>` stopped
being `#[cfg(windows)]`: whether a mapping's view has to be held is a property of
*which kind of `h` arrived*, not of which kernel is running, and that `Option` is
now also what `Drop` reads to decide whether `munmap` applies. The `SIGBUS` guard
stays Unix-only and that is still right — it defends against a client
`ftruncate`ing its pool smaller, which is a thing an open fd allows and a named
section does not.

Three receive-side sites genuinely need a real descriptor and now say so:
`security_context` (a `UnixListener` to accept on), `virtual_keyboard` (an fd to
`mmap`), and both refuse a name with a protocol error or a warning rather than
guessing. `vendor/PATCHES.md` already recorded that sandboxing this way is not
portable and wants AppContainer instead, so the refusal is the position the fork
already held, now enforced by the type.

### 79.6 The doors, and why one of them needs a flag

`wc-compositor` sets the dialect per accepted connection:

* **the ring door needs no flag.** A connection arriving as a ring slot *is*
  `wc-proxy --upstream-ring`, by construction — nothing else can claim one — so
  it is set `InBand` unconditionally.
* **the socket door takes `--in-band`.** A unix socket carries no identity, and
  the relay legs put the proxy on one (`wc-vm-client.sh` runs `wc-proxy
  --upstream /tmp/up.sock` over a virtio-serial pair). So the operator who
  arranged the relay declares it. That is still "the transport picks" — it is a
  property of how the compositor was launched, not of anything negotiated in the
  stream, which §72.3 measured and rejected.

The setter is deliberately separate from `insert_client` rather than a parameter
on it: `insert_client` has seven signatures across two backends and
`wayland-server`, and a connection cannot have read anything between the two
calls because nothing is dispatched until the next turn. `Handle::set_client_fd_encoding`
returns `io::Result` for one honest reason — **the `libwayland` backend refuses
`InBand`**. It is a binding to a library that reads `SCM_RIGHTS` and nothing else,
and silently accepting would reproduce §72.3's desync one layer down.

### 79.7 What is proven, and what is only compiled

**Proven, by tests that run in the gate:**

* `an_in_band_h_round_trips_on_this_platform` — a `wl_shm.create_pool` written
  and read back **on Linux** in the in-band dialect, asserting that the `h` costs
  body bytes and comes back as the same `Descriptor`. Before this, no code on
  Linux could write those bytes or read them.
* `reading_in_band_bytes_out_of_band_does_not_silently_succeed` — the mismatch is
  detectable rather than invisible.
* `an_open_fd_cannot_be_written_in_band` — the write side refuses rather than
  guessing, which is `MessageWriteError::WrongDialect`.

**Not proven, and not claimed:**

1. **`scripts/wc-pooltest.c` through the proxy to a Linux compositor has not been
   run.** That is §72.3's acceptance test and it is the next thing to do. What is
   now in place is everything it needs on the compositor side; what has not
   happened is the run.
2. **`wc-proxy` is untouched**, so
   `the_upstream_dialect_is_still_assumed_rather_than_chosen` **still passes and
   is deliberately still there**. Its assertion is that `session.rs` spells both
   dialects as constants with no transport consulted, and that is still exactly
   true. Deleting it now would be deleting a true statement because a *different*
   statement became false.
3. **A keymap still cannot be sent to an in-band peer on Linux.** `SealedFile` is
   a `memfd` there, so `proto_fd()` can only return the open arm, and
   `rs/wire.rs` will refuse with `WrongDialect`. **Loudly, which is the change** —
   the same client previously desynchronised the stream with nothing logged.
   Fixing it means backing `SealedFile` with `wc_handle::Handle::create_shared_file`
   on Unix, which is real work and is the next step rather than this one. The
   same applies to the clipboard and drag pipes.

So the pool path — the one §72.3 names — is built end to end and the keymap path
is not. That is the honest split, and 2 is why `wayland-info` over the relay is
still expected to fail where `wc-pooltest` is not.

### 79.9 The acceptance test, both legs

`scripts/wc-pool.sh` runs `scripts/wc-pooltest.c` through `wc-proxy` to a
**Linux** `wc-compositor`, on one host, and it is in the tree because §72.3 asked
for exactly this: "that is the regression test, and it has to go from failing to
passing".

| leg | what it is | client exit | pools the proxy published |
|---|---|---|---|
| **fixed** | compositor told its socket peer is a proxy (`--in-band`) | **0** | **4** |
| **control** | identical, without telling it | **124 (timeout)** | **1** |

**The control leg is half the test.** The fixed leg alone would pass just as well
if the compositor had quietly started ignoring `h` arguments; the control leg
asserts that removing one flag brings back **exactly** the failure §72.3
describes — the client publishes one pool, its next round trip never returns, and
neither log says anything. Not an error, not a disconnect: a hang. That is what
makes "it works now" mean "the dialect is chosen" rather than "something
changed".

**`the_upstream_dialect_is_still_assumed_rather_than_chosen` is deleted, and it
is worth saying why the obvious objection does not hold.** Its assertion — that
`session.rs` spells both dialects as constants — is *still literally true*, since
`wc-proxy` is untouched. But that grep was never the point; it was a stand-in for
the defect, and its own doc comment names the condition for removal. Its opening
sentence, "on Unix the vendored backend's `Argument::Fd` is a raw descriptor with
nowhere to put a `wc_handle::Descriptor`, so a rewritten `wl_shm.create_pool`
handed to a **Linux** `wc-compositor` desynchronises its reader", is now false in
every clause. Keeping a test whose premise is dead because its assertion still
parses is the failure §35.10 warns about — a claim that outlives its truth — and
it is replaced by the harness above, which asserts the defect's absence against
the thing itself rather than against a proxy for it.

The proxy's upstream dialect being a constant is no longer a *defect*; it is a
limitation with a name: `wc-proxy` can only speak to a compositor that expects in
band. That is every compositor this project ships. A stock third-party compositor
behind `wc-proxy` was never supported and is not what §72.3 was about.

### 79.8 The gates

| gate | result |
|---|---|
| `nix develop --command cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | **89 binaries, 2644 passed, 0 failed** |
| master `c2330a4` before this | 89 binaries, 2642 passed |
| `scripts/wc-pool.sh` | both legs pass — 79.9 |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` | exit 0 |
| `cargo check --workspace --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` | exit 0, and it found 79.4 |
| `the_upstream_dialect_is_still_assumed_rather_than_chosen` | passes, and stays — see 79.7 |

2644 is 2642 plus three minus one. The three are the wire tests in 79.7; the one
is `the_upstream_dialect_is_still_assumed_rather_than_chosen`, deleted for the
reason 79.9 gives. No test moved binaries.

## 80. The keymap crosses the other way, and §79's loud refusal was the right shape

### 80.1 Status in one paragraph

§79 built the direction a compositor **reads** an `h` and said plainly that the
direction it **writes** one was not done: `SealedFile` is a `memfd`, so a keymap
to an in-band peer was refused by `rs/wire.rs` with `WrongDialect`. It is done.
`SealedFile` now mints a named twin on first in-band use, `KeymapFile::with_fd`
takes the peer's dialect instead of a `cfg`, and `scripts/wc-keymap.sh` runs
**`wayland-info`** — a client that is not ours — through `wc-proxy` to a Linux
`wc-compositor` and gets its keyboard. Both directions of §72.3 are now closed.

### 80.2 The refusal was load-bearing, which is the argument for building it that way

§79 chose to make the unsupported case fail loudly rather than skip it, and this
section is what that bought. The control leg's log line is:

```
[proxy] client 1 failed: compositor: wl_keyboard.keymap (event):
        argument 1 claims 35572 bytes, 0 available
```

The proxy reads its upstream in band, so it takes the length word of an
out-of-band `h` — which occupies **no body bytes at all** — and finds nothing
behind it. That is §72.3's defect seen from the end that happens to have a length
check in front of it, and it named the failing message, the argument index and
the exact byte count. Compare the pool direction, where the same class of error
produced a hang and two silent logs. **A defect that reports itself is a
morning's work; one that hangs is a section of this document.**

### 80.3 `SealedFile` grows a named twin, lazily

A sealed `memfd` is a descriptor and nothing else: it has no name a peer could
open. A peer reached through `wc-proxy` is handed a *name*. Those are different
objects, so serving both means having both.

```rust
named: std::sync::Mutex<Option<Handle>>,
```

Three decisions worth recording:

* **Lazy.** A compositor serving only stock clients never creates one. The cost
  of the named form is a file in `--shared-dir`, and it is paid per keymap per
  compositor by the peers that need it.
* **`Mutex`, not `OnceLock`.** Minting can fail — `publish::mint()` depends on
  `--shared-dir` — and a failure has to be retryable. A `OnceLock` would let the
  first keymap, sent before the compositor was configured, poison every later
  attempt.
* **The two objects are never synchronised, and do not need to be.** A
  `SealedFile` is immutable by construction; that is what "sealed" means. The
  bytes are read back out of the `memfd` at mint time rather than kept in a
  second buffer for the lifetime of every keymap.

The Windows arm is unchanged and is now simply the case where the named form
already exists: `named()` hands back the `Handle` the file has always held.

### 80.4 `with_fd`'s `cfg` became a question about the peer

`KeymapFile::with_fd` used to branch on the platform: Windows had no
`tempfile` fallback and Unix did. It now branches on the connection.

The unsealed fallback exists **only for the out-of-band dialect** — it hands the
client a plain `tempfile` descriptor, and an in-band peer is handed a name, so
there is nothing to select between. A client on version < 7 of `wl_keyboard`
behind a proxy therefore gets the sealed object anyway, which is *more*
permissive than the protocol requires rather than less: `keymap` says nothing
about sealing. Windows is now simply the platform on which every peer is in band,
which is what the `cfg` was really encoding all along.

The dialect reaches the call site through `Resource::fd_encoding()`, a default
method on the trait every generated protocol object implements. It reconstructs
the client from the object exactly as `Resource::client()` already does, so no
call site had to start carrying a `DisplayHandle` it did not have. It returns
`OutOfBand` for a dead object, deliberately: a dead object has no client to ask,
and guessing *in band* would turn a harmless no-op into a wrong-format write.

### 80.5 The evidence, and why the client is `wayland-info`

`scripts/wc-keymap.sh`, the mirror of `scripts/wc-pool.sh`:

| leg | `wayland-info` exit | `repeat_info` lines | keymap objects minted |
|---|---|---|---|
| **fixed** — compositor told its peer is a proxy | 0 | **1** | **1** |
| **control** — identical, without telling it | 0 | **0** | **0** |

**The client is not ours**, which is the point: `wayland-info` is in the dev
shell already and binds `wl_seat` and creates a `wl_keyboard`, which is what
makes a compositor send a keymap at all. `wc-pooltest.c` binds nothing but
`wl_shm`, so §79's passing pool leg was never evidence about this direction —
stated because it would have been easy to assume otherwise.

**The assertion is deliberately not the exit code.** `wayland-info` exits 0 in
both legs: it prints the globals it was told about and stops. What differs is
whether the *keyboard* answered — `wl_keyboard.repeat_info` follows
`wl_keyboard.keymap`, so a keymap that desynchronised the stream takes the repeat
lines with it, in a run whose exit status says everything was fine. Asserting on
the exit code would have called the control leg a pass. This is §71.1's rule
again: a client's exit status is not a session check.

`scripts/wc-pool.sh` still passes both legs, unchanged.

### 80.6 The clipboard and the drag pipes needed no change, and that is a claim

They were named alongside the keymap as "the same shape". They are not, and it is
worth saying why rather than leaving the absence of a diff to be read as an
oversight.

1. **Forwarding already works within a dialect.** `SelectionSourceProvider::send`
   takes a `ProtoFd` and passes `fd.borrow()`, so a pipe arriving on one
   connection goes out on another as whichever arm it arrived as. §79 built
   `WireFd::borrow()` for exactly this.
2. **Cross-dialect forwarding is not implementable today and not because of
   this code.** Naming a pipe means a `Descriptor::Pipe`, and `wc-handle` has no
   pipe support on *either* platform — the variant exists and nothing constructs
   or opens one. That is a `wc-handle` gap, not a wire one. **§81 closed it**, in
   the direction that needs no relay.
3. **This compositor sends no clipboard `h` at all.** `wc-compositor`'s
   `send_selection` and `ServerDndGrabHandler::send` drop the descriptor and say
   so in a printed line; the bytes go through `wc_clipboard_v1`, which `wc-proxy`
   binds instead (§29.6). So there is no site here that would need the change.

If a clipboard `h` ever is sent to a peer of the wrong dialect, `rs/wire.rs`
raises `WrongDialect` and names it, which is 80.2's property and is why leaving
this alone is safe rather than merely untested.

### 80.7 The gates

| gate | result |
|---|---|
| `nix develop --command cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | **89 binaries, 2644 passed, 0 failed** — unchanged from §79 |
| `scripts/wc-keymap.sh` | both legs pass |
| `scripts/wc-pool.sh` | both legs pass, unchanged |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` | exit 0 |
| `cargo check --workspace --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` | exit 0 |

No unit test was added, and that is the honest description: what changed is
reachable only with three processes and a real client, so the evidence is two
harnesses rather than a number in the suite.

## 81. `Descriptor::Pipe` stops being a variant nothing constructs

### 81.1 Status in one paragraph

§80.6 named the last gap of this class and located it correctly: not a wire gap
but a **`wc-handle` gap** — `Descriptor::Pipe` had existed since stage 1 and
nothing on either platform constructed or opened one. It does now.
`Handle::create_pipe`/`open_pipe`/`pipe_end` are real on Unix, backed by a FIFO,
with **five unit tests that move actual bytes**; `wc-proxy`'s `materialise` grew
the arm that turns an arriving pipe descriptor into a real fd. What is still not
built is the *other* direction, and 81.5 is precise about why that is a relay
rather than a descriptor.

### 81.2 Windows needs none of it, and that is a proof rather than an excuse

The obvious reading of a Unix-only implementation is "half done". It is not, and
the argument is short enough to check:

* `Descriptor::Pipe` is needed only to carry an `h` between two peers speaking
  **different** dialects — a name has to stand in for a descriptor that one side
  cannot receive.
* On Windows there is no ancillary channel, so no peer can speak the out-of-band
  dialect at all. §79.4 already made `FdEncoding::default()` `InBand` there, and
  this section makes `set_client_fd_encoding` **refuse `OutOfBand` outright**
  rather than leaving `rs/wire.rs` to discover it one message at a time.
* Two in-band peers need no conversion: the `h` is already a name, and
  `WireFd::borrow()` forwards it unchanged.

So a cross-dialect transfer cannot arise on Windows, and an implementation there
would be code with no caller and no test. `platform/windows.rs` says so in place
of the functions, and names `crates/sv-transport/src/winpipe.rs` — which already
has `CreateNamedPipeW` and a working `Pipe` — as the file to lift if that ever
changes. A pointer to an afternoon's work beats an afternoon of untestable work.

### 81.3 The one subtle thing is `O_RDWR`, and it is asserted rather than described

A FIFO with no writer gives readers EOF; a FIFO with no reader gives writers
`SIGPIPE`; and `open()` for reading **blocks until a writer arrives**, which in a
compositor's event loop is not a slow path but a deadlock. Opening the creator's
own end `O_RDWR` fixes all three at once, and it is the standard answer — written
down because a reader who has not hit it before will read `O_RDWR` on a
unidirectional object as a mistake.

`opening_the_peer_end_does_not_block_on_the_other_end_appearing` is that hazard
as a test. Note what it does *not* do: no thread, no timeout. If the keepalive
were wrong the test would **hang rather than fail**, which is exactly the failure
mode being excluded, and a timeout would only convert it into a flake.

### 81.4 `peer_reads` is carried rather than inferred

Wayland's pipe `h` arguments are unidirectional and **which way round they go is
per request**: `wl_data_source.send` hands the source a descriptor to *write*,
`wl_data_offer.receive` hands the requester one to *read*. A shim that assumed
either would be wrong half the time, which is why the flag is in the descriptor
and why `Handle::open_pipe` resolves it centrally. A boolean that means the
opposite thing depending on who is asking is how a clipboard transfer ends up
reading its own writes, and both directions have a test.

### 81.5 What is built, and the one thing that is not

**Named → Open is complete and needs no relay.** A pipe descriptor arriving at
`wc-proxy` is opened, and the local client is handed one end of the same FIFO the
compositor created. The bytes then flow between those two processes without the
proxy touching one.

**Open → Named is not built, and it is not an arm of the same shape.** Nothing
can give an *existing* anonymous pipe a name after the fact. Converting one means
creating a FIFO, handing over its name, and **copying between the two** — a byte
relay, with a policy question attached about who runs it, how much it buffers and
what happens when one end goes away. That is a different kind of change from
anything in §79–§81, all of which moved descriptors rather than bytes.

It also does not arise in this project yet, which is worth stating so the absence
is not read as a blocker: `wc-compositor` sends no clipboard `h` at all — the
bytes go through `wc_clipboard_v1`, which `wc-proxy` binds (§29.6). The case
needs a *client* source behind the proxy and a *stock* client requesting, on one
compositor, which is arrangement 3's shape and not one any harness runs today.

### 81.6 The tests broke a sibling before they passed, and the fix is the rule they test

Written first as a `mod pipe_tests` inside `lib.rs`, they cost **one failing test
that was not theirs**: `publish::tests::a_published_directory_mints_two_spellings_of_one_name`
opens with `assert!(mint().is_none(), "nothing may be minted before `set`")` — an
assertion about the state of the **whole process** — and its own comment says the
tests touching that registry must not run concurrently. A module in the same
library shares the process and calls `set`, so it broke that sibling from another
thread while every new test passed.

Cargo gives each file under `tests/` its own process, which is why the four
binaries beside `pipe.rs` already exist. Using the same escape hatch is the fix,
and it is worth recording because it is the same rule as the object under test:
**some things are global, and the way to have two of them is to have two
processes.** A FIFO has a name in one filesystem; `publish` has one directory per
process. Neither gets a second by being asked politely.

It is also the argument for `--no-fail-fast` stated as an incident. The new tests
all passed; the failure was somewhere else entirely, in a crate the change did
not appear to touch. A run that stopped at the first failing binary would have
reported the pipe work as green.

### 81.7 The gates, and this time the count moves

| gate | result |
|---|---|
| `nix develop --command cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | **91 binaries, 2704 passed, 0 failed** |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` | exit 0 |
| `cargo check --workspace --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` | exit 0 |
| `scripts/wc-pool.sh`, `scripts/wc-keymap.sh` | both harnesses, both legs, unchanged |

**The delta is attributed from the diff rather than by subtracting two runs**, and
that is the more useful form here: master moved three times while this was being
gated, so a subtraction would have been measuring someone else's commits as much
as this one. The change adds **exactly one test file containing exactly five
`#[test]`s and alters no test anywhere else** — `git diff` shows zero `#[test]`
lines added or removed outside `crates/wc-handle/tests/pipe.rs`. That is checkable
without re-running anything.

**The five are the pipe tests, in the one new binary, and the contrast with §80 is
the point.** §80's
count did not move because what changed there was reachable only with three
processes and a real client. A pipe is the one kind of `h` whose whole behaviour
fits inside one process — create it, open it as the peer would, move bytes, check
which side got them — so here the evidence *is* a number in the suite. Neither
answer is better than the other; what would be wrong is reporting one shape of
evidence as though it were the other.

## 82. Firefox's tabs in the title bar by default, and the first drag of a folded window

### 82.1 Status in one paragraph

Until this section Firefox reached Windows' caption only under `--decorations
tabs`, a flag no deployment passes. The default `auto` treated Firefox as
`Negotiated` and never folded it. The launcher hard-coded `titlebar = none`, and
`wc-session` said the frame-extending compositor "does not exist yet", although
§31 had built it. Now the defaults produce the goal clause end to end:
`wc-launch` gives Firefox `MOZ_GTK_TITLEBAR_DECORATION=client`, preferences
that turn off Firefox's own window buttons, and a `userChrome.css` that sizes
its tab strip to Windows' caption and leaves the caption-button corner empty.
The compositor's `auto` folds the caption of any window whose client *asked* to
decorate itself. `titlebar = none` is the per-application opt-out.

**Windows draws minimise, maximise and close, and Firefox draws none** (§82.3
gives the evidence). The first real drag of a folded window found two defects
in code that §22.7 and §45.11 had written and nobody had exercised, and one
misdiagnosis of my own (§82.6):

* `xdg_toplevel.move` entered the *keyboard* move;
* GTK's maximise pushed the window off its monitor;
* a "Wine parks maximised windows differently" fix, which was the second
  defect seen from the wrong side and has been reverted.

What was measured: Linux headless with Firefox 157 (11 passed, 0 failed) and
Wine with real `SendInput` gestures (20 passed, 0 failed). What was not
measured: the real guest. Wine has no DWM, so DWM's buttons, snap layouts,
Windows 11's real metrics, 125%/150% and the launcher's reservation against
DWM's real button bounds are still unmeasured. §82.10 is the command that
measures them.

### 82.2 Why `auto` left Firefox's tab strip under the caption

§49 made `auto` fold the caption only for `Decorator::ProbablyItself`, which
means a client that bound no decoration protocol and draws a margin.
GTK binds KDE's manager, so Firefox was `Negotiated` on every run. That variant
said *that* it negotiated and threw away *what*. Started without
`MOZ_GTK_TITLEBAR_DECORATION=none`, Firefox asks for `Client` whatever the
default (§22.3's table). The compositor echoes the request (§22.4) and then drew
Windows' caption above Firefox's tab strip: two title bars, under the default.

The per-surface record is now a map from surface to the mode last agreed:
KDE's object starts at the manager's default and moves with every echoed
`request_mode`, and `xdg-decoration` records whatever this compositor
configured. A new `Decorator::AskedForClient` is folded by `auto`. The decision
rests on what the client *said* on the protocol that exists for saying it, not
on a correlate, and it has to: `report_decorator` logged Firefox's inset as
`0,0` at map, though its trace says `(26, 23)`. The geometry arrives a commit
after the first buffer, so the inset is not a signal anyone can lean on at that
moment.

Measured on Linux, no `--decorations` flag, `scripts/wc-firefox.sh tabs-default`:

| client | Firefox asked | compositor |
|---|---|---|
| `titlebar = tabs` (env `client`) | `request_mode(1)` | `asked to decorate itself (Client) and was told yes, so this window's caption is folded` |
| `titlebar = none` (env `none`) | `request_mode(2)` | `negotiated its decorations`, caption kept |

One run of the compositor can therefore hold both, which a run-wide flag could
not. `--decorations server` and `client` still fold nothing. Under them an
insisting client is now reported as `THIS WINDOW HAS TWO TITLE BARS` rather than
"agreed", because that is what it has.

### 82.3 Who draws minimise, maximise and close: Windows

| | Windows draws them (DWM) | Firefox draws them |
|---|---|---|
| snap layouts | `DwmDefWindowProc` answers `HTMAXBUTTON` over DWM's button (§31.5). `caption::hit` answers it too (§82.5) | Windows needs `HTMAXBUTTON` over Firefox's maximise button, and no protocol says where that is (§22.8) |
| look | the system theme, hover and press states, DPI, Windows 11's shapes | GTK symbolic icons in 24 px circles (`browser.css`: `--titlebar-button-size: 24px`, Adwaita backgrounds). These would be the only GNOME-styled controls on the desktop |
| measured on the guest | yes, `tabs.png` (§31.1) | only as the `nobuttons` control (§31.8) |
| can the other side's be removed? | Firefox's: **yes, all three**, with `ui.GtkCSD{Minimize,Maximize,Close}Button=0` (§82.4) | DWM's: yes, `--caption-buttons off` |
| height | the caption's (30 px at 100%) | stretched to Firefox's strip |

The last row is the only one that favours Firefox. §82.4 removes the difference
by making the strip the caption's height.

**This overturns one conclusion of §22.9 and §31.9, and narrows another.** Both
said Firefox's close button "cannot be removed". What they measured is that
`gtk-decoration-layout` cannot remove it, and that is still true. The preference
names `ui.GtkCSDCloseButton` and its siblings are in Firefox 157's `libxul.so`
as LookAndFeel overrides. Setting the three to 0 in `user.js` removes all three
buttons, close included. This was measured on a frame dump of the Linux
compositor: the corner held the tab-list button and three round GTK buttons
before, and only the tab-list button after (`/tmp` experiment; the harness
control leg in §82.4 re-measures it).

### 82.4 Firefox's half: the corner and the height, measured

The sheet is two variables and one width
(`wc_launch::plan::user_chrome_css`):

```css
:root { --tab-min-height: 29px !important; --tab-margin-block: 1px !important; }
#TabsToolbar .titlebar-buttonbox-container { min-width: 146px !important; }
```

* **Height.** Firefox computes `--tabstrip-min-height` as
  `--tab-min-height + 2 × --tab-margin-block` (`tabs.css`). Setting a 29 px tab
  with 1 px margins gives a 31 px strip, which is the guest's `folds 31 px`.
  29 px is the value of Firefox's own compact density, so nothing is smaller
  than a size Firefox ships.
* **Corner.** The button box stays in the tab strip with its buttons hidden, and
  gets a `min-width` equal to §31.5's measured `146x30` strip.
  `#TabsToolbar` is required in the selector. The first version left it out and
  brought back the navigation bar's own button box, which Firefox hides while
  tabs are shown, and the hamburger menu moved left by 146 px.

From frame dumps of the geometry rectangle, `tabs-default`, 96 DPI numbers:

| leg | tab-strip rows (x = 700, from the top) | share of the 146x31 corner in its commonest colour |
|---|---|---|
| launcher profile | **31** | **99.5%** (the rest is the window's rounded corner) |
| env var only, no profile (control) | 44 | 67.5% (tab-list button plus Firefox's three buttons) |

The crops are `docs/tabs-in-titlebar/linux-tabs-default-top.png`,
`linux-tabs-noprofile-top.png` and `linux-none-top.png`. They are the
compositor's frame dumps and contain no Windows frame. A visual check by a
separate agent confirmed the following:

* in the default crop, only the tab-list button is in the right 150 px;
* in the control, Firefox's three round buttons are there;
* the opt-out has a 44-row strip with no window buttons.

**The two DPI-dependent numbers come from the launcher**, which runs on the
guest:

* The height is `AdjustWindowRectExForDpi`'s top inset for the compositor's own
  window style, at `GetDpiForSystem`. The thread is made per-monitor aware first,
  because an unaware caller is told 96.
* The width is §31's 146 px scaled with rounding up. No API reports the caption
  buttons' bounds without a window on screen.

`TitlebarFit::at` is unit-tested at 96, 120 and 144 DPI (31/146, 39/183,
47/219). **CSS pixels are assumed to be device pixels.** That holds because the
one `wl_output` is scale 1 and the launcher sets no `layout.css.devPixelsPerPx`.
A host with GTK text scaling would break it, and §82.5's corner check is what
would say so.

### 82.5 The compositor's half: hit test, metrics and buttons, as functions

`platform/caption.rs` is new and pure. It is compiled on every target and has
12 unit tests. `win32.rs` gathers the numbers and asks it.

* **`caption::hit`**, for a point `DefWindowProc` called `HTCLIENT`, applies these
  rules in order:
  1. The top resize band of a *restored* window is `HTTOP`, `HTTOPLEFT` or
     `HTTOPRIGHT`, and it wins over the buttons, as on a native window.
  2. The button strip in thirds is `HTMINBUTTON`, `HTMAXBUTTON` or `HTCLOSE`.
  3. Everything else is `HTCLIENT`, empty tab strip included. §22.8 still
     holds: no protocol says which of Firefox's pixels are a title bar, so a
     drag there is Firefox's to start, with `xdg_toplevel.move`, and a
     double-click is Firefox's `set_maximized`.

  A maximised window has no band, and its top row over the close button is
  `HTCLOSE`. `DwmDefWindowProc` is still asked first on Windows. Answering the
  buttons here as well is the documented way for a custom frame to keep snap
  layouts, and on Wine it is the only way.
* **DPI.** Every caption metric is now taken at the *window's* DPI:
  `GetDpiForWindow`, `GetSystemMetricsForDpi` and `AdjustWindowRectExForDpi`,
  resolved at runtime. Where those are missing, `caption::rescale` stands in
  with `MulDiv` rounding, tested at 125% and 150%.

  Before this section, `frame_border` and `top_inset` used `GetSystemMetrics`
  and `AdjustWindowRectEx`, which answer at the *system* DPI. On a 150% monitor
  beside a 100% primary, the top band was 8 px instead of 12, and the DWM margin
  was a 100% caption. §31.13 item 3 called this right "by construction"; that
  was true only on one monitor.
* **Fallback buttons.** Wine's `DwmGetWindowAttribute` returns `E_NOTIMPL`
  (§67.4), so until now a folded window under Wine had no buttons at all, and
  with Firefox's own buttons off it had no way to close. Where DWM will not
  say, the window now draws the system's buttons with
  `DrawFrameControl(DFC_CAPTION)`: three `SM_CXSIZE` buttons at the window's DPI,
  the folded caption's height, at the right edge. `caption::hit` hit-tests
  them. They are still Windows' rendering (the classic one), so §31.5's rule
  ("do not draw the buttons, uncover them") holds wherever there is something to
  uncover.
* **The corner check.** `caption::corner_is_clear` asks whether almost every
  opaque pixel under the button strip is one colour. Transparent pixels are
  skipped, because the CSD window's rounded corner is alpha 0. Before that
  change Wine reported a false `DRAWS UNDER THE CAPTION BUTTONS` from 2% of a
  54x30 strip. The compositor logs the verdict whenever it changes. This is
  §31.14 item 4, *warn when the levers disagree*, for the one lever whose
  failure showed only in a photograph.

### 82.6 The first drag, and what it found

`wc-desk` gained `hittest`, which sends `WM_NCHITTEST` at window-relative
points, and `mouse`, which sends real `SendInput` drags, clicks, double-clicks
and hovers and prints the window rectangle before and after. `wc-firefox.sh
wine-tabs` runs both against Firefox in a Wine HWND under the defaults. The
first runs found three things, and the third was not what it first looked like.

1. **`xdg_toplevel.move` was the keyboard move.** §22.7 posted bare `SC_MOVE`
   with `lParam = 0`, which is Alt+Space → *Move*. It warps the cursor to the
   caption's middle and moves the window by the distance from *there*. A drag
   of (+120, +80) on empty tab strip moved the window by **(+286, +82)**. The
   extra 166 px is the distance from the press point to the middle of the
   1288 px window. It is now `SC_MOVE | HTCAPTION` with the cursor in
   `lParam`, the form a caption click produces, and the same drag moves the
   window by **(+110, +74)**. The 10 px shortfall on each axis is GTK's drag
   threshold, crossed before the move is requested.
2. **GTK's maximise moved the window off the monitor.** §45.11's `ShiftOrigin`
   moved the `HWND` whenever the window's geometry origin changed, declared or
   not. GTK re-declares `(26, 23)` as `(0, 0)` when Firefox maximises: the
   shadow goes, the buffer is replaced, and the window rectangle stays the same.
   The compositor logged `origin shifted by -26,-23` and pushed the maximised
   window off its monitor, and the 31-row tab strip with it. The Wine capture
   showed the navigation bar at the top of the screen. `ShiftOrigin` now fires
   only for the bounding-box extent that §45.11 was about. Every Wayland
   compositor keeps the window geometry where it is when it is re-declared, and
   §45.11's own unit test says the same for the synthetic Win32 ("a declared
   inset leaves the window where it was put"). It also removes a smaller
   symptom: every window used to move by its shadow inset just after it mapped,
   because the geometry arrives a commit late (§82.2).
3. **A diagnosis that was wrong, corrected in the same section.** The shifted
   maximised window sat at `-30,-27`. That was read as "Wine parks a maximised
   window a caption above the screen", and `3e8d5bd` moved the maximised client
   top to the work area's top. With item 2 fixed, Wine parks it at `-4,-4`: one
   band, as Windows does. The `-26,-23` was the shadow shift and nothing else, so
   `a3406ca` puts the band back. A new log line on every maximise compares the
   client's top with the work area's top. It reports any future mover as
   `MISMATCH` instead of absorbing it the way the work-area rule would have.
   This is §55.3's rule again: a symptom is not a diagnosis.

Also measured: the Wine console that `cmd /c` opens sits over the top-left
665x434 of the desktop and takes `SendInput` presses aimed there. The first
top-edge drag, at x = 600, "did not resize" for that reason and no other. Hit
tests are messages and are unaffected. The leg aims its gestures to the right of
the console and says why.

### 82.7 The Wine leg, and what it does and does not prove

`scripts/wc-firefox.sh wine-tabs` passed 20 of 20. Its assertions cover:

* the fold under the default;
* `folds 30 px` (Wine's caption);
* the fallback buttons at `client rect 1226,0 54x30`;
* the compositor's own corner check reporting clear;
* hit tests of `HTTOP`, `HTTOPLEFT`, `HTCLIENT` (empty tab strip and below it),
  `HTMINBUTTON`, `HTMAXBUTTON` and `HTCLOSE`;
* the top edge resizing (`904 px at y=0 -> 843 px at y=61`);
* `handed a move to Windows`, with the window following the drag;
* a double-click on empty tab strip maximising the window;
* maximised: the monitor's top row is `HTCLIENT`, with the client's top at the
  work area's top;
* the maximised capture's first 31 screen rows being the tab strip.

The captures are `docs/tabs-in-titlebar/wine-tabs-{restored,moved,maximised}.png`.
**They are Wine:** Xvfb, Wine's own frame, no DWM, and the classic fallback
buttons. A separate visual check found the following:

* the strip is the window's top row in all three captures;
* the buttons sit about 100 px clear of Firefox's tab-list button;
* the buttons are 30 px tall against a 31 px strip. Wine's caption is 30 px and
  the launcher's 100% number is Windows 11's 31;
* nothing is cut off when maximised.

It found one artefact: a few black pixels at the window's rounded top-left
corner. That corner is alpha 0 in Firefox's buffer, and GDI's blit ignores
alpha (§31.6). On the guest the same pixels fall inside the DWM-extended
region, where alpha 0 is a hole onto the frame; that has not been looked at.

The Wine leg also does not show the following, and cannot:

* DWM's buttons;
* `DwmDefWindowProc`'s answers;
* the snap-layouts flyout;
* Windows 11's metrics;
* any scale but 96 DPI;
* whether the launcher's 146 px covers DWM's real strip.

The leg is **not perfectly stable**. On the final tree it ran six times: five
passed 20 of 20, and one lost all three gestures. That run printed each
gesture's "before" line and never its "after" line, so `wc-desk` did not finish
inside the leg's 60 s wait, and the leg reported 14 passed, 6 failed. The cause
was not found. The run kept no artefacts, and every rerun with `WC_KEEP=1`
passed. It is recorded rather than averaged away.

### 82.8 The launcher and `wc-session`

* `[app.*] titlebar` defaults to `tabs`, and the shipped example says so. It
  accepts `tabs`, `none` (alias `server`) and `client`, the last being §31's
  picture without the profile, kept as a control. A typo is refused by name,
  because Firefox treats an unknown `MOZ_GTK_TITLEBAR_DECORATION` as "decorate
  yourself".
* `wc-session run` gets two words where it used to get one: the env value and
  the sheet. It writes the sheet only under the launcher's own profile tree. When
  an app opts out it removes a sheet that carries the launcher's mark, and leaves
  any other `userChrome.css` alone. The stale "does not exist yet" comment is
  replaced by the arrangement as it now is.
* **Empty words now cross as `-`.** `wc-session` splits
  `$SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND` on whitespace, so an empty base64 argument vanished
  and every later one arrived one place early. An `exec` without `--profile`
  sent its preferences into the profile slot. Nothing had hit this because the
  shipped `exec` names a profile.
* `wc-launch --write-firefox-profile TITLEBAR DPI DIR` writes exactly what a
  launch sends, on every platform. The harnesses use it, so they measure the
  launcher's output and not a copy of it.

Every row was run on this branch at its final code (`a3406ca` plus this

row is the guest.**

### 82.10 What is not proven, and the guest run that proves it

1. **DWM's buttons against the reservation.** This needs the default leg on the
   guest, where the corner check compares the launcher's 146 px with DWM's real
   bounds. That leg is new:

   ```
   WC_HOST=<host-user>@<host-ip> WC_HOST_FIREFOX=<absolute path of firefox on the host> \
     scripts/wc-titlebar.sh deploy
   WC_HOST=<host-user>@<host-ip> WC_HOST_FIREFOX=<same> scripts/wc-titlebar.sh default
   ```

   It asserts the following:
   * the fold with no `--decorations`;
   * Firefox asking for `Client`;
   * the profile arriving on the host;
   * `DwmExtendFrameIntoClientArea ok`;
   * `keeps Windows' own caption buttons`;
   * **`leaves the caption-button corner clear`** against DWM's bounds;
   * `HTTOP` at the top edge, `HTCLIENT` on empty strip, and `HTMAXBUTTON` and

2. **Snap layouts, the drag, the top edge and the double-click on the guest's

     scripts/wc-titlebar.sh default

   The leg hovers the maximise button for 1.5 s while `wc-desk shot --screen`

## 83. The arena moves onto an ivshmem device, and root leaves the launcher's path

### 83.1 Status in one paragraph

Until this section every session the desktop shortcut started became root on the
VM host twice: once to locate the guest's arena through QMP and
`/proc/<qemu-pid>/fd`, and once to run `wc-proxy` against QEMU's memory backend
(§12.9, §28.9 item 4). The arena now lives in **BAR2 of a QEMU `ivshmem-plain`
device** whose memory backend is a file at a path,
`/run/windows-vm/wc-arena/arena`, mode 0660 `root:wc-arena`. The guest compositor
maps the BAR through the WHQL-signed ivshmem driver (`--arena-ivshmem 0`) and
writes a header at the front of it; the VM host opens the file **as the user**,
reads the header, and runs the proxy in a *user* unit. `wc-session`'s `up`,
`proxy` and `down` do not call `$ROOTC` on this path, and there is no fallback to
the old one. The developer harnesses keep `--arena-guest-ram` and their root.
On the guest, the device was hot-plugged into the running VM, the driver is
installed, a non-administrator process mapped it and its bytes were read on the
host by `sirati`, and the launcher ran end to end in session 0 with no root
(83.8). The interactive desktop was not available, and 83.9 lists what that
leaves unrun.

### 83.2 The reason, which security-model.md R6 asked for

R6 closed with an instruction: *"If a driver is ever proposed again, this entry is
why it has to be argued from a stated new reason rather than revived from the old
one."* The old reason ivshmem was dropped was a mechanism: a BAR is
`VM_IO|VM_PFNMAP`, host-pointer import pins pages, and the pinning path refuses
such pages (docs/design.md §5.1). That reason is about **importing the arena into a
GPU driver**, and it still stands for shared_vulkan's arena, which stays guest RAM.
The compositor's arena is never imported into anything. The guest compositor
reads it with the CPU and the host proxy writes it with the CPU, so the mechanism
objection never applied to this path. Nobody had a reason to use a device here
until now.

The new reason is **root in the product path**. §12.9 said what it would take to
avoid it, in order of preference, and ruled out each option for its own reason:
running QEMU as the user is a real question on a VFIO machine; a helper that
returns a *name* "cannot be written" because a memfd has no name; passing the
descriptor over `SCM_RIGHTS` breaks the one invariant the design has. §12.9 also
named the thing that would change the second answer, in parentheses: *"a
`memory-backend-file` would have one — a path on tmpfs — and swapping the backend
is another VM change with its own consequences."* This section makes that change
for a dedicated region rather than for the guest's whole RAM. That keeps the
consequences down to one device, one file and 128 MiB.

### 83.3 Why this is not the file arena, and what §28.2 now says

§28.2's rule is that the file-backed arena must not be reachable from the
launcher, because "a launcher that could quietly degrade to a file would produce
a window that works and pixels that tear". The host now opens a path, so the rule
has to be read for what it was about. The file arena is a file **each side maps
through its own filesystem**: on the Wine fixture that is one kernel's page
cache, and on a virtio-fs export it is two, which §10.3 measured incoherent for
live mappings (65280 of 65536 bytes wrong). The ivshmem file is not mapped by the
guest at all. The guest maps a PCI BAR, and QEMU makes that BAR **the same RAM
pages** as the host file (`hw/misc/ivshmem-pci.c` registers the backend's own
`MemoryRegion` as BAR2, docs/research-vulkan-forwarding.md §2.2). That is the same
relationship guest RAM had with `/proc/<qemu-pid>/fd/<n>`, which was also a path
naming QEMU's backing object.

So `the_arena_is_ivshmem_and_never_a_file` (the old
`guest_ram_is_the_only_transport`) keeps every refusal it had. `--arena`,
`--arena-provide`, `--shared-dir` and the source grep for them are all still
there, and it adds `--arena-guest-ram` and `--arena-frames` to the refused list,
because a launcher that emitted them would start a session the host's `up` can
no longer serve without root. `wc-substrate.sh` gains an `ivshmem` substrate that
removes `SV_ALLOW_FILE_ARENA` exactly as `guest-ram` does.

docs/design.md §1a is satisfied in the same way it was before: the host opens a
name it can resolve itself, and what crosses the VM boundary is a 64-bit run id.

### 83.4 The header, and why it is outside the arena

The plan that `wc-arena-host` used to write held four facts: an object, a length,
a run id and the outbound window. With a device, QEMU was told the object before
the guest booted, so the other three have to travel some other way. They travel
in the region itself. `wc_handle::ivshmem` defines a 64-byte header in the first
4 KiB page: magic `WCIVSHM1`, version, header size, run id, generation, region
length, arena id, and the outbound window. It is encoded and decoded by one
platform-independent module, so the Windows writer and the Linux reader cannot
disagree about a field offset, and the test pins the offsets as numbers.

**The page is not part of the arena.** The arena's offset 0 is the region's byte
4096, on both sides. `Attached` gained a `base` for this, and the proxy's plan is
one run at file offset 4096. If the header lived at arena offset 0, the proxy's
first-fit allocator would write pixels over it on the first frame. That is
§12.10's lesson about the stamps, which also had to be found again later and
could not be because a pool had overwritten them.

**Ordering.** `attach_ivshmem` clears the previous compositor's magic before it
registers anything. `publish_ivshmem` runs after the outbound window is reserved
and before the socket is bound. It writes every field, then a release fence, then
the magic. The launcher waits for the line printed *after* publishing, `header
published: run 0x…`. `wc-session up` then checks the magic and the run id with
`od`, and the proxy checks them again together with the arena id and the file
length (`Plan::from_ivshmem`). A header left by a compositor that has exited
therefore fails at `up`, with both run ids in the message.

**What the guest side no longer does.** It does no `VirtualLock`, no stamps, no
frame list and no deferral of gifts. The BAR's pages are not in the compositor's
working set and are not charged against the guest's RAM. The launcher also no
longer runs the Superfetch frame-list query (security-model.md R28), which stays
in use for shared_vulkan's arena and the developer harnesses.

### 83.5 What it costs

* **128 MiB of host RAM**, pinned under VFIO like the guest's own. The file is on
  `/run`'s tmpfs. On testhost that comes out of the ~1.4 GiB the host has left
  after the guest's 13 GiB (`free -m` before the change: 1419 MiB available).
  The guest gets the matching amount back, because the arena is no longer carved
  out of its RAM and pinned.
* **No growth.** A BAR is the size QEMU gave the device. The proxy refuses
  `--arena-grow` with `--arena-ivshmem` rather than arm growth with nothing
  behind it, which was §28.12's "armed and inert" state. The compositor reserves
  no growth channel. A session that fills the arena refuses pools, which it
  survives (§20). 128 MiB less the header page and the 1 MiB outbound window is
  about twice the 64 MiB peak §28.12 measured.
* **One mapping per device.** The driver gives the BAR to one handle and takes it
  back when that handle closes. So one compositor per VM uses it, and a second
  one fails at start-up with the reason in the message.
* **A group that can stop the VM.** security-model.md R29.

### 83.6 The VM side

`virtualisation.windowsVm.waycomposeArena` in nix-config, on branch
`wc-arena-ivshmem`, adds the `memory-backend-file` and the `ivshmem-plain` device
on a pinned root-bus slot (`pci.0`, because testhost's machine type is
i440fx). It adds a root `ExecStartPre` that recreates the file for every VM start
(directory 0750, file 0660, truncated to the size QEMU is told), an
`ExecStopPost` that removes it, and `users.groups.wc-arena.members =
[ "sirati" ]`. It also sets `restartIfChanged = false` on `windows-vm.service`:
before this the unit had no such setting, so any `switch` that changed it would
have restarted the VM somebody is logged into. 83.8 and 83.9 record which of the
persistent change and the hot-plug were applied, and how.

### 83.7 The guest side

The driver is the WHQL-signed `ivshmem` from the Looking Glass B7 host
installer, the only signed build available (docs/research-vulkan-forwarding.md §2.2).
`wc_handle::platform::windows::map_ivshmem` finds the device by interface GUID
`{df576976-569d-4672-95a0-f57e4ea0b210}`, asks `IOCTL_IVSHMEM_REQUEST_SIZE`, and
maps with `IOCTL_IVSHMEM_REQUEST_MMAP` in **`IVSHMEM_CACHE_CACHED`**. That is
write-back, the same class as the host's mapping of a tmpfs page, which is what
R10 requires of two page tables over one page. The driver's default for a BAR
is uncached, and the compositor is the side that *reads*, so write-combining
would be the wrong choice too.
The IOCTL codes are `CTL_CODE(FILE_DEVICE_UNKNOWN, 0x801/0x802/0x803,
METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_ANY_ACCESS)`, written out by hand. The `IVSHMEM_MMAP`
layout is taken from the driver's own `Public.h`.

`wc-ivshmem-probe` is the guest's half of the core measurement. It goes through
the same `attach_ivshmem`, writes a marker carrying its pid and run id at arena
offset 0, reads it back, and with `--bench` times one 1920×1080 RGBA copy out of
the mapping against the same copy between two heap buffers.

### 83.8 What was run, on 2026-10-15

The guest had been reset at 14:37 after an unrelated hang, and **nobody was
logged in** for any of this. So everything below ran from ssh: the driver steps
in the ssh session, and the launcher's runs in session 0, where the compositor's
windows exist but nobody sees them. Before and after each step that touched the
VM (hot-plug, driver install, every probe and every launcher run), `ssh true` to
the guest and `ping <guest-nat-ip>` from testhost were checked, and all passed.

**The slot, read before anything was added.** `query-pci` on the running VM:
root-bus slots 0–15, 26 (the CD xHCI, pinned) and 31 (the IGD's mock LPC) are
in use, and every auto-addressed device is at 15 or below. `info qtree` shows
`PIIX4_PM` with `acpi-root-pci-hotplug = true`. The 64-bit PCI window is
`0x7000000000–0x7080000000` (2 GiB, `pci-hole64-size`), of which
`0x7000000000–0x701104bfff` is assigned, so a 128 MiB prefetchable BAR fits.
Slot `0x1c` (28) is free and above every auto-addressed device. Adding a device
there assigns nothing to any existing device, and a cold start with the device
on the command line gives the auto-addressed devices the slots they have now.

**The hot-plug: done, on the running VM, with no restart.** The file was
created as root through `sudokey`. The `wc-arena` group exists only once the
NixOS change is active, so sirati was given access by ACL: directory
`root:root 0750` + `u:sirati:r-x`, file `root:root 0660` + `u:sirati:rw-`. Then
over QMP `object-add memory-backend-file` (`share=true`, 134217728 bytes) and
`device_add ivshmem-plain,id=wcarena0,memdev=wcarena,bus=pci.0,addr=0x1c`
returned `{}` each. `info pci` lists `Bus 0, device 28: RAM controller: PCI
device 1af4:1110`, and every other device is where `query-pci` had it. Windows
enumerated it at once as "PCI standard RAM Controller", status OK.

**The driver.** The ssh account is an administrator (`IsInRole(Administrator)`
true) and its session is elevated, so `pnputil /add-driver ivshmem.inf
/install` ran directly. It published `oem158.inf` and installed it on
`PCI\VEN_1AF4&DEV_1110&SUBSYS_11001AF4&REV_01\3&267a616a&0&E0`. The device is
now "IVSHMEM Device", status OK, provider Red Hat, Inc., driver version
`100.10.100.10000`.

| file | SHA-256 (identical on this machine and on the guest) |
|---|---|
| `looking-glass-host-B7.zip` (looking-glass.io/artifact/B7/host) | `c2415a5a0c405f1d6aa936986bdd4b806c50574b4521747e113c3be2be047b1b` |
| `looking-glass-host-setup.exe` (inside it) | `9d789e8e18a45aab415d40cd1fc3f07aba54e6871122f26031ac44c7250e5032` |
| `ivshmem.inf` | `e41554a07eee128aee07cebdd2423dcfcde45e3868e2ae90f7ba8caf52af8f1c` |
| `ivshmem.cat` | `40cc6242b8bf05600e5361b81ec4f5150b23bfdcbab538b68e406f8ac57e979d` |
| `ivshmem.sys` | `416c73f68f1bdaf10bdd86f2c29c62370edbdd9d3aeb109cb618eccfd050a45d` |

`Get-AuthenticodeSignature` on the guest: `ivshmem.cat` and `ivshmem.sys` are
both **Valid**, signer *CN=Microsoft Windows Hardware Compatibility Publisher*,
issuer *CN=Microsoft Windows Third Party Component CA 2014*, timestamped by
*Microsoft Time-Stamp Service*.

**The core claim, measured.** `wc-ivshmem-probe --bench` was run under a token
with **`BUILTIN\Administrators` deny-only** (`runas /trustlevel:0x20000`;
`whoami /groups` in the same process confirms it). It printed:

```
mapped ivshmem device 0 (\\?\pci#ven_1af4&dev_1110&…#{df576976-569d-4672-95a0-f57e4ea0b210}) in 7.704 ms:
  region 134217728 bytes, arena 134213632 bytes
wrote and read back at arena offset 0 (region byte 4096): WCPROBE1 pid 9804 run 0x92bab4552df52363 -> identical
```

On testhost, as `sirati` (uid 1000, not root, not in any group the file
names), an earlier probe's marker read back out of
`/run/windows-vm/wc-arena/arena` with `xxd -s 4096 -l 32`:

```
00001000: 5743 5052 4f42 4531 c81f 0000 0000 0000  WCPROBE1........
00001010: 35eb 7abc dc17 8967 0000 0000 0000 0000  5.z....g........
```

`0x1fc8` is that probe's pid, 8136, and `0x678917dcbc7aeb35` its run id. So
bytes written by a non-administrator Windows process into the BAR are in the
host's file, at the same offset, read by an unprivileged Linux user.

What that token was **not**: its integrity level stayed High, because `runas
/trustlevel` removes the group and not the label. A UAC-filtered desktop token
is Medium. The device opened for a non-administrator; whether it opens at
Medium integrity is shown by the first launcher run on the interactive desktop
(83.9 item 1). An S4U scheduled task with `RunLevel Limited` was tried first
and turned out to get a full administrator token, so it proved nothing and is
not counted.

**The cost of a CACHED mapping, as a copy.** The compositor logs no per-frame
blit time, so what was measured is the copy its blit makes: one 1920×1080 RGBA
frame out of the mapping into private memory, 15 successive frames, 5 reps.

| | best | mean | best rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| ivshmem CACHED → heap | 0.521–0.565 ms | 0.557–1.063 ms | 14.7–15.9 GB/s |
| heap → heap (control, same process) | 0.517–0.533 ms | 0.521–0.566 ms | 15.6–16.1 GB/s |

Three runs. The best figures are the same to within 7%, so a cached BAR reads
at memory speed. The means are noisier on the BAR (one run's mean was 1.06 ms),
and three runs cannot say why.

**The launcher, functionally, in session 0.** `wc-launch.exe firefox` was run
over ssh from its own directory (`C:\Users\<guest-user>\wcivs`, its own key restricted
to `~/wc-launch-ivs/wc-session`) against a session nobody can see. The first
attempt found a real bug: the forced command's `wc-session` defaulted its
binaries to `~/wc-launch/bin`, so a second installation started the *first*
installation's `wc-proxy`, which rejected `--arena-ivshmem` as an unknown
argument. `wc-session` now runs the binaries installed beside it. After that,
every run went through:

```
arena: run 0x23c00e145e1fdd27, 655 ms
up: ivshmem run 0x23c00e145e1fdd27 generation 2, 134217728 bytes at /run/windows-vm/wc-arena/arena | up ok … (214 ms)
proxy: proxy ok /tmp/wc-launch/wcl-428/wl-proxy (as sirati, ivshmem) (266 ms)
cold start: 1164 ms
CLICK-TO-WINDOW 2336 ms (cold, 0 window(s) before)
```

`ps` on testhost: `sirati 146229 … ~/wc-launch-ivs/bin/wc-proxy
… --transport arena --arena-ivshmem /run/windows-vm/wc-arena/arena`. The proxy
logged `transport arena 0: 134213632 bytes of ivshmem BAR2 … (nothing located,
nothing opened as root …)`. `$ROOTC` was called on none of `up`, `proxy` and
`down`. `scripts/wc-launch.sh verify` against the live session:
**6 passed, 1 failed**. The six include the live compositor's command line
(`--arena-ivshmem`, no file flag), wc-proxy running as `sirati`, 6 connections
on one region and one allocator, and `1 fds in, 2 out (2 from the arena)`. The
one failure is that the main connection's pool counts had not been printed.
The proxy prints them when a connection closes, and on this run the main
connection outlived Firefox until the unit was stopped. The proxy's per-pool
lines show four 217600-byte pools published into arena slices, the closed
connections show `0 overflows, 0 refusals`, and the compositor logged
`window 1 pixels served by wl_shm (mapped: 0 section, 0 shared-file, 3
arena-slice)`, `window 1 mapped 1264x713 (xrgb)` and 101 commits.

| | ivshmem, session 0 (this section) | guest RAM, §28.4 / §28.12 |
|---|---|---|
| cold click to window | **2336, 3002, 1930 ms** | 5.7–7.1 s, of which the locate was 2.8–4.1 s |
| `up` (was the locate) | 205–233 ms | 2832–4098 ms swept |
| warm click to window | **1015, 1371, 1375 ms** | 1414–1601 ms; 1494–1554 at 64 MiB |
| `sv-guest.exe` with Firefox up | **private 11.5 MB, working set 40.9 MB** | private 101 MB, working set 120 MB |

**These numbers are not like for like, and the table says so by its column
heading.** Session 0 has no visible desktop, no DWM composition of the windows
and no user. §28.4's figures were the interactive desktop, through the shortcut
and the scheduler's interactive route. The memory row compares like with like
in what it counts, since a BAR mapping is not private bytes and the old arena
was 64 MiB of pinned private memory. The click rows bound the cost of the
locate and the root steps, which are gone, and do not stand in for the
desktop's numbers. The shortcut (`Firefox (Linux, ivshmem).lnk`, wearing
Firefox's icon) is installed on the desktop and has not been clicked.

**Cleanup.** Every launcher session was ended with `wc-launch.exe --stop`. No
process from `C:\Users\<guest-user>\wcivs` is running, and no `wc-proxy` or Firefox of
this run is left on testhost. Left in place on purpose: the hot-plugged
device, its file, the installed driver, the shortcut and both installation
directories. These are the deployment.

### 83.9 What is not proven

1. **Nothing has run on the interactive desktop.** Nobody was logged in. Not
   yet run: the shortcut clicked through the scheduler's interactive route, its
   cold, warm and photographed window, and with them the device opening at
   Medium integrity. The commands are:
   ```
   export WC_LAUNCH_DIRNAME=wcivs WC_LAUNCH_HOSTDIR=~/wc-launch-ivs \
          WC_LAUNCH_TITLE="Firefox (Linux, ivshmem)" WC_LAUNCH_PORT=57441 WC_LAUNCH_SHOTDIR=ivshmem
   nix develop -c scripts/wc-launch.sh deploy   # the guest's copy predates the merge of §82
   nix develop -c scripts/wc-launch.sh install
   nix develop -c scripts/wc-launch.sh cold
   nix develop -c scripts/wc-launch.sh warm
   nix develop -c scripts/wc-launch.sh verify
   nix develop -c scripts/wc-launch.sh shot     # images to docs/ivshmem/, judged by a separate agent
   nix develop -c scripts/wc-launch.sh stop
   ```
2. **The persistent VM change has not booted, and is not set to.** The nix-config
   branch `wc-arena-ivshmem` evaluates and builds. It was **not** activated, by
   `switch` or by `boot`. testhost runs a system with nixpkgs from 2026-08-19
   that no commit reproduces, and the branch sits on a master 418 commits and a
   two-month nixpkgs bump ahead of it. A `boot` would have put all of that, not
   this change, into the next reboot. Until the branch is deployed, a natural
   restart of the VM drops the device. The launcher then fails at `up` with
   "no ivshmem arena", as designed, and does not fall back.
3. **The `SIGBUS` of R29 is the documented behaviour of a truncated shared
   mapping, not a measurement.** Triggering it would stop the VM.
4. **The blit is measured as a copy, not as the compositor's present.** The
   compositor has no per-frame timing for it.
5. **A full session's pool accounting was not read** (83.8): the main
   connection's counts print on close, and it closed only when the unit stopped.

On the tree after merging master (fe24480, §82):

| gate | result |
|---|---|
| `nix develop --command cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | **93 binaries, 2740 passed, 0 failed** |

| `scripts/wc-pool.sh`, `scripts/wc-keymap.sh` | both OK, both legs |
