## 88. Scrolling at 60: a frame timeline across both machines, and a frame clock that does not cross ssh.exe

Written 2026-10-16, on branch `scroll-fps`, from master cd08c7a. The brief:
§87 measured 40–45 fps while scrolling accelerated Firefox on the guest; find
where a frame's time goes, end to end, fix what costs most, and reach a
steady 60 on a 60 Hz output. Every guest run was in session 0, over ssh, on the
`wcgpu` test installation until the last step; a health watchdog (ssh to the
guest, ping from the VM host, every 15 s) ran throughout. The reports and
harness records are in `docs/scroll-fps/`.

### 88.1 Status in one paragraph

**60 fps on the guest.** The scroll harness of §87 (the long page, 40 wheel
steps, a `requestAnimationFrame` counter, now three rounds with every frame's
timestamp) went from **44.6 / 45.3 / 43.7 fps** with frame times p50 21.7,
p95 27.7, p99 38.3 ms to **60.4 / 60.3 / 60.3 fps** with p50 17, p95 18, p99 18
ms. A 150 s tour afterwards (27 loads, WebGL every round, real sites) ended
with 59.9 fps and no fault. The cause was not the GPU, the copies or the host's
CPU: Firefox draws its next frame when the compositor answers
`wl_surface.frame`, and that answer came back through the launcher's ssh
tunnel, where **Windows' `ssh.exe` holds a small message from the guest until
the host next sends something** — 18.8 ms a frame. wc-proxy now answers frame
callbacks itself on a 60 Hz grid, at most three ahead of the compositor
(88.4). Four smaller fixes went with it. All are deployed in `wcivs` (88.6).

### 88.2 The instrument: `WC_FRAME_TRACE`

`sv_transport::frametrace` writes `<us> <event> k=v …` lines to the file
`WC_FRAME_TRACE` names (`%p` is the pid), on a clock every process on one
machine shares (the wall clock read once, advanced by `Instant`). Off, it is
one `OnceLock` load per call site. Five processes write their half:

| process | events |
|---|---|
| the ICD, in Firefox | `icd.present`: the gap since the last present, the round trips in it by opcode, and the present's phases; `icd.put`: the `wl_shm` buffer wait, the copy, the commit |
| wc-proxy | `px.frame`, `px.c`, `px.attach`, `px.commit` (with its copy time); `px.gdone` and `px.release` arriving from the compositor; `px.done` sent to the client, and by whom |
| the compositor | `wc.c` per commit, `wc.done`/`wc.done_sub` per answered callback, `wc.present` (read and compose time), `wc.turn` per loop turn that handled a commit, `wc.paint` on the UI thread (wait for `WM_PAINT`, `SetDIBitsToDevice`) |
| the GPU side | `gs.ops`: each ring's second, by opcode and execution time |
| the harness | `harness.scroll-begin`/`-end` around each round |

`scripts/wc-frame-timeline.py` joins them. The guest's wall clock is not the
host's (it ran 1.570–1.573 s behind); the offset is estimated NTP-style from
the k-th commit and the k-th answered callback both sides saw, which assumes
the two directions' fastest crossings are equal, so the split between them is
an estimate and is labelled as one. `scripts/wc-cpu-sample.py` samples the
host's CPUs and threads. `sv-firefox-soak.py` gained `SOAK_MODE=scroll` and
reports rAF percentiles; `sv-firefox-wayland.sh scroll` runs it locally.

### 88.3 Where a frame went, before

Medians per frame, while scrolling, one run (`timeline-base.txt`):

| stage | p50 | p95 |
|---|---|---|
| present to present | **21.2 ms** | 31.5 ms |
| Firefox between presents | 17.8 | 28.6 |
| … of it blocked on GPU-side round trips (5 a frame) | 7.3 | 10.4 |
| … `vkWaitForFences` ×1, `vkResetCommandPool` ×2.1, `vkWaitSemaphores` ×1 | 4.5, 1.65, 0.74 | |
| present: reset + submit, fence wait, copy into `wl_shm` | 0.05, 2.0, 1.2 | |
| proxy: copy into the compositor's arena | 1.3 | |
| compositor: read the arena, compose the window | 0.8, 1.6 | |
| **`wl_surface.frame` to its `done`, at the proxy** | **18.8** | 24.8 |
| host CPUs 14 and 15 (`user.slice`'s cpuset; the VM has 0–13) | 34 %, 33 % | peaks 48–50 % |

So the host was not CPU-bound, the GPU-side copies were small, and the frame
period was the callback round trip. The order on the wire showed why: the
compositor answered each callback at once (`wc.done_now`, a subsurface) and
flushed, and the proxy received the answer only **after the host's next
commit had reached the guest**, every frame. With nothing else crossing
(Firefox idle at start-up) answers took 22–35 ms.

**The tunnel, measured alone.** `probe-tunnel-latency.exe` on the guest sends
a timestamped 24-byte message every 47 ms through an `ssh.exe -N -T -R` forward
shaped like the launcher's, to `wc-tunnel-latency.py` on the host, which can
also send an 8-byte ping every N ms that the guest echoes:

| host-to-guest traffic | guest's unprompted message, wait above the fastest | prompted round trip |
|---|---|---|
| none (two runs) | p50 0.5 / 29.9 ms, p99 22.6 / 46.6 ms | — |
| a ping every 10 ms | p50 14.4, p90 24.3 ms | p50 12.2, p90 22.1 ms |
| a ping every 2 ms | p50 2.3, p90 7.2 ms | p50 3.0, p90 9.0 ms |

The guest-to-host direction of `ssh.exe` (OpenSSH_for_Windows 9.5p2) moves
when something arrives from the host. It is not Nagle's algorithm: answers 50
to 80 ms apart, long since acknowledged, waited just as long, and the relay's
socket with `TCP_NODELAY` (88.4 item 5) changed nothing (`timeline-a1.txt`:
41 fps, `done` 14.1 ms after the compositor sent it). Nothing of ours reaches
inside `ssh.exe`.

### 88.4 The fixes

1. **wc-proxy keeps the client's frame clock** (`crates/wc-proxy/src/pace.rs`,
   `--pace-frames 60`, passed by `wc-session`). Each `wl_surface.frame` is still
   forwarded; the proxy answers it on its own 60 Hz grid, and the compositor's
   later `done` is swallowed and returns a credit. At most `--pace-depth` (3)
   callbacks may be answered ahead of the compositor, so a compositor that
   stops answering stops the client after three frames, as it would have
   directly. Two rules came from running it. A compositor answer that arrives
   first must not reach the client: forwarding those gave Firefox two clocks
   and **120 fps under Wine**; it pre-pays the credit instead and the client
   still hears the grid. And the compositor's `delete_id` for such a callback
   is held until the proxy's own `done` has gone, or the client would be told
   its callback is gone while still waiting on it. `done` carries
   `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` milliseconds, which Firefox evidently uses as its vsync
   time: rAF timestamps became whole milliseconds, hence the 17/18 ms
   percentiles.
2. **The compositor's frame clock** (`tick::FrameClock`). Window callbacks were
   answered on the first 5 ms turn at least 16 ms after the last answer — every
   20 ms — and subsurface callbacks at once. Now every callback asked for
   before a tick is answered on it, the loop sleeps no later than the next
   tick, and the grid lies on DWM's vblank when DWM reports one (an interactive
   session; not exercised here) or runs free at 60 Hz. For a proxied client it
   now only paces the credits; for a client on the guest itself it is the
   display rate.
3. **Two round trips gone.** `vkResetFences` and `vkResetCommandPool` are sent
   without asking for a reply, as `vkQueueSubmit` already was (D15):
   `VK_SUCCESS` is synthesised and a refusal makes the ring fatal. The rings
   keep the order (later waits share the device ring, later submits carry a
   barrier past it). Round trips per frame went from 5 to 2 (p50).
4. **A pipelined present** (`crate::wsi::Presenter`). `vkQueuePresentKHR`
   resets and submits the copy and returns; the swapchain's presenter thread
   waits for it on the **queue** ring (on the device ring the wait would hold
   that ring for the copy's length) and puts the frame into `wl_shm`.
   `vkAcquireNextImageKHR` waits for an image whose copy is still being shown.
   The present costs Firefox's renderer thread 0.06 ms instead of 3.3.
   `SV_PRESENT_SYNC=1` restores the old order.
5. **Small things.** wc-proxy is deployed in release (it parses every message
   and copies every frame on the host's two cores; the debug build's commit to
   copy was 24 ms at p99). `probe-relay.exe` sets `TCP_NODELAY` and an ACK per
   segment on its socket to `ssh.exe` — not the cause, but a byte pipe for an
   interactive protocol should not wait for ACKs.

Not changed, because the timeline said they were not where the time went: the
GDI blit (not measurable in session 0, where `WM_PAINT` never came, 88.7), the
two 4 MB copies (1.0 ms each, off the renderer thread now), the compositor's
5 ms turn, and the host's cpuset.

### 88.5 After

The same harness and build shape, one run each; the first four on `wcgpu`:

| | before (`base`) | relay + grid, no proxy clock (`a1`) | all five (`a2`) | 150 s tour (`soak`) | deployed `wcivs` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| scroll fps (three rounds) | 44.6, 45.3, 43.7 | 42.0, 38.6, 43.1 | **60.4, 60.3, 60.3** | 59.9 (one round) | **60.4, 60.2, 60.4** |
| rAF frame time p50 / p95 / p99 | 21.7 / 27.7 / 38.3 ms | 22.4 / 34.8 / 47.5 | **17 / 18 / 18** | 17 / 18 / 18 | 17 / 18 / 18 |
| present to present p50 / p95 / p99 | 21.2 / 31.5 / 45.5 | 22.7 / 34.2 / 47.0 | 16.6 / 20.5 / 22.9 | 16.6 / 20.6 / 21.8 | 16.7 / 20.1 / 22.2 |
| `frame` to `done` at the proxy, p50 | 18.8 | 20.2 | 14.2 (the grid) | | |
| round trips per frame (p50) and their time | 5, 7.3 ms | 2, 7.5 | 2, 6.5 | | |
| present on the renderer thread | 3.3 ms | 0.08 | 0.06 | | |
| `wl_shm` buffer waits | 0 of 720 | 0 of 691 | 1 of 960 | 0 of 320 | 0 of 960 |
| host CPUs 14 / 15 | 34 / 33 % | 32 / 31 % | 40 / 40 % | | 25 / 25 % |

Firefox's own time from a `done` to its next present is p50 12.3, p95 16.0,
p99 17.6 ms (13.0, 16.8, 18.7 before): 60 is reached, with little room. The
GPU side's driver spends 5.7 ms a frame in `vkWaitForFences`, Zink waiting for
the Intel GPU.

Locally (Wine compositor, RADV, wc-proxy, same harness) the grid alone gave
60.3 fps with p50 16.66 ms where the 5 ms turn had given 175 fps unpaced, and
the proxy's clock kept it at 60.3; the first version of the proxy's clock
gave 120.

On the guest: three scroll runs and one tour on `wcgpu`, four tunnel probes

## 89. Input in under a millisecond: the Wayland connections leave ssh for rings in the ivshmem region

Written 2026-10-16, on branch `tunnel-latency`, from master 03b0585. The brief:
§88 left input (keyboard, pointer, wheel, from Win32 on the guest to Firefox
on the host) waiting behind `ssh.exe`'s hold on small guest-to-host messages;
measure the input path end to end, choose a low-latency transport for the
Wayland stream with evidence, build it with the old path as a loud fallback,
verify on the guest, and enable it in `wcivs`. Every guest run was in session
0 over ssh, on the `wcgpu` test installation until the last step, with a
health watchdog (ssh to the guest and ping from the VM host, every 15 s) that
never failed. The results are in `docs/tunnel-latency/`.

### 89.1 Status in one paragraph

**Input from Windows to the client's socket now takes 0.70 ms at the median,
2.40 ms at p99 and 3.17 ms at worst, against 14.93, 34.98 and 50.91 ms
before** (Firefox on a static page; the animated and wheel cases are in 89.6).
The Wayland connections are §36's rings, at last used by the launcher: the
compositor keeps the last 6 MiB of its ivshmem BAR (§83) for a 32-slot
shared_vulkan control region, the header says where, and a second
virtio-serial port, `org.sirati.wcbell.0`, carries the wakes in both
directions, as §87's port does for the GPU. The crossing itself is 0.02 ms,
below what the clock can resolve. Two smaller fixes in the compositor took the
rest: the Wayland thread is woken by queued input instead of finishing a 5 ms
wait, and pumps the rings again after it flushes. ssh keeps authentication,
control, the sound, the GPU's cold path and the icon and clipboard feeds; a
session without the port falls back to the tunnel and says so, in capitals,
at four layers. Scrolling stays at 60 fps and sound is unchanged. Deployed in
`wcivs`; the port was hot-added to the running VM and its NixOS persistence is
built and dry-activated but not switched (89.8).

### 89.2 The instrument

§88's `WC_FRAME_TRACE` gained an input timeline and a clock that can be
compared across the two machines.

| stamp | where | what |
|---|---|---|
| `inj` | `probe-input-latency.exe` (guest) | posts `WM_MOUSEMOVE`, or a move and a `WM_MOUSEWHEEL`, into the largest window of `sv-guest.exe`, every 25–75 ms (jittered so nothing that ticks hides its share) |
| `wc.in` | compositor, UI thread | the window procedure has the event |
| `wc.in_tx` | compositor, Wayland thread | the event leaves the UI channel for smithay |
| `wc.flush` | compositor, Wayland thread | the turn's flush: its bytes are in the socket, or the ring |
| `px.in` | wc-proxy | the event parsed from the compositor's stream, with its `time` |
| `px.out` | wc-proxy | the write to the client's socket that carried it returned |

`WC_FRAME_TRACE_CLOCK=mono` stamps with `QueryPerformanceCounter` on the guest
and `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` on the host, which every process on a machine shares
whatever the wall clock is doing. The offset between the two counters is
measured, not estimated from the traffic being timed: `wc-clock-sync.py`
pings `probe-tunnel-latency.exe` every 5 ms over a second tunnel made with Git
for Windows' ssh (whose guest-to-host direction does not hold, 89.4), keeps
the fastest ping of every two-second window and fits a line through them. In
every run the fastest round trips were 0.17–1.35 ms, the drift 1–4 ppm, and no
window lay more than 69 µs off the line; a crossing below about 0.1 ms is
therefore below the instrument, which is why two medians in 89.6 read −0.00
and −0.02. `scripts/wc-input-latency.py` pairs the stamps (by the event's
`time` where it has one, by position for `wl_pointer.enter`) and reports each
gap. In session 0 the real cursor is never over the window, so the
compositor's `TrackMouseEvent` answers every posted move with
`WM_MOUSELEAVE` and every move becomes an `enter`; it takes the same path from
`wc.in` on.

### 89.3 Where an input event went, before

`wcgpu`, accelerated Firefox, 60 s each, ms:

| stage | static page p50 / p90 / p99 / max | animated page (60 Hz) | wheel (scrolling) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Windows to the window procedure | 0.15 / 0.22 / 0.33 / 0.55 | 0.15 / 0.22 / 0.32 / 0.51 | 0.13 / 0.23 / 0.36 / 0.73 |
| waiting for the Wayland thread's turn | 2.88 / 5.16 / 7.13 / 8.59 | 2.47 / 5.02 / 5.42 / 6.03 | 2.92 / 6.00 / 8.39 / 9.32 |
| smithay to the flush | 0.25 / 2.03 / 3.78 / 4.59 | 0.20 / 0.38 / 0.67 / 1.54 | 0.29 / 2.35 / 4.30 / 5.17 |
| **the crossing** (relay, ssh.exe, sshd, the socket) | **11.39 / 23.17 / 30.84 / 46.33** | **14.73 / 28.19 / 37.42 / 55.47** | 0.45 / 1.32 / 20.49 / 25.62 |
| wc-proxy | 0.03 / 0.07 / 0.65 / 3.16 | 0.03 / 0.05 / 0.12 / 0.97 | 0.03 / 0.19 / 0.95 / 3.02 |
| **Windows to the client's socket** | **14.93 / 26.93 / 34.98 / 50.91** | **17.95 / 31.42 / 38.96 / 56.31** | 4.83 / 9.26 / 24.36 / 34.22 |

The hold is not cured by the client drawing: with a square turning at 60 Hz
the crossing was worse, because the frames go over the GPU rings and the
proxy now answers frame callbacks itself (§88), so little Wayland traffic
flows from host to guest to release the guest's messages. Scrolling releases
them, by commits, most of the time and not at p99.

### 89.4 The candidates, and the choice

| candidate | crossing, measured or expected | authority the guest gains | robustness | fit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ssh.exe as now | p50 11.4, p99 30.8 ms (89.3) | — | works | — |
| a host-to-guest keepalive at 2 ms (§88's probe) | p50 2.3, p90 7.2 ms | none | costs a wake every 2 ms on both machines for as long as a session is up | a workaround for another program's bug |
| **Git for Windows' ssh** (OpenSSH 10.3, MSYS2) as the tunnel | **p50 0.58, p99 0.99, max 1.75 ms** end to end; 0.65/1.06 ms above the fastest crossing alone | none: the same key, forced command and forwards | depends on a third-party install being on the guest; its key-permission check passes only because MSYS2 mounts with `noacl`; it refused to start the launcher's tunnel because stale tunnels of other sessions still held the audio port (Windows' ssh.exe binds beside them) | the data stays in ssh, encrypted, through a relay process and TCP |
| plain TCP on the host-only link with a per-session secret | ~1 ms (the link's ping is 0.73–1.15 ms) | a new listener on the host reachable from the guest's network; the secret is the only thing keeping anything else on that link out | needs a firewall rule on the host (a networking change, which this work may not make) | a second authenticated channel beside ssh |
| vsock | tens of µs | a new device class and a host listener on a vsock port any host process could bind first | `/dev/vhost-vsock` exists on the host, but the guest has **no viosock driver** (virtio-win's installed set is balloon, ivshmem, viofs, vioinput, viorng, vioscsi, vioser, viostor, netkvm, viomem): a new kernel driver and a Winsock provider on a machine a family member uses daily | a second transport family |
| a virtio-serial port carrying the Wayland bytes | tens of µs (§36.6.3: 17.6 µs round trip) | none new (89.9) | one opener per port, so Firefox's several connections, the feeds and resynchronisation after a session all need a multiplexing layer | §36.3 rejected one stream for several connections: head-of-line blocking and an id-rewriting layer |
| **§36's rings in the ivshmem region, a virtio-serial port as the doorbell** | **0.02 ms** (89.6) | none new (89.9) | the driver is already installed and the port is hot-pluggable (§87.5); the ring code is shared_vulkan's, Miri-checked; a missing port falls back | the design's own answer: §36.2 calls a Wayland connection a ring slot and "the real one" |

The last is chosen. It is the only candidate whose latency is the hypervisor's
rather than a network's, it moves no authority (89.9 and security-model.md
R31), it needs no driver the guest does not have, and it is what §36 said the
Wayland connection should have been from the start. Git's ssh is the measured
runner-up and the cheapest; it is recorded here because a fallback that wanted
to be faster could use it, not built.

### 89.5 What was built

**The region.** `wc_handle::arena::attach_ivshmem_with_rings` keeps the BAR's
last `Geometry::for_wayland().control_size` (6 MiB) out of the arena: the
arena's offset 0 stays at byte 4096 and only its length shrinks, by 6 MiB of
128. The header (`wc_handle::ivshmem`) is version 2: `rings` at offsets 64 and
72, in region offsets, refused anywhere but the region's tail; a version-1
header reads as one with no rings, so a host updated first still serves an
older compositor. `Geometry::for_wayland` is 32 slots of 64 KiB lanes (a
Wayland message is at most 4 KiB; 32 is below the doorbell byte's 64 slots).

**Slots come back.** `Control::kill_ring` kept a dead slot dead for the
region's life, which was right for a test and wrong for a twelve-hour session.
`Control::recycle_ring` (owner only, `DEAD` only, never the reverse ring) zeroes
the control block and stores `FREE` with release; the proxy marks `DEAD` as its
last touch of a connection (`RingUpstream`'s `Drop`, after its end of stream);
the compositor's `RingLink::reap` treats `DEAD` with an empty lane as the end
of the stream, ends the client, and recycles slots no link of its own still
uses. `scripts/wc-rings.sh` runs 40 clients in a row through one recycled slot.

**The doorbell.** The compositor opens `org.sirati.wcbell.0` (half a second's
wait, not the ten `PortHandle::guest_port` gives a port being hot-added) and
installs its writer as the process's `CrossWake`; `Bell::ring` pokes it when
the proxy is parked. wc-proxy connects to QEMU's socket for the port, installs
its writer the same way, and runs one thread (`rings::BellHub`) that turns a
byte naming a connection's reply lane into a write to that connection's
`eventfd`, which is in the pump's `poll` set. Both sides park on the lane they
read before they sleep and look once more after, `Bell`'s handshake with a
`poll` and a waitable timer where the futex was. A ring with a doorbell sleeps
like a socket; the 20 ms timeout is only the bound on a lost byte.

**The compositor's turn.** `tick::Ticker` gained a `Waker` (an auto-reset
event on Windows) that the UI thread sets when it queues an event and the
doorbell's reader sets on every byte, so the loop handles input on arrival.
That took the turn from p50 2.88, p99 7.13 ms to 0.09 and 1.81. The rings are
pumped again right after `flush_clients`, so what smithay flushed leaves in the
same turn instead of the next.

**The launch path.** `wc-launch` passes `--wayland-rings <wayland-bell>`
(default `org.sirati.wcbell.0`, empty to turn it off) and logs what the
compositor said. `wc-session up` reads the header's version and rings and
checks the port's socket; `proxy` adds `--wayland-rings --wayland-bell` only
when both are there and reports what the proxy made of them. The proxy keeps
`--upstream`: the icon and clipboard feeds use it, and so does any connection
that cannot have a ring. The tunnel is opened exactly as before.

### 89.7 Two things found that are not this section's

**Stale tunnels in `wcgpu`.** Three Windows `ssh.exe` tunnels started on
2026-10-15 between 18:36 and 18:51 (the §87 sessions, parent processes gone)
still listen on `wcgpu`'s audio port 57472, and Windows' ssh.exe binds a fourth
beside them; the launcher's sound then connects to one of the stale ones and
plays nothing ("0.0 s played"), which is how every `wcgpu` session of this
section ran until the audio checks moved to port 57475. They were not started
by this work and were not killed; whoever owns them can end them by pid (2860,
8300, 5840) or let the next guest restart do it. `wcivs`'s ports were free.
The launcher now kills its relay and tunnel when a cold start fails after
starting them, which is one way such a tunnel was being left behind.

**An idle sink drops and underruns.** On a page that plays nothing, the
launcher's player counted 44 dropped chunks and 6.25 underruns a second, on
the rings and on the ssh path alike (`wcivs`, 41 s and 74 s); with a tone
playing the counts stop growing after the first seconds. The PCM of an idle
null sink arrives in bursts. It is inaudible (it is silence) and predates this
section; it is recorded because the counters look alarming.

### 89.8 The VM side

The port was hot-added to the running VM over QMP as root, with the ids the
persistent configuration uses: `chardev-add` of a server socket
`/run/windows-vm/wc-arena/wcbell.sock` with id `wcbell`, `device_add
virtserialport,bus=vioserial.0,chardev=wcbell,name=org.sirati.wcbell.0,id=wcbellport`,
then `chgrp wc-arena`, `chmod 0660` and `setfacl -m u:sirati:rw` on the
socket. `query-status` said `running` before and after, the watchdog never
failed, and the guest opened the port by name at once.

nix-config branch `testhost-wc-wayland-rings` (6511e8a, on c1cd31a, which
builds to exactly generation 53's `g9vz217c…`) adds
`waycomposeArena.waylandBell` beside `doorbell`: the same chardev and port on
the QEMU command line, the socket in the `ExecStartPost` that gives the GPU's
socket its group and named ACLs, and removal with the arena's files. testhost
enables it. The system `k77fwidz…` is built, copied to testhost, pinned by
`~/wc-tl/system-wcbell`, and `switch-to-configuration dry-activate` says
**"would NOT stop the following changed units: windows-vm.service"** and
nothing else. **It is not switched**: switching is the owner's step. Until it
is, the next VM start drops the port and every session falls back to the
tunnel, loudly. The switch is
`sudokey run -- /nix/store/k77fwidz52c4s2ghd9wff2q08sadfnx3-nixos-system-testhost-26.11.20260819.ffb3c9b/bin/switch-to-configuration switch`
together with `nix-env -p /nix/var/nix/profiles/system --set` on that path for
a boot entry; `windows-vm.service` has `restartIfChanged = false`, so the VM
keeps running.

### 89.9 Security

The guest gains no authority (security-model.md R31 has the argument). In
short: what crosses is bytes into a region the guest could already write
(the ivshmem arena, R29) and one byte per wake into a socket QEMU made, `0660
root:wc-arena` with a named ACL for `sirati`, exactly like §87's. Nothing new
listens on the host: QEMU's chardev is the listener, the filesystem is its
authentication, and wc-proxy *connects* to it. The guest's port has one opener,
and whatever guest process holds it can only send wakes to, and write Wayland
bytes for, the proxy that already parses everything the guest sends. The
proxy still checks the header's run id before it attaches the rings, the ring
layout against its own, and bounds every offset. ssh keeps the guest's one
authority on the host: the forced command, its verbs and its forwards are
unchanged. No descriptor can cross: the ring takes `&[u8]` and the doorbell a
`u8` (§14.7, §36.5).

### 89.12 What is not measured, and what is not done

* **The interactive desktop.** As in §88, nobody was logged in: input was
  posted into a session-0 window, so the time from a real device to the window
  procedure (Windows' own input stack) is not in these numbers, and every move
  was an `enter`. From the window procedure on, the path is the one a person's
  input takes.
* **The client's own reading.** The path ends at wc-proxy's write into the
  client's socket; Firefox's read of it is a local `AF_UNIX` hop.
* **Host to guest** is faster too (the doorbell wakes the compositor when the
  proxy writes, where a commit used to wait for the next 5 ms turn) and was not
  timed separately; §88's scroll numbers are its check.
* **Still on ssh:** the clipboard and icon feeds (one each per connection; a
  paste from Windows into Firefox still waits for the hold), the sound (host to
  guest, which ssh.exe does not hold), and the GPU's cold path. Moving the feeds
  onto rings is two more claims per connection and is the next step if a
  paste ever feels slow.
* **The NixOS switch** (89.8).

## 90. The desktop test: Firefox from the shortcut, on the desktop a person uses

Branch `desktop-e2e`, 2026-10-16, 03:56–04:47. The first run of the whole
product on the guest's interactive desktop (session 1), with a person logged in
for it, against the checklist of `docs/goal-firefox.md`. Everything before this
ran in session 0, under Wine, or both. The evidence is in `docs/desktop-e2e/`.

### 90.1 Status in one paragraph

Through the click route the harnesses have always used, Firefox works on the
desktop:
- **the window.** A real window that drags, maximises, snaps and resizes, with
  its tabs in the caption.
- **the title.** It is correct and follows tab switches.
- **rendering.** Hardware WebRender on zink on the Intel UHD, at 58–60 fps
  while scrolling.
- **input.** Keyboard, mouse, menus, cursors and the clipboard in both
  directions.
- **two windows.** A second window renders.
- **the session end.** Closing the last window ends the session after 60 s.

Four things are wrong.
1. **A real double-click gets a much worse product.** The harnesses' click
   runs elevated; Explorer's runs at medium integrity, and at medium integrity
   the virtio-serial doorbells cannot be opened. That cold start took 12.7 s
   instead of 2.3 s, Firefox fell back to software WebRender, and the window
   came minutes late (90.3).
2. **The taskbar and Alt-Tab icon was Windows' generic one.** The launcher's
   Firefox package has no `share/`. **Fixed** and proven on the guest (90.4).
3. **Hardware video decode produces empty pictures.** H.264 and HEVC play with
   advancing clocks and no error, and every pixel is (0,77,0). VP9, decoded in
   software, shows the same clip correctly through the same path (90.5).
4. **Windows' caption buttons vanish now and then**, while still working
   (90.6).

The second window also opens at 252x304 in the screen's corner (90.7).

### 90.2 Verdicts against the goal

| requirement (goal-firefox.md) | verdict | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| appears as a window on Windows | **pass** | `A-window.png`, `B-after-drag.png`, `B-maximised.png`, `B-snap-hover.png`, `B-after-topedge.png`, `H-win1.png`, `H-win2.png`; hit tests and rectangles in `actions.txt` (`w2`, `b1`, `b2`) |

| title correct | **pass** | Alt-Tab `alttab-*.png` ("Mozilla Firefox"); `actions.txt` `h3`: Ctrl+T gives `Mozilla Firefox`, Ctrl+Tab back gives the page's title; every navigation's title reached `GetWindowText` within 110–705 ms (`c1`, `d1`, `d2`, `e1`) |
| Firefox paints its UI into the title bar | **pass, with bug 90.6** | `A-window.png` (tabs in the caption; buttons at x 780–923 clear of the tab-list button at 761), `B-snap-hover.png` (snap-layouts flyout on hover), `B-maximised.png`; `caption-buttons-*.png` for the bug |

### 90.3 Bug: a real double-click runs at medium integrity, and the doorbells refuse it

The guest's Explorer starts a shortcut at medium integrity. The first click of
this run was exactly that: `Start-Process` on the `.lnk`, from a process in
session 1 at the `Limited` run level. The launcher's log (`medium-launcher.log`):

```
SSH FALLBACK: the Wayland connections will cross the ssh tunnel this session -- wc-compositor: WAYLAND RINGS UNAVAILABLE: the doorbell port org.sirati.wcbell.0 did not open (CreateFileW (virtio-serial port) failed: errno 5)
gpu: [gpu] no doorbell on org.sirati.svbell.0 (CreateFileW (virtio-serial port) failed: errno 5); waits will run out their slice
cold start: 12711 ms
CLICK-TO-WINDOW never (cold); no window mapped in 120 s
```

Firefox's own log said `Failed to create EGLConfig for WebRender!` and then
`Fallback WR to SW-WR`. A window was up at 04:09, 4.5 minutes after the click,
at 516x128. It later grew to the profile's 931x525. It rendered, with its tabs in
the caption (`medium-window.png`).

**The cause, measured.** One `CreateFileW` of
`\\.\Global\org.sirati.wcbell.0` and `…svbell.0` (`GENERIC_READ|WRITE`):

- from a scheduled task at the `Limited` run level (`S-1-16-8192`, medium):
  both fail with error 5;
- from the ssh session, which holds the administrator's full token: both open.

The ivshmem devices (the arena and the GPU slot) do open at medium integrity
(`arena 0 provided from ivshmem`, `mapped in 12.44ms`). So §83.9's question
about the device at medium has a split answer: ivshmem yes, virtio-serial no.

**Why no earlier section saw it.** `wc-launch.sh`'s `runint.ps1` registers its
task with `-RunLevel Highest`, so every click of every harness ran the launcher
elevated. The same shortcut through that route: rings and both doorbells up,
cold start 2.3 s, and a window in **4302 ms** (later 4430 ms and 3963 ms).
Everything else in this section used that route, because it is the one the brief
names.

**Not fixed.** The fix is a security descriptor on the virtio-serial port
devices that lets the interactive user open them. That is a change to the guest
system and to the security argument of security-model.md R31 (any medium
process of that user could then write to the ports). It is the owner's step. The
alternative is a launcher that runs elevated, which would put a UAC prompt on
every click.

### 90.4 Bug, fixed: the generic icon

The compositor's log: `icon published for "firefox": 0 image(s) []`, and the
proxy's: `app id "firefox": nothing to show (no firefox.desktop in any data
directory, and no theme has "firefox" either)`. Since §87.14 the launcher runs
`firefox-readback`, a package with `bin/` and `lib/` and no `share/`, so neither
a theme nor §18.5's walk up from the executable finds anything. The desktop
shortcut still showed Firefox's icon only because it was installed before that
switch.

The package's pixels are `lib/firefox/browser/chrome/icons/default/default{16,32,48,64,128}.png`
(Thunderbird uses `chrome/icons/default/`). `icons::bundled_icons` collects
`default<N>.png` from beside the client's `/proc/<pid>/exe`, and `resolve` uses
them only when no theme has the name, so a user's theme still wins. A new unit
test covers the layout, the precedence and Thunderbird's variant.

On the guest after the deploy (90.10):

```
[proxy] client 2: icon: app id "firefox": icon "firefox" -> 3 image(s) [48x48 32x32 16x16] from …/firefox-readback-157.0.1/lib/firefox/browser/chrome/icons/default/default16.png (24.3 ms)
wc-compositor: window 1 icon set: 2 of 2 slots from 3 image(s) [48x48 32x32 16x16]
```

Two visual checks agreed: before the fix, the taskbar button and the Alt-Tab
entry wore the generic icon; after it, both show Firefox's
(`taskbar-before.png`, `taskbar-after.png`, `alttab-before.png`,
`alttab-after.png`).

### 90.5 Bug: hardware decode returns empty pictures

Hardware decode is advertised, and it is used:
- about:support Media lists H264 and HEVC under hardware decoding
  (`C-support-codecs.png`);
- the GPU side serves `VK_KHR_video_decode_h264` and `…h265`.

But the picture is empty. One 30 s clip (a navy frame, a yellow running
timestamp, and a white flash with a beep every second) was played in three
encodings, about 4 s into each:

| encoding | decoded by | video area |
|---|---|---|
| VP9 (`P-vp9.png`) | Firefox, in software | correct: 7008 colours, mean (36,37,64), timestamp `00:00:03.833` |
| H.264 High (`P-h264.png`, and `E-video.png` 20 minutes earlier) | the GPU side, Vulkan Video | **one colour, (0,77,0)** |
| HEVC Main (`P-hevc.png`) | the GPU side, Vulkan Video | **one colour, (0,77,0)** |

(0,77,0) is BT.709 limited-range YUV with all three planes zero. In every case
the page's own counters advance: 102 frames in 3.4 s with 0 dropped, and over a
16 s run 479 frames with 2 dropped, all `err=none`. No `GUARD`, fault or error
line appears in the GPU log, so the failure is silent.

**Not known: whether this is the new driver.** The guest's driver went from
101.7076 to 101.7092 just before this run. §87.13 and §87.14 checked frame
counts and about:support on the guest, never the decoded pixels, so there is no
earlier picture to compare with. It is reported here for whoever evaluates the
driver; nothing was rolled back or changed.

**Audio.** Played and consumed. The launcher's player counted 20.4 s that was
not silence over the first session, which is the clip's 0.1 s beep per second.
A/V sync was not measured, and nobody confirmed hearing it.

### 90.6 Bug: Windows' caption buttons vanish, and still work

Windows' minimise, maximise and close glyphs are sometimes missing from a
maximised window, in both sessions:
- the corner shows only the tab strip's colour (`caption-buttons-scroll-vs-webgl.png`,
  `caption-buttons-X-series.png`, `caption-buttons-Y-series.png`,
  `caption-buttons-P-h264.png`);
- they come back for single frames (`Y03` in the series) and after some
  navigations;
- a second session stayed correct through the same sequence
  (`caption-buttons-session2.png`) and then lost them on a video page.

The buttons still work while invisible: hit tests answer `HTMAXBUTTON` and
`HTCLOSE`, and two closes in this run clicked an invisible close button.

The only paint path, `WM_PAINT`, does `SetDIBitsToDevice` and then `FillRect`s
the button strip with alpha 0 inside the same clip, so neither half of
`uncover_caption_buttons` is skipped by a partial update. Something else makes
the strip opaque again between paints. Not found. Candidates for the next look:
- DWM's caption-colour updates (`match_caption_colour` sets
  `DWMWA_CAPTION_COLOR` many times a second while Firefox animates its tab strip;
  the log has runs of 10–14 lines);
- `DwmDefWindowProc` not seeing the non-client mouse messages;
- the 1 px rounding between DWM's bounds and `nc_top`.

Smaller things seen in the same captures:
- a 1 px black row above the buttons of a restored window (§82.7's corner
  alpha);
- a 1 px dark line under the button strip after scrolling
  (`caption-buttons-session2.png`, rows 2 and 4).

### 90.7 Bug: the second window opens at 252x304, in the corner

A second click while Firefox ran: **758 ms** to a new window, which is the
warm number. That window is real Firefox and renders (`H-win2.png`), so the
black second window of §85.7 is Wine's. But it was mapped at 252x304 at (0,0),
and it stayed that size, with its toolbar clipped. The medium-integrity first
window also started small (516x128) before it took the profile's size. Both
look like the size Firefox commits before it has read its own saved geometry,
taken by the compositor as final. Not investigated further.

## 91. A double-click gets the doorbells, the fallback takes seconds, and two window bugs

Branch `medium-il`, 2026-10-16. The three bugs §90 left open that are not the
video decode: a real double-click ran without the ring and GPU doorbells
(§90.3), Windows' caption buttons vanished from maximised windows (§90.6), and a
second window opened at 252x304 in the screen's corner (§90.7).

### 91.1 Status in one paragraph

All three are fixed.
- **Bug 1.** The two virtio-serial ports carried vioser's admin-only descriptor.
  They now admit the interactive user at medium integrity (91.2,
  security-model.md R32). The first real double-click after the change,
  <guest-user>'s own at 05:48, had rings, both doorbells and a window in 3173 ms.
- **The slow fallback.** The guest's waits cost a 15.6 ms timer tick per rung
  when no doorbell was attached, and the port open retried access denied for
  10 s. Both are fixed (91.3).
- **The harness** now clicks with a double-click's token by default and checks
  the route from the launcher's own `token:` line (91.4).
- **Bug 2.** `DefWindowProc` painted the caption over the button strip on every
  title change (91.5).
- **Bug 3.** The map echoed the client's first size back as a configure, which
  Firefox obeyed, and read the window's position before Windows had chosen it
  (91.6). A maximise asked for before the first frame was undone by the map,
  and a client that commits only its minimum now gets a default size.
- **GTK dialogs** (reported from real use while this ran): the file chooser's
  *Open* sat under Windows' buttons. A session-private GTK sheet pads every
  header bar by the buttons' width (91.8).

On the guest (91.7) the double-click route is proven. The caption buttons and
the dialogs are measured on the Linux build only, because <guest-user>'s session was
locked for the rest of the run.

### 91.2 Bug 1: the ports' descriptor

**Measured.** `QueryDosDevice("Global\org.sirati.wcbell.0")` is `\Device\00000042`,
the PDO of `{6FDE7547-…}\VIOSERIALPORT\4&34687BC8&0&05`, and `svbell.0` is
`…&0&04` (`\Device\00000041`). Both device objects had
`D:P(A;;FA;;;SY)(A;;FA;;;BA)S:AI(ML;;NW;;;LW)` and no PnP `Security` property.
That is vioser's `WdfDeviceInitAssignSDDLString(…, SDDL_DEVOBJ_SYS_ALL_ADM_ALL)`
for its raw port PDOs (vioserial `Port.c`). The `Global\` alias is not a
different object with a different descriptor, as `winpipe.rs` had guessed; it is
a link to the PDO. The ivshmem devices, by contrast, admit Everyone (R32 quotes
their descriptor), which is why §90.3 saw them open at medium.

**The options.**

| option | verdict |
|---|---|
| descriptor on the two port PDOs | **chosen**: no resident component, one account, medium and up, survives reboots through the PnP property |
| doorbell on the ivshmem device (`ivshmem-doorbell`; the Looking Glass driver has `IOCTL_IVSHMEM_RING_DOORBELL` and event registration) | needs the VM reconfigured and restarted and an `ivshmem-server` on the host |
| a guest service owning the ports, relaying over an ACL'd pipe | a new resident component, a hop per wake, and the same grant as a pipe ACL |
| an elevated launcher | a UAC prompt per click, and an administrator token for the session |

**The fix**, `scripts/wc-port-access.ps1` (`show`, `apply`, `revert`, `install`,
`uninstall`). It sets
`D:P(A;;FA;;;SY)(A;;FA;;;BA)(A;;FRFW;;;<SID>)S:(ML;;NWNR;;;ME)` both as the
device's PnP property (`SPDRP_SECURITY_SDS`, applied by PnP at every device
start) and on the live device object (`SetSecurityInfo` on a handle). `install`
also copies itself to `C:\Program Files\waycompose` and registers the SYSTEM
task `waycompose port access`, which runs `apply` at every startup and finds the
ports by name. `wc-launch.sh deploy` runs `install -User <guest-user>`
(`WC_LAUNCH_PORT_ACCESS=skip` leaves the guest alone). R32 is the security
argument.

**Applied on testhost's guest at 05:34** (`docs/medium-il/port-access.txt`):
both live descriptors and both PnP properties read back as the new one, with
<guest-user>'s SID `S-1-5-21-2794265523-3702185664-1359551570-1001`. Then, from
`docs/medium-il/probe.txt`:

| token | `CreateFileW(GENERIC_READ\|GENERIC_WRITE)` on each port |
|---|---|
| session 1, scheduler `Limited` run level: `S-1-16-8192`, not elevated | opened |
| a Low-integrity copy of that token | error 5 |
| ssh, the administrator's token | opened |
| a Low-integrity copy of the administrator's token | error 5 |

**What was not tested:** a reboot, and a vioser update. The PnP property is the
documented mechanism for both (the PnP manager applies a device's `Security`
property to its device objects when it starts the device), and the startup task
applies the descriptor whatever PnP does. Restarting a port's device to prove it
was not done: vioser creates a port's symbolic link from a work item when the
host names the port, and a restarted PDO might come back without it until the
next boot.

**A worry, tested and retired.** vioser's create handler answers a second open
of a held port with `STATUS_OBJECT_NAME_EXISTS`, which is a success code, and its
close handler then clears `GuestConnected` and tells QEMU the guest closed the
port. If a second open reached it, opening a held port even for `READ_CONTROL`
would cut the holder's host-to-guest wakes. It cannot reach it: vioser also sets
`WdfDeviceInitSetExclusive`, and the I/O manager refuses the second open. A
process that held `wcbell.0` and asked vioser (`IOCTL_GET_INFORMATION`) before
and after another process's `READ_CONTROL` open read `guest_connected=1` both
times, and the second open failed with error 5. So `wc-port-access.ps1` can run
beside a session. A held port keeps its live descriptor until it is free, and
the tool says so.

### 91.3 The fallback that took minutes

§90.3's medium-integrity session had its window 4.5 minutes after the click. Two
causes, both fixed.

**A timer tick per rung.** `Futex::first_slice` says the guest's first rung is
1 ms. Measured on the guest with a 40-sample loop: `WaitOnAddress` with a 1 ms
timeout returns after p10 15.51, p50 15.98, p90 16.22 ms; 2 ms and 8 ms timeouts
return after the same. The timeout is rounded up to the 15.625 ms tick in a
process that has not raised the timer resolution, and none of ours does
(`tick.rs`). With a doorbell this is invisible, because a delivered wake ends the
wait. Without one, every rung of every guest wait was a tick, a forwarded call
cost two ladders of 16-31 ms, and Firefox's GPU process came up so slowly that
its EGL setup failed and WebRender fell back to software. The fix is
`park::sleep_the_rung`. On Windows, in a process with no cross-VM doorbell, a
rung shorter than a tick is a `std::thread::sleep`, which is a high-resolution
waitable timer since Windows 10 1803 (0.57 ms for a 100 µs request and 1.58 ms
for 1 ms, on the same guest). Nothing on that kernel would have rung the word
anyway. With a doorbell nothing changes.

**Ten seconds of retrying access denied.** `open_virtio_port` retried every
failure for 10 s, because a hot-added port appears a moment after QEMU adds it.
That port is `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND`. Access denied is a descriptor or a holder,
and neither changes in 10 s, so it now retries for 1 s, and the error names both
causes and the script. §90.3's `gpu ok … (10378 ms)` and most of its 12.7 s cold
start were this.

The measurement of the fallback after the fix is in 91.7.

### 91.4 The harness clicks like a double-click

`runint.ps1` takes `-RunLevel`. `wc-launch.sh`'s clicks (and the native
Firefox measurement) use `Limited` unless `WC_LAUNCH_CLICK=elevated`. That is
the filtered medium token in session 1 that Explorer uses. `wc-launch.exe` logs
`token: medium integrity (S-1-16-8192), not elevated` (or what it got) once per
launch, and the cold leg checks three things: that the token is a double-click's,
that the Wayland connections are on the rings (`transport rings:`, no
`SSH FALLBACK`), and with a GPU that the GPU side has its doorbell.

Two harness bugs turned up while running a second installation beside the
deployed one. `--stop`, `--ping` and `--install` were sent without
`--session-name`, so they acted on the default session `wcl`, which is the
deployed installation a person uses. `kill_host_firefox` killed every process
matching `wc-launch/firefox`, which includes the deployed profile, and
`WC_LAUNCH_FRESH` deleted `~/.wc-launch/firefox` whatever profile the run used.
All of them now use the installation's own session and profile.

### 91.5 Bug 2: the caption buttons

The window extends DWM's frame into its client area, makes the caption-button
strip transparent in `WM_PAINT`, and lets DWM draw the buttons behind it (§82).
`DefWindowProc` answers `WM_SETTEXT`, `WM_SETICON` and `WM_NCACTIVATE` by painting
the caption it believes the window has, synchronously and outside `WM_PAINT`,
into that strip. The strip turns opaque, the buttons behind it disappear, and
hit testing still finds them. They come back when a later paint's damage covers
the strip, which is why navigations brought them back. Every capture in §90.6
that lost them was of a page that retitles itself several times a second (the
scroll counter, the video clock), and the compositor forwards each title with
`SetWindowTextW`. That the losses were all maximised follows from the order of
§90's run: every retitling page was shown after the window was maximised.

The fix is what WPF's `WindowChrome` does for this frame. For a folded window,
`WM_SETTEXT` and `WM_SETICON` go to `DefWindowProc` with `WS_VISIBLE` cleared for
the call (`defproc_without_caption_paint`), and `WM_NCACTIVATE` goes with
`lParam` -1, which tells it not to repaint the non-client area. After each, the
strip is invalidated, so the next `WM_PAINT` clears it again whatever drew there.

### 91.6 Bug 3: the second window's size and place

**The size.** `map_window` shows the window and then sizes it to the client's
first commit. `ShowWindow` on a `CW_USEDEFAULT` window sends a `WM_SIZE` with the
cascade's default size, and the `SetWindowPos` sends one with the committed
size. `on_size` turned each into an `xdg_toplevel.configure` with that size.
A configure with a size is an instruction. Firefox commits a first geometry
before it has read its saved one (252x304 for the second window, 516x128 for the
medium session's first), was told that size back, and kept it. Nothing on the
Win32 side followed a later commit either. This is also the "configured twice at
map" that the stage-38 comment in `map_window` could not explain.

Now `placing` covers the map's `ShowWindow` and `SetWindowPos`, `on_size` reports
nothing inside it, and `settle_placement` decides afterwards: a client that got
what it committed hears nothing, and one the work area shrank gets one configure
with the size it got. While a toplevel has never been configured with a size
(no user resize, maximise or fullscreen), a commit at a new window geometry is
the client choosing again. `state.rs` sends `ToUi::Resize` and the window
follows (`follow_client_size`), except during the user's own move or size loop
and while maximised or minimised. `xdg_toplevel.set_min_size` and `set_max_size`
reach Win32 as `ToUi::SizeHints` and are answered in `WM_GETMINMAXINFO`, before
the first placement.

The maximise configure used to inherit its size from the configure every window
got at map. It now carries the size of where the window's popups may go (the
monitor's work area on Windows, the output headless), and the `WM_SIZE` that
follows corrects it.

**The place.** The origin was read before `ShowWindow`, when a `CW_USEDEFAULT`
window has no position yet, and the work-area fit clamped that placeholder to the
work area's top-left corner. The `SetWindowPos` then moved the window there, over
the cascade position Windows had just chosen. It is now read after `ShowWindow`,
so a new window opens where Windows' cascade puts it, fitted to the work area.

**What Firefox commits, traced.** With `WAYLAND_DEBUG` against the Linux build:
a window Firefox opens maximised (a new window from a maximised one, or a fresh
profile on a small screen) sends `set_maximized` *before its first commit*. The
compositor answered with a maximised configure carrying 0x0, and GTK then
commits its own fallback, 252x304: that is §90.7's number. On win32,
`set_window_state` then maximised a window that had never been shown, and
`map_window`'s `SW_SHOWNORMAL` restored it at 252x304. Now a request that
arrives before the map is kept (`maximize_at_map`) and the map shows the window
with `SW_SHOWMAXIMIZED`, whose `WM_SIZE` gives the client the work area as its
size.

**Two more, found on the guest with a fresh profile.**
- Firefox's first commit there is a 1x1 geometry. Windows will not make an
  overlapped window smaller than its minimum track size (166x47 at 125%), and
  `settle_placement` first reported that larger size as a configure, which took
  the size away from Firefox: the window stayed 148x38. A placement larger than
  the commit is now not reported; only a smaller one is.
- Firefox then commits 500x120, which is exactly its own `set_min_size`. With no
  saved geometry Firefox sizes a window from `screen.availWidth`/`Height` (90%,
  at most 1280x1040), and on the guest those are not known yet when the window
  is made. A resizable toplevel with no parent, still choosing its size, whose
  commit is exactly its minimum, has chosen nothing. The compositor configures
  it to Firefox's own rule against the work area it is on and resizes the window
  to match. Dialogs, fixed-size windows (min = max) and any other size are left
  alone. This is also §90.3's medium first window, 516x128 with its frame.

**Tests.** The headless stand-in sent a `Resized` at map to mirror win32 and no
longer does (`showing_a_window_does_not_tell_it_its_own_size_back`).
WLCS headless: `XdgToplevelStableConfigurationTest.defaults`, which expects no
size in the first configure and failed on both legs before (the old comment in `control.rs` said so), now passes, and
`window_can_maximize_itself` still passes.

### 91.8 GTK's dialogs under Windows' caption buttons

Reported by the user from real use: in Firefox's Ctrl+O file chooser, the
*Open* button, at the right end of the GTK header bar, sat behind Windows'
caption buttons. The compositor's default `auto` folds the caption of every
window whose client asked to draw its own title bar, and GTK's dialogs (the file
chooser, Save As, Print) ask exactly as Firefox's main window does. Only the main
window had its corner reserved, by the launcher's `userChrome.css` (§82). The
user's ruling: keep folding the dialogs, and make GTK leave the corner empty.

**The fix.** `plan::gtk_css` renders a `gtk.css` with
`headerbar { padding-right: <reserve>px; }` at the same reservation as the tab
strip's (146, 183 and 219 px at 100, 125 and 150%), and square top corners,
because the window is opaque to GDI and the pixels outside a rounded corner
were drawn black. The launcher sends it to `wc-session run` as a seventh word,
next to the `userChrome.css`. `wc-session` gives the application a
session-private `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, because GTK 3 and 4 read `gtk.css` and
`settings.ini` from `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/gtk-{3,4}.0` and the user's own
`~/.config` is not the launcher's to write. The private directory is an overlay.
Every entry of the real one is a symbolic link back to it, and only `gtk.css`
(which imports the user's own first) and `settings.ini` (the user's, with
`gtk-decoration-layout=:` so a GTK window draws no window buttons of its own)
are replaced. A bare private directory was tried first and was wrong: the file
chooser's sidebar lost Documents, Downloads and the other user folders
(`user-dirs.dirs`), its bookmarks (`gtk-3.0/bookmarks`) and the icon theme
(dconf). On testhost the overlay also keeps `~/.config/mozilla` and
`fontconfig` reachable. A file an application creates at the top of the
directory lands in the overlay and is gone with the session.

**Measured** with Firefox 157 against the Linux compositor in `auto`, frame dumps
of the dialog (`docs/medium-il/gtk-dialogs/run.sh`; a page whose only element is
a full-window file input, a download link with downloads set to ask where, and
a print button with `print.prefer_system_dialog`, each opened by a scripted
click). The colours in the rightmost 146 columns of the header bar's rows, where
Windows draws its buttons:

| dialog | without the sheet | with it |
|---|---|---|
| Open (file chooser), 1096x869 / 1231x949 | 179 (Search and Open) | 2 (header background) |
| Save As, 1231x949 | 181 (Search and Save) | 2 |
| Print, 614x505 | 92 (Print) | 2 |

A visual check of the six frames: with the sheet, Open and Save end at x=1084
of 1231 and Print at x=467 of 614, each exactly at the boundary; no dialog has a
GTK close button either way; the overlay variant's sidebar lists the same places
with the same icons as the unmodified one. The header bars are in
`docs/medium-il/gtk-dialogs/*-headerbar.png` (cropped to the bar, because the
full frames show this workstation's volumes and printers). `about:preferences`'
file pickers are the same `GtkFileChooser`. The `settings.ini` and a GSettings
keyfile arm measured identically, so the layout override is not needed for these
three dialogs, which show no window buttons in either case; it stays for GTK
windows that would. The measurement on the guest is in 91.7.

## 92. Pinning Linux applications to the taskbar, and their jump lists

Branch `taskbar-pins`, 2026-10-16. The brief: a Linux application can be
pinned to the Windows taskbar, from its running button or from a Start menu
entry; the pinned button and the running windows are one button; right-clicking
it shows the application's own actions, and for Firefox the same jump list
Windows' Firefox shows (Frequent pages, then Open new tab, Open new window and
Open new private window); all of it survives the session ending and a reboot.
The evidence is in `docs/taskbar-pins/`.

**Status.** It works on the guest's real desktop, through clicks on the real
taskbar:
- the running button wears Firefox's name and icon (`Firefox (Linux) – 1 aktives
  Fenster`);
- "An Taskleiste anheften" from the running window's jump list pins it, and
  the pin and the window are one button;
- the jump list matches Windows' Firefox's: Häufig with the profile's pages and
  their favicons, then Neuen Tab öffnen, Neues Fenster öffnen and Neues privates
  Fenster öffnen with Firefox's glyphs. Each task works, and the private window
  is private (`Mozilla Firefox Private Browsing`);
- after the session ends, a click on the pin starts it cold (3.1 s, 4.0 s
  deployed) and the window lands on the pin;
- the Start menu entry pins to the same button.

The user's taskbar has exactly one Linux pin, the deployed `Firefox (Linux)`
(92.9).

### 92.1 One identity for the pin, the shortcuts and every window

Windows puts a window on a pinned button when the window's
`PKEY_AppUserModel_ID` equals the pinned shortcut's `System.AppUserModel.ID`.
Stage 32 already gave every window an identity derived from its Wayland app id,
`Waycompose.app.firefox` for Firefox, and that string is the same in every
session, so it is the right key for a pin. (`Waycompose.unnamed.c1` is what a
window carries between its creation and the client's `set_app_id`; Firefox's
windows move to their real identity before they are first shown.)

What was missing was the other half: nothing on the Windows side carried the
same string. The desktop shortcut was written by PowerShell's `WScript.Shell`,
which cannot set `System.AppUserModel.ID`, so a pin of it (the user had made
one, `Firefox (Linux, ivshmem)`) was a button of its own, grouped by
`wc-launch.exe`'s path, beside the windows' button.

So `wc-launch` now writes its shortcuts through `IShellLinkW` and sets the
identity on them (`src/shell.rs`, hand-written COM like the compositor's), and
it derives that identity with the compositor's own function: `taskbar.rs` is
compiled into `wc-launch` with `#[path]`. The app id it feeds in is the one
the windows will carry: `app-id` in the `[app.*]` section if set, else the
desktop entry's `StartupWMClass` (which exists to say exactly that), else the
desktop id. For Firefox all three are `firefox`.

### 92.2 Pinning from a window: the relaunch properties

`win32.rs` used to set `PKEY_AppUserModel_PreventPinning` on every window, on
the reasoning that a pin made from a window runs whatever the shell can work
out about it, which is `sv-guest.exe`. That reasoning stands; what changed is
that the launcher can now say what a pin should run. For each application it
writes `<exe dir>\apps\<identity>.relaunch`:

```
command=C:\Users\<guest-user>\wcivs\wc-launch.exe firefox
name=Firefox (Linux)
icon=C:\Users\<guest-user>\wcivs\firefox.ico,0
```

and passes the directory as `--relaunch-dir`. When the compositor stamps an
identity on a window it reads that file. If the file is there, the window gets
`PKEY_AppUserModel_RelaunchCommand`, `…RelaunchDisplayNameResource` and
`…RelaunchIconResource`, and `PreventPinning` is cleared. If not, the three
are removed and `PreventPinning` is set, as before. A window of a client the
launcher did not start (a harness's `weston-terminal`) still cannot be pinned.
The first launch of an application writes its file before starting it, so its
first window is pinnable. Every later launch refreshes the file after the
window is up.

### 92.3 The Start menu entry

Every launch (and `--install`, and `wc-launch.exe --refresh <app>`) writes
`Programs\<title>.lnk` with the identity, the icon and `wc-launch.exe <app>`.
"Pin to taskbar" on it pins a shortcut with the same identity, which is the
same button as the windows'.

### 92.4 Where the facts come from: the host's desktop entry

The application's name, icon and actions are in its desktop entry, on the VM
host. On NixOS that is the package's own store path, or for the readback Firefox
(which has no `share/`, §90.4) the stock package of the same name.
`wc-proxy desktop` (`crates/wc-proxy/src/desktop.rs`) reads it by the
specification: localised names, `Actions=` in order, `Exec=` quoting, and the
field codes. `wc-session app APPID B64EXE THEME` returns it with the icon and,
for Firefox, three task glyphs. The glyphs are the Linux package's own SVGs
(`new-tab.svg`, `window.svg`, `privateBrowsing.svg`), drawn in `context-fill`.
The host fills them in the colour of the jump list's text (the guest sends the
taskbar's theme) and rasterises them with `rsvg-convert`.

The guest keeps the answer (`apps\<app>.meta`) and refreshes it on every
launch, so a pin made today and an updated Firefox tomorrow agree.

### 92.5 The jump list

`ICustomDestinationList` under the same identity. For Firefox the list follows
Windows' Firefox:

* **Häufig / Frequent**: the launcher profile's most visited pages, read by
  `wc-session frequent` from copies of `places.sqlite` and `favicons.sqlite`,
  sorted by visit count as Windows' Firefox sorts its own (`SORT_BY_VISITCOUNT_
  DESCENDING` in `WindowsJumpLists.sys.mjs`), with their favicons (an SVG
  favicon is rasterised). Firefox's own prefs are respected: `browser.taskbar.
  lists.enabled`, `…frequent.enabled`, `…recent.enabled` (a Recent category),
  `…tasks.enabled`, `…maxListItemCount` (7) and `…refreshInSeconds` (120). A
  page the user removes from the list is remembered and not put back.
* **Aufgaben / Tasks**: Open new tab, Open new window, Open new private window,
  named as Windows' Firefox names them in the UI's language (German here) and
  wearing Firefox's own glyphs. Windows' Firefox's strings are not in the Linux
  package (they are built for Windows only), so the launcher carries English
  and German. The desktop entry's Profile Manager is not offered: the launcher
  pins the profile with `--profile`, so a profile manager could only start a
  second Firefox beside the session.
* Windows adds its own footer: the application, and Pin/Unpin.

Any other application gets its desktop entry's actions, by `Name[<lang>]`.

Each entry runs `wc-launch.exe <app> --action <id>` or `--url <URL>`. A warm
click is one ssh exec (`wc-session action|open`); a cold one starts the
session first and then runs the action, with the profile, preferences and title
bar the shortcut would have given it. While a session runs, its owner rebuilds
the list every `refreshInSeconds`, so the Frequent pages follow the history.

### 92.6 The security argument

docs/security-model.md R33, in short: the guest names a desktop id and an
action id, or a URL, and never a command. The host builds the argv from its
own desktop entry, checks the program against the entry's and the launcher's,
and runs it as an array. URLs are `http`, `https` or `file:///` only, one
word, and go into the slot the entry's `%u` marks. **What it does not close is
`run`**, which has carried a whole command line from the guest since §28. A
holder of the guest's key could already run any program as `sirati`. R33
records it, and what closing it would take.

### 92.7 Found on the way

- **Windows' `ssh.exe` stalls on a reply written in pieces.** With its standard
  output on a file (§28.6's arrangement), `app` delivered its first 1417 bytes
  and then hung for ever: the host side had finished, no process of ours was
  left on either machine, and the MSYS `ssh` on the same guest received all
  20520 bytes. `icon`, which prints 18 KB at once, never had the problem. So
  `app` and `frequent` now run again under a command substitution and answer in
  one write (`wc-session`, before its `case`).
- **`frequent` exited 1** on a list whose last page had no favicon: the
  pipeline's status under `pipefail`. The launcher took it as a failed reply
  and the session-0 run's jump lists had no pages until it exited 0.
- **This guest's Start button opens Open-Shell**, which UI Automation cannot
  see into. Its program list is the Start menu's Programs folder, and its
  right-click menu is the shell's. So the Start menu route was driven through
  a File Explorer window on `shell:Programs`: Windows 11's context menu, then
  "Weitere Optionen anzeigen", then "An Taskleiste anheften". The classic menu
  shows UI Automation none of its items from another process, so the agent
  reads them from the menu (`MN_GETHMENU`, `GetMenuString`, `GetMenuItemRect`).
- **Windows builds a pin from the Start menu shortcut when one carries the
  window's identity.** The pin made from the running window's jump list is a
  copy of `Programs\Firefox (Linux).lnk` (target `wc-launch.exe firefox`,
  identity `Waycompose.app.firefox`), not the window's relaunch command. The
  relaunch properties are what make the window pinnable at all, and what a
  pin would be built from if the Start menu entry were deleted.
- **The user's earlier pin `Firefox (Linux, ivshmem)` was already gone** by the
  first session-1 run (09:53). It was in `User Pinned\TaskBar` at 06:24 and
  absent at 09:53. Nothing of this branch touched it.
- **The screen locked twice during the work**, once for three hours. The agent
  now refuses every command while LockApp has the foreground (`LOCKED: … no
  command of this file was run`). It also never sends the Win key, and it
  refuses a shell click whose point another process's window covers.
