### 92.11 What is not proven, and what is next

1. **A reboot.** Everything a pin needs is a file: the pin's `.lnk`, the Start
   menu entry, the relaunch file, the icon. The jump list is Windows' own
   `CustomDestinations` file for the identity. Nothing depends on a session,
   and the relaunch after the session ended is the run that shows it. The VM
   was not rebooted (guest-safety rules).
2. **`run` still carries a command line** (security-model.md R33). The next
   step is `run` naming an application by desktop id, with the deployment's
   profile and executable in a file on the host.
3. **Removed pages and the Recent category** are implemented and unit-tested,
   but were not exercised on the guest: nobody removed a page, and
   `browser.taskbar.lists.recent.enabled` is off by default.
4. **Languages.** The jump list's Firefox strings are German and English. Other
   UI languages get English task names; a desktop entry's own `Name[<lang>]`
   is used for other applications.
5. **A second application** would get its own identity, pin and jump list from
   its desktop entry. Only Firefox has been run.
6. **Multiple installations shared an identity.** `wcivs`, `wcpins` and `wcmil`
   all launch `firefox`, so they all wrote `Waycompose.app.firefox`'s jump
   list, and the last one to refresh won. Fixed in 92.12: the identity is
   per installation, and only the installation whose pin already carries the
   old identity keeps it.

### 92.12 One identity per installation

Branch `session-fixes-aumid`, 2026-10-19.

**The cause.** `taskbar::identity` was a function of the app id alone. Every
installation of Firefox put its windows, shortcuts, pins, jump list and
relaunch file under `Waycompose.app.firefox`. The test installation "Windows
7 (Linux, no ssh)" shared `Waycompose.app.atp-nested` with the user's "Windows
7 (Linux)". `ICustomDestinationList` keys a jump list by that string and the
last writer wins, so a test run replaced the user's Firefox jump list with
the test profile's pages. Since §107 one compositor serves every
installation, so windows of two installations of one application shared one
button, and a pin made from either relaunched whichever installation's
relaunch directory came first in boot order.

**The scheme.** An installation's applications carry
`Waycompose.install.<installation>.<app id>`, for example
`Waycompose.install.wclinux.atp-nested` (`taskbar::installed_identity`).
`install.` is a segment of its own beside `app.` and `unnamed.`, so no
installation name and no client's app id can produce another namespace's
string. The installation's name has no dot (the session service allows
letters, digits, `-` and `_`, at most 32), so the segment after it is the
app. Windows does not document whether it compares AUMIDs with regard to
case, so the scoped form is lower case only. An upper-case letter is
lowered, and the name then counts as mapped: it carries the hash of the
original, as `identity` already did for spaces and long names. Two
installations, or two app ids, that differ at all get different strings,
and every string fits Windows' 128 characters with no space
(`every_scoped_identity_fits_what_windows_documents` checks 30 pairs of
odd names, all distinct). A client that never set an app id keeps
`Waycompose.unnamed.c<N>`: the connection number is unique in the
compositor, and such a window cannot be pinned.

**The one exception: the user's existing pin.** The old identity is in the
user's pinned shortcuts, desktop shortcuts and Explorer's own copy of the
pins (the Taskband blob). Two ways were weighed:

* (a) rewrite every shortcut's AUMID at deploy and rebuild the jump list
  under the new id. Changing a pinned shortcut's identity under a running
  Explorer splits the pin and its windows into two buttons until Explorer
  restarts, because Explorer reads its cached copy. That is a visible change
  to the user's taskbar, or an Explorer restart, and neither is allowed.
* (b) keep `Waycompose.app.<app>` for the one installation whose pin already
  carries it. Nothing the user sees changes, by construction: the pin, its
  windows and its jump list keep the string they have.

So (b), with (a)'s rewrite only where it is invisible. Deploy runs
`wc-launch.exe --taskbar-ids` on the guest (`taskbar_id::decide`). For each
`[app.*]` of the installation:

1. A decision an earlier deploy made is kept. Deploy copies the old ini to
   `wc-launch.ini.prev` before it copies the new one, and the verb reads
   `taskbar-id` from it. A decision never flips.
2. A test installation always gets its own identity: `WC_LAUNCH_TEST_HOME`
   set for the deploy, a `test-home` file beside its `wc-session` on the VM
   host, or `WC_LAUNCH_TASKBAR_ID=install`.
3. A claim file, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\waycompose\taskbar\<identity>.owner`, names
   the `wc-launch.exe` that holds an old identity. If it names another
   installation that still exists, this one gets its own.
4. Otherwise the user's shortcuts decide: those in `User Pinned\TaskBar`, on
   the desktop and in the Start menu's programs, read through `IShellLinkW`
   and its property store. A pin with the old identity that runs this
   installation keeps it. A pin that runs another installation gives it to
   that one. With no pin, a desktop shortcut decides, unless another
   installation has one too; then neither keeps it. Start menu entries are
   not evidence, because every launch writes one. A shortcut of a removed
   installation is not evidence either.
5. Anything else gets its own identity.

The result is written into the installation's `wc-launch.ini` as
`[app.<id>] taskbar-id = legacy` or `install` (absent is `install`). A
`legacy` decision writes the claim file. An `install` decision gives this
installation's own unpinned desktop and Start menu shortcuts the new
identity (`shell::set_link_aumid`, which keeps everything else in the
file), and removes the relaunch file of the form it no longer uses. Its pin,
if it has one with the old identity (only a test installation can), is left
alone and the log says so: its windows get their own button until the user
pins again. A shortcut whose identity cannot be read is taken to carry the
old one, so it can only keep it where it is, and it is never rewritten.
`scripts/wc-launch.sh taskbar-plan` is the same verb with `--dry-run`: it
prints the shortcuts it found and each decision, and changes nothing.

**Two installations never carry one identity.** The claim file is checked
before any shortcut. The compositor checks again: a session whose boot
claims an old identity that another live session holds does not get it, and
the log says `taskbar: session N … asked for the application-wide identity of
…` (`Registry::add_session`).

**The compositor.** The launcher sends its scope in the boot line,
`taskbar=INSTALL[:APP,…]` (107.3), where the apps are the window app ids that
keep the old identity. The scope must name the boot's own installation. A
one-session compositor gets it as `--taskbar-scope`. Each window remembers its
client's session, and `taskbar::identity_in(app_id, client, session)` stamps
the session's installation's identity. A session with no scope (a launcher
from before §92.12) keeps the old identity, as before. A launcher whose boot
is refused with `unknown boot field "taskbar"` is talking to a compositor
from before §92.12 (another installation started it); it boots again without
the field and logs that its windows carry the old identity until that
compositor ends.

**Relaunch, per installation.** A window's relaunch file is looked up only in
the directory of the session whose scope owns the identity
(`Registry::relaunch_dirs`). Before, every session's directory was searched
in boot order, and a stale `Waycompose.app.firefox.relaunch` left in a test
installation's `apps` could give the user's window the test installation's
command. An identity no scope owns is looked up in the unscoped sessions'
directories, as before.

**The jump list.** `ICustomDestinationList::SetAppID` gets the same string as
the windows and shortcuts. The jump list's own files (icons, removed pages,
refresh period) were in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\waycompose\jumplist\<app>`, shared by
every installation too. An installation with its own identity now keeps them
in `jumplist\<installation>\<app>`; the one with the old identity keeps the
old directory, and with it the pages the user removed.

**Removal.** `wc-launch.exe --uninstall-taskbar` (`scripts/wc-launch.sh
uninstall-taskbar`) deletes the installation's own jump list
(`ICustomDestinationList::DeleteList` on its own identity). It deletes the
old identity's list only while this installation holds the claim, and then
removes the claim. It removes its desktop and Start menu shortcuts, its
relaunch files and its jump-list directory. It never touches another
installation's, and it lists its pins, which only the user can unpin
(`taskbar_id::plan_removal`).

**What deploy does to the user's installations.** On the next deploy of
each, with this build, nothing else running:

| installation | expected decision | what the user sees |
|---|---|---|
| `wcivs` ("Firefox (Linux)") | `legacy`: the pin `Firefox (Linux)` in `User Pinned\TaskBar` carries `Waycompose.app.firefox` and runs `wcivs\wc-launch.exe` (92.9). Claim written | nothing changes: the pin, its windows and its jump list keep their identity. The list's pages are rebuilt at the next launch from the user's profile, which replaces whatever a test run left in it |
| `wclinux` ("Windows 7 (Linux)") | `legacy` if its pin or desktop shortcut is the only one with `Waycompose.app.atp-nested`; `install` if the test installation's desktop shortcut carries it too and neither is pinned | `legacy`: nothing. `install`: nothing visible either; the unpinned desktop and Start menu shortcuts get `Waycompose.install.wclinux.atp-nested`, and a pin made afterwards joins its windows |
| `wcmc` (Minecraft) | `legacy`, from its pin or desktop shortcut | nothing |
| the test installations | `install` | their windows leave the user's buttons and get their own; their Start menu entries move with them |

The real decisions are in each deploy's log (`taskbar-id: <app> legacy|install
<identity>: <why>`); `taskbar-plan` shows them before anything is written.
Not run on the guest from this branch.

**The tests.**

| where | what |
|---|---|
| `taskbar.rs` `install_tests` (both crates) | the scheme: legible ids, case and mapping, uniqueness over 30 odd pairs, the 128-character limit, no dot in the installation segment, the scope's parse and render, legacy only where the scope says, a shared compositor naming three sessions' windows by their installations, a second legacy claim refused, the one-session default, relaunch files found only in the owning installation's directory |
| `session_svc.rs` | the boot line carries `taskbar=`, and a scope of another installation or a bad app id is refused |
| `taskbar_id.rs` | the decision: the user's situation (pin of `wcivs`, a test installation's Start menu entry), never two `legacy` in either deploy order over six shortcut layouts, test installations, a persisted decision that does not flip, claims (another's, ours, stale), shortcuts of removed installations and Start menu entries are not evidence, unreadable identities, path comparison, removal |
| `config.rs` | `taskbar-id` parsed, defaulted and refused; read from any ini text; set in place, CRLF kept |
| `plan.rs`, `appmeta.rs` | the scope the launcher sends, and the launcher's identity equal to the compositor's for the same installation |

Under Wine (`/mnt/datasets/builds/evidence/session-fixes/aumid/wine-taskbar-ids.txt`):
two installations `wcivs` and `wcpins` of one Firefox, both first configured as
before §92.12 and `--install`ed, `wcivs`'s shortcut copied into `User
Pinned\TaskBar`. Then the deploy's step: `wcpins --taskbar-ids` decided
`install` ("the user's pin carries it and runs …\wcivs\wc-launch.exe") and
removed its old relaunch file; `wcivs --taskbar-ids` decided `legacy` and wrote
the claim. A second deploy kept both ("kept from the installation's ini").
`--refresh` then wrote `Waycompose.app.firefox.relaunch` in `wcivs\apps` and
`Waycompose.install.wcpins.firefox.relaunch` in `wcpins\apps`.
`wcpins --uninstall-taskbar` removed its two shortcuts and its relaunch file
and left `wcivs`'s three. Wine's shell links do not implement
`IPropertyStore::GetValue` (`E_NOTIMPL`) and do not store the identity, so
every identity read as unreadable, which is the path the rule above takes
for that; `DeleteList` is `E_NOTIMPL` too.

On a real Windows 11 (a throwaway clone of the local test image, 24H2,
build 26100; `/mnt/datasets/builds/evidence/session-fixes/aumid/vm/`), the
same scenario with two throwaway installations whose shortcuts our
`--install` wrote, `wcivs`'s copied into `User Pinned\TaskBar`, and a cached
host answer for Firefox:

| step | result |
|---|---|
| the property store read | every shortcut read `[Waycompose.app.firefox]`, the same as the shell's own `System.AppUserModel.ID` column; nothing unreadable |
| `--taskbar-ids`, `wcpins` first | `wcpins`: `install` ("the user's pin carries it and runs …\wcivs\wc-launch.exe"), its desktop and Start menu shortcuts rewritten, the shell then reads `Waycompose.install.wcpins.firefox`; `wcivs`: `legacy`, claim written |
| `--taskbar-ids`, `wcivs` first | `wcivs`: `legacy`, claim written; `wcpins`: `install` ("…\wcivs\wc-launch.exe holds the claim") |
| the pinned `.lnk` | SHA-256 the same before and after, in both orders |
| `--refresh` for both | `SetAppID` and `CommitList` succeeded for both identities (`jump list 3 task(s)`, 10 slots); two `customDestinations-ms` files, one whose links run `wcivs`, one `wcpins`; relaunch files `Waycompose.app.firefox.relaunch` in `wcivs\apps` and `Waycompose.install.wcpins.firefox.relaunch` in `wcpins\apps` |
| `--uninstall-taskbar` of `wcpins` | its list file gone (`DeleteList` succeeded), `wcivs`'s list unchanged; its two shortcuts and its relaunch file gone, `wcivs`'s three shortcuts and relaunch file still there; `jumplist\wcpins` removed |

The first run left an empty `jumplist\wcpins` after the removal; the removal
now takes the installation's directory too once it is empty.

**Not run:** per-session identities on window properties in a shared
compositor. A session's clients reach the compositor only through the
ivshmem rings that the VM host's session service serves; a socket client is
always session 0. That path is covered by the registry's and the boot line's
unit tests above, and the code that writes the property (`win32.rs`,
`set_taskbar_identity`) is §92's, unchanged.

**Gates.** `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast`: 114 binaries, 3291
passed, 0 failed, 9 ignored. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets`, and
`-p wc-launch -p wc-compositor --all-targets` for Windows: no warning in a
line this section wrote. `cargo check --workspace --target
x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` and `-p wc-launch -p wc-compositor --target
x86_64-apple-darwin`: exit 0. `scripts/wc-xref.sh --list` and
`design_citations`: no missing citation.

## 93. Two bugs from real use: the clipboard, and a menu that closes instead of opening

Branch `clip-submenu`, 2026-10-16. The user reported both from the guest's
desktop. First, the clipboard is not shared between Windows and Linux
programs ("last time i tried this didnt work"). Second, in Firefox's menu,
choosing an item that opens a submenu, such as Help on the way to About
Firefox, closes the whole menu. The evidence is in `docs/clip-submenu/`.

### 93.1 Status in one paragraph

**The menu** is found and fixed. Clicking a menu item moved Windows'
activation and keyboard focus to the popup's HWND. Firefox heard its window
lose focus and rolled its menus up, so the click landed on a menu that was
already closing. Popups now refuse activation, and the compositor no longer
passes a focus move between a window and its own popups on to the client
(93.2). This is proven under Wine, where it reproduced, for three cases:
Help → About Firefox, a nested bookmarks folder, and a `<select>`. On the
guest, after <guest-user> unlocked the session, the same three work with this
branch's build (93.4). **The
clipboard**: the paths §90 tested work on the guest, including the real
double-click route, and Unicode, emoji, line breaks and HTML arrive intact
(93.4). Three defects were found that a person meets and a test does not
(93.3):
- whatever was on the Windows clipboard before a session started was never
  offered;
- **a copy over 4 MiB ended Firefox's connection**, so Firefox showed its
  crash reporter and the clipboard died;
- pictures did not cross at all.

All three are fixed and tested under Wine; `scripts/wc-clip.sh` covers
pictures, 17 passed. On the guest the start-up paste and Firefox → Word
work; Word → Firefox, Notepad, the big copy, pictures and the ssh fallback
were cut off when TeamViewer locked <guest-user>'s session at the end of a remote
session, at 06:38 and again at 09:28 (93.6). Deployed to `wcivs`, 13 passed
(93.8).

### 93.2 The menu: a click activated the popup

Under Wine with `wc-compositor.exe` from master, the first click opened the
hamburger menu as window 2. The click on "Help and Report" then produced
this (`wine-menu-logs.txt`):

```
wc-compositor: window 1 lost keyboard focus
wc-compositor: window 2 has keyboard focus
wc-compositor: window 2 pointer button 0x110 pressed
wc-compositor: window 2 pointer button 0x110 released
wc-compositor: xdg_popup destroyed -> window 2
```

The compositor sent no `popup_done`; Firefox closed the menu itself. Its
popups are created `WS_EX_NOACTIVATE`. That style keeps a window from
becoming the *foreground* window, and that is all it promises. Under Wine
a click on it still activated it and gave it focus within the active
thread, so window 1 got `WM_ACTIVATE(WA_INACTIVE)` and `WM_KILLFOCUS`.
Whether real Windows does the same was not measured (93.8). The client
heard `wl_keyboard.leave` and lost `activated`, and Firefox rolls every
menu up when its window loses focus (§85.4 found that Firefox never grabs
its popups, so nothing on the Wayland side held them open either).
`keyboard_target`'s comment said the focused HWND "is always a toplevel
because a popup is `WS_EX_NOACTIVATE`", and that was the false premise.

A menu in the menu bar opens its submenu on hover, so it never showed
this. Only a click inside a popup does. Hamburger items such as Help,
Bookmarks and More Tools need a click, and so does any item in a nested
popup.

The fix has two halves. Each one alone fixes the reproduction
(`wine-menu-logs.txt`):
- **The platform.** A popup answers `WM_MOUSEACTIVATE` with `MA_NOACTIVATE`.
  That is what Windows' own menus and tooltips do: the click is delivered,
  and neither activation nor focus moves.
- **The compositor.** It no longer trusts the platform here. A popup that
  gets focus or activation anyway hands it to its toplevel; in Wayland a
  popup without a grab never has the keyboard. A loss of focus or
  activation is held for 30 ms (`HeldLoss`, `FOCUS_MOVE_GRACE`). If the
  same window, or one of its popups, takes it back in that time, the
  client hears nothing. A real move to another window is told as before,
  the held loss first.

After the fix, under Wine, with this branch's binaries:

| gesture | result |
|---|---|
| hamburger → "Help and Report" | the panel stays open on the Help subview (`wine-after-help-panel.png`; before: `wine-before-after-help-click.png`, no menu) |
| → "About Firefox" | `window 3 title -> "About Mozilla Firefox"` |
| Bookmarks (Alt+B) → hover "Mozilla Firefox" → click the first item of the nested popup | both popups open (`wine-after-bookmarks-nested.png`); the click navigated to "Firefox Help" (`wine-after-bookmarks-item-clicked.png`) |
| a `<select>`: open, click "gamma" | `title -> "SEL:gamma"` (`wine-select-open.png`) |

The About window is black under Wine. That is §85.7's second window, which
§90.7 showed is Wine's: the same Firefox renders it on the guest. WLCS
headless gives the same result as master (93.7), so the protocol's grab
behaviour is unchanged. Context-menu submenus such as "Send to device"
appear only with a signed-in account and were not exercised.

### 93.3 The clipboard: three defects

**The clipboard as it was at start-up was never offered.** The compositor
announced the Windows clipboard to Wayland only on `WM_CLIPBOARDUPDATE`,
which reports a *change*. Take the ordinary sequence: copy a URL in another
program, double-click the shortcut, paste into Firefox's address bar. It
pasted nothing until something was copied again. The same happened to
every window opened after a session ended; a session ends 60 s after its
last window closes. The platform now announces the clipboard once, after
it registers its listener:

```
wc-compositor: at start-up, the clipboard already holds: [CF_UNICODETEXT] -> 5 mime type(s)
```

That line is from the guest (`guest-clipboard.txt`). The paste that should
follow it was not made there (93.6).

**A copy over 4 MiB ended Firefox.** This reproduced under Wine with master's
binaries. The test page's button runs `execCommand('copy')` on 6,291,488
characters (`wine-clipboard-logs.txt`):

```
[proxy] client 2: the client's selection is 7077924 byte(s) across 1 mime type(s): text/plain;charset=utf-8
wc-compositor: client ... disconnected: ProtocolError(... "more staged bytes than the compositor holds")
[proxy] client 2 failed: Broken pipe (os error 32)
wc-compositor: window 2 title -> "Firefox Crash Reporter"
```

Three faults are in line here:
1. `wc_clipboard_manager_v1.chunk` past `MAX_SELECTION_BYTES` (4 MiB) was a
   protocol error, which ended the feed.
2. The proxy went on writing the queued chunks into the closed socket.
3. The pump's `?` turned that EPIPE into the end of Firefox's own Wayland
   connection, and Firefox reports a lost display as a crash (§85.3).

4 MiB is a long page selected with Ctrl+A once its HTML comes along. Fixes:
- The cap is 32 MiB on both sides, and a test pins the two numbers to each
  other.
- The proxy leaves out what does not fit, HTML before text (`fit_selection`).
- The compositor refuses an oversize selection without ending the feed
  (`Staging::overflowed`).
- `ClipLink` stops writing once it gives up.
- The pump drops a failed feed and answers every open paste; the icon feed
  gets the same treatment. The client goes on.

With the new proxy against the old compositor, the feed is dropped and
Firefox lives ("CSMALL:true" after the refusal). With both halves new, the
7 MB selection is published and the next small copy works.

A smaller fault in the same path: the copy deadline (2 s) counted from the
start of the pull. A client still writing a long selection after 2 s was
published cut off in the middle. The deadline now counts from the last byte
received. Past the cap it stops reading, so a client that never goes quiet
cannot grow the buffer without end.

**Pictures did not cross.** The proxy pulled only text and HTML, and the
compositor knew only `CF_UNICODETEXT`, `"HTML Format"` and `CF_HDROP`. The
proxy dropped Firefox's "Copy Image" as "none of which this clipboard
carries", and a screenshot copied in Windows was offered to no one. Now:
- `image/png` goes on as the registered `"PNG"` (browsers, Office and the
  Snipping Tool read it) and as `CF_DIB`: 32-bit BGRA, bottom-up, for Paint
  and everything else.
- A `"PNG"` or a `CF_DIB` on the Windows clipboard is offered as
  `image/png`.
- The DIB reader takes the shapes Windows hands out: a 40-byte header or a
  V4/V5 one; 32-bit `BI_RGB` or `BI_BITFIELDS`; 24-bit; and 1-, 4- or 8-bit
  with a palette; top-down or bottom-up. An all-zero fourth byte means
  opaque.
- A paste now reads only the formats that can answer its type. Before, a
  request for `text/html` also read `CF_UNICODETEXT`, and `GetClipboardData`
  on a program that renders late (Word) makes that program render.

Under Wine: the page's "copy image" button (`navigator.clipboard.write`)
published `[PNG 280 bytes, CF_DIB 12328 bytes]`. A `CF_DIB` put there by
`probe-clip.exe` was pasted into a contenteditable as `image/png(104)`.
`wc-clip.sh` checks both directions with `wl-copy` and `wl-paste`.

### 93.4 On the guest

The test install is `C:\Users\<guest-user>\wcclip`, session `wcc`, port 57521, with
the host half in `~/wc-launch-clip`. It was launched as a double-click is: a
ShellExecute of its `.lnk` from a process at the Limited run level. The
launcher ran at integrity `0x2000`, and §91's port access gave it the rings
and both doorbells (`guest-clipboard.txt`). Input came from the session-1
agent of §90 (`SendInput`, guarded to our windows).

| check | result |
|---|---|
| Windows → Firefox, `Set-Clipboard` then Ctrl+V in a textarea | `Grüße ✓ 漢字 😀`, LF, `https://example.org/?q=1&r=ü`: every code point |
| Firefox → Windows, Ctrl+A Ctrl+C in the textarea | the same text with CRLF; owner `sv-guest.exe`; `CF_TEXT`, `CF_OEMTEXT` and `CF_LOCALE` synthesised by Windows |
| Firefox page selection → Windows | `CF_UNICODETEXT` and `"HTML Format"` |
| start-up paste (09:24, after the unlock) | text on the clipboard before the double-click pasted into the textarea: `TA:PRE-SESSION ü 42 wcc-pre` |
| hamburger → "Help and Report" | the popup stays and shows the Help subview (`guest-menu-popup.png`, `guest-help-popup.png`); the compositor logged only the press and release, no focus or activation change |
| → "About Firefox" | `About Mozilla Firefox`, 746x427 (`guest-about.png`) |
| Bookmarks (Alt+B) → "Mozilla Firefox" → first item | the nested popup opened on hover (`guest-bm.png`, `guest-bm-nested.png`); the click opened "Firefox Help" |
| a `<select>` | an option clicked in its list became the value (`SEL:beta`) |
| Firefox → Word (a document opened through COM, `Content.Paste()`) | `wcc-ff2word Gruesse ok` |
| Word → Firefox, Notepad, the 6 MB copy, pictures, master's compositor for the before, the ssh fallback | **not run**: the session locked at 09:28:48 (93.6) |

Two facts about the guest bear on what the user saw:
- **One session at a time.** The ivshmem device allows one mapping, and the
  doorbell port one opener. A second install's double-click while another
  install's session is up gets `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` on the port and error
  548 on the device, and no window. Within one install the launcher's mutex
  prevents this; across installs nothing does. The coordinator's guest
  lease exists for this.
- The clipboard feeds still cross ssh in every arrangement (§89.12).
  Nothing in this run showed them slow.

### 93.5 What the user probably met

It cannot be known which of these it was. The ones a person meets in
normal use:
1. Copying before opening Firefox, then pasting (93.3, the first defect).
2. Before §91, a real double-click gave a session whose window came minutes
   late, rendered in software, with everything on ssh (§90.3).
3. Copying a large selection: Firefox ended and showed its crash reporter
   (93.3, the second defect).
4. Copying or pasting a picture (93.3, the third defect).

Short text in a running session worked before this branch, and still does.

### 93.6 Incident: <guest-user>'s session locked, twice, and the clipboard history

**The locks were TeamViewer's.** <guest-user>'s session locked at 06:38:14 and
again at 09:28:48. TeamViewer's own log on the guest
(`C:\Program Files\TeamViewer\TeamViewer15_Logfile.log`) records both:

```
06:38:14.966  Carrier[95]::CmdEndSession(): Received CMD_ENDSESSION with reason: PartnerDisconnected_WithError
06:38:14.994  tvdesktop::WorkstationLocker::LockWorkstation: Start locking workstation ...
06:38:15.086  SERVICE_CONTROL_SESSIONCHANGE session=1, statusCode=WTS_SESSION_LOCK, console=1
09:20:27.296  WorkstationLockerWin::ShouldAutoLockWorkstation: Autolock: yes, ...
09:28:48.625  tvdesktop::WorkstationLocker::LockWorkstation: Start locking workstation ...
09:28:48.710  SERVICE_CONTROL_SESSIONCHANGE session=1, statusCode=WTS_SESSION_LOCK, console=1
```

TeamViewer is set to lock the computer when a remote session to it ends.
The first session ended because the partner's connection dropped and the
reconnect failed. This branch's first report blamed the 06:38 lock on its
test agent, which was replaying an input batch with a malformed Win+R chord
at that moment. The log shows otherwise, and that report is withdrawn. The
second lock came 12 s after the agent's last keystroke (Ctrl+C in its own
Firefox window at 09:28:36). The agent refused its next batch because of the
lock screen. Practical consequence: while TeamViewer's autolock is on, a
dropped remote session locks the desktop and ends every test that needs
input until someone unlocks it. Turning the option off is <guest-user>'s choice,
and nothing here changed it.

**The agent's loop was real**, 06:34–06:38. A command had overwritten the
variable that held the batch's file, so the batch was never removed and ran
39 times. What it did:
- **Clipboard history.** Each run copied, so the copies filled the Windows
  clipboard history (25 entries) and pushed <guest-user>'s older entries out. The
  25 entries, all this branch's, were then deleted through the WinRT
  `Clipboard` history API from a non-interactive process.
- **<guest-user>'s clipboard.** The text on it at 06:19 was saved only in the
  agent's memory, and was lost when the agent was stopped.
- **The clipboard now.** It still holds this branch's test string
  (`PRE-SESSION ü 42 wcc-pre`). It cannot be cleared while the session is
  locked, and it is to be cleared only if it still holds exactly that.

The agent is fixed:
- The loop variable is its own, and a command file is removed before it
  runs.
- It never sends the Win key, and drops the chords that needed one.
- It refuses input while LogonUI is up.
- It sends a click or a key only while the foreground window and the point
  belong to a process the test started.

The rules for every agent are in `visual-check-instructions.md`.

## 94. The guest names an application, never a command line

Branch `run-appid`, from master `59a6e8e`, 2026-10-16. The brief:
security-model.md R33 (added with §92) recorded that `wc-session run` took a
whole command line from the guest, base64'd, and ran it. So any process on the
Windows guest that can read the launcher's key could run any program on the VM
host as `sirati`, through the very forced command whose job was to stop that
(§28.5: "the guest cannot run anything on the VM host except the verbs"). Close
it: the guest names an application by id, the host owns the definitions, the
old form is removed with no way back for the key, and every other verb is
audited the same way.

**Status.** Closed, and the audit found two more holes of the same family and
several narrower ones (94.4). `wc-session` now refuses any request that is not
made of the characters some verb needs, any verb with the wrong number of words,
and any word that is not of its verb's type; `run`, `action` and `open` start
only an application defined in the host's `apps.ini`. A harness runs the real
script with 133 hostile requests and 12 hostile definitions (94.5); against master it fails eleven of
its fifteen tests, among them a command line accepted and run, and a run id
that reached the root step. Deployed to `wcivs` (94.7).

### 94.1 What the guest could send

| verb (until §94) | guest-chosen words | what they reached |
|---|---|---|
| `run ID CMD PROFILE PREFS TITLEBAR [CHROME [GTK]]` | the command line; a profile path; the whole `user.js`; the value of `MOZ_GTK_TITLEBAR_DECORATION`; the whole `userChrome.css`; the whole `gtk.css` | the first word went through `resolve_exec` and the rest were the program's arguments: **any program, any arguments**. `user.js` set **any preference** of the profile, `devtools.chrome.enabled` and the remote debugger among them |
| `action`, `open` | as `run`, plus the executable (`B64EXE`) | the argv came from the desktop entry, but the executable, profile and files were the guest's |
| `app APPID B64EXE THEME`, `icon APPID [EXE]` | an executable path or name | which package's directories were searched; `icon` then followed the entry's `Icon=` as a path fragment |
| `frequent B64PROFILE` | any directory under `~/.wc-launch` | **any launcher profile's history**, another installation's included |
| `up ID RUNID PAGES OUTBOUND` | the run id | checked only if it began with `0x`; `1;cmd` passed and was printed with `%s` into the script `up` pipes to `$ROOTC`: **a root command injection** in design, not exploitable on testhost only because `~/rootc` no longer exists (§12.9; the memory note of 2026-08-21) |
| every verb | every word | `set -- $SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND`, unquoted: each word was glob-expanded against the home directory, and extra words were ignored |

### 94.2 The host's definitions

One file, `apps.ini`, beside `wc-session` in the installation's directory
(`~/wc-launch-ivs/apps.ini` for `wcivs`), written by `wc-launch.sh deploy` and
read by nothing else. It is not in the stage that goes to the guest, and no
verb writes under the installation's directory. A section per application:

```
[firefox]
exec     = ~/wc-launch-ivs/bin/firefox-readback/bin/firefox
args     =
profile  = ~/.wc-launch/firefox
prefs    = middlemouse.paste=false
titlebar = tabs
desktop  = firefox
gpu      = on
```

(`env = NAME=value`, repeatable, is the eighth key.) `load_app` refuses a key
it does not know, an `exec` that is not an absolute path to an executable file,
a `profile` that is not one plain directory name under `~/.wc-launch`, and a
`titlebar`, `gpu`, `desktop` or `env` outside its alphabet. `wc-session apps`
(an operator verb, refused from the guest) checks the whole file, and deploy
runs it as a PASS line.

Every word `run` used to carry, and where it is now:

| was | now |
|---|---|
| the command line's first word, resolved by `resolve_exec` at every launch | `exec`, absolute. A name in `WC_LAUNCH_FIREFOX` is resolved **at deploy time** by the operator verb `wc-session resolve`, and a store path it lands on is GC-rooted at `bin/app-firefox` |
| `--profile DIR` in the command line, and the profile word | `profile`; `--profile DIR` is added to the argv, and `user.js`/`userChrome.css` are written there and only there |
| the rest of the command line | `args` (fixed, split on whitespace; Firefox has none) |
| `user.js`, rendered on the guest from `[app.*] prefs` and the title bar | rendered **on the host** from `prefs` and `titlebar` by `wc-launch --render-app-files`, which is `plan::host_files`: the same tested renderer, built for Linux and deployed as `bin/wc-launch`. `wc-session` still appends its own lines (crash count, `gfx.webrender.all`, the decode prefs, the null audio context) |
| `userChrome.css`, `gtk.css` (§82, §91.8) | rendered by the same call, sized from the guest's two numbers (94.3); the private `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` overlay is built from the host's `gtk.css` as before |
| `MOZ_GTK_TITLEBAR_DECORATION` | from `titlebar` (`Titlebar::moz_env`, printed by the renderer) |
| the GPU environment (`gpu.env`, §86) | unchanged, and applied only where the definition says `gpu = on` |
| the readback Firefox (§86) | chosen by `exec` pointing at it; its `.wc-vulkan-readback` marker still turns the decode prefs on |
| audio (§86) | unchanged: per session, from `audio.state` |
| the jump list's `B64EXE` | the definition's `exec`, whose basename must still be the desktop entry's program |
| `frequent`'s profile | the definition's `profile` |

On the guest, `[app.*]` is now display and identity only: `title`, `icon`,
`desktop`, `app-id` (§92's taskbar identity) and `host-app`, the host's id
(the section's by default). `exec`, `prefs` and `titlebar` are refused by name
with a message that points at `apps.ini`, so a pre-§94 ini fails at the line
rather than being half-read.

### 94.3 What the guest still sends, and how it is typed

Before any verb runs, the request must be at most 16 KiB and 12 words, and made
only of letters, digits, space and `+ / = . _ -` (spelled out, not as ranges, so
the locale's collation cannot widen it). It is split with `read -a`, which does
no pathname expansion. Then each verb checks its word count exactly and each
word's type:

| verb | words | types |
|---|---|---|
| `run` | `ID APP DPI CAPTION` | session id: a letter or digit, then `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`, ≤ 64. App id: a letter or digit, then `[A-Za-z0-9._+-]`, no `..`, ≤ 64, and a section of `apps.ini`. DPI: decimal 48..960, no leading zero. CAPTION: decimal 0..512 (0 = not measured) |
| `action` | `ID APP ACTION DPI CAPTION` | ACTION: a letter or digit, then `[A-Za-z0-9-]`, ≤ 64, and one the desktop entry lists (`wc-proxy desktop`) |
| `open` | `ID APP B64URL DPI CAPTION` | base64 of ≤ 4096 bytes; the URL `http(s)://` or `file:///`, every byte printable ASCII, no quote, backslash or newline; checked again by `desktop::url_ok` and put in the `%u` slot |
| `app` | `APP [light\|dark]` | |
| `icon`, `frequent` | `APP` | |
| `up` | `ID RUNID ivshmem` | RUNID `0x` + 1..16 hex digits; the guest-RAM form (`ID RUNID PAGES OUTBOUND [frames]`) is refused unless the host's own environment sets `WC_LAUNCH_GUEST_RAM=1` |
| `proxy`, `down`, `status`, `logs`, `audio` | `ID` | |
| `gpu` | `ID [N]` | N 1..8 |
| `ping` | none | |

DPI and CAPTION are the only free values left, and they are numbers: the
desktop's DPI and Windows' caption height there (`AdjustWindowRectExForDpi`),
which only the guest can measure and from which the host sizes Firefox's tab
strip and the GTK header bars (§82, §91.8). The renderer checks the ranges
again. A launch's words are built in `plan::launch_verb`, and its test checks
that every word is in the request alphabet.

`wc-proxy desktop` now reads its options only before its first word (`--dirs`,
or `--`): until §94 a positional that read `--dirs` was taken as the option.
`wc-session` passes the options first.

### 94.4 The audit, verb by verb

| verb | finding | fix |
|---|---|---|
| all | unquoted `set -- $SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND` globbed every word; extra words ignored; no size limit | the alphabet, size and word limits of 94.3; `read -a`; exact word counts |
| `run` | command line from the guest (R33) | app id; argv from `apps.ini` |
| `run`, `action`, `open` | `user.js`, `userChrome.css`, `gtk.css` as guest text: any preference, any sheet | rendered on the host from the definition and two numbers |
| `action`, `open`, `app`, `icon` | the guest chose the executable, so the package directories searched | the definition's `exec` |
| `icon` | an `Icon=` value was used as a path fragment (`…/apps/$NAME.png`) | only a theme name (`[A-Za-z0-9._+-]`, no `..`) is followed |
| `frequent` | any profile under `~/.wc-launch` | the definition's profile |
| `up` (guest RAM) | run id without `0x` unchecked and printed with `%s` into the root script | `^0x[0-9a-fA-F]{1,16}$` on both paths, `%q` throughout, and the guest-RAM path refused unless the host sets `WC_LAUNCH_GUEST_RAM=1`; `proxy` and `down` take their root steps only under the same condition |
| `up` (ivshmem) | `0x` with no digits, or extra words, passed | the same regex; exactly three words |
| ids, app ids, action ids | a leading `-` was allowed | a letter or digit first |
| `open` | the URL became a positional of `wc-proxy desktop`, which looked for `--dirs` anywhere | options before the first word; the URL's scheme checked in `wc-session` first |
| `proxy` (ivshmem), `gpu`, `audio`, `status`, `logs`, `down`, `ping` | arguments are a checked id (and `N`); every path is under `$RUNROOT/$ID`; units are `wc-launch-…-$ID` | word counts only |
| environment | `WC_LAUNCH_ROOTC` is `eval`ed and every `WC_LAUNCH_*` changes paths, so a guest that could set the environment would own the script | none needed: testhost's sshd has no `AcceptEnv` and `PermitUserEnvironment` is off (checked), so the guest sets nothing |

Two operator verbs, `apps` and `resolve`, are served only from argv: the forced
command names the script with no arguments, so the guest never reaches argv.

### 94.5 The tests

`crates/wc-launch/tests/wc_session.rs`, in the style of `sv-testkit`'s
`kill_safety`: the real `scripts/wc-session`, run as the guest reaches it (the
request in `$SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND`), in a scratch host with an `apps.ini`, a
live session (a bound `wl-proxy` socket) and stand-ins for the application and
`wc-proxy` that write down their argv. The renderer is this crate's own binary.
`$WC_LAUNCH_ROOTC` is a command that leaves a file. Every hostile request must
exit non-zero, say `wc-session:` why, start nothing, reach no root step and
create no file it names.

* five positive tests: `run` (argv, `user.js`, `userChrome.css` at 144 dpi and
  a 45 px caption, the environment, the GTK overlay), a definition with no
  profile and `titlebar = none`, `action` (the options-first call to
  `wc-proxy`), `open` (`https://example.org/a?q=[a]*&x=%41#f` arrives as one
  argument, unexpanded), `frequent`;
* the old forms: `run` with a command line in four shapes, a base64'd program
  as the app id, `sh` and `bash` as app ids, the old `action`, `open`, `app`,
  `icon` and `frequent`;
* shell metacharacters (`;`, `&&`, `|`, `$(…)`, backticks, newline, CR, tab,
  `*`, `?`, `[`, `~`, quotes, `>`, `${HOME}`, backslash, non-ASCII, a control
  character); `..` and paths in every verb that takes an id; `-`-leading words
  in every slot; numbers out of range, octal-looking and hex; URLs that are
  options, `javascript:`, `data:`, `file:/`, `about:`, `chrome:`, or carry a
  space, newline, quote, backslash, non-ASCII or a bell; 20 000-byte and
  13-word requests; 16 unknown verbs (`sh`, `scp -t`, `rsync --server`,
  `internal-sftp`, …); the operator verbs from the guest;
* the root steps: master's injection shape `up t94 1;id 16384 1048576`, the
  guest-RAM `up` in every form, `proxy` and `down` of a session with a plan;
* definitions outside the rules (relative, missing or directory `exec`;
  profile outside, with `..`, nested; an unknown key; bad `titlebar`, `gpu`,
  `env`, `desktop`; no `apps.ini`).

Run against master's `wc-session` the harness fails 11 of 15: `run` accepted the
command line and started it (`run ok … audio=none`), `up t94 1;id 16384 1048576`
**reached the root step**, `status -rf` and a 13-word `status` were accepted, and
a refused `up` had already removed the session it named. The positive tests fail
there too, because master has no `apps.ini`.

Also new: `plan::launch_verb` and `plan::host_files` with their tests,
`config` tests for the refused keys and `host-app`, and
`desktop::options_end_at_the_first_word`.

fault.

### 94.8 What is not done

1. **The started application is as powerful as its interface**
   (security-model.md R33): a guest process that can drive the desktop can make
   Firefox save files, open `file:///` pages or run its Browser Console as
   `sirati`. The key no longer runs commands; the application it starts can.
   Running applications as another user or in a sandbox is a product change and
   is not made here.
2. **The other installations need a redeploy to launch again**, from this
   branch (it writes their `apps.ini`); until then they serve every verb but
   `run`, `action`, `open`, `app`, `icon` and `frequent`. Their keys could
   instead be removed from `authorized_keys`, which is the owner's decision.
3. **`/tmp/wc-launch` is shared by every installation** and by any local user
   who creates it first. That is a host-local concern, not one the guest can
   reach beyond the session ids, and is unchanged.

## 95. The desktop checks: menus, the clipboard, dialogs and a day's use, on the deployed launcher

Branch `desktop-checks`, 2026-10-16 11:10–15:11 and, after the VM restart and the
third deploy, 2026-10-17 07:04–07:31. The checks §91 and §93.8
left pending, run against the deployed `wcivs` on <guest-user>'s desktop (session 1)
the way a person starts it: a click on the pinned `Firefox (Linux)` taskbar
button, at medium integrity. The evidence is in `docs/desktop-checks/`.

### 95.1 Status in one paragraph

**Every multi-step menu works on real Windows.** That includes the one the
user asked about: Hamburger, Help and Report, About Firefox. So do the clipboard
in every direction asked for, the GTK dialogs, a second window from a
maximised one, the pin, a typed URL, scrolling, H.264 video with sound, and
the ssh fallback. Five bugs were found:
- **Firefox crashed four times in two hours of ordinary use.** Two causes,
  found and reproduced locally by a background agent (95.4):
  - **The lost device:** a short stall of the guest made the ICD declare the
    GPU side gone. Fixed: the ICD waits 5 s, drops late replies, and gives
    a slot back when its process exits.
  - **The arena:** the 64 MiB arena of a GPU session ran out with two
    windows open. Not fixed here. Larger fixed slots (2 x 112 MiB) were
    tried on the guest and starved Firefox's parent of a slot at start-up
    (95.4.10). The user ruled for dynamic allocation on the ivshmem device,
    which another agent now owns, so the guest keeps 3 x 64 MiB.
- **A `<select>` dropdown wore a thick black frame**: a translucent
  subsurface was copied over the page instead of blended. Fixed (95.5).
- **Windows' caption buttons still vanished after page loads** in a new
  window: `WM_NCPAINT` painted the caption over the strip §91 clears.
  Fixed (95.6).
- **Closing the last window crashed Firefox once**, during shutdown (95.4).
  Reproduced locally later the same day and found to be ours: the ICD's
  pipelined present (§88) can still attach a frame to Firefox's `wl_surface`
  after Firefox has destroyed it. The fix is on branch `quit-crash`.
- Two harmless log oddities: the audio player's drop counter while the stream
  is silent, and Firefox's `Broken pipe` warnings on a selection (95.8).

**The third deploy, checked on the desktop** (95.7): §97's GPU pool, §99's
doorbell hub and §98's fix for the crash at quit. Every check passed: hardware
WebRender on the Intel GPU, the select, the caption glyphs 8 of 8, video with
sound, and four quits with frames still being presented, none of which crashed.
60 fps on the guest with and without §98's synchronous present.

### 95.4 Firefox on the forwarded GPU: an arena too small, and a guest pause taken for a dead peer

This is the record of the background agent this branch started for the
crashes (branch `gpu-oom`, merged here). Where it proposes larger fixed
slots as the arena fix (95.4.6, 95.4.9), that was overtaken: the 2 x 112 MiB
geometry starved Firefox's parent of a slot on the guest (95.4.10, 95.7), and
the user ruled that GPU memory be allocated dynamically on the ivshmem device
instead, which another agent now owns. The ICD and GPU-side fixes stand.

Branch `gpu-oom`, from master `ab009e9`, 2026-10-16. The brief was two Firefox
crashes on the deployed `wcivs` install. Crash 2 (session 12:34:29 to 12:45:02)
printed 120 `ZINK: vkCreateBuffer failed`, then `wr_renderer_render:
OutOfMemory` at t=208.8 s and `Fallback WR to SW-WR`, and at about t=630 s
`zink: DEVICE LOST!`, `vkCreateSampler failed (VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST)` and a
SIGSEGV in the parent. Crash 1 was an idle Firefox during a screen lock:
`DEVICE LOST!` and `vkCreateBufferView failed (VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST)` 2.3 s after
the iGPU went from D3 to D0. The GPU side logged nothing either time. Two more
sessions arrived during the work: wcl-1332 fell back to SW-WR with **no**
`vkCreateBuffer` failure but ten `zink: couldn't allocate memory: heap=3
size=2097152`, and later died of the same `vkCreateSampler` DEVICE_LOST while an
image was pasted.

**Status.** Two causes, both reproduced on this workstation's RADV and both
ours. The OOM is the 64 MiB arena: Firefox with two windows has a working set
that fills the application's 56 MiB of it, and the free space fragments below
one 2 MiB slab (95.4.2). The lost device is the ICD declaring the GPU side gone
after 150 ms without a heartbeat, which a guest that is not scheduled for that
long produces with nothing wrong on either side (95.4.3). The ICD now waits five
seconds, drops a late reply instead of handing it to the next call, frees a
half-built swapchain, and says once, whatever `SV_DEBUG` says, why it failed a
call. The GPU side says when its driver returns a lost device or an
out-of-memory. What the 120 `vkCreateBuffer` failures of crash 2 were is **not
established** (95.4.4); the next one will say. The arena fix is an ini change on
the guest (95.4.6); nothing here ran on the guest or on testhost.

#### 95.4.1 Where "ZINK: vkCreateBuffer failed" comes from

Mesa 26.2.4 (the deployed kopper build's source,
`/nix/store/9s209y4515mm50m7kpxlqc6nji1rw13v-source`) prints it in one place,
`zink_resource.c:1295`, `create_buffer()`, when `vkCreateBuffer` itself returns
anything but `VK_SUCCESS`. It is the first Vulkan call of a buffer resource:
there is no requirements query before it, the result is not printed, and
`zink_screen_handle_vkresult` is not called, so a `VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST` there
does not even mark the device lost. The memory comes after it, in
`zink_bo_create`, whose failure prints `zink: couldn't allocate memory: heap=N
size=M` instead (`zink_bo.c:269`; `heap` is Zink's own heap enum, not a Vulkan
heap index), after one retry with its slab and BO caches emptied.

So crash 2's 120 lines are a non-success from our `vkCreateBuffer`, and arena
exhaustion cannot produce them: the ICD's `create_buffer` never touches the
allocator. They are either the GPU side's forwarded result or a `LowerError`
(a transport failure, or a lowering error such as `ChainTooLong`), and before
this section both were silent without `SV_DEBUG`. wcl-1332's
`couldn't allocate memory` lines are the other path, and that is the one the
local runs reproduce.

#### 95.4.2 The arena: a working set, not a leak

`scripts/sv-firefox-wayland.sh two-windows SECS` is a new mode of the existing
harness: weston (pixman, `wl_shm` only), `sv-gpu-server` on RADV, Firefox 157.0.1
through the ICD and the deployed kopper Mesa, `SVWL_FORCE=wr` (the deployed
`gfx.webrender.all`). `sv-firefox-soak.py` opens a page that retitles itself ten
times a second, a second window, sets both to 1280x752 and then 1296x768, and
tours local pages and three real sites in both windows. At the end it closes
one window and quits from the other. `SV_DEBUG` now prints the arena's use, with
the time, whenever it moves by 2 MiB.

| run | arena | result |
|---|---|---|
| 300 s, `SV_DEBUG` | 64 MiB (56 MiB to the application, 8 MiB blob reserve) | `the arena is exhausted: 2162688 bytes asked for, arena 48928 KiB of 57344 KiB in use`, `zink: couldn't allocate memory: heap=5 size=2162688` twice, `wr_renderer_render: OutOfMemory`, `Fallback WR to SW-WR`; 25 of 63 compositor samples `WebRender (Software)` |
| 300 s, `SV_DEBUG` | 64 MiB | no failure; largest free run down to **2048 KiB** at t=276 s, against the 2112 KiB the first run failed on |
| 240 s, no `SV_DEBUG` | 64 MiB | `vkAllocateMemory: the arena is exhausted: 2097152 bytes asked for, arena 51040 KiB of 57344 KiB in use in 21 allocation(s), largest free run 1936 KiB, high water 51040 KiB`, then the same fallback |
| 600 s, `SV_DEBUG` | 256 MiB | no failure, 129 page loads; in use between 42 and 51 MiB for the whole run, high water **53152 KiB** at about 120 s and never higher |
| 300 s, `SV_DEBUG`, this branch with master 2982bdd merged in (a trial merge, not committed) | 112 MiB, the size 95.4.6 recommends (98 MiB to the application) | no failure, WebRender throughout, high water 53088 KiB, largest free run never below the 34 MiB of the end; the same run at 64 MiB exhausted again (`53024 KiB of 57344 KiB in use … largest free run 1876 KiB`) and fell back |

At 256 MiB the use rises to a plateau within two minutes and stays there for
ten, so nothing leaks over this workload; Zink's BO cache gives memory back
(the use falls by 6 MiB at a time) and its retry empties it before failing. The
working set is about 21 allocations: Zink's 2 MiB slabs, and the ICD's own
swapchain readback buffers, one per swapchain image at the window's full size
(kopper asks for two, so 1296x768 costs 7.6 MiB a window). At 64 MiB the
high-water mark is 95 % of what the application gets, and readback buffers of
several window sizes (4.4 MiB, 3.3 MiB) leave holes no 2 MiB slab fits, so whether
a run fails is a matter of fragmentation timing: one of two 300 s runs did.

`vkAllocateMemory` used to fail this silently (R11 calls exhaustion "a normal
condition an application handles", which is true and was the whole of the
diagnosis). It now says so once with the request, the use, the largest free run
and the high-water mark. Two leaks on the failure path are also closed: a
swapchain whose second image could not get its readback buffer kept the first
one's for the life of the process, and an allocation whose slab the GPU side did
not import stayed allocated with no handle anyone could free.

#### 95.4.3 The lost device: 150 ms of silence

Every wait the ICD makes on a ring passed a 50 ms liveness interval to
`wait_until`, which builds its peer-gone window as three intervals. So a GPU side
whose heartbeat did not move for 150 ms of the ICD's running time was gone, and
the call returned `VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST`. The GPU side beats every 20 ms from a
thread of its own, but when the guest is not scheduled every one of its threads
stops, and the ICD, which kept running, has no stall of its own to credit. The
GPU side's ring threads poll at 200 ms (a 600 ms window) for the same reason
and judge the app side gone only after `APP_GONE_AFTER`, five seconds (`session.rs`).

`SVWL_STALL_MS=N` makes the harness `SIGSTOP` the GPU side for N ms every
`SVWL_STALL_EVERY` seconds (default 20) from 30 s on, which is what a paused
guest looks like from the host.

| build | stalls | result |
|---|---|---|
| master (plus the diagnostics) | 400 ms | the second stall, t=51 s: `transport: peer of ring 2 is gone; returning VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST`, three `zink: DEVICE LOST!`, `swapchain killed`, `vkCreateImage failed (VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST)`, a minidump. The signature of crashes 1, 2 and 3 |
| this branch | 12 x 400 ms | alive at 243 s, WebRender throughout, no failure line |
| this branch | 12 x 2000 ms | alive at 245 s, WebRender throughout, no failure line |
| this branch | 25 x 1000 ms, every 10 s | alive at 302 s, WebRender throughout, no failure line, then a clean quit |

The window is now `PEER_GONE_AFTER`, five seconds, for every ICD wait, through one
helper (`wait_for_peer`) and a new `sv_transport::park::wait_until_gone_after`
that takes the window separately from the poll interval.

A second defect made a lost device worse than it had to be. A call that gave up
left its command on the ring, and a GPU side that was only slow answered it
later. The next call read that reply, saw the wrong sequence number and failed
with `Shape("a reply arrived out of order")`, leaving its own reply for the call
after it, so every later call on that ring failed for the rest of the process.
A reply older than the call's own sequence number is now dropped.
`transport::abandoned_calls` stops a fake GPU side's heartbeat for twice the
window before it answers: the first call is `DeviceLost`, the second gets its own
reply. Without the fix the second call fails.

#### 95.4.4 What crash 2's vkCreateBuffer failures were

Not established. By 95.4.1 they were a failed `vkCreateBuffer` from the ICD, and
three things could produce it: the Intel driver's own result (forwarded
unchanged, and until now not logged by the GPU side), a transport failure
(printed only under `SV_DEBUG`), or a lowering error. The ring desynchronisation
of 95.4.3 would fail every call on the device ring, `vkCreateImage` and
`vkCreateSampler` with it, and crash 2's log has only `vkCreateBuffer` failures
until t≈630 s, so it is the least likely of the three. The next occurrence will
name its layer:

* the ICD says the first `vkCreateBuffer` result the GPU side refused, with the
  size, the usage and the arena's use;
* the ICD says the first transport failure of each kind and the first lowering
  failure of each kind (`a call failed in this ICD: …`), unconditionally;
* the GPU side says, once per command and result, when its driver returns
  `VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST`, `VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_DEVICE_MEMORY` or
  `VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_HOST_MEMORY` (`sv-gpu-server: the driver returned … from …`).
  The generated dispatch calls a new `GpuHost::note_driver_error` after every
  driver call that returns a `VkResult`; the hand-written `vkCreateBuffer`,
  `vkCreateImage` and `vkAllocateMemory` call it too.

#### 95.4.5 Crash 1: what can be said

The old ICD returned `VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST` for a ring wait that saw 150 ms of
heartbeat silence, a call that took over 10 s (`CALL_TIMEOUT`), a ring the GPU
side marked fatal, or a GPU side that restarted. The last two leave a line in
the GPU side's log, and it had none. The driver itself could also have returned
it, and the old GPU side would have forwarded that silently. 95.4.3 shows that the
first produces this exact signature, and a guest that stalls while its
passed-through iGPU changes power state, 2.3 s before the failure, is the kind of
pause that triggers it. So the likeliest reading is the ICD's window, which this
branch widens to five seconds. If the next occurrence instead logs `the driver
returned VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST`, Intel's driver lost the device across D3, and
neither side can repair that: a lost `VkDevice` stays lost, its objects with it.
Surviving it would be Firefox's job (a robust context and a renderer reset; it
crashed instead), and avoiding it would mean keeping the iGPU out of D3 while a
GPU session is open, either by a power setting on the guest or by
`disable_idle_d3` on the host's vfio-pci. Neither was tried.

#### 95.4.6 The geometry, and what it costs

The GPU arena is a 256 MiB ivshmem device cut into `gpu-sessions` slots of
16 MiB control plus `gpu-arena-mib` arena (§87.2). `sv-hostd` takes each slot's
geometry from the guest's extent, so the split is the guest's ini alone.

| ini | slots | arena a session | application's share | against the 53 MiB measured |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `gpu-sessions = 3`, `gpu-arena-mib = 64` (deployed) | 3 x 80 MiB | 64 MiB | 56 MiB | 95 %, fails |
| `gpu-sessions = 3`, `gpu-arena-mib = 69` | 3 x 85 MiB | 69 MiB | 61 MiB | 87 % |
| `gpu-sessions = 2`, `gpu-arena-mib = 112` | 2 x 128 MiB | 112 MiB | 98 MiB | 54 % |
| a 384 MiB device, `gpu-sessions = 3`, `gpu-arena-mib = 112` | 3 x 128 MiB | 112 MiB | 98 MiB | 54 %, and 128 MiB more host RAM |

The second row is not a fix. The third is the one this section recommends: it
costs no host memory and gives up the third concurrent session, which §87.2 kept
for `glxtest`, the browser and an RDD or a restart. `glxtest` exits before the
browser asks for its slot, and a slot comes back when its session ends, so two
cover the browser and its video decoder. The fourth row needs memory testhost
does not have (244 MB available at crash 2, 412 MB and 723 MB later). Two things
about the third row are unverified on the guest: that Intel's driver imports a
112 MiB host pointer as it does a 64 MiB one (§87.3), and that a Firefox start
never needs a third slot at once.

#### 95.4.7 The quit crash

A session on the deployed build (wcl-2652) crashed when its last window closed,
in `xpcom-shutdown-threads`, and the crash reporter deleted the minidump. Here, a
two-window session that ends by closing one window and quitting from the other
exited 0 with no minidump in three 60 s runs and in a 300 s run at 64 MiB
and in a 300 s run with 25 one-second stops of the GPU side. It is not
reproduced. Closing the *last* window over WebDriver
leaves this Firefox running with no window, so the harness quits through
`Marionette:Quit`, which takes the same shutdown path but not the same click.
`MOZ_CRASHREPORTER_NO_DELETE_DUMP=1` in the launcher's environment would keep the
next dump.

#### 95.4.10 Two slots and Firefox's start: a slot held five seconds after its process exits

The deploy of 95.4.9 (gpu-oom merged with master, `gpu-sessions = 2`,
`gpu-arena-mib = 112`) showed that Intel's driver takes the 112 MiB import
(`2 session slot(s) of 128 MiB (16 MiB control + 112 MiB arena)`), and that two
slots broke Firefox's start. Sessions 1 and 2 (367 and 11 commands) held both
slots. Clients 3 to 6 were refused (`all 2 GPU session slots are taken`). The
browser process was among them, so it had no `libsv_icd.so` mapped and drew on
llvmpipe.

**A slot outlived its process by five seconds.** `RingTransport::shutdown`
sets the control region's `SHUTDOWN` flag, which the GPU side's ring threads
check every 50 ms, and nothing called it. So the GPU side learned that a
session was over only when its heartbeat had been silent for `APP_GONE_AFTER`.
Measured with `scripts/sv-slot-release.sh`: `vulkaninfo` exits and its session
ends 5156 ms later. Firefox's `glxtest` exits and the browser asks for its slot
well inside that time. **And a refused ICD gave up at once**, for the life of
the process.

Two changes, both in the ICD:

* At exit the ICD sets `SHUTDOWN` on every control region it attached (an
  `atexit` handler, `transport::arm_goodbye`). The same measurement: the
  session ends 67 ms after `vulkaninfo` exits.
* A connection refused because every slot is taken waits for one, retrying
  every 250 ms. The budget is 10 s for the process as a whole, kept in
  `$TMPDIR/sv-icd-slot-wait-<pid>`, because the loader loads the ICD up to
  three times in one process and a refused load leaves nothing loaded to
  remember the wait. The refusal reaches the ICD only as text through
  `sv-hostd`, so it is matched by the guest's words
  `GPU session slots are taken`. Any other refusal fails at once, as before.

`sv-gpu-server serve --slots N` refuses past N concurrent sessions with the
guest's message. It reads the client's `AttachRequest` first, as `sv-hostd`
does, so that the refusal does not race the client's write. This is how the
fixed slots were measured here.

| `scripts/sv-slot-release.sh` (one slot) | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `vulkaninfo` exits; its session ends | 5156 ms later | 67 ms later |
| a holder is SIGKILLed (no `atexit`); a second client asks at once | refused at once, no GPU | served after 5.3 s (`sv-icd: got a GPU session slot after 5.3s`) |
| the holder stays; a second client asks | refused at once | refused after 10070 ms in total |

| `sv-firefox-wayland.sh two-windows`, `SVWL_SLOTS=1`, 112 MiB | result |
|---|---|
| before | the guest's failure exactly: four `sv-icd: refusing to load rather than answering locally`, the browser with `libsv_icd.so` unmapped, `ZINK: vkCreateInstance failed (VK_ERROR_INCOMPATIBLE_DRIVER)`, no GPU-side submission after `glxtest` |
| after, 3 runs | the browser connected at the first attempt (`glxtest`'s slot was already back); submissions in every window, a clean quit |

Locally Firefox 157 opens two sessions at start (`glxtest`, then the browser),
with or without the deployed Vulkan-decode prefs (`SVWL_VULKAN_DECODE=1`). The
guest's 11-command session is not reproduced here. If it belongs to a process
that stays alive, two slots leave nothing for a third (a video decoder, or a
restart that overlaps), and that process waits 10 s and then runs without the
GPU.

**The 69 MiB alternative.** Three slots of 16 + 69 MiB fill 255 of the 256 MiB.
Four 300 s two-window runs at a 69 MiB arena passed with no allocation failure.
The application's share is 60.4 MiB against the 53 MiB high water of 95.4.2, so
88 %, against 95 % at 64 MiB, where one run in two failed. That is less margin
than four runs can prove.

### 95.5 Bug, fixed: the `<select>` dropdown's black frame

On the guest the open list of a `<select>` had a thick black frame with black
showing outside its rounded corners (`guest/g1b-6a.png`). The compositor's
log had no popup for it, only `wl_surface created`. Traced against the Linux
build with `WAYLAND_DEBUG`: GTK makes the dropdown a `wl_subsurface` of the
window (`wl_subcompositor.get_subsurface` after the click), not an `xdg_popup`
as every menu is. Its buffer has a transparent margin for the shadow.

`Shadow::compose` copied every surface of a window's tree onto the canvas. Its
own note (stage 9) said a copy was right until a translucent subsurface
arrived, and that it would then show as a hard edge. That is what happened: the
margin's premultiplied (0,0,0,0) replaced the page under it.

**The fix.** The root of a tree is still copied. Every later surface goes
through `Shadow::compose_over`, a premultiplied "over"
(`dst = src + dst·(1 − α)`):
- an `Xrgb8888` source is copied, since its fourth byte is padding;
- a row that is all opaque is copied, which is every row of Firefox's content
  subsurface, so the common frame costs one scan of the alpha bytes more than
  before;
- a tree whose bounds reach past the root starts from transparent, not from
  the last frame.

**Proof.** The same page and click against the Linux compositor, before and
after (`select-linux-before.png`, `select-linux-after.png`, `select-run.sh`):
the black frame is gone and the page shows round the corners. Three unit tests
pin the blend, the XRGB copy and the opaque case. Under Wine the dropdown has
no frame and `gamma` still sets the value. On the guest: 95.7.

### 95.6 Bug, fixed: the caption buttons, a third time

§91.5 stopped `DefWindowProc` painting the caption over the folded button strip
on `WM_SETTEXT`, `WM_SETICON` and `WM_NCACTIVATE`. In this run the glyphs still
vanished, but differently:
- **Not on title changes.** 24 captures with the page retitling 10 times a
  second, restored and maximised: all visible.
- **Not on activation or caption-colour changes.** 8 captures while switching
  the foreground between two windows, with the colour animating: all visible.
- **After a page load in a window that had just been created**, in three
  sessions (`caption-lost-g0-test.png`, `caption-lost-g4-long.png`), and back
  after a later scroll (`caption-back-g4-scrolled.png`). The same loads in an
  older window: 20 captures, all visible.

The pixels say who painted. Where the glyphs should be, a lost capture holds
one colour, (40,29,68): Firefox's own tab-strip pixel. A good capture shows
DWM's caption colour (41,30,69) behind the glyphs. So the strip had been
painted opaque from outside `WM_PAINT`, whose blit always clears it inside its
update region.

**The fix.** `WM_NCPAINT` is the general form of what §91 handled for three
messages. A folded toplevel still needs the default handler for its frame, so
after it the strip is invalidated again. `present()` also adds the strip to
every frame's invalidation, so anything else that paints there lasts until the
client's next frame at most. That is one 146x31 blit and fill per frame,
inside a paint that is happening anyway. Under Wine (fallback buttons) the
window and its buttons are unchanged. On the guest: 95.7.

### 95.8 Two log oddities, not defects

- **The audio player's drop counter.** Every session logs about 434 dropped
  chunks and 62 underruns per 10 s played. That happens only while the stream
  is silent: the null sink's monitor then delivers about 15 chunks per burst,
  the queue holds 8, and the rest are dropped. While the H.264 clip played, the
  10 s that were all sound had 0 drops and 0 underruns. The counter misleads,
  and the sound is fine.
- **`Error writing selection data: Broken pipe`** in Firefox's log, once per
  copy. A reader closed a selection pipe before Firefox finished writing to it.
  Every copy arrived whole (95.2).

The grey patch that is in every capture near (104,141) is the capture tool's
privacy mask over some other process's transparent window that sits above
ours; `WindowFromPoint` there answers our window.
