| Wine | the menu paths of 95.2; after the fixes: the window, the fallback caption buttons through a navigation, the select without a frame |
| `wc-launch.sh deploy` (`wcivs`) | 16 passed, 0 failed, both times (95.7) |
| privacy | every committed capture is of a private window, a test page, a menu of Firefox's own, a caption corner or a dialog's header bar; a separate check of all 22 found one with two history rows (masked) and slivers of the desktop at the edges (masked) |

## 96. Minecraft: a pointer that holds still, a window that follows, and three forwarder gaps a game found

Branch `minecraft`, from master `59a6e8e` with `ab009e9` (§94) merged in,
2026-10-16. The brief: run Minecraft on the VM host and play it on the guest —
the window through waycompose, the rendering on the guest's Intel iGPU through
shared_vulkan — once **stock**, whose OpenGL is Zink on our ICD, and once with
**VulkanMod**, which renders Vulkan on our ICD directly; demo mode only, no
Microsoft account. Phase 1 is the workstation: the deployed topology with the
VM taken out (Wine for Windows, RADV for the GPU). `docs/minecraft.md` is the
procedure and the user's view; this section is the engineering.

### 96.1 Status in one paragraph

**Both forms play on the workstation, through the whole stack**: the game as a
native Wayland client of `wc-proxy`, `wc-compositor.exe` under Wine drawing its
window, the frames rendered by `sv-gpu-server` on the AMD iGPU. Keyboard,
**mouse-look**, F3 (renderer `… (RADV RAPHAEL_MENDOCINO) (MESA_RADV)` for stock,
`Vulkan 1.4.0`/`VulkanMod 0.6.8+1.21.11` for the mod), F2, fullscreen and back,
sound to PulseAudio and a clean quit from the close button, every run of
`scripts/sv-minecraft.sh`. Four things had to change, and each is a general
defect a game happened to be the first to reach: the compositor had **no pointer
lock and no relative motion** (96.3), a window did not follow a size its client
declared **by geometry alone** (96.4), **fullscreen** was declined (96.5), and the
forwarder **lost three output structs and returned ids for pipelines that do not
exist** — the last of which crashed the GPU side inside RADV once Zink knew which
driver it was on (96.6).

### 96.2 The setup

Prism Launcher 11.1.1 and OpenJDK 21 from nixpkgs; Minecraft 1.21.11, Fabric
loader 0.19.5 and VulkanMod 0.6.8+1.21.11 (Modrinth, sha1 checked); a data dir
of its own under `/tmp/svmc`. Demo mode is Prism's own path with no account —
setup wizard *Finish* without logging in, *No Accounts* → No, *Play demo?* →
Play Demo, a player name — after which Prism launches with `--demo` and an
access token of `0`. `scripts/sv-minecraft.sh setup` clicks those buttons on an
Xvfb by position, never by key: the wizard's focused widget is "Add Microsoft
account", and the keyboard version of this script started Microsoft's
device-code login twice. Nothing was entered and no account exists; the script
now also gives Prism a refusing `xdg-open`, no session bus, and a watchdog that
kills it if its log ever mentions a Microsoft login.

Prism's *wrapper command* records each launch (argv, environment, the launch
script it writes to the game's stdin), and `run` replays it in the session's
environment: the same `NewLaunch.jar`, classpath, `--demo` and
`-Dorg.lwjgl.glfw.libname`. That last is Prism's "use system GLFW"
(`UseNativeGLFW`), which on nixpkgs is `glfw3-minecraft`; LWJGL's own GLFW
crashes in `glfwInit` on a compositor without a `wl_seat`, which rules out a
headless pixman weston as the control (GLFW 3.4 dereferences the missing seat).
GLFW picks Wayland by itself when `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` is set and `DISPLAY` is not.

The GL environment is Firefox's (§87's `gpu.env`): our ICD alone in
`VK_DRIVER_FILES`, `nix/mesa-kopper-wayland.nix`'s EGL, Zink forced,
`LIBGL_KOPPER_DRI2=1`. The game runs under `bwrap` with an empty `/dev/dri`:
Mesa's EGL probes every DRM device before it settles on kopper, and on this
workstation the first is the NVIDIA card (`pci id for fd 16: 10de:2b85`). It
found no driver and let go; the harness must not open it at all, and an empty
`/dev/dri` is what testhost has anyway.

### 96.3 Holding the pointer

A first-person game turns the view by how far the mouse moved. On Wayland it
asks for a **lock** (`zwp_locked_pointer_v1`: the pointer stops, and cannot leave
the window) and for **relative motion** (`zwp_relative_pointer_v1`: the distance,
while the pointer stands still). GLFW does both for `GLFW_CURSOR_DISABLED`, which
is Minecraft's mouse-look, and without the globals it logs `65548: Wayland: The
compositor does not support pointer locking` and the view never turns. WLCS had
both protocols in its GAP list: "ClipCursor and SetCursorPos exist on Win32;
nothing binds them yet", "WM_INPUT raw motion exists on Win32; nothing binds it
yet". Now:

* **The globals** are smithay's (`PointerConstraintsState`,
  `RelativePointerManagerState`). The fork (`vendor/smithay`) gains one hook,
  `PointerConstraintsHandler::constraint_removed`: upstream drops a constraint
  silently when its object is destroyed, and a compositor that enforces it
  outside the protocol — a clipped system pointer — had no way to hear that
  GLFW had let go (it does, on every pause menu and inventory).
* **The policy** (`State::update_pointer_hold`): a constraint is active while
  its surface is the one under the pointer, **in the window with the keyboard**,
  and the pointer is in its region. The keyboard half is the safety property:
  Windows moves the keyboard on Alt-Tab, a taskbar click, the Start menu, a
  toast — and the lock ends with it, `oneshot` constraints gone. It is
  re-evaluated on pointer motion, keyboard focus (one wrapper around
  `set_keyboard_focus`, so a sixth caller cannot forget), constraint creation
  and removal, commits of the held surface and window destruction, and the
  platform hears only a change: `ToUi::PointerHold { id, Some(Locked |
  Confined(rect)) | None }`.
* **Motion**: platform motion now carries its distance. While locked the
  pointer does not move and only `relative_motion` is sent; while confined the
  position is clamped (`crate::hold::clamp_into`, last pixel inclusive, the
  number WLCS asks for); otherwise `relative_motion` rides in the same
  `wl_pointer.frame` as the absolute motion.
* **Win32** (`platform/win32_hold.rs`): a lock is `ClipCursor` to one pixel at
  the window's centre plus `RegisterRawInputDevices` for the mouse; `WM_INPUT`
  becomes `FromUi::PointerRelative`, and `WM_MOUSEMOVE` (and the motion before a
  click) is not forwarded while locked. A confinement is `ClipCursor` to the
  region's bounding box (`crate::hold::region_bounds`; a region with holes is
  bounded, not shaped, and says so). Raw input that reports **positions** — a
  tablet, a VM's absolute pointer, remote-desktop injection — is turned into
  distances (`AbsoluteMotion`, scaled from `0..65535` to the screen or the
  virtual desktop). The clip is let go **by the UI thread itself** on
  `WM_KILLFOCUS`, `WM_ACTIVATE(WA_INACTIVE)` and destruction, before the
  Wayland thread has heard, and put back on `WM_SETFOCUS` if the Wayland side
  still holds it (§93's focus grace); it follows the window on
  `WM_WINDOWPOSCHANGED`, and is re-asserted from `WM_INPUT` if something else
  changed it. A pointer left clipped to a window the user has left is the one
  failure this must not have, so it does not depend on one thread's message.
* **The synthetic Win32** (`control.rs`) now does what `ClipCursor` and raw
  input do to the suite's moves: a new verb `pointer-move-by` (the shim's
  `move_relative`, which until now was turned into an absolute move from the
  shim's own idea of where the pointer was) moves from where the pointer *is*,
  clipped; under a lock it produces `PointerRelative` and moves nothing. And it
  **raises and activates on a click**, before delivering it — `WM_MOUSEACTIVATE`,
  `WM_ACTIVATE` and `WM_SETFOCUS` precede `WM_LBUTTONDOWN` on Windows — with a
  Z order of its own (`Control::stack`: new windows on top, clicked ones on top,
  popups with their owner). Until §96 a click on a background window did nothing
  here.

`wc-proxy` learns both XML files (`wayland-protocols` 0.32.12, as the
compositor's smithay), and its table test grows to 47 interfaces.

**WLCS, headless**: the two suites now run (they were skips): 18 tests, 16 pass.
The other two are the `persistent` ones: they destroy the window that took the
keyboard and expect the constraint back on the window underneath within the
same round trip; here the keyboard comes back on the platform's next turn, as on
Windows (the UI thread's `DestroyWindow` activates the next window), and the
constraint does come back — the log shows it after each of the three cycles —
one round trip after WLCS looks. Both are in the expected-failure table with
that reason. Click-to-activate also fixed
`XdgToplevelStableConfigurationTest.activated_state_follows_pointer`, and the
whole suite went from master's **429 passed, 37 failed, 759 skipped** to **448
passed, 36 failed, 741 skipped**, 30 of the failures expected (master 28).

**Minecraft**: every run locks, takes 30 raw-input motions while locked and turns
the view by them (F3's `Facing` from `-37.8 / -17.9` to `2.7 / -17.9` after 300 px
right, to `2.7 / -40.4` after 150 px up), and releases the clip on Escape, on
F11 and when the window closes. Wine reports `xdotool`'s XTEST motion as raw
input, so this is the Win32 path end to end, minus the hardware.

### 96.4 A window that follows a size declared by geometry alone

GLFW with libdecor maps its first frame *with* client-side decorations — 854x480
of game inside 902x552 of frame and shadow subsurfaces — learns a moment later
that the decorations are the server's, destroys the frame and declares
`set_window_geometry(0, 0, 854, 480)` **with no new buffer**, because its content
did not change. §91 made a window follow a client that is still choosing its
size, but only on the buffer path; the geometry-only commit path (§37's crop fix)
moved the crop and left the `HWND` at 902x552, with a band of background under
the game for as long as it ran. That path now follows too, by the same rule
(`client_chooses`, the window mapped, a different size): `window 1 client chose
854x480 by its geometry alone; the window follows`.

### 96.5 Fullscreen

`xdg_toplevel.set_fullscreen` was smithay's default — a bare configure, which
declines the request — so Minecraft's F11 did nothing. It is now honoured like a
maximise (§45): `ToUi::Fullscreen` and the `Fullscreen` state in the same
configure with the output's size. On Win32 that is the borderless fullscreen
games use: the style and outer rectangle saved, `WS_POPUP`, the window over the
monitor's `rcMonitor` (not the work area, so the taskbar is under it), the size
reaching the client through `WM_SIZE`; `unset_fullscreen` puts both back.
(96.10: the *placement* is saved and replaced too, since a restore from the
taskbar goes back to it.)
Measured: `fullscreen on its monitor (1600x1000 at 0,0)`, F3 `Display:
1600x1000`, and back to 854x480.

### 96.6 Three forwarder gaps, and a GPU-side crash they were hiding

With the validation layer inside the game (`SVMC_APP_VALIDATE=1`) the stock
game reported, on every start:

* `VUID-VkSwapchainCreateInfoKHR-imageColorSpace-parameter` and
  `-imageFormat-01273`: **Zink on Wayland creates every swapchain with
  `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT`**, unconditionally since Mesa 26.2
  (`zink_kopper.c`), and that colour space belongs to `VK_EXT_swapchain_colorspace`,
  which our ICD did not have. It is also the true description of our WSI — the
  present copies the bytes as they are — so the ICD now advertises the instance
  extension and lists the pass-through colour space beside sRGB for all four
  formats (sRGB first, so nothing else changes its choice).
* `VUID-VkDescriptorSetLayoutCreateInfo-flags-00281`: push-descriptor layouts with
  `maxPushDescriptors (0)`. vulkaninfo through the forwarder showed the whole of
  `VkPhysicalDeviceVulkan14Properties` zero (`maxPushDescriptors`,
  `defaultRobustness*`, `copySrcLayoutCount`, …) against RADV's real values.
  **The generator refuses a writeback for a struct with a pointer-valued member**
  — it cannot know the caller's capacity — and a refused link was left as the
  application left it. Three such links matter: the 1.4 properties,
  `VkPhysicalDeviceHostImageCopyProperties`, and
  `VkPhysicalDeviceLayeredApiPropertiesListKHR`, which is how **Zink identifies
  the driver**: it passes a capacity of one, an untouched link says "one layered
  API, all zeros", and Zink takes the zero as the driver id — `zink Vulkan
  1.4(… (Driver Unknown))` — and applies **none of its per-driver workarounds**,
  RADV's or Intel's. The generated `store_pnext` now hands a refused link to
  `sv-icd-entry/src/writeback.rs`, which writes those three by hand: every scalar,
  the layered list's count and entries up to the caller's capacity, and the copy
  layouts' counts as zero (the arrays are not carried, and `hostImageCopy` is not
  advertised). F3 now says `(MESA_RADV)`.

Knowing it was on RADV, Zink took its RADV paths, and **the GPU side died in
`radv_CmdBindPipeline`** (SIGSEGV, `coredumpctl`), with the GPU-side layer's
`VUID-vkCmdBindPipeline-pipeline-parameter: Invalid VkPipeline Object 0x0` just
before. The cause is in the generated GPU side: a batch create answered the app
side's minted ids **whether or not the driver made the object**. Zink's
fast-link path calls `vkCreateGraphicsPipelines` with
`FAIL_ON_PIPELINE_COMPILE_REQUIRED`, RADV answers `VK_PIPELINE_COMPILE_REQUIRED`
(`[trace] vkCreateGraphicsPipelines -> VkResult(1000297000)`) and a null pipeline,
and Zink tests the *handle* to decide whether to compile; given an id back it
bound a pipeline that existed nowhere, the GPU side translated it to null, and
RADV dereferenced it. The generator now returns `VK_NULL_HANDLE` for every
element the driver left null and binds only the rest (`Out::Array` in
`emit/gpu_entry.rs`). This is not a RADV matter: on the guest, Zink identifies
Intel's driver the same way and takes Intel's paths.

The VUIDs that remain on the GPU side, for stock only and around F2, F11 and
world loading, are `VUID-vkCmdBeginRendering-pRenderingInfo-09592` (an internal
image or a swapchain image used as an attachment while in
`SHADER_READ_ONLY`/`PRESENT_SRC`) and the related
`VUID-vkCmdDrawMultiEXT-imageLayout-00344`. **The first is Zink's own**: with Zink
on this RADV *without* the forwarder — sway headless on the iGPU as the
compositor, a virtual keyboard from `wtype`, the layer inside the game, F2 and
F11 pressed the same way — it appears in both forms, `SHADER_READ_ONLY` and
`PRESENT_SRC`. The second did not appear in the 120 s native run. VulkanMod's
runs have no VUID on the GPU side. (The layer *inside* the game crashes Zink
eventually on native RADV as well, in `zink_gfx_program_update_optimal` or
`check_pool_alloc`; it is a diagnostic, not a gate.)

### 96.7 Measurements

The workstation, the AMD iGPU (RADV, Mesa 26.2.0 on the GPU side), 854x480
windowed, render distance 8, the 30 s steady window of a run, the rate from our
ICD's `icd.present` trace:

| | vsync | frames/s | present interval p50 / p95 / p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| stock (Zink, MESA_RADV) | off | 238 | 3.0 / 8.7 / 17.1 ms |
| VulkanMod | off | 347 | 2.0 / 8.1 / 11.7 ms |
| stock | on | 32 | 19.4 / 71.2 / 114.8 ms |
| VulkanMod | on | 195 | 3.1 / 17.8 / 37.2 ms |

Before 96.6 (Zink not knowing its driver) stock ran at 317 frames/s: RADV's
workarounds include turning push descriptors off. With vsync on, stock is paced
by Mesa's Wayland swap interval — it waits for `wl_surface.frame` — and runs at
half the 60 Hz frame clock with a long tail: the timeline (§88) puts 17 ms of
each frame in `vkWaitSemaphores` round trips and 14 ms in the present fence,
against well under 5 ms of each with vsync off. That points at the iGPU's clocks
under a light load rather than at the path, and it is the number to measure
again on the guest, where the frame clock is DWM's. VulkanMod's vsync is a
present mode, and our ICD's `FIFO` is not tied to a display (`wsi.rs`), so it is
not capped.

### 96.9 What is not done

1. **Phase 2**: the guest, its Intel iGPU, a launcher app and the session's
   sound. Played by the user on the guest, both renderers, with sound; what
   that found is 96.10 and 96.11, and what is still to be seen there is at the
   end of 96.11.
2. **Absolute pointers**: mouse-look from a remote desktop (TeamViewer injects
   absolute positions) is implemented (`AbsoluteMotion`) and not measured; it
   stops at the edge of the remote screen by construction.
3. **vsync pacing on the workstation** (96.7).
4. **The Wine leg cannot drive a pointer**, so the Win32 half of 96.3 is measured
   by Minecraft under Wine, not by WLCS.

### 96.10 On the guest: a fullscreen game minimises when it loses focus, and the test helper took focus

The user played both games from the deployed launcher. Two reports came back:
a fullscreen VulkanMod "went to the taskbar and could not be restored", and
stock Minecraft did the same earlier.

**The minimising is GLFW's, and it is right.** GLFW's `GLFW_AUTO_ICONIFY`
(default on) minimises a fullscreen window when it loses focus: on Wayland
`xdgSurfaceHandleConfigure` calls `xdg_toplevel_set_minimized` when a configure
clears `activated` while the window has a monitor (glfw3-minecraft 3.4,
`wl_window.c:636`), and GLFW's Win32 backend does the same on Windows. What
took focus was the test helper: a scheduled task in session 1 starting
`powershell.exe -WindowStyle Hidden`, which Windows 11 hosts in Windows Terminal
regardless, so a terminal window came up and took the foreground. Every look at
a fullscreen game minimised it.

**A real click restores it.** `wc-desk mouse` (SendInput, real input) on the
game's taskbar button brought the window back and focused. The helper's own
`ShowWindow(SW_RESTORE)` + `SetForegroundWindow` from a background process
cannot, because Windows' foreground lock refuses `SetForegroundWindow` from a
process the user did not just interact with. That is not something to fix.

**What was wrong: the placement.** The restored window came back 1296x768 at
-8,-8, borderless, with the taskbar showing beneath it: the maximised placement
it had before F11. `set_fullscreen` had saved and moved only the window's
rectangle (`GetWindowRect`, `SetWindowPos`). Windows keeps a second answer,
`WINDOWPLACEMENT` (the normal rectangle and whether the window is maximised),
and a restore from the taskbar uses that one. Now `set_fullscreen` saves the
placement and, for as long as the window is fullscreen, sets it to normal (not
maximised; minimised stays minimised) with the monitor as its normal rectangle
and without `WPF_RESTORETOMAXIMIZED`. Leaving puts the saved placement back,
maximised if it was, and a window that is on the taskbar at that moment stays
there. `rcNormalPosition` is in workspace coordinates unless the window is a
tool window. That arithmetic is `platform/fullscreen.rs`, pure and tested on
every target (6 tests: taskbar at the bottom, top and left, a tool window, a
second monitor, the show states).

**The helpers, for anyone testing a fullscreen application on the guest:**

* **Keys**: `/tmp/wcrun/guest-keys.sh f11 esc e shift+w …` injects through
  QEMU's virtual keyboard (QMP `input-send-event`). No guest process starts, so
  nothing takes focus. It refuses the Windows key. The VM has only a PS/2
  mouse (relative motion), so avoid clicks while a game is fullscreen.
* **Looking**: `wc-desk` is now a GUI-subsystem program, with no console, so
  started by a scheduled task it shows no window and takes no foreground.
  `--stdout FILE` takes its output to a file, which is how a scheduled task
  gets it back. Started from ssh or `cmd /c … > file` it writes to the handles
  it was given, and from an interactive console it attaches to that console.
  Measured on the guest: `wc-desk windows` from the scheduled task with a
  restored fullscreen Minecraft in front, and the game stayed in front and was
  not minimised. With the old helper, every run minimised it.

### 96.11 Minecraft's icon, and Prism Launcher from Windows

**Minecraft names no app id.** On the guest its window was
`Waycompose.unnamed.c4`: the generic icon, a taskbar button of its own,
nothing to pin. GLFW 3.4 takes its Wayland app id from the
`GLFW_WAYLAND_APP_ID` hint, and Minecraft does not set it. On plain
`xdg_toplevel` GLFW then sends `set_app_id("")`. On libdecor, which
glfw3-minecraft uses when libdecor is there, it sends nothing at all
(`libdecor_frame_set_app_id` only `if (strlen(appId))`, `wl_window.c:822`).
The local run showed the second: the proxy saw no `set_app_id`.

**The launcher says it in the environment, and the proxy acts on it.** The
proxy already reads `/proc/<pid>/exe` of each client (§18.5). It now also
reads `/proc/<pid>/environ` for two variables (`icons::client_env`):

* `WC_APP_ID`: a toplevel of that client starts with this app id, sent right
  after `xdg_surface.get_toplevel`, and an empty `set_app_id` is replaced by
  it. A client that names itself is never overruled: its own non-empty
  `set_app_id` follows and replaces the default, as any second one does. The
  value must be a desktop id (`icons::app_id_ok`, the launcher's rule).
* `XDG_DATA_DIRS`: joins the icon search after the proxy's own directories and
  before the executable's prefix. An application installed under a home
  directory and run by an interpreter (`~/wc-mc`, Java) is found nowhere else.

What a client can choose this way is the name of its own icon and where its
own desktop entry is, which it could already choose with `set_app_id`.

`minecraft-demo` sets `WC_APP_ID` to the desktop id of its shortcut
(`wc-minecraft`, `wc-minecraft-vulkanmod`) and puts the installation's
`share/` first in `XDG_DATA_DIRS`. Since the launcher derives the shortcut's
identity from that same desktop id (§92.1), window and pin are one button.
Measured locally (Phase 1 harness, `SVMC_GAME_ENV` with the two variables):
`xdg_toplevel@28 starts with app id "wc-minecraft"`, the icon resolved from
the bundle's `48x48/apps/wc-minecraft.png` (Minecraft's own, from the game's
assets), `window 1 icon <- 1 image(s) published for "wc-minecraft"`, and the
window moved to `Waycompose.app.wc-minecraft`. Every other check of the run
passed, including a clean quit.

**Prism Launcher from Windows.** `prism` is an application like the others
(`scripts/sv-minecraft-apps.ini`): Prism 11.1.1 from nixpkgs on Prism's data
in `~/wc-mc/prism`, with both instances, named "Minecraft 1.21.11" and
"Minecraft 1.21.11 (VulkanMod)". It gets a desktop shortcut, a Start menu
entry and a pinnable identity like Firefox's.

* **Qt on Wayland, Windows' caption.** `env = QT_QPA_PLATFORM=wayland` (never
  X11) and `QT_WAYLAND_DISABLE_WINDOWDECORATION=1`, so Qt draws no frame of its
  own and the compositor gives the window Windows' caption (`titlebar = none`,
  §82). On the guest: Windows' caption with Prism's icon and three buttons, and
  nothing of Qt's above the page.
* **One identity.** Qt's app id is the desktop file's name,
  `org.prismlauncher.PrismLauncher`. The launcher would have derived the
  shortcut's identity from the entry's `StartupWMClass` (`PrismLauncher`),
  making window and pin two buttons, so the guest block sets
  `app-id = org.prismlauncher.PrismLauncher`. On the guest:
  `aumid="Waycompose.app.org.prismlauncher.PrismLauncher"`, a relaunch command
  (`wc-launch.exe prism`), and Prism's own 256 px icon resolved by the proxy
  from its package.
* **The game Prism starts** inherits everything from Prism, which has it from
  `wc-session`: the session's Wayland display (GLFW picks Wayland by itself
  with no `DISPLAY`), its sound (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/pulse/native`), the GPU
  environment (`gpu.env` and the session's `SV_SOCKET`). From the instances it
  gets system GLFW (`UseNativeGLFW`), the narrator off and Prism's 1 GiB heap.
  The one thing Prism cannot pass on is the identity. Prism's global wrapper
  command, `bin/minecraft-prism-wrap`, sets `WC_APP_ID` by instance (`INST_ID`)
  and the data directory, then `exec`s the game. It is a global setting, so an
  instance the person adds later has it too. A game from Prism and the same
  game from its shortcut are the same taskbar button with Minecraft's icon,
  separate from Prism's: that is how Windows shows a launcher and the game it
  started.
* **No account, and none prevented.** With no valid account Prism opens its
  Quick Setup page ("Add Microsoft account") at every start
  (`Application::createSetupWizard`: `login = !anyAccountIsValid() &&
  SupportsMSA`); **Finish** goes on without one. Play then asks "No
  Accounts" (No), "Play demo?" (Play Demo) and a player name (OK), and the game
  starts with `--demo`. A person who wants their own Microsoft account adds it
  in Prism. Nothing here stops that, and the automation never enters
  credentials. The login watchdog and the refusing `xdg-open` of 96.2 belong to
  `sv-minecraft.sh setup` and are not in the deployed path.
* **`ship` keeps what the player owns**: worlds, `options.txt`,
  `servers.dat`, `accounts.json`, logs and screenshots are excluded from the
  copy and from `--delete`. The bundle's `options.txt` goes only where an
  instance has none.

**Prism's main window died, and the fault was smithay's.** On the guest Prism's
setup page worked, and its main window broke the connection the moment it
appeared ("The Wayland connection broke"). Reproduced under Wine
(`scripts/wc-prism-icon.sh`), the compositor said: `ProtocolError { code: 3,
xdg_toplevel_icon_v1, "The provided buffer has been destroyed before the
toplevel icon" }`. Qt gives every window with an icon three shm buffers on an
`xdg_toplevel_icon_v1`, calls `set_icon`, destroys the icon, then the pools and
buffers. That is the protocol's order. The setup page had sent
`set_icon(nil)`, so it never hit this. smithay registers a destruction hook on
each icon buffer and removes them when the icon is destroyed, but its
`ShmBufferUserData::remove_destruction_hook` compared with `!=`: it removed the
first hook that was *not* the one asked for, so a buffer's only hook was never
removed. The vendored smithay now compares with `==` (a `WAYCOMPOSE FORK` note
in `wayland/shm/mod.rs`). With it Prism's main window opens, lists both
instances, and wears its own icon from its three buffers (`icon <- 3
buffer(s) from the client's own xdg_toplevel_icon_v1`). `wc-prism-icon.sh` is
the gate: PASS. It should go upstream: any smithay compositor kills a Qt 6
window with an icon this way.

**Not yet seen on the guest** (the desktop was the user's): a game started
from Prism, and Minecraft's icon on the guest's taskbar. Both need one short
slot: open Prism from its shortcut, Finish, select an instance, Play, then the
three dialogs, then a look at the taskbar.

Gates on `ed365b4` (master 86a6261 merged): `cargo test --workspace
--no-fail-fast` **102 binaries, 2986 passed, 0 failed**, 8 ignored (new:
`platform::fullscreen`'s 6, `icons`' 2 environment tests, and the session test
of the app id on the wire); `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` exit 0,
no warning in a line this branch wrote; `cargo check --workspace --target
x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` exit 0; `scripts/sv-minecraft.sh run stock 150` with
`WC_APP_ID` PASS.

## 97. The GPU arena becomes one pool: leases instead of slots, and a device carved out of the guest's RAM

Branch `gpu-arena-dyn`, from master `2982bdd` with `gpu-oom` (§95) and
`minecraft` (§96) merged in, 2026-10-16. The brief: two Firefox windows, or
Firefox and Minecraft, must fit on the forwarded GPU whenever their total does;
memory a session frees must be another session's at once; running out must be
an ordinary `VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_DEVICE_MEMORY` and never a lost device; and every
byte shared between host and guest stays on the ivshmem device, never a file
path and never a copy.

### 97.1 Status in one paragraph

The GPU ivshmem device is now **one pool** that every session of the guest's
GPU process leases from: a control region when a session starts, a blob
reserve, 4 MiB chunks for small allocations and a lease of its own for
anything of 1 MiB or more, each lease its own host-pointer import, each given
back the moment it empties. Fixed slots are gone (`gpu-arena = slots` keeps
§87's path for a rollback). The device does **not** grow at run time: vfio
pins every byte of an ivshmem BAR, the host has no RAM to spare, and adding a
device takes QEMU's monitor, which is root's. Instead the device grows from 256
to 1024 MiB at the VM's next start, carved out of the guest's RAM (13312 →
12544 MiB), so the host pins exactly what it pinned before (97.3). Locally, two
Firefox windows ran on a 256 MiB pool with hardware WebRender throughout, and
the guest's own code path ran end to end on lavapipe with two applications
filling the pool at once (97.6). Not yet run on the guest (97.8).

### 97.2 What ran out, measured

§95 measured the crash: the arena (memory types 1–3), not the blob space and
not device-local memory. Firefox's two-window working set was 42–53 MiB in a
56 MiB share, and fragmentation finished it: the largest free run fell to
1.9 MiB, below Zink's 2 MiB slab, with 6 MiB free. §96 then moved every buffer
an application never maps out of the arena (type 0), which roughly halved
Firefox's arena use, and measured VulkanMod at more than 240 MiB of mappable
memory: two 64 MiB staging buffers and its host-coherent pools.

What the pool's own accounting says about the same two-window Firefox on this
branch (RADV, `serve --pool 256M`, 120 s, the lines `[gpu] pool high water`):

| | |
|---|---|
| sessions at start | `glxtest` (2 leases, given back at its end), then the browser |
| browser, first 30 s | 32.9 MiB leased: blob reserve 8, 2 chunks, 2 dedicated (8.9) |
| browser, high water | 68.0 MiB leased, of which 24–26 MiB in allocations (`SV_DEBUG`) |
| largest free block at the high water | 186.6 MiB of 188 MiB free (3 free blocks) |

The gap between 68 MiB leased and 26 MiB used was the first chunk policy
(8 MiB chunks, a lease of its own from 4 MiB): Zink's slabs here are
2,310,144 bytes, three fill a chunk and leave 1.4 MiB of it unusable. From
1 MiB up an allocation now gets its own lease, rounded to the pool's 64 KiB, so
the waste is at most 64 KiB a slab (97.5).

### 97.3 Growth: decided by what vfio pins, and by the host's RAM

The brief offered three ways to grow past the device; each was measured or
read before it was chosen or refused.

* **Lazily populated host pages: impossible.** On testhost QEMU's `VmLck` is
  14024576 kB, which is 13312 + 128 + 256 MiB exactly — the guest's RAM and both
  ivshmem devices — with `-overcommit mem-lock=off`. That is vfio's type-1
  accounting: it maps every RAM-backed region into the IOMMU, ivshmem BARs
  included, and pins every page. Both backing files are fully allocated
  (`stat` blocks = size). A sparse file buys nothing here. The VM's
  virtio-balloon is inhibited by vfio for the same reason.
* **Hot-plugged regions: rejected.** QMP `device_add` works (slots 0x10–0x19,
  0x1b and 0x1e were free), but each added region is pinned host RAM for as
  long as it is plugged, and driving QMP takes root on the host. The user
  rejected a root helper in the launch path. The host's RAM decides it anyway:
  MemAvailable was 636 MB at 14:27 and **186 MB** at 14:50, because the
  applications the guest runs live on the host (the minecraft agent's Java was
  1057 MiB RSS; Firefox is the same kind of process). The host's own baseline is
  about 1 GB: 280 MiB of service RSS, 450 MiB of kernel (slab 268, page tables
  42 + 80, stacks) and 230 MiB of page cache. A pinned region would come out of
  the applications' RAM, and an out-of-memory host kills QEMU first, by size, and
  QEMU is <guest-user>'s VM. The pool code keeps a regions table (a pool offset is
  `region << 32 | offset`), so a second device configured at boot needs no
  change of format; nothing grows while the VM runs.
* **A larger device at the next VM start: chosen, at no host cost.** The guest
  had 7.3 GiB of its 12.9 GiB free and 8.7 GiB committed of a 13.75 GiB commit
  limit. 768 MiB moves from the guest to the device: `memoryMB` 13312 → 12544,
  `waycomposeArena.gpu.sizeMiB` 256 → 1024 (a BAR is a power of two). QEMU pins
  13696 MiB before and after. The 1 GiB BAR fits OVMF's 64-bit window, which is
  at 448 GiB, 2 GiB long, and holds the iGPU's 256 MiB aperture, the GPU device
  and the arena today; QEMU widens the window to cover what is mapped.

The demand it is sized for: Firefox's three sessions and two windows, about
130 MiB with today's per-session costs; VulkanMod, more than 240 MiB of
mappable memory plus a session's start; together about 430 MiB. 512 MiB is the
smallest device that holds both with almost no room; 1024 leaves room for a
larger window, video, or a second game.

The change is nix-config branch `testhost-wc-gpu-pool` (56bda9b, on
6511e8a): system `y0yxfch0…`. Its only difference from the running system
(`k77fwidz…`, which building 6511e8a here reproduces exactly) is
`windows-vm.service`'s arguments. It takes effect at the VM's next start, and
that start must be a planned cold restart right after the switch: a
hibernation written with 13312 MiB that resumes onto 12544 MiB is discarded by
Windows. `windows-vm-shutdown` asks qemu-ga for `guest-shutdown` (a full
power-off) on a plain `systemctl restart windows-vm`, and hibernates only while
`switch-to-configuration` is running, so the restart goes after the switch has
exited.

### 97.4 The design: one owner, leases, and a session heap

**The pool** (`sv_arena::pool`) lives in the guest's GPU process, the one
process that maps the device (its driver gives the BAR to one handle, §87.2).
It hands out leases at a 64 KiB granule from a TLSF allocator per region and
keeps an account per session: what it holds, its high water, its refusals.
Two rules keep one application from stopping the others:

* **A cap per session**: three quarters of the pool, control region excepted
  (192 of 256 MiB, 768 of 1024). With the cap at the pool less 48 MiB, a second
  process beside a full one started and then could allocate nothing (97.6).
* **A reserve for starting**: the last `control + blob reserve` bytes of region
  0 only take the two leases a session cannot start without. With only the
  control region allowed in, a process started beside a full one got its rings,
  was refused its blob reserve, and its ICD refused to load.

**The protocol** is three commands on the existing rings, hand-written in
`sv_proto::sv` like `svImportArenaSlab`: `svArenaInfo` (asked once at attach,
carrying the process name for the pool's log; answers fixed or leased),
`svLeaseArena` (a length and a purpose; answers a pool offset and the memory
type the lease was imported as, or `VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_DEVICE_MEMORY`) and
`svReleaseArena`. `WIRE_VERSION` went 2 → 3, so a stale peer is refused at
attach rather than on its first allocation. The GPU side imports each lease on
its own (`VK_EXT_external_memory_host`, the same call §87.3 measured on Intel)
into the session's device, records it in the session's object table, and
resolves every `(memory, offset)` the application names only inside leases of
its own. A command blob is read only if it lies in one of the session's
leases. A release frees the import before the range goes back, so no range is
another session's while this device still holds it.

**The host** (`sv-hostd ivshmem-serve`) checks a pooled session's control
region by its stamps as before, and the pool header's nonce (the first 64 KiB
of the device, `sv_transport::poolhdr`) against the one the `Hello` carries
(`Locator::IvshmemPool`): a GPU process that restarted, or the wrong file, is
refused by name. The ICD is handed the device's file **by name** and the
control region's offset, as §87 did; it reserves the pool's address space and
maps the file at offset 0, so a pool offset is an offset into one mapping. No
descriptor crosses (docs/design.md §1a), and nothing is copied: a mapped
`VkDeviceMemory` is a pointer into the device's pages, as before.

**The session heap** (`sv_arena::heap`) is the app side's allocator, as
docs/design.md §5.2 always had it. It asks for a lease when nothing it holds fits,
with the state lock dropped across the round trip, and gives a lease back when
its last allocation is freed. A dedicated lease goes back at once, a chunk once
another chunk is already empty. The arena heap the ICD advertises is what the
session may lease (the cap, or the pool if smaller); the first build advertised
the address space it reserves, which took the whole size away from the
device-local heap, and Zink refused every device-local allocation ("can't
allocate … from heap that's only 0 bytes").

A session's control region is now the layout's size, 8.06 MiB, not §87's
16 MiB: sixteen rings of two 256 KiB lanes are 8 MiB, and the other half was
never written. On a pool, a byte a control region does not use is a byte no
session can lease.

### 97.5 The allocator, and its tests

`sv_arena::tlsf` is a two-level segregated-fit allocator: classes by the top
set bit of the size and sixteen subdivisions of each, a bitmap per level, free
lists of physical blocks that merge with both neighbours the moment they are
freed. A search rounds the request up to the next class, so any block found
fits. One step the textbook leaves out: when that finds nothing, the request's
own class is walked, because on a nearly full pool an exact fit just below the
rounded class is the memory a refusal would leave on the table. Everything is
in private memory: the allocator never touches the range it manages.

| test | what it holds |
|---|---|
| `tlsf::random_sequences_never_overlap_never_leak_and_coalesce` | 40 seeds × 4000 random allocations and frees, 4 KiB and 64 KiB granules: no two live blocks overlap, the used bytes always equal the sum of the live blocks, every invariant (`Tlsf::check`: the blocks tile the range, links agree both ways, no two free blocks touch, every free block is in its class's list and the bitmaps say so) after every step, and one free block of the whole range once everything is freed |
| `tlsf::firefoxs_churn_keeps_a_two_mib_run_free` | §95's workload replayed (2 MiB slabs and three readback sizes churning at 46 of 64 MiB), and a 2 MiB request always fits |
| `tlsf::an_exact_fit_below_the_rounded_class_is_found` | the fallback |
| `pool::random_pool_traffic_never_overlaps_or_leaks` | 20 seeds × 3000 steps of five sessions leasing, releasing and closing while regions are added and removed: no overlap within a region, accounts that balance, a cap never exceeded, and every region one free block at the end |
| `pool::firefox_and_minecraft_fit_when_the_total_does`, `a_session_cannot_take_the_reserve_or_more_than_its_cap`, `a_draining_region_…`, `closing_a_session_…` | the policies |
| `heap::random_heap_traffic_through_a_pool_balances` | 16 seeds × 3000 steps of every size through a real pool: allocations inside their lease, never overlapping, and the pool gets every byte back |
| `heap::two_windows_resizing_never_run_out_and_give_memory_back` | two windows' readback buffers resized every 500 steps among 1280×752, 1296×768 and 1920×1080 while 2 MiB slabs churn, 20000 steps on a 256 MiB pool: never refused, and never more slack than two chunks and a granule a lease |
| `sv_gpu_server::pool::a_refused_lease_returns_instead_of_hanging` | the first build logged a refusal by re-locking the pool it held (a guard in a `match` scrutinee lives to the end of the `match`) and hung the GPU process on the first full pool; found by 97.6 |
| Miri, `cargo miri test -p sv-arena --lib -- tlsf pool heap` | 18 passed, no undefined behaviour (the random tests at 1–2 seeds and 250–600 steps under Miri; 3716 s) |

### 97.10 On the guest with the 1024 MiB device: two failures, and the soak

The VM restarted at 18:20 with the 1024 MiB GPU device and 12544 MiB of
RAM (97.3). `wcgpu` and `wcmc` were redeployed from master `ad406ac`
(`gpu-arena = pool`, 15 of 15 checks each). The first Firefox crashed twice
before the soak ran, for two reasons, neither of them the pool's allocator.

**A quiet session was ended while its application lived.** Firefox sat
idle for two minutes before the soak driver connected. The guest's GPU
process ended the browser's session with "ring 1: nothing for 120s; the app
side is gone" (`session::IDLE_LIMIT`), although the ICD was beating every
20 ms. The pool gave the freed control region to the next session, Firefox's
RDD process, and re-creating its rings reset the generation under the live
browser: "peer restarted: generation 1 became 0", `VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST`, and
Zink took the browser down. The 120 s limit was older than the pool (the slot
path shares `session::drain`), but a slot path's freed slot was not handed on
at once. Fixed in `efb7b03`: a live heartbeat resets the idle clock, so
`IDLE_LIMIT` applies only to an app side that never beats; and a pooled
session the GPU side ends with an error keeps its control region and leases
instead of handing them on. Locally, a session holding 184 MiB with no ring
traffic for 135 s beside a second session kept working and freed and
reallocated normally.

**A stale session held the doorbell.** Redeploying `wcgpu` stopped the
guest's launcher, but the crashed session's host units
(`wc-launch-gpu-wcg-13688` and its proxy and audio) kept running. Its
`sv-hostd` kept QEMU's only connection to `svbell.sock`; the next session's
hub connected into QEMU's backlog, never to be accepted, and the ICD's socket
to the hub filled. Firefox's renderer thread then sat in `send()`
(`PortWake::poke`, inside `vkCreateGraphicsPipelines`) and its main thread in
a synchronous `FlushRendering`, until the ICD's calls timed out. Fixed for
the application in `8b68865` (the host-side doorbell writer queues to a
thread of its own and drops a byte rather than block); fixed at the cause in
§99, which takes the port away from sessions altogether.

**The soak**, 19:06–19:37, `wcgpu` on the 1024 MiB pool, Firefox's two
windows with the first playing a looping 720p H.264 clip
(`SOAK_MODE=two-windows SOAK_VIDEO=1`, the driver on the workstation over a
forward of Marionette):

| check | result |
|---|---|
| page loads, compositor samples | 375; WebRender in all 375 |
| step errors, DEVICE_LOST | 0, 0 |
| video | 55,861 frames, 190 dropped (0.34%), `err=none` |
| quit | clean from the last window, no minidump |
| pool high water | 97.7 of 1024 MiB: browser 74.1, RDD (video decode) 23.5 |

Minecraft on the same pool (`wcmc` and the `wcl` installation): stock
1.21.11 rendered through Zink on the Intel iGPU at 52 fps, and VulkanMod
0.6.8 at 30 fps, both with F3 showing the renderer and no artifacts
(`/tmp/wcrun/minecraft-shots/`). The user played both from TeamViewer. One
compositor bug was found and left for its owner: leaving fullscreen (F11 on
a fullscreen window) minimised the window to (-32000,-32000), and neither
`ShowWindow(SW_RESTORE)` nor a click on its taskbar button brought it back.

## 98. Firefox's crash at quit: a frame shown after its surface was gone

**Superseded in part by §100:** with `libsv_wlshim.so` preloaded, a Wayland
swapchain pipelines again, safely; without it, everything below still holds.

Branch `quit-crash`, from `desktop-checks` 8d8c32b, 2026-10-16. The brief: §95.4
saw Firefox crash once when its last window closed on the guest, and the
gpu-arena-dyn agent reproduced a crash at quit on the workstation (two windows
and a video; not caused by its pool). Find the faulting stack, decide whose it
is, and fix it if it is ours.

### 98.1 Status in one paragraph

**It was ours.** The pipelined present of §88 shows a frame from the
swapchain's `sv-present` thread, with `attach`, `damage` and `commit` on the
application's `wl_surface`, after `vkQueuePresentKHR` has returned. Firefox
destroys that surface before the swapchain: when it closes a window, and at
quit, where it never destroys the swapchain at all. A frame still in flight
then marshals on a freed proxy: SIGSEGV twice, and once SIGABRT from glibc's
futex check, all three in `present::wayland::Surface::put` on `sv-present`
(98.3). That broke an invariant Mesa writes down and Firefox builds on: a
Wayland surface is touched only inside the application's own swap call (98.4).
**A Wayland swapchain now presents on the calling thread**, as Mesa's own WSI
does; X11 and headless keep the presenter. With the window widened on purpose
(a 30 ms sleep before the frame is shown), the old order crashed in 4 of 4 runs and
the new one in none of 6 (98.6). The price is the present's wait back on the
renderer thread for Wayland frames: at most a frame in a hundred on the
workstation, and nothing measurable on the guest, where §88 had put the
wait at 3.3 ms (98.7).

### 98.2 The recipe

From gpu-arena-dyn's harness change, taken here without its pool:

```
SVWL_VIDEO=1 SVWL_VULKAN_DECODE=1 SVWL_FORCE=wr scripts/sv-firefox-wayland.sh two-windows 120
```

The first window plays a looping 720p H.264 clip for the whole run, so it is
presenting at 30 fps when the browser quits; the tour runs in the second. With
`SVWL_EXTRA_ENV=MOZ_CRASHREPORTER_DISABLE=1` the fault leaves a core for
`coredumpctl` instead of a minidump. It crashed in
about one run in five here (98.6), and in 2 of 3 for gpu-arena-dyn.

`SVWL_RUNROOT` puts the run directory somewhere other than `/tmp`. The harness
now starts Firefox with `MOZ_CRASHREPORTER_NO_DELETE_DUMP=1`, and its verdict
counts minidumps where the crash reporter keeps them, `$HOME`'s
`Crash Reports/pending`, as well as in the profile. Before, a crash at quit with
the reporter on read "exit 11, 0 minidump(s)" with the dump sitting in
`pending` (checked with the widened window of 98.6), and no core either,
because the reporter handles the signal.

### 98.3 What the stacks and the protocol say

`docs/quit-crash/stacks.txt` has the crashing thread and the main thread of all
three cores. The crashing thread is always `sv-present` (abridged, innermost
first):

```
arg_count_for_signature        (libwayland-client)  <- in one; __pthread_mutex_lock in the other two
wl_closure_init, wl_closure_marshal
wl_proxy_marshal_array_flags   (libwayland-client)
sv_icd::present::wayland::Surface::put
sv_icd::wsi::finish_present
sv_icd::wsi::Presenter::start::{closure}
```

In two of the three the main thread is deep in shutdown
(`QuotaManager::Observer::Observe` from `nsXREDirProvider::DoShutdown`); in the
third it is running JavaScript. In the one core searched for it, no thread was
in WebRender's renderer or in Zink. Both fault
sites read through the proxy: the message signature in one, the display's mutex
in the other. That is what a freed `wl_surface` proxy looks like.

To see the order, a temporary build of the ICD logged swapchain creation and
destruction, `vkDestroySurfaceKHR`, and each present's queueing, start and end,
with the thread; `WAYLAND_DEBUG=client` logged every request. Both go to
Firefox's stderr, so they interleave in time. The run that crashed
(`docs/quit-crash/protocol-crash.txt`, times UTC):

| time | thread | what |
|---|---|---|
| 50.379800–.379852 | Firefox | the toplevel destroyed; `wl_surface#23` (Firefox's surface for EGL) unmapped with `attach(nil)` and committed |
| 50.413301 | `sv-present` | our attach and commit of the previous frame on `#23` |
| 50.413858 | renderer | `vkQueuePresentKHR` on swapchain `0xe91`, image 1, returns |
| 50.413877 | `sv-present` | starts that present: the wait for the copy |
| 50.415026, .415106 | Firefox | `wp_viewport#26.destroy()`, `wl_surface#23.destroy()` |
| | `sv-present` | `Surface::put` on `#23`: "The futex facility returned an unexpected error code", SIGABRT |

The run before that frame took 50 ms from start to commit (`.363887` to
`.413319`), so a present may be in flight for far longer than the 1.2 ms the
crash needed.

A run that quit cleanly (`docs/quit-crash/protocol-clean.txt`) shows the same
order without the bad luck, and shows that closing an ordinary window has it
too: `wl_surface#46.destroy()` at .130606, then `vkDestroySwapchainKHR` for its
swapchain at .130791. For the last window, `wl_surface#23` is destroyed and
swapchain `0x1005` never is; the process ends with it alive.

### 98.4 Whose fault, and why only the call itself is safe

Firefox destroying the surface before the swapchain breaks Vulkan's rule that a
native window outlives its swapchain. But Firefox and Mesa between them
guarantee something narrower, and both write it down:

- **Firefox** takes `WaylandSurfaceLock` around `SwapBuffers()`
  (`gfx/webrender_bindings/RenderCompositorEGL.cpp`: "Rendering on Wayland has
  to be atomic (buffer attach + commit) and wayland surface is also used by
  main thread so lock it"), and `~WaylandSurface`, which destroys the
  `wl_surface`, asserts the surface is not locked
  (`widget/gtk/WaylandSurface.cpp`).
- **Mesa's Zink** presents synchronously on Wayland, inside the swap
  (`src/gallium/drivers/zink/zink_kopper.c`, 26.2.4, at `cdt->async`): "Wayland
  EGL has a driver invariant which requires that any `wl_surface` …
  calls happen inside the client's call to eglSwapBuffers(). Submitting surface
  messages after eglSwapBuffers() returns causes serialization issues with the
  Wayland surface protocol and can lead to the compositor booting the app. This
  means we can't do async submit on Wayland."

So `vkQueuePresentKHR` runs inside `eglSwapBuffers`, which runs inside
Firefox's lock, and nothing may touch the surface after it returns. §88's
presenter was the one link that did.

**No later check can make an asynchronous frame safe.** Libwayland gives a
client no notice that another part of the program destroyed a proxy. A proxy
*wrapper*, made while the surface is alive, would stop the use-after-free,
because marshalling through it never reads the application's proxy. But the
request would still name object id 23 after the compositor had deleted it:
`invalid object`, a protocol error that ends the connection. Or, once the id
is reused, the request goes to whatever object now has it. Either is worse
than the crash.

### 98.5 The fix

`crate::wsi::pipelines(target, SV_PRESENT_SYNC)` decides whether a new
swapchain gets a presenter: not on a Wayland surface; yes on X11, whose frames
go out on a connection of our own by a window id whose death is an error that
connection ignores (`present::x11`), and on headless. `SV_PRESENT_SYNC=1` still
presents everything on the calling thread. `SV_PRESENT_SYNC=0` now also
pipelines Wayland, to measure what that is worth, and brings the crash back.

Regression test: `wsi::tests::a_wayland_present_is_finished_before_vk_queue_present_returns`.
It fails on the old rule (Wayland pipelined), which was checked by putting the
old rule back. Two more tests pin X11, headless and `SV_PRESENT_SYNC`. Nothing
else changed: the synchronous path is the one §88 kept for comparison.

### 98.6 The runs

Every run is the recipe of 98.2, 120 s. A run counts only if Firefox stayed on
hardware WebRender to the end. Seven did not: the harness's 64 MiB arena ran out
(§95.4) and Firefox logged `Fallback WR to SW-WR`, after which its frames no
longer go through this ICD's present. All seven quit cleanly, and every crash
came from a run that had not fallen back.

| build | runs that count | crashed at quit |
|---|---|---|
| before, as deployed | 4 | **2** (SIGSEGV, SIGSEGV) |
| before, with the logging of 98.3 | 8 | **1** (SIGABRT, run p) |
| before, by `SV_PRESENT_SYNC=0`, crash reporter on | 2 | 0 |
| **after** | 9 | **0** |
| before, by `SV_PRESENT_SYNC=0`, and a 30 ms sleep before the frame is shown | 4 (2 on a 64 MiB arena, 2 on 256 MiB) | **4** (SIGSEGV, SIGSEGV, SIGABRT, SIGSEGV) |
| **after**, and the same 30 ms sleep, which now happens inside `vkQueuePresentKHR` | 6 (2 on 64 MiB, 4 on 256 MiB) | **0** |

The first three rows say the crash comes in about one run in five (3 of 14), so
9 clean runs after the fix would still happen by luck about one time in eight.
The last two rows settle it. The sleep (a temporary build, not committed) holds
each frame back before its `attach` and `commit`. Pipelined, that only widens
the window between `vkQueuePresentKHR` returning and the frame reaching the
surface, and Firefox crashed in `Surface::put` on `sv-present`, the same stack
as 98.3. After the fix the same sleep runs inside Firefox's swap, under its
lock, so Firefox waits for it before destroying the surface.

### 98.7 What it costs

On the workstation, `scroll` mode (40 wheel steps, three rounds), Firefox on
Zink on this ICD on RADV:

| | after (synchronous) | before (`SV_PRESENT_SYNC=0`) |
|---|---|---|
| scroll fps, no frame trace | 60.3, 60.2, 60.3 (p99 17.7, 17.7, 17.4 ms) | 60.2, 60.1, 60.2 (p99 18.9, 18.7, 18.9 ms) |
| scroll fps, frame trace on | 59.6, 59.5, 59.5 (p99 20.4, 20.5, 20.4 ms) | 60.3, 60.0, 60.2 (p99 18.2, 18.7, 18.2 ms) |
| present on the renderer thread, median | 5.2 ms (fence wait 4.96, `wl_shm` put 0.28) | 0.01 ms |
| Firefox between presents, median | 11.1 ms | 16.7 ms |

Here the renderer thread's 11 ms of its own work plus the 5 ms wait still fit in
a 16.7 ms frame, so the rate holds; with the trace on (more work per frame) it
slips by about one frame in a hundred. On the guest §88 measured the wait and
the copy at 2.0 and 1.2 ms, and the scroll there reached 60 fps only with every
change of §88 in place. **On the guest** (2026-10-17, deployed `wcivs` with §97's
pool, §95.7): a page scrolling 12 px each animation frame, three 5 s rounds,
made 60.0, 60.0, 60.0 fps (p50 17, p99 18 ms) as deployed, and 60.2, 60.0,
60.2 fps (p50 17, p99 18 ms) in a session with `SV_PRESENT_SYNC=0` in `gpu.env`.
One session each, so a cost under a frame in a hundred would not show; nothing
larger does. If it ever costs frames, the way to win them back without the
crash is to make the wait shorter, not to move it off the calling thread: for
example, a `wl_shm` pool on the arena itself, which removes the 1.2 ms copy.
