## 99. The doorbells belong to no session: one hub per user, every installation and every application on it

Branch `bell-hub`, from master `0f486c4`, 2026-10-16. The user's requirement,
after 97.10: **any number of applications must be able to run together**, so
a doorbell is a shared resource, and no session, crashed or alive, may hold
one against the others.

### 99.1 What held what

| port | QEMU's socket | held by, until §99 | consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `org.sirati.svbell.0` (GPU rings, §87) | `svbell.sock` | each session's `sv-hostd ivshmem-serve`, from its start to its end | the first session's hub owned the port; a later one's connection sat in QEMU's backlog (97.10) |
| `org.sirati.wcbell.0` (Wayland rings, §89) | `wcbell.sock` | each session's `wc-proxy`, directly | the same shape, with no hub at all |

QEMU's chardev serves one connection. A later connection is accepted into
the backlog and never served, so a session that came second could write
its bells and never be read, and, until `8b68865`, blocked on them.

On the guest each port has one opener, and that is already right: one GPU
process maps the GPU device (§87.2) and serves every session over one port
handle (`vdoorbell::attach_set`), and one compositor holds the Wayland port.
Any number of applications share those two processes; nothing more is
needed there.

### 99.2 The hub

`sv-hostd bell-hub --port UPSTREAM=HUB …`, the user unit
`wc-bell-hub.service` (`Restart=always`), started (never restarted) by `wc-launch.sh deploy`
and by `wc-session` if a session finds it down. It runs as the user and
refuses to run as root.

* It holds `svbell.sock` and `wcbell.sock` for as long as the VM runs,
  retrying every 500 ms while they are absent and reconnecting when QEMU
  restarts; clients stay connected across that.
* Every session's ICDs connect to `/run/user/<uid>/wc-bell/sv.sock`
  (`SV_BELL`) and every session's `wc-proxy` to `…/wl.sock`
  (`--wayland-bell`). `sv-hostd ivshmem-serve` no longer touches the port.
* A byte from the guest goes to every client; a byte from any client goes
  to the guest. A doorbell byte names a ring slot and lane, not a session
  (`park::lane_token`), so it cannot be routed by session without changing
  the wire; every client rings that lane in its own sessions, the right one
  wakes, and the others pay one spurious wake, as the doorbell's framing
  argument always priced it.
* **Nothing blocks on anybody.** Each client has a writer thread fed by a
  bounded queue of its own (256 writes), and so does the upstream. A full
  queue drops the byte and counts it; a client that stops reading, crashes
  or hangs costs only its own bells, and a client that leaves is forgotten.

**A hub restart costs running sessions their bells.** Clients (an ICD's
doorman, a proxy's ring wake) do not reconnect, so after a restart every
session then running waits out its slices until it ends: slower, never
wrong. So `wc-launch.sh deploy` starts the hub when none runs and never
restarts a running one; a new binary takes effect at its next start.
Clients since 99.4 reconnect, which removes even that for new sessions.

Without the hub, a session falls back to holding the port itself and says
so in capitals (`NO SHARED DOORBELL HUB`), which is the pre-§99 behaviour.
Every installation must therefore be redeployed with this `wc-session`: an
old one would take QEMU's socket away from the hub.

### 99.3 Tests

| test | holds |
|---|---|
| `bellhub::a_stalled_client_blocks_no_other_and_not_the_guest` | 4 MiB from the guest with one client never reading: the guest's writes return, the other clients get bytes, the stalled client's are dropped and counted, and a client's byte still reaches the guest |
| `bellhub::clients_survive_the_upstream_reconnecting` | the upstream closes (the VM stops): the hub reconnects by itself and a client connected before carries on both ways |
| `bellhub::a_client_leaving_affects_no_other` | a client leaving is forgotten, the rest still get the guest's bytes; the socket is 0600 |
| `vdoorbell::a_doorbell_nobody_reads_never_blocks_the_poker` (`8b68865`) | the ICD's side: two million pokes into a socket nobody reads return at once |

### 99.4 Clients reconnect to a restarted hub

An ICD's doorman and a proxy's ring wake now attach through
`vdoorbell::attach_host_reconnecting`: the installed writer is a
`SwapWriter`, and when the hub's socket closes the doorman reconnects every
500 ms and swaps the new socket in. In the gap pokes are dropped and waits
use their slices; nothing fails and nothing waits for the hub. An ICD whose
hub is not up yet at bring-up now keeps trying instead of giving up.
`vdoorbell::a_client_reconnects_to_a_restarted_hub`: the hub's socket closes
and is bound again on the same path, and the client's pokes reach the new
hub and the new hub's bytes ring its target.

Sessions started by a build before this one do not reconnect, so deploy
restarts a changed hub only while no `wc-launch-*` unit is active, and
otherwise says the change waits for the hub's next start.

### 99.5 One application killed stopped every session: the guest's port write

2026-10-17, 07:39–08:01, `wcmc` on master `6bd5cac`, on the hub. Firefox
(two windows, one playing the 720p clip) and stock Minecraft ran together,
each with its GPU session's doorbell on the hub and the proxy's Wayland
doorbell beside them. The hub was restarted under them at 07:40:53, and all
three clients reconnected within a second (99.4); pages kept loading. Then
Minecraft's `java` was killed with SIGKILL at 07:41:06.

From that moment the guest's GPU process served no session at all. Firefox's
next page load waited 30 s, its ICD timed out ("wait on ring 2 timed out")
and Zink crashed the browser on `DEVICE_LOST`. The GPU process logged nothing
after 07:40:27, not even the end of Minecraft's session, which its 5 s
heartbeat check should have noticed. `Stop-Process` left it half-exited with
one thread in a kernel `Executive` wait and one in `ExecutionDelay`. That is
Windows' I/O-cancel loop. At 08:00:43 the guest logged **VirtioSerial event
54, `0x80040036`, `IO_DRIVER_CANCEL_TIMEOUT`** ("failed to complete a
cancelled I/O request in the allotted time"), and only then did the process
finish exiting. There was no TDR or display event, and DWM stayed responsive.
The Intel driver was not involved.

**What stopped every session** was the one thing they all share and can block
on: the process's doorbell writer. Every ring thread pokes it after
publishing a reply. On Windows it was an overlapped `WriteFile` waited for
with no timeout, under one mutex. One write that never completed held the
mutex, and every session's ring threads queued behind it. Why the virtio-serial
port stopped draining at the kill is not known: the hub kept reading its
upstream, and QEMU's side showed nothing queued. Whatever the trigger, the
writer must never be able to stop a serving thread.

**While the process cannot exit, it keeps the GPU device's one mapping**
(`map_ivshmem`: "the driver allows one per device and keeps it until the
handle that made it closes"). For those 8 minutes a new GPU process of any
installation would have been refused the device and its applications would
have rendered in software. It was not a reboot's worth, but it was not
harmless either.

Fixed:

* The guest's port writer is now the detached writer the host side got in
  `8b68865`: a thread of its own and a bounded queue that drops on overflow.
  A ring thread never waits on the port again.
* An overlapped write waits at most 500 ms, is then cancelled
  (`CancelIoEx`), and is waited for, since its buffer must outlive it. The
  driver may not complete the cancel for minutes (the event above), and then
  only the writer thread waits; bells are dropped meanwhile.

Measured locally on both drivers the guest path can be stood in for: two
survivors rendering frames continuously while a third client was killed
with SIGKILL five times. Survivors had 0 failures on lavapipe through
`pool-guest` and 0 on RADV through `serve --pool`. Neither path has a
virtio-serial port, so neither could reproduce the stall itself. The guest
confirmation is the multi-app run again.

Not fixed: a process with a pending virtio-serial request still takes up to
the I/O-cancel timeout to exit, and holds the GPU device until then.

### 99.6 The confirmation, a port the driver leaked, and a hub that never closes QEMU's connection

**The kill, again** (2026-10-17, 08:09–08:20, `wcmc` and `wcivs` on master
`558b2bd`). Firefox (two windows, one playing the clip) and stock Minecraft
ran together. The hub was restarted at 08:11:19, and both GPU doorbells and
the proxy's Wayland doorbell reconnected. Minecraft was killed with SIGKILL
at 08:11:35. The guest ended its session within about 5 to 8 seconds
("27 lease(s) and the control region given back"), and Firefox ran the full
10 minutes: 110 page loads, WebRender in all of them, 0 errors, a clean quit.

**The stale session.** A `wcgpu` session's guest side was killed, and its
host units and Firefox were left running with their hub connections. A new
`wcmc` session started beside it in 10 s, attached to the hub, and ran 21
page loads with 0 errors. The same hub process held both QEMU ports
throughout.

**But that run had no GPU doorbell on the guest.** The GPU process logged
"no doorbell on org.sirati.svbell.0 (… access denied … or another process
holds it)". At 08:08 `wc-port-access`, running as SYSTEM, opened `wcbell`
and got error 5 on `svbell`. Vioser ports are exclusive, so that means held,
and no process of ours existed. Since 99.5's process finished exiting on
`IO_DRIVER_CANCEL_TIMEOUT`, the port has stayed open with nobody behind it:
the driver leaked the open it failed to cancel. QEMU's `svbell` socket held
543 host-to-guest bytes with nobody to read them, for as long as it was
watched. So the run proved that a kill no longer stops other sessions, but
not yet the detached writer under a kill. Without the doorbell, the clip
dropped 43% of its frames, against 0.34% with it (97.10).

`pnputil /disable-device` on that port answered "the system must be
restarted" (3010) and left the device marked disabled for the next boot
(`ConfigFlags` 0x1), with the enable refused until then. No reboot was made.
The boot task now defuses that (`wc-port-access.ps1`, `6ccd1b2`):

* every run records our ports by name in `ports.json`, since a port's name
  exists only while it is started;
* the SYSTEM boot task re-enables a recorded port that is disabled, with
  `pnputil /enable-device`, before it applies the ACLs, and logs to
  `wc-port-access.log`. Run once as at boot, it found `svbell` disabled and
  was refused only because the restart is still pending;
* the boot task had applied nothing since §91. Through `powershell -File`,
  `-Ports a,b` is one string, so it looked for a port named "a,b". The
  script now splits it.

**What started 99.5's stall is still not proven.** The best-supported
reading: the hub's restart, 13 s before the kill, closed and reopened
QEMU's chardev connection, and after that the Windows port stopped
completing the GPU process's writes. It is the same driver that then could
not complete the cancel. Rather than wait for proof, the hub no longer
closes that connection.

**QEMU's connections in systemd's store.** `wc-bell-hub.service` is
`Type=notify` with `FileDescriptorStoreMax=8` and
`FileDescriptorStorePreserve=yes`. The hub gives systemd a copy of each
upstream connection (`FDSTORE=1`, `FDNAME=svbell-up`) and each listening
socket (`svbell-listen`), replacing an entry when it reconnects and removing
it when QEMU closes. A restarted hub takes them back (`LISTEN_FDS`,
`LISTEN_FDNAMES`, `sdfd::take`). systemd holds a copy while the old process
exits, so QEMU never sees a disconnect, and clients reconnect to the same
listening socket at once. Measured on this workstation under systemd 261,
with a stand-in for QEMU that logs every connection: two restarts of the
service, **one connection, never closed**, bytes from the hub to QEMU until
the end, and two descriptors in the store throughout.

The first restart that installs this unit still closes the connection once,
because the old process has nothing stored.

### 99.7 The missing test, with the doorbell back

2026-10-17, after the guest restarted at 08:43:48. The boot task re-enabled
`svbell` ("was disabled … pnputil /enable-device exit 0") and applied both
ACLs. `wcmc` was deployed from master `33d86be`, which installed the
fd-store unit; that one restart closed QEMU's connection once, as intended,
with no session running. The guest's GPU process then logged "doorbell
attached on org.sirati.svbell.0".

**Hub restart mid-run with the fd store** (08:49:28, Firefox with two
windows and the clip, plus stock Minecraft): the new hub "inherited 4
descriptor(s) … [svbell-listen, svbell-up, wcbell-listen, wcbell-up]" and
"kept … open across the restart" for both ports. QEMU's two connections were
the same sockets before and after (`ss`: unchanged inodes), so QEMU saw no
disconnect. Both GPU clients and the proxy reconnected.

**SIGKILL of Minecraft** at 08:49:46: the guest ended its session 6 s later,
polling included. Firefox ran the full 10 minutes: 119 page loads, WebRender
in all of them, 0 errors, a clean quit, no `DEVICE_LOST`. This time the GPU
process held `svbell` throughout, so the detached writer was on the path.

**The doorbell is used.** `sv-pool-stress` through the same session, run
twice:

| | ring waits | parked | mean | under 1 ms | 10–100 ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| with the doorbell (the hub) | 583 | 534 ms | **0.92 ms** | 381 | 1 |
| without (`SV_BELL` unset) | 583 | 1750 ms | 3.0 ms | 310 | 58 |

**Video drops.** On `wcmc` (stock Firefox) the drop rate was 4–5% alone,
15–29% while Minecraft loaded and ran, and 3.5% after the kill. On `wcgpu`
alone (the readback Firefox build, as in 97.10), over 4 minutes, it was
**2.84%** (2–3% per interval), against 0.34% in 97.10's 31-minute soak and
43% with no doorbell (99.6). What makes up the rest of the difference to
97.10 is not measured. Candidates: the hub's extra socket hop on each wake,
and the host's state, with 1.1 GB available. An A/B with the session holding
QEMU's socket directly would separate the two.

### 99.8 Hub or direct: the video drop rate, and a session that trusted a dead socket

2026-10-17, 09:04–09:50, with no user session running. The setup was
`wcgpu` (the readback Firefox build, as in 97.10), two windows with the 720p
clip, 4 minutes per run. Each figure excludes the first sample (start-up).
**Hub**: the session's clients on `wc-bell-hub`. **Direct**: the hub held
off by a runtime drop-in (`ConditionPathExists=` a path that does not exist)
with its descriptor store cleared, so the session's own `sv-hostd` and proxy
hold QEMU's sockets, as before §99.

| run | path | frames | dropped | rate | host available | swap used |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | hub | 6090 | 173 | 2.84% | 594–732 MB | 181 MB, flat |
| A2 | hub | 6093 | 146 | 2.40% | 587–716 MB | 177 MB, flat |
| A3 | hub | 5952 | 131 | 2.20% | 558–667 MB | 176 MB, flat |
| (B3, B4) | hub, see below | 6076, 6107 | 141, 186 | 2.32%, 3.05% | 541–707 MB | 175 MB, flat |
| A4 | hub | 6087 | 124 | 2.04% | 547–653 MB | 175 MB, flat |
| D1 | **direct** | 6067 | 132 | **2.18%** | 575–678 MB | 175 MB, flat |
| D2 | **direct** | 6030 | 113 | **1.87%** | 541–544 MB | 175 MB, flat |

Hub runs: 2.04–3.05%, mean 2.48%. Direct: 1.87 and 2.18%, mean 2.03%. The
hub may cost a few tenths of a point, inside the spread of its own runs, so
it is not what separates today from 97.10's 0.34%. Neither is the host's
memory. Available memory stayed at 540–730 MB, swap flat at 175–181 MB, and
swap-ins were 3–75 pages per 4-minute run. The host's load was 3–5. What
does separate them is not measured. The plain difference in code is that
since 97.10 every doorbell write goes through a writer thread, on the host
(`8b68865`) and on the guest (`495802e`): one more thread handoff per wake.
A non-blocking inline write on the host socket would remove that handoff
without giving back the guarantee. The guest's Windows port cannot do that
without the thread.

**Found on the way: `wc-session` trusted a dead hub socket.** Its `hub_up`
checked that `/run/user/<uid>/wc-bell/{sv,wl}.sock` existed. They outlive
the hub, and with the fd store they are meant to. With the hub stopped (the
first two "direct" runs, B1 and B2), a session pointed its ICDs at a dead
socket (no GPU doorbell) and its proxy at a dead `wl.sock`. That sent every
Wayland connection over ssh ("SSH FALLBACK"), and the clip dropped 96–100% of
its frames. `e9a168e`: `hub_up` asks systemd whether the hub is active,
starts it if it can, and otherwise falls back to holding QEMU's ports
itself. B3 and B4 then turned out to be hub runs after all: `systemctl
--user mask --runtime` does not override a unit file in
`~/.config/systemd/user`, so `wc-session` started the hub. That is why the
direct runs use a drop-in.

### 99.9 Where the video frames went: the doorbell's writer thread, and §98's synchronous present

2026-10-17, 09:52–11:36. The setup was `wcgpu` (the readback Firefox build),
two windows with the 720p clip, 4-minute runs, start-up sample excluded.
Absolute rates drift with the host's load over an hour (the same build gave
1.75% at 10:00 and 3.9% at 11:20), so every comparison below alternates its
two arms and compares only within one block.

**The host's doorbell writer thread, then inline (`7467cdc`).** Through the
hub, alternating T, I, T, I: thread 2.65% and 2.22%, inline (`MSG_DONTWAIT`
on the socket, no thread) 1.75% and 1.78%. Kept.

**The build behind 97.10's 0.34%** (`efb7b03`), run direct with the hub
held off: 0.90%, 0.33%, 1.01%. Bisecting over the merges since then, also
direct: `883e70e` 3.14%, `9076288` 3.09%, `6873327` 2.57%. `6873327` is
`efb7b03` merged into a master that already had `4fe941b` (desktop-checks).
In `crates/`, that adds only `sv-icd/src/wsi.rs` (§98) and three compositor
files. `6873327` with the compositor files reverted: 3.12%, so not those.
`6873327` with `SV_PRESENT_SYNC=0`, which restores the pipelined Wayland
present §98 removed: 1.36%.

**§98's synchronous present, today's build, alternating S, P, S, P:**

| run | present | dropped |
|---|---|---|
| S5 | synchronous (default since §98) | 3.96% |
| P5 | pipelined (`SV_PRESENT_SYNC=0`) | 2.27% |
| S6 | synchronous | 3.87% |
| P6 | pipelined | 2.22% |

So most of the gap to 0.34% is §98: presenting a Wayland frame inside
`vkQueuePresentKHR`, which the quit crash required, costs the clip about
1.7 points of its frames. The host's writer thread cost about 0.7, and is
gone. The hub costs at most a few tenths (99.8). The pipelined present cannot
come back as it was: it marshalled on a `wl_surface` the application may
already have freed. What would keep both is to pipeline everything up to the
surface requests and make only `attach`, `damage` and `commit` inside the
application's next call, since Mesa's own WSI touches the surface only
there. That is §98's owner's to decide.

## 100. The pipelined Wayland present comes back, guarded: `libsv_wlshim.so`

Branch `present-async`, from `desktop-checks` b173cfa with master bfac0ce merged,
2026-10-17. The brief (from §99.9): §98's synchronous Wayland present costs
the 720p clip about 1.7 points of its frames on the guest. Keep §98's crash
fixed and get the frames back. The coordinator proposed pipelining everything up to the
surface requests and making `attach`, `damage` and `commit` inside the
application's next call. The answer here is a different design, for the
reasons in 100.2.

### 100.1 Status in one paragraph

**The present is pipelined again on Wayland, and it is safe.** A small C
library, `libsv_wlshim.so`, preloaded into the application by `wc-session` (and
by `sv-firefox-wayland.sh`), stands in front of libwayland's request entry
points. For a surface the ICD registers, it marks the surface dead before the
application's `destroy` is forwarded, and counts the application's unmaps
(`attach` of a NULL buffer). Both happen under the lock the ICD's present thread
holds around its own `attach`, `damage` and `commit`. A frame whose surface died or was
unmapped after the application presented it is dropped. Without the shim the
ICD presents inside the call, exactly as §98 left it. Locally, with each frame held back 30 ms (the window §98's crash needed), 8
of 8 runs quit cleanly, against 4 of 4 crashes for the unguarded order. The
guard dropped 4 to 7 frames at each quit, so the race was caught, not missed.
**The guest's video A/B is still open (100.6).**

### 100.2 Why not the next call

The proposal was to keep the GPU wait and the readback copy on the present
thread, and make the three surface requests inside the application's next
`vkQueuePresentKHR`, where Mesa's WSI touches the surface. Two things rule it out.

- **The last frame would not be shown.** A frame's commit would wait for the
  application's next present, and an application presents only when something
  changed: Firefox's WebRender after a page or a key press, GTK 4 after a
  redraw. The frame that ends a burst — the letter just typed, the last scroll
  position, a page that has finished loading — would stay on the screen's
  previous frame until something else changed. It works for a video playing
  and fails for everything that stops.
- **The other calls are not safe points either.** The application's lock covers
  `eglSwapBuffers` only (98.4). `vkAcquireNextImageKHR` is called by Zink while
  it builds the next frame, outside that lock, and `vkDestroySwapchainKHR`
  comes after the surface is already gone: in §98's protocol log `wl_surface#46`
  was destroyed at .130606 and its swapchain at .130791, and at quit the
  swapchain is never destroyed at all.

So no point inside the application's own calls both comes soon enough and is
safe. The alternative suggested with it, committing from a frame callback dispatched on the
application's event queue, has the race of §98 in another place. Firefox
destroys the surface on its main thread, the thread that dispatches that queue,
but a `done` event already read from the socket is still dispatched after a
destroy the same thread made a moment before.

### 100.3 The shim

What the ICD cannot see — that the application has destroyed its surface — is
visible to anything between the application and libwayland, because the
destroy is a request the application makes. `crates/sv-icd/shim/sv_wlshim.c`
defines `wl_proxy_marshal_flags`, `wl_proxy_marshal`,
`wl_proxy_marshal_array_flags`, `wl_proxy_marshal_array` and `wl_proxy_destroy`.
Preloaded, it takes those calls from libxul and GTK before libwayland does.

- **Every call is forwarded.** The variadic ones are turned into a
  `wl_argument` array from the request's signature in the proxy's interface,
  exactly as libwayland's own `wl_argument_from_va_list` does, and passed to
  the real `wl_proxy_marshal_array_flags`. The real functions come from the
  `libwayland-client.so.0` the process has loaded, by its handle. They never
  come from `RTLD_NEXT`, because in Firefox that finds `libmozwayland.so`'s
  link-time stubs (libxul is linked against them, `NEEDED libmozwayland.so`).
- **For a registered surface**, under one mutex: `wl_surface.destroy` (opcode
  0, or any request with `WL_MARSHAL_FLAG_DESTROY`) and `wl_proxy_destroy` mark
  it dead *before* forwarding; `attach` with a NULL buffer bumps its
  generation. The forwarded call is made with the mutex held, so it cannot fall
  between the present thread's checks and its requests.
- **The ICD's side** (`svwl_shim_v1_track`, `_untrack`, `_generation`,
  `_begin`, `_end`) is found with `dlsym(RTLD_DEFAULT)`. The ICD registers the
  surface inside `vkCreateSwapchainKHR`, reads its generation inside each
  `vkQueuePresentKHR` (so a frame carries the generation it was presented at),
  and on the present thread wraps its `attach`, `damage` and `commit` in
  `begin`/`end`. `begin` fails if the surface is dead or the generation moved,
  and the frame is dropped. The ICD's own libwayland calls go through its own
  `dlopen` handle, not through the shim, so it never re-enters it.
- **No `DT_NEEDED` on libwayland**, and the ICD-facing names carry a version.
  In a process that never uses Wayland the shim does nothing. An ICD without
  the shim, or with an older one, finds no `svwl_shim_v1_*` and presents in
  the call (`pipelines(target, SV_PRESENT_SYNC, guarded)`).

Two things it does not do, on purpose. It does not order the present thread's
`commit` against the application's own pending state on that surface (a
viewport change and its commit). Neither did §88's present, and a frame
committed between the two takes the new viewport one frame early. And it is
an `LD_PRELOAD`: an application started some other way gets §98's
synchronous present, which is correct and only slower.

### 100.4 Built, shipped, started

- `crates/sv-icd/build.rs` compiles the shim with the Linux compiler
  (`CC_x86_64_unknown_linux_gnu`, else `CC_FOR_BUILD`, else `gcc`). It cannot
  use `CC`, which the dev shell points at mingw. It is built with `-Wall
  -Wextra -Werror` and put beside `libsv_icd.so` in `target/<profile>/`.
- `wc-launch.sh deploy` copies it to the host's `bin/` with the ICD and checks
  it arrived byte for byte.
- `wc-session` adds `LD_PRELOAD=<base>/bin/libsv_wlshim.so` to the GPU
  environment of an application that gets the GPU, when the file is there.
  `ini` and `gpu.env` are unchanged.
- `sv-firefox-wayland.sh` preloads it unless `SVWL_SHIM=0`, and its
  per-minute sample says whether Firefox has it mapped (`shim-mappings=`).

### 100.5 The crash, locally

The recipe of 98.2 (two windows, the looping 720p clip, 120 s, quit from the
last window), with the crash reporter on and core dumps off. A run counts if
Firefox stayed on hardware WebRender. The harness's 64 MiB arena still runs out
in some runs (§95.4), and those fall back to software.

| build | runs (that count) | crashed at quit | frames the guard dropped |
|---|---|---|---|
| shim, and a 30 ms sleep before each frame is shown (a temporary build) | 8 (7) | **0** | 4–7 per run, all at the quit |
| shim | 10 (7) | **0** | (not logged) |
| for comparison, 98.6: unguarded pipelined, the same sleep | 4 (4) | **4** | |

In the delayed runs the dropped frames came in the last second of each run, a
slot at generation 0 and then a slot at generation 1. That is one surface
destroyed outright, and one unmapped (`attach(NULL)`) and then destroyed:
Firefox closing its two windows.

### 100.6 The video frames

**Locally**, alternating synchronous (`SVWL_SHIM=0`) and shim, 120 s each, a
256 MiB arena so none fell back: synchronous 109, 17 and 13 of about 3600 frames
dropped (1.28% in all); shim 32, 8 and 29 (0.64%). The workstation's GPU is too
fast for this to be more than a direction.

**On the guest**, `wcgpu` with the arena agent's 4-minute two-window run
(`gad-out/ab-run.sh`, as in §99.9). Both arms had the same `libsv_icd.so`,
`sv-hostd`, `wc-proxy` and `wc-session`; only the shim file was there or not:

| run | arm | frames after the first sample | dropped |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | synchronous | 5980 | 0.54% |
| A1 | shim | 1077 (cut short) | 3.90% |
| S2 | synchronous | 5972 | 0.28% |
| A2 | shim | 6089 | 0.31% |

Two things make this block inconclusive. The synchronous arm was not regressed
that day at all: 0.28–0.54%, against §99.9's 3.9% for the same present. And the
runs were disturbed. A1, and in a second block A3 (shim) and S3 (synchronous,
26% dropped), lost Firefox's windows a minute in: `no such window` from
Marionette, then a clean quit (`Stopped listening`). There was no minidump, no
core and no lost device, and the synchronous arm was hit as well. Our own stack was checked and ruled out:

- **Not a timeout.** The windows went at 54 s (A3), 77 s (A1) and 182 s (S3).
- **Not the soak driver.** It closes the windows only at the end of its 240 s,
  and its fatal line was Marionette closing the connection.
- **Not the compositor on its own.** Its only `xdg_toplevel.close` comes from
  `FromUi::CloseRequested`, which only the window's `WM_CLOSE` sends
  (`platform/win32.rs`). The session's 60 s exit-when-empty ends a session
  after its last window closes; it does not close one.
- **No automation on the guest.** No agent, `wc-desk` or script was running,
  and the scheduled tasks were idle.
- **Not the shim.** S3 had no shim, and nothing was killed, faulted or logged a
  lost device.

What is left is a `WM_CLOSE` from Windows itself, or Firefox's own close
button. Either is a person at the desktop, and the 26% drop rate of S3 says the
guest was busy. The block was stopped and `wcgpu` restored byte for byte.
**To repeat on a free desktop.**

## 101. The desktop is the user's first: an activity sentinel, and a lease that waits for it

2026-10-17, branch `present-async`. The user's rule, for every agent: the
Windows guest's desktop is ours when there has been no real keyboard or mouse
input for two minutes; while there is, wait. It came out of §100.6, where
somebody at the desktop closed the windows of an A/B run, twice. What this
section builds is the measurement that makes "real" mean something.

### 101.1 What counts as the user

Every agent's input on the guest goes through `SendInput`: the session agent
of §95, `wc-desk`. Windows flags all of it as injected, and a low-level hook
sees the flag (`LLKHF_INJECTED`, `LLMHF_INJECTED` and their `LOWER_IL`
variants). So the rule is decidable inside the guest, with one exception. Keys
injected through QEMU (QMP `input-send-event`: `guest-keys.sh`, and
`unlock-guest.sh`, which has to reach the secure desktop) arrive as
hardware.

### 101.2 The pieces

| piece | where | what |
|---|---|---|
| `wc-activity.exe` | `scripts/wc-activity.c`, built with mingw; on the guest in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\waycompose\tools` | No window, no focus. `WH_KEYBOARD_LL` and `WH_MOUSE_LL` on one thread. Injected events are skipped, and so is a mouse move under 2 px from the last one counted. A second thread writes `%LOCALAPPDATA%\waycompose\activity.txt` every 2 s, replaced atomically: a heartbeat, whether the hooks are installed, the start time, and the last 64 real inputs, coalesced to 250 ms, newest first. The hooks never wait on the disk (Windows silently drops a slow low-level hook) and are reinstalled every minute. One per session (a named mutex). |
| scheduled task `wc-activity` | `scripts/wc-activity-install.sh` | Starts it at <guest-user>'s logon, at unlock, at a console or remote connect and every 5 minutes (one copy: `IgnoreNew`), interactive, limited, no time limit; the script also starts it at once. The program registers with `RegisterApplicationRestart`. On 2026-10-19 an Office update's Restart Manager ended it, and with only the logon trigger nothing started it again for 80 minutes. Safe to run while somebody uses the desktop |
| `guest-idle.sh` | `scripts/wc-guest-idle.sh`, installed as `/tmp/wcrun/guest-idle.sh` | Reads the file and the guest's clock over ssh. Exit 0 `idle N s` at 120 s or more (`GUEST_IDLE_SECS`). Exit 2 `active N s ago`. Exit 1 unknown (no file, a heartbeat over 15 s old, no hooks), which counts as not idle. With no file or a stale heartbeat it first runs the task once (`schtasks /Run`, invisible) and reads again (`GUEST_IDLE_NO_RESTART=1` skips this). Input from 0.5 s before to 2 s after a line of `/tmp/wcrun/qmp-inject.log` is ours: the clocks are matched through the middle of the ssh round trip. If every input kept is ours, the last real one is older: the sentinel's start, or the oldest entry when all 64 slots are full |
| QMP injection log | `/tmp/wcrun/guest-keys.sh`, `/tmp/wcrun/unlock-guest.sh` | A line before and after each injection, host milliseconds first |
| `guest-lease.sh take` | `/tmp/wcrun/guest-lease.sh` | Takes a free lease only once the desktop is idle. Renewing does not wait. `GUEST_LEASE_NO_IDLE=1` is for work that opens no window and sends no input |
| the instructions | `/mnt/datasets/builds/visual-check-instructions.md` | Every agent rechecks before each input step, and pauses until two idle minutes if the user comes back |

### 101.3 Checked

- **On the guest**, installed 13:42. Running in session 1, both hooks in place,
  a heartbeat every 2 s. In the first 40 s it recorded 15 real mouse inputs and
  no keyboard. No agent drives the VM's pointer: nothing of ours sends QMP
  pointer events, and no automation process was running. So somebody was moving
  the mouse at that moment, which is also what §100.6 suspected.
- **The check's logic**, against canned files (`GUEST_ACTIVITY_TEXT`):
  - a real input 30 s ago reads `active 30 s ago`, exit 2;
  - the same input inside a logged injection, with a real one 200 s before
    it, reads `idle 200 s`, exit 0;
  - a heartbeat 60 s old reads unknown, exit 1;
  - no input since a start 600 s ago reads `idle 600 s`;
  - only our injection in the ring reads idle since the start.
- **A run under the rule:** `/tmp/dc/ab4-block.sh` waits for an idle desktop
  before each run. During a run it checks every 10 s, and if the desktop is
  used it aborts the run, ends its session, and repeats it after two idle
  minutes. The soak drives Firefox through Marionette, which is not OS input,
  so activity during a run is the user's.

**First use**, 2026-10-17. The block S5, A5, S6, A6 of 100.6 started S5 twice
on a desktop idle for 124 s (13:50:08, 14:02:05). Both tries were aborted
2:23 and 2:30 into the run, on real input. The second time it was keyboard
input from 14:04:27 to 14:04:51, which went on after the run's session had
ended. No QMP injection was logged. Both times it came about two minutes after
the run's Firefox windows appeared on the desktop, so the person at it reacts
to them. The block was stopped rather than repeated every few minutes, and
`wcgpu` restored.

### 101.4 Remote use: injected input counts, ours is tagged, and TeamViewer is asked

The first sentinel had it backwards for one case the user pointed out. Working
through TeamViewer arrives as `SendInput`, flagged injected, and the sentinel
skipped exactly that, so remote use read as idle. TeamViewer's log for the day
shows a remote-control session from 10:20:13 to 13:20:14. That covers A1, A3
and S3 of 100.6, the runs whose windows were closed.

- **Every input counts** (sentinel version 2). The kind letter keeps the path:
  `k`/`m` arrived as hardware (QEMU's virtual devices included), `K`/`M` were
  injected by something that is not ours.
- **Ours is tagged, not timed.** Every tool of ours that calls `SendInput` puts
  `WC_AGENT_TAG` ("WCAGENT1", `0x57434147454E5431`) in `dwExtraInfo`, which a
  low-level hook receives unchanged. The sentinel skips those events and counts
  them (`ours N`). That is `wc-desk` (`send_mouse`, `send_rel`, `send_key`),
  `probe-cursor.c`, `probe-scroll.c`, and §95's session agent
  (`docs/desktop-checks/session1-agent.ps1`). `click.ps1` sends no input (it
  starts the shortcut). A tag is exact where a time window is a guess. For a
  tool of ours that cannot tag, the guest-side `%LOCALAPPDATA%\waycompose\inject.log`
  (`<unix ms> <who>` per line) is discounted with the QMP rule. That rule now
  applies only to injected-kind input, and the QMP log only to hardware-kind.
- **TeamViewer is a second signal.** `guest-idle.sh` reads the last
  `ConnectionGuard:` line of `TeamViewer15_Logfile.log`, or of `_OLD.log` after
  a rotation. TeamViewer writes "incoming remote control in sessions: N" when a
  session starts and "no restrictions" when the last one ends; the pairs match
  `Connections_incoming.txt` for the day (UTC there, local in the log). While
  the line says a session runs, the desktop is in use (exit 2) whatever the
  input says.
- **An old sentinel reads as unknown**, since it cannot see remote input.

Checked against canned files:

| case | answer |
|---|---|
| TeamViewer session running, no input for 10 min | `in use: TeamViewer remote control since 2026/10/17 13:37:20`, exit 2 |
| the session ended ("no restrictions"), no input for 10 min | `idle 600 s`, exit 0 |
| injected mouse input 30 s ago, not ours | `active 30 s ago`, exit 2 |
| injected input inside a guest-logged injection, real input 200 s before | `idle 200 s`, exit 0 |
| hardware-kind input inside a QMP injection, real input 300 s before | `idle 300 s`, exit 0 |
| injected-kind input inside a QMP window (not discounted) | `active 39 s ago`, exit 2 |
| sentinel version 1 | unknown, exit 1 |

Live after the update (14:25): version 2 running in session 1. It showed
hardware keyboard input seconds old, and TeamViewer's last line was "no
restrictions", so somebody was at the VM's own console.

## 102. The future Linux desktop as one window on Windows: a nested login screen and KWin, clients of the proxy

2026-10-17 to 19, branch `nested-linux`, and nix-config branch
`testhost-win7-nested`. The user's goal: one click on the Windows desktop
shows testhost's future native Linux desktop as one window. First the nested
login screen that nix-config's `win7-desktop.nix` already runs on the
user's laptop (`atp-nested login`: the patched COSMIC greeter on a seat of its
own, `seat-atp`, with greetd), then <desktop-user>'s AeroThemePlasma or Windows 11
style Plasma session as a nested KWin. Input, sound, resizing, a taskbar
identity of its own, and everything gone when the window is closed.

### 102.1 Status in one paragraph

**Works end to end on the real guest.** A medium-integrity click on the
desktop shortcut "Windows 7 (Linux)" shows the nested login screen in one
Windows window in 4.4 s, and the Aero session in 5.3–5.4 s (autologin
armed by root for the test, 102.9). In that window the start menu opens on a
click, typing reaches its search field and finds applications, Dolphin opens,
sound from the session plays on Windows, the window resizes and maximises and
KWin's output follows (1000×600, 1280×729), and the close button ends KWin,
the session, greetd and the seat, unloads `vkms` and lifts the memory cap.
About 31 frames a second with an animating client at 1280×729, KWin
compositing in software. A border drag and a caption double-click resize and
maximise it; a wrong password is rejected by PAM with the greeter's message,
and a real password login (a throwaway user, removed again) starts a session.
The guest runs found eight bugs, all fixed (102.9, 102.13): a recycled pool id
froze KWin's frames, clicks were delivered at a frozen origin, the nested
Plasma locked itself, the login screen outlived a session ended under it, a
second login user had no socket, the greeter typed y and z swapped on the
German keyboard, wc-desk's combined move-and-button input never started
Windows' size loop, and the activity sentinel never recognised our tag. Locally the NixOS test passes 10 of 10. The VM runs
with 2 GiB less RAM (10496 MiB) since 2026-10-17.

### 102.2 The path

| step | where | what |
|---|---|---|
| shortcut | guest, installation `wclinux` | `wc-launch.exe linux-desktop`: desktop shortcut and Start menu entry "Windows 7 (Linux)", identity `Waycompose.app.atp-nested` (§92) |
| session | VM host, `~/wc-launch-linux` | `wc-session` as for any application (§94): the ivshmem arena, the rings, the proxy, the session's PulseAudio (§86); the compositor with `--nested-compositor-globals` |
| `run` | `apps.ini [linux-desktop]` (`scripts/wc-linux-desktop-apps.ini`) | `exec = /run/current-system/sw/bin/atp-nested`, `args = login 1280x800 guest`, `env = WC_APP_ID=atp-nested`, `gpu = off`, `titlebar = none` |
| launcher | `atp-nested`, as `sirati` | ACLs for <desktop-user> and cosmic-greeter on the session's Wayland and PulseAudio sockets and on the closed directories on the way; `wc-foreign-app-ids` for the proxy (102.4); `sudo -n atp-nested-seat … guest` |
| seat | `atp-nested-seat`, root | checks every argument (security-model.md R36), caps the two users' slices at 2 GiB, loads `vkms`, starts greetd on `seat-atp`; the greeter is cosmic-comp in winit mode on the proxy's socket |
| login | greetd, PAM `atp-nested-login` | <desktop-user>'s password. No face login: both USB controllers, the cameras on them, are the guest's |
| session | `atp-nested-session`, as <desktop-user> | `PULSE_SERVER` = the session's PulseAudio; `plasma-kwin_wayland` pointed at the proxy's socket by a runtime drop-in; `startatp-wayland` |
| end | the window's close button | `xdg_toplevel.close` → KWin quits → Plasma's session ends → in `guest` mode the greeter runs only once, so greetd gives up → the seat's cleanup |

`guest` is new in the module: no "Start Windows" button (the window is on
Windows already), and the seat ends with the session instead of showing the
login screen again in a new window.

### 102.3 KWin's Wayland backend, and what it needs from the host

KWin 6.7.4's nested backend refuses a host without `wl_compositor` ≥ 4,
`wl_subcompositor`, `xdg_wm_base`, `wp_single_pixel_buffer_manager_v1`,
`wp_viewporter`, `wl_seat`, `zwp_pointer_constraints_v1` and `wp_presentation`
(`wayland_display.cpp`). The first local run ended right there: "wp_single_pixel_buffer_manager_v1
isn't supported by the host compositor", and KWin restarted until Plasma gave up.
Its window is a 1×1 single-pixel buffer viewported to the output's size; the
picture is in synchronized subsurfaces with viewports; the render loop advances
on presentation feedback.

`wc-compositor --nested-compositor-globals` (launcher `[session]
nested-compositor-globals = on`, deploy `WC_LAUNCH_NESTED_GLOBALS=1`) offers
the three. Off, a session sees exactly the globals it saw before: GTK binds
`wp_viewporter` whenever it is offered, and Firefox's path has not been
through §95's checks with it.

* single-pixel buffers are read as one-pixel buffers, alpha kept;
* a viewported surface is held at its destination size everywhere (sizing,
  layout, hit tests, damage); the source rectangle is scaled nearest-neighbour,
  and a 1:1 viewport keeps the old fast path; a commit that only changes the
  viewport recomposes, which is how KWin resizes;
* presentation feedback is answered on the frame tick: `presented`, or
  `discarded` for a frame replaced before it. `wc-proxy` rewrites `clock_id`
  and every `presented` timestamp to its own `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` when it forwards
  them: the guest's clock is not the client's (§88).
* not behind the flag: a subsurface no longer maps a window whose root has
  never had a buffer and declares no geometry. KWin's window first appeared at
  32×32 and jumped; Firefox declares a geometry and keeps the old path.

**Compositing: QPainter, and why.** KWin's backend offers OpenGL only with a
render node and `linux-dmabuf` from the host (`supportedCompositors`).
testhost's host has no render node (the iGPU is the guest's) and the proxy
has no dmabuf; so KWin composites in software, as it reported locally. The cost
is the Aero glass: KWin's blur and contrast effects need OpenGL, so the
taskbar is transparent rather than frosted. Running KWin on the forwarded GPU
would need a render node, or KWin's Vulkan or EGL device paths without one, and
dmabuf from the proxy to the guest; neither exists. The module can hand
plasmashell the forwarded GPU (`nestedTest.gpuForwarding`, 102.10); it is off.

Locally (Wine, `weston-presentation-shm` inside KWin): 3330 frames presented
and 73 discarded in 62 s, a resize followed, close quits KWin.

### 102.4 Two Wayland clients of other users, named as one application

The window on Windows is two Wayland clients in turn, of two users: the login
screen's cosmic-comp as `cosmic-greeter`, then KWin as `<desktop-user>`. §96 named a
client by its `WC_APP_ID`, read from `/proc/<pid>/environ`, which is closed to
the proxy for another user's process. So `atp-nested` writes
`wc-foreign-app-ids` into the session's directory: `<uid> <app id> <title>`
per user. `wc-proxy` reads it only for a client whose `SO_PEERCRED` uid is
not its own, only if the file is a regular file of its own user that nobody
else can write, at most 4 KiB. The app id names the window (`set_app_id` after
`get_toplevel`, as §96); the title replaces every title the client sets
("KDE Wayland Compositor WL-0 — Press right control key to grab pointer",
"Smithay"). Both windows are `Waycompose.app.atp-nested`, "Windows 7 (Linux)",
with the icon of the module's desktop entry `atp-nested` (ATP's start orb).

### 102.5 One window: the successor takes the place

The session's window is a new toplevel of a new client, and Windows' cascade
would open it somewhere else. A toplevel's first map now takes the place, and
the maximised state, of the last window of the same named identity that closed
less than 20 s before (`platform::Succession`). Only named identities, and
only once. The identity matched is the one the compositor meant to give the
window, not what the shell's property store took (Wine's has none).

### 102.6 Sound

The session's PulseAudio (§86) is `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/pulse/native` of the
application `run` starts; `atp-nested` passes it to the seat as a socket
path, the seat checks it like the Wayland socket, and `atp-nested-session`
sets `PULSE_SERVER` in <desktop-user>'s user manager, so every application of the
session plays there; the launcher plays its monitor on Windows as for Firefox.
testhost's host has no sound server of its own, and must not get one: Plasma
would turn PipeWire on, which would open the sound card QEMU plays the guest's
sound into. `linux-desktop.nix` forces it off and adds Plasma's volume applet.

### 102.7 The NixOS side

nix-config branch `testhost-win7-nested`, on `56bda9b` (generation of
2026-10-16):

* `win7-desktop.nix` and its directory from master; the aerothemeplasma-nix and
  gaze inputs; testhost's nixpkgs is two months older, so the patched greeter
  is built from a vendored cosmic-greeter 1.9.1 package (the patch does not
  apply to 1.5).
* the module: the seat takes any socket of the caller at a path only it or root
  controls (R36), a PulseAudio socket argument, `guest` mode, a one-shot
  autologin root can arm for tests, `nestedTest.memoryMax`, sessions named
  so that Aero sorts first (the greeter preselects the first name until a user
  has chosen), the `atp-nested` desktop entry and icon, and the greeter's user
  and daemon on a machine without COSMIC's login screen.
* `testhost/linux-desktop.nix`: the module for <desktop-user> (password from
  laptop's config, set once by activation because `mutableUsers` keeps an

  power-profiles-daemon and fwupd off, `memoryMax = 2G`.
* the VM's RAM 12544 → 10496 MiB; the GPU ivshmem device stays 1024 MiB.

`nix store diff-closures` against the running system: only additions (Plasma,
ATP, the greeter, Steam from the module), no version changes; QEMU's
derivation unchanged. `dry-activate`: windows-vm not restarted.

all passing (2026-10-19):

| subtest | checks |

| Windows side | `wc-compositor.exe --nested-compositor-globals` under Wine on Xvfb |

### 102.9 On testhost

**The system.** testhost runs nix-config `a036e81`'s system
(`sw708k1…`), switched after `dry-activate` each time; `windows-vm` was never
restarted by a switch. The RAM change took effect at a clean restart on
2026-10-17 18:31, made while the guest was idle and locked: `qemu-ga`
shutdown, "guest powered down cleanly", QMP `base-memory` 11005853696
(10496 MiB). After it the iGPU, both IVSHMEM devices and the virtio-serial
ports were started, the boot task re-enabled and re-permitted `svbell` and
`wcbell` (`wc-port-access.log` 18:31:53), the bell hub reattached to both, and
the guest's memory reads 10.2 GiB visible, 5.6 GiB free at the desktop. One
surprise: the guest's LAN adapter came up link-local, and `ipconfig /renew`
over the host link brought back <guest-ip>. <guest-user> was signed back in with
one `unlock-guest.sh`. Host memory available went from 1.1 GiB to 3.1 GiB.

**The installation.** `wclinux` (guest `C:\Users\<guest-user>\wclinux`, host
`~/wc-launch-linux`, port 57541, `nested-compositor-globals = on`,
`copy-scope = buffer`), deployed with `WC_LAUNCH_EXTRA_APPS`,
`WC_LAUNCH_EXTRA_APP_BLOCKS` and `WC_LAUNCH_INSTALL_APPS=linux-desktop`: 15
passed (`docs/nested-linux/deploy-102b.txt`).

**The runs** (2026-10-19, 07:20–08:50, the guest idle per `guest-idle.sh`,
under the lease; it had been locked overnight and was unlocked once with the
PIN and locked again after each block; input through `wc-desk`, one step at a
time; captures of our window only, judged by separate agents):

| run | what | result |
|---|---|---|
| A | login screen | the greeter in the window, titled "Windows 7 (Linux)", taskbar identity `Waycompose.app.atp-nested`, pinnable; 376 MB in the greeter's slice |
| B | autologin to Aero | the desktop drawn at login, but no later frame reached the window |
| D | frame trace (`WC_FRAME_TRACE`) | the compositor received and painted KWin's frames (`wc.present` 1264×713, `wc.paint`), yet the window's pixels did not change while Dolphin opened |
| E | `copy-scope = buffer` | Dolphin appears (139 000 pixels changed); sound: a tone in the session played on Windows (2.6 s not silent of 5 s); resize through `SetWindowPos` → KWin output 1000×600, maximise → 1280×729; ~31 fps (63 commits/s, two per frame) with `weston-presentation-shm`; 1.3–1.6 GB in <desktop-user>'s slice, 2.0–2.3 GiB available on the host |
| F | the pointer fix, `copy-scope = buffer` | the start menu opens on a click, "sea" typed into its search finds nine applications; close button → seat, session, `vkms`, ACLs, cap all gone; 486 frames presented |

**Frames frozen after the first map: a recycled pool id.** The guest's window
kept KWin's first frame. The trace showed every frame composited and painted
from the arena slice, so the slice held stale pixels. The cause was not the
damage arrears but the proxy's pool table: KWin imports each swapchain slot as
`create_pool`, `create_buffer`, `pool.destroy`. When the compositor's
`delete_id` for the first pool came back before that buffer's release,
libwayland gave the same id (29) to the second slot's pool, and `create_pool`
overwrote the zombie entry. From then on the first buffer's commits copied the
second pool's memory into the second slice, and the slice the compositor read
for the first buffer (`slice 0`) kept frame 1. The guest's late releases over
the rings made the reuse likely; Wine's prompt ones did not. Fixed in
`f48a63c` (`retire_pool_id`, test `a_recycled_pool_id_does_not_steal_a_live_buffer`,
which fails at frame 3 without it); live under Wine with a forced late release
the animation advances with the id reused. On the guest with `--copy damage`
again: Dolphin appears (138 600 pixels changed), the start menu opens and
closes without remnants. `$BASE/copy-scope` stays as an option; `wclinux` no
longer sets it.

**Clicks inside KWin.** `wl_pointer` coordinates on KWin's layer subsurface
were frozen at the origin they had when the button went down (smithay's
`ClickGrab`), so with motion during a click KWin saw the pointer elsewhere and
its start menu did not open. `TreeClickGrab` resolves the origin from the
surface tree at every event, on one input clock (five tests).

**Faults.** None: no `Display`/`dxgkrnl` events and no application crash on the
guest in the window of the runs; GPU forwarding was not used (`gpu = off`).

**Our input counted as the user's.** The activity sentinel recorded
`wc-desk`'s clicks as injected input that was not ours. A hook probe on the
guest showed why: a low-level hook receives `dwExtraInfo` truncated to its low
32 bits (`extra=00000000454e5431` for every tagged move). `wc-activity`
accepts the low half since `a7a1daa`; redeployed, a tagged hover counts as
ours (`ours 2`) and the desktop stays idle.

### 102.13 Demo gaps closed on 2026-10-19

**Border drag and caption double-click.** Not the compositor: `wc-desk` sent
each press as one `MOVE|ABSOLUTE|LEFTDOWN` input, and Windows did not start its
modal size loop from that. Moves and presses are now separate (tagged) inputs,
and `wc-desk` prints where each press lands. On the guest: a drag of the
bottom-right corner (`HTBOTTOMRIGHT`) took the window from 1280×752 to 980×552
and KWin followed to 964×513; a double-click on the caption (`HTCAPTION`)
maximised it (KWin 1280×729) and a second one restored it. Locally the
harness can show it only with Wine drawing the frame itself (`Decorated=N`):
without a window manager Wine gives a frame press nothing.

**The login path.** A wrong password for <desktop-user>: `pam_unix(atp-nested-login:auth):
authentication failure … user=<desktop-user>`, `AUTH_ERR`, and the greeter shows
"Incorrect password. Please check your keyboard layout and try again." with the
field cleared. A real login: a throwaway user `nestedtest` with a known
password, added on the branch for the check and removed again (account, home,
files): it logged in and its Aero session ran in the window; the close button
ended it cleanly. Two bugs found on the way: the launcher's ACLs, the cap and
the user-manager clean-up covered only `nestedTest.user`, so a second user's
session had no socket (now every user the login screen offers); and
cosmic-comp keeps its own keymap, US, so on the German Windows keyboard a y and
a z were swapped in the password (`nestedTest.login.keyboardLayout = "de"` on
testhost; with it the login typed as labelled succeeded).

**A UAC prompt after every PIN unlock.** Twice, right after `unlock-guest.sh`,
`consent.exe` came up on the secure desktop, requested through the Appinfo
service, not by our tools (they run at the Limited level). While it is up,
`SendInput` reaches nothing. It went away by itself after 2–4.5 minutes; we
never answered it. Which application asks for elevation at unlock is
<guest-user>'s to look at.

**Test VMs.** The user's rule: no more RAM than the test needs. The NixOS
tests now record the peak of `MemTotal - MemAvailable`: `nested-waycompose`
1426 MiB → 2048 (was 8192), `nested-login` 1194 MiB → 1792 (was 6144).

### 102.14 One window per application: clicks that wait, and a launch that says it failed

**The bug, 2026-10-19 on the guest.** Nothing appeared at once after a click
on "Windows 7 (Linux)", so the user clicked several more times within a second.
Each click was a `run` on the host, six seats started at once and tore each
other down, and the user got no window and no message. The host now takes a
lock (a second `run` fails with "a nested session is already running"). The
launcher stops sending those runs.

**`single = on`** in an `[app.*]` block (set for `linux-desktop` and
`linux-desktop-win11` in `scripts/wc-linux-desktop-apps-guest.ini`) applies to
a plain click (`Request::Run`). Jump-list tasks and pages are unchanged.

1. **A window is up.** The launcher looks for a visible, unowned top-level
   window of the session's compositor. The compositor's pid comes from the
   state file, and only counts while the session's mutex exists, which is the
   same test that makes a click warm (`session_alive`, `OpenMutexW`, never
   creating it). The window must carry the application's identity
   (`PKEY_AppUserModel_ID` = `appmeta::aumid`, §92). If the identity cannot be
   read (Wine), the window's exact title must equal the block's `title`, which
   is also the title `wc-proxy` gives both nested windows (102.4). If such a
   window exists, the launcher restores it when minimised (`ShowWindowAsync`),
   calls `SetForegroundWindow` (the click's own process may take the
   foreground), logs one line and exits 0 without contacting the host.
2. **A launch is in progress.** The launching click holds
   `Local\waycompose-single-<session>-<section>` from the gate until its window
   is found, or for at most 90 s. A click that finds the lock held waits (95 s
   at most) for that window and then does 1. If the lock is let go with no
   window, the first launch failed and has told the user, so this click exits
   quietly. A lock left by a crashed launcher (`WAIT_ABANDONED`) counts as free.
3. **A failed launch says so.** The cases are: the session could not start,
   the host refused the `run`, or no window appeared within 90 s. The launcher
   lets the lock go first, then shows a `MessageBoxW` captioned with the
   application's title. The text is German when the UI language is
   (`GetUserPreferredUILanguages`, as for the jump list), otherwise English.
   The host's "already running" becomes "läuft bereits oder wird gerade
   beendet … versuchen Sie es dann erneut". The dialog runs on a thread of its
   own, so a session owner keeps supervising while the dialog is open. The
   process waits for the dialog before it exits.

The decisions (`crates/wc-launch/src/single.rs`) are pure functions with unit
tests. The Win32 half in `main.rs` enumerates windows, waits on the mutex and
focuses the window.

**Under Wine** (`scripts/wc-launch-single-wine.sh`, 20 checks; the 90 s case
with `WC_SINGLE_SLOW=1`), the real `wc-launch.exe` runs with
`scripts/wc-launch-single-fake.rs` standing in for `ssh.exe`, the compositor
and the relay:

| case | result |
|---|---|
| a cold click | one `run`; the lock is taken and let go when the window appears |
| a click on a minimised window | restored and foreground; exit 0; still one `run` |
| five clicks 150 ms apart | one `run`, one window; four clicks waited and focused it |
| the host refuses, three clicks | one `run`, one dialog ("already running"); the two others exit 0 quietly |
| the session cannot start, `LANG=de_DE` | the German dialog |
| accepted, no window in 90 s, plus a second click | one dialog; the second click exits 0 quietly |

Wine has no window property store, so these runs exercise the title path
only. The identity path is checked on the guest. Log lines on the guest
(`%LOCALAPPDATA%\waycompose\wc-launch-<session>.log`):
`single: <section>: a window is already up (hwnd …, by identity); …; no run sent`,
`… another click is launching it; waiting up to 95 s …`,
`… the other click's window is up after N ms …`,
`… the other click's launch ended without a window …`,
`CLICK-TO-WINDOW N ms (cold|warm, single; …)` and
`single: <section>: FAILED after N ms (…); lock released; telling the user: …`.

**With §107's shared compositor.** The installation has no compositor of its
own then, and its state file says `comp-pid=0` so that `--stop` never kills
the compositor every other installation's windows are in. The window lookup
needs a process all the same: the launcher keeps the shared compositor's pid
from its answer to `ping` (`compositor <pid>`) as `shared-pid` in the state
file, and looks among that process's windows (`single::window_pid`). Several
installations' windows share that process; they are told apart by identity
(the AUMID from the app id), so two installations that give a `single`
application the same app id would also share one taskbar button, and the
lock (`Local\waycompose-single-<session>-<app>`) stays per installation.
Checked on the guest when the shared compositor is deployed there; before
that, by unit tests (`a_shared_compositors_windows_are_looked_for_…`,
`the_shared_compositors_pid_comes_from_its_ping`).

### 102.10 The GPU

`nestedTest.gpuForwarding` (off) lets the seat pass the session's GPU
environment (`wc-session run` with `gpu = on`) to plasmashell only, word by
word: a fixed list of names, store paths for the libraries and manifests, the
caller's sockets for `SV_SOCKET` and `SV_BELL`. KWin stays on QPainter
(102.3), so a GPU-rendered plasmashell would be read back and composited in
software. Not enabled and not measured on the guest: `gpu = off` in the
definition.
