### 105.12 What is not done, and what is left on ssh

* **Nothing of a session is left on ssh.** What ssh still does on these
  machines: the developer's deploy and harness channel, workstation to guest
  and workstation to host. The installations that have not been redeployed
  since §105 still use their old forced-command keys until they are (105.10
  lists them).
* **Two installations' sessions at the same moment** remain impossible. The
  ivshmem driver gives one mapping per device (§93.4). Every installation
  shares the one service and the one hub, one after another.
* **A microphone.** The sound ring carries input streams (§103.16). The
  Windows side announces none, because there is no `waveIn` capture yet.
* **A start answered before it runs** (105.13) means a `run` that the host's
  `wc-session` refuses after the answer reaches the launcher only as "no
  window". The refusal is in the proxy's log with the request. Everything
  `wc-session` would refuse for the words themselves is checked before the
  answer.
* **The jump list's answers can be up to 30 s old** (`ctlfast::STALE`). That
  is the price of answering in microseconds, and it is below the jump list's
  own refresh period (at least 30 s, §92).
* **`gpu-arena = slots`** (§87's fixed slots) still has only the TCP cold
  path, and the forward that reached it is gone, so that mode no longer
  works. The pool (§97) is the default and is what every installation uses.
* **The installation key is not rotated.** Delete `$HOSTDIR/session.key` and
  redeploy to replace it.
* **The debug transport** (105.7) is kept on purpose, off by default.

### 105.13 The control round trip, below 0.2 ms

The user's bound, after 105.9's 18–27 ms: a mean below 0.2 ms. Those
milliseconds were not the crossing. They were a `bash wc-session` per request
(process creation, a shell, its `od`s), the launcher's new connection per
request, and both ends parking on their lanes between a request and its
answer. So:

* **The host answers in-process** (`wc_proxy::ctlfast`):
  * `rtt` (a no-op, for measuring) and `status` at once;
  * `app`, `icon` and `frequent` from a cache that the proxy fills at its start
    for every application of the installation and refreshes after serving an
    answer older than 30 s;
  * `run`, `action`, `open` and `gpu` checked here (an application of
    `apps.ini`, an action its desktop entry lists, the two numbers in range),
    answered, and started on a thread afterwards. Only starting a process
    still spawns one, and that spawn is out of the reply's round trip;
* **both ends spin before they park** (200 µs on the host, 300 µs on the
  guest), so a request's answer, or the next request of a burst, needs no
  doorbell;
* **one connection serves many requests** between the launcher and the
  compositor, and the compositor reads its socket in chunks;
* `wc-launch.exe --ping` measures it: `WC_PING_N` round trips of
  `WC_PING_VERB` (default `rtt`), with `WC_PING_GAP_MS` between them so that
  each one finds the host parked and crosses by doorbell, as a single click's
  request does. `scripts/probe-ctl-rtt.c` does the same on Linux.

Measured locally (`wc-no-ssh.sh`: the Linux compositor, a file for the
device, socat for QEMU's port, the real hub, service and proxy):

| request | n | mean | p50 | p90 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `rtt` | 10000 | 5.6–6.6 µs | 5.1–6.6 | 6.8–7.4 | 11–16 |
| `status` | 1000 | 9.2–12.1 µs | 8.7–11.1 | 10.2–13.8 | 16–33 |
| `frequent` (cached) | 1000 | 8.0–10.4 µs | 7.6–9.8 | 8.8–11.2 | 15–28 |

**On the guest this is not measured yet**: the fast path's build is deployed to
`wcns`, and the guest was in use (105.10). The crossing there is a virtio-serial
byte each way when a side is parked; §89 measured the Wayland rings' crossing
at 0.02 ms. Until the guest's mean over 10 000 round trips is below 0.2 ms, the
user's installations stay on their current build.

**The cold start**, from 105.9's 0.9–1.3 s, stage by stage:

* the GPU process now starts before the compositor, instead of after the
  session is up;
* its host half (`wc-session gpu`) is started by the service at boot, beside
  the proxy, not after it on a request;
* `wc-session`'s waits for sockets poll every 10 ms instead of 50, and the
  launcher's waits for the compositor's lines every 5 ms instead of 25.

What remains is the work itself: mapping the device, `up`, starting
PulseAudio and the proxy as user units, and the proxy attaching. The service
logs `up`, `proxy` and `gpu` separately for each session, so the next guest
run gives the breakdown.

**And a fix found on the way.** A session's PulseAudio "had no session bus"
by unsetting `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`. Under a user unit, libdbus then falls
back to `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/bus`, and a second PulseAudio on that bus (here, an
unrelated program's) still took the name `org.PulseAudio1`, so the session had
no sound. The address now points nowhere.

**After the guest measurement** (master `a27ca12`, installation `wcns`,
session 0, the real virtio-serial crossing):

| request | n | mean | p50 | p90 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `rtt` | 10000 | **20.9 µs** | 19.8 | 21.9 | 45.5 |
| `status` | 1000 | 27.1 µs | 25.1 | 29.5 | 58.7 |
| `frequent firefox` (cached, 601 bytes) | 1000 | 29.9 µs | 27.6 | 32.0 | 66.5 |
| `icon firefox` (18 KB) | 1000 | 198.6 µs | 174.0 | 250.6 | 439.1 |
| `app firefox light` (20.5 KB) | 1000 | 213.9 µs | 193.5 | 277.0 | 423.8 |
| `rtt`, 20 ms between requests (each crosses by doorbell) | 200 | 24.3 µs | 20.6 | 23.5 | 43.9 |

The bound is met for every request without a payload. The two that carry an
icon were not slow on the ring: a 20 KB packet through a lane costs 0.7 µs
(`wlbytes::throughput_probe`). They were slow in the launcher and the
compositor's copy of the answer, which deploy built in **debug**. Locally, the
same path in release takes 8–14 µs for 20 KB. A 256 KiB answer took 5.2 ms,
because a writer facing a full lane slept 1 ms at a time. It now spins, then
yields, then sleeps 200 µs, and takes 0.11 ms. Deploy now builds the
Windows binaries in release. The guest's icon and app answers are to be
measured again with that build.

**The cold start's 303 ms from the record to the host's answer** was the
service's three verbs. On the guest: `up` 66 ms (a `bash wc-session` and its
`od`s), `proxy` 233 ms (PulseAudio started as a unit and waited for, then the
proxy as a unit and waited for), and `gpu` 108 ms (beside them). PulseAudio
now starts beside the proxy instead of before it. The remaining cost is two
`systemd-run`s and the proxy attaching; `up` in-process is the next cut if it
is needed.

**Two tests that failed under load, and why.** They were run 200 times each,
with full suites alongside as load.

* `poolcold::a_ring_lost_across_a_reopen_is_recovered_by_the_rescan` failed
  63 times in 208. Its premise is that nothing wakes the guest between a
  silent reply and the port's reopen. The open-rescan that §103.15 put on the
  doorman's own thread could arrive inside that window, so the guest
  answered early. That is right for the product and wrong for the test, which
  now waits for the open's wakes before it replies: 0 failures in 208.
  `guest_doorman` also marks the bell before it returns again, so a waiter
  never takes the bell-less slice while the doorman thread has not run yet.
* `two_processes` failed 3 times in 200 with "never created hostd.sock within
  30s". The daemon had **exited** at once with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL … errno 17`:
  two daemons started in the same instant had chosen the same run id, the
  clock's nanoseconds alone, for the name of their shared object. The pid is
  now part of the id, and the test now reports a daemon that exited, with its
  stderr, instead of waiting out its 30 s budget: 0 failures in 200.
* On the way, the load also found a **use-after-free in a test**.
  `soundring::two_links_talk_both_ways` dropped the memory under its region
  while the links' threads still ran (SIGSEGV in `wake_epoch`, 1 run in 18 of
  the whole suite at 32 threads). The test now uses an owned region, and
  `soundring::spawn`'s thread keeps the `Control` alive as long as it runs: 24
  parallel suite runs, 0 failures.

### 105.14 An isolated request: the hop timeline, and what each hop cost

105.13's numbers were for requests that followed each other. The user's bound
is for every request, and the common one is the opposite: a click after the
machine sat idle, which finds every thread on both sides parked and every
core in an idle state. Measured on the guest before this section
(installation `wcivs`, session 0, release build, `rtt`):

| gap between requests | mean | p50 | p90 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none (back to back) | 21.3 µs | 18.6 | 21.6 | 40.2 |
| 20 ms | 694.9 µs | 418.8 | 1496.3 | 1943.3 |
| 1 s | 1061.5 µs | 922.1 | 1683.0 | 3614.2 |

**The instrument.** `WC_HOP_TRACE=FILE` (`%p` is the pid) makes a process
stamp each hop of a request with the machine's monotonic counter in
nanoseconds (`frametrace::hop`: a counter read and a push under an
uncontended lock; a thread of its own writes the file every half second).
The guest's stamps are `QueryPerformanceCounter`, the host's
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`, which is also what bpftrace's `nsecs` reads, so the
proxy's stamps line up with a kernel trace of the same run
(`scripts/wc-hop-host.bt`: wakeups, the C-state each woken thread's CPU
came out of, KVM's halt wakeups, and the one-byte bell reads and writes of
QEMU, the hub and the proxy). The two machines' clocks are fitted from the
back-to-back runs before and after each measurement, where both sides spin:
per request the guest writes the ring (g1), the proxy reads it (h1) and
answers (h2), and the guest sees the answer (g2); the fastest tenth gives
the offset to 0.2 µs, and the line through two such runs follows the drift,
which was 40–100 ppm between QPC and the host's slewed monotonic clock.
`scripts/wc-hop-timeline.py` and `scripts/wc-hop-host.py` print the tables
below. The harness that drives the guest (session 0 only, one lease per run)
and every run's raw data are kept out of the repository, with the evidence.

Stamps, in order: `L.send`/`L.recv` (the launcher around one request),
`C.line` (the compositor has read the request from the launcher's socket),
`C.ringtx0`/`C.ringtx1` (around writing it into the control ring),
`bell.poke` (the doorbell rung), `bell.wr0`/`bell.wr1` (the old detached
writer thread around its `WriteFile`) or `bell.issued` (the new inline
write issued), `door.rx` (a doorman read a bell byte), `P.unpark`/`P.rx`/
`P.tx` (the proxy's control thread woke, read the request, wrote the
answer), `C.park`/`C.unpark`/`C.reply` (the compositor gave up spinning,
was woken, saw the answer), `C.socktx` (the answer written to the
launcher's socket).

**Before**, 20 ms between requests (µs after `L.send`; p50 and mean):

| hop | p50 | mean |
|---|---|---|
| the compositor's request thread wakes on its socket (`C.line`) | 39.7 | 45.2 |
| request in the ring, bell rung (`bell.poke`) | 44.5 | 50.1 |
| the detached writer thread wakes and starts its `WriteFile` (`bell.wr0`) | 105.3 | 407.6 |
| the proxy's doorman has the byte (`H:door.rx`) | 308.4 | 550.2 |
| the proxy's control thread is awake and has the request (`H:P.rx`) | 366.6 | 593.1 |
| the answer written (`H:P.tx`) | 369.7 | 609.7 |
| the compositor sees it (`C.reply`); 154 of 500 had stopped spinning at 1 ms and waited for a bell back | 384.8 | 664.3 |
| the launcher has it (`L.recv`) | 418.3 | 693.2 |

At 1 s between requests the same hops were 61.6 (the compositor's wake),
389 (the writer thread's wake, mean 598), 608 (the doorman), 660 (the control
thread), 793 (the compositor) and 859 µs (the launcher; mean 1050).

The host's half, from the kernel trace (815 requests that found the proxy
parked; p50/mean):

| hop | p50 | mean |
|---|---|---|
| QEMU's main thread woken by the vCPU's kick (ioeventfd) until it runs | 2.6 | 4.4 |
| QEMU's virtio-serial work until it writes the byte to the hub | 33.1 | 32.3 |
| the hub's reader woken and running | 5.5 | 15.5 |
| the hub reads the byte, then sends it to every client in turn | 6.0 + 20.1 | 6.7 + 26.0 |
| the proxy's doorman woken and running | 24.9 | 41.1 |
| the doorman reads the byte, rings the lane (`door.rx`) | 10.1 | 17.3 |
| the control thread woken by the doorman's futex wake and running | 17.3 + 6.4 | 32.3 + 10.2 |
| **QEMU woken to the proxy reading the request** | **156.6** | **184.5** |

The CPUs those threads ran on came out of C1 or C2 almost every time
(the hub and the proxy on the host's two user cores, 14–15; C3, with its
1 ms exit latency, in 4%), so this was not the deep idle states 105.13
suspected. It was the number of thread wakes in a row, each a few to tens
of microseconds on a core that had been idle and clocked down, on both
machines.

**What changed, hop by hop.**

1. **The guest's bell is written by the thread that rang it** (Windows
   only: `winpipe::AsyncWriter`). The detached writer (§99.5) handed every
   bell byte to a thread of its own, and on an idle guest that thread's
   wake was the slowest hop on the guest: 61 µs p50 at 20 ms gaps, 318 µs at
   1 s, with a tail past a millisecond. The ringing thread now issues the
   overlapped `WriteFile` itself (the virtqueue kick happens inside that
   call) and never waits for it: the request and its byte live in one of 32
   slots until the write completes, which the next write notices. A pool
   whose writes all still pend (a host end that stopped draining) has them
   cancelled and the byte refused, which the bell counts as dropped as it
   counted a full queue; §99.5's promise, that a port that stops draining
   never stops a ring thread, is kept with no thread. The call itself costs
   20–50 µs on the guest (vioser's request path and the kick's exit).
   `WC_BELL_INLINE=0` puts the detached writer back, to compare.
2. **The hub rings the lane itself** (shared: `bellhub::DirectRings`,
   `--port UPSTREAM=HUB,rings=FILE`). The hub already reads every byte the
   guest rings; the lanes' wake words are in the ring region at the tail of
   the shared-memory file, which the hub maps as the proxy does, and a
   `FUTEX_WAKE` on a shared file mapping reaches a waiter in any process that
   maps the file. So the waiting thread is woken by the hub's own thread,
   and the two wakes after it (the proxy's doorman, then the doorman's futex
   wake of the waiter: 71 µs p50, 90 mean, from the hub's read to the control
   thread being woken) are gone from the path. The clients still get every
   byte; for a futex waiter their wake is a spurious one, and a waiter that
   waits some other way (the proxy's eventfd per Wayland connection) still
   needs it. The hub attaches only the ring layout
   (`Control::attach_for_bells`: the protocol's ids are read from the region,
   the layout is checked as for any attach), follows the header's run id to
   a new compositor, and rings nothing while the file has no rings.
   `bellhub::tests::the_hub_wakes_a_lane_waiter_in_a_shared_file_with_no_client`.
3. **The hub lets the thread it woke run first** (shared, Linux host). The
   kernel trace showed the proxy's control thread, once the hub woke it,
   waiting a median 60 µs for a CPU: in 40 of 41 traced requests the
   scheduler had put it on the hub's own CPU (the wake is "affine"), where
   the hub went on to send the byte to every client. The hub now yields
   once after ringing a lane that had a waiter parked on it, before the
   fan-out; with nobody waiting, the yield returns at once.
4. **Every wait for an answer yields while it spins, and only the side that
   must spin does** (shared). 105.13's spins were busy loops. On the guest a
   busy spin held its vCPU against the very thread it was waiting for (the
   launcher spinning kept the compositor's request thread off the vCPU, and
   two busy spinners on one vCPU lost it for a 15.6 ms tick). The
   compositor's wait for the host's answer now yields (`SwitchToThread`) for
   up to 2 ms (it was a busy 1 ms; a third of the 20 ms-gap requests used to
   outlast it and need a bell back), and the proxy's 200 µs spin yields
   too. The launcher no longer spins at all: on a loaded guest its yielding
   spin and the compositor's shared a vCPU and lost it to the load for
   10–25 ms. `WC_LAUNCH_SPIN_US` and `WC_CTL_SPIN_US` set them, to measure.
5. **Tried and taken out: the request's threads above normal priority.** On
   a guest loaded by a game, 7 requests in 2000 took 2–53 ms, all of it the
   guest's scheduler (a readied thread waiting one or two 15.6 ms ticks for
   the quantum of the thread running where it was queued). Raising the
   launcher's and the compositor's request threads to
   `THREAD_PRIORITY_HIGHEST` for the request, and yielding with `Sleep(0)`,
   made it worse: a high-priority thread that spins starves the
   normal-priority threads the request needs. Measured in one lease, 1000
   requests 20 ms apart and 60 1 s apart per configuration:

   | bell writer | request threads | 20 ms: mean / p50 / p99 / max | 1 s: mean / p99 |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | inline (this section) | HIGHEST | 255 / 160 / 567 µs / 35 ms | 322 / 834 µs |
   | **inline (this section)** | **normal** | **180 / 158 / 353 µs / 8.8 ms** | **298 / 470 µs** |
   | detached thread (before) | HIGHEST | 440 ms / 480 ms / 612 ms / 2.0 s | 56 ms / 501 ms |
   | detached thread (before) | normal | 310 / 160 / 1387 µs / 47 ms | 481 / 868 µs |

   With the detached writer the starved thread was the bell writer itself,
   and the bell then went out with the next lease ping, half a second
   later. The change is not kept; what the loaded guest's ticks cost is
   left to the guest's own scheduling.

**Which hops are whose.** For another platform (the real Mac, §103.17):

| hop | where it lives | platform |
|---|---|---|
| the launcher's request to the compositor (a local socket) | `wc-launch`, `session_svc` | Windows only: on macOS the launcher and the main process are one |
| the compositor's thread wakes on that socket | guest scheduler | Windows only |
| the bell's write (vioser `WriteFile`, the kick) | `winpipe` | Windows (a virtio-console write and its kick on Linux/libkrun) |
| the hypervisor carrying the kick to the host's port (QEMU's main loop: 33 µs here) | QEMU | QEMU; HVF/libkrun on the Mac has its own |
| the hub reading the byte and ringing the lane | `bellhub` | shared |
| the waiting thread's wake | `park`, `wlbytes` | shared (a futex on Linux, a shared word on macOS) |
| the answer back while the asker spins (no bell) | `session_svc`, `macsvc` | shared |
| a yielding spin, never a busy one, on the side that expects the answer | `session_svc`, `macsvc` | shared |
| the hub yielding to the thread it just woke (the wake is affine) | `bellhub` | Linux hosts; any host whose hub and proxy share few cores |
| a guest freeze while the passed-through GPU leaves D3 (up to ~6 s, about once a minute) | the guest's GPU driver, vfio | this VM; samples within one are set apart below |

**After.** The same instrument on the final build (test installation
`wcil`, shared compositor, release, session 0). At 1 s between requests,
p50 µs after `L.send`:

| hop | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| the compositor's request thread has the request | 61.6 | 55.0 |
| request in the ring, bell written | 389 (the writer thread's wake) | 104.8 (`WriteFile` issued inline) |
| the compositor sees the answer | 793 | 247.2 |
| the launcher has it | 859 | 275.0 |

On the host, from the hub's read of the byte to the control thread being
woken: 71 µs p50 before, 10 µs after; and the thread then ran on the
other core instead of waiting for the hub's fan-out.

**Measured.** One lease, one guest state, master at the merge base
(bc19340) against this branch, each deployed in turn to the same test
installation, hop trace off:

| | master bc19340 | §105.14 |
|---|---|---|
| 20 ms between requests (n = 1000): mean / p50 / p99 | 487 ms / 480 ms / 503 ms | 268 / 141 / 363 µs |
| 1 s between requests (n = 200): mean / p50 / p99 | 57 ms / 405 µs / 685 ms | 317 / 262 / 1341 µs |
| idle, 60 s with the session up: the guest's compositor / the host's proxy | 0.72 s / 0.32 s CPU | 0.22 s / 0.33 s CPU |

Master's 480 ms is a parked proxy answering on its 500 ms slice: since the
shared compositor (§107), a byte through the proxy's own doorman no longer
wakes the control thread. Here the hub wakes it, which is why this branch
does not show it; the plain path is a separate fix.

The larger runs, with the hop trace on, so that every sample can be placed
against the GPU's power transitions (`scripts/wc-hop-stats.py`). The statistics
script converts both ends of each request with the timeline's fitted clock
offset and drift. It refuses GPU-wake attribution without a clock fit; RTT
statistics without a wake file still work with guest stamps alone. The
machine-readable fit is available through `wc-hop-timeline.py RUNDIR
--clock-json`. Regression checks run with `python3 scripts/test-wc-hop-stats.py`.
Reanalysis of `final-c` with this conversion leaves the table below unchanged:


| gap | n | mean | p50 | p99 | max | within a GPU wake (set apart) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| none | 2000 | 20.0 µs | 19.4 | 30.1 | 187 | 0 |
| 20 ms | 2000 | 240.0 µs (257.1 outside the wakes) | 144.7 | 604.7 | 53 ms | 295, mean 140.9 |
| 20 ms, final configuration | 1000 | 180.2 µs | 158.0 | 352.8 | 8.8 ms | not traced |
| 1 s | 300 | 306.7 µs | 275.0 | 812.9 | 5.4 ms | 32, mean 309.0 |
| 1 s, final configuration | 60 + 200 | 298–317 µs | 262–287 | 470–1341 | 5.5 ms | not traced |

The mean target is met back to back and in the 180.2 µs final-configuration
20 ms run. The larger 20 ms run fails it at 240.0 µs, despite its 144.7 µs
median. The 1 s mean also fails at about 300 µs. Where it goes is in
the timeline above: on the guest ~105 µs before the request is in the
ring (a thread's wake on a halted vCPU and the vioser write), ~140 µs
through QEMU, the hub and the proxy and back, and ~30 µs for the
launcher's wake. The means at 20 ms also carry the guest's own scheduling
outliers (a game in session 1 had them at 2–53 ms, 7 in 2000), which no
change on our side removed (item 5).

**Idle CPU.** Nothing added spins or polls while idle: every spin is
bounded by an outstanding request, and the hub's yield runs only when a
byte rang a parked lane. Host: hub 0.01 s and session service 0.02 s per
minute, as before.

**What is left on the path, and why it is not software here.** The kick
reaches the host through QEMU's main loop: its main thread is woken by the
vCPU's ioeventfd, runs virtio-serial's handler and writes the byte to the
hub's socket (33 µs of work on an idle P-core, and on a loaded guest that
loop also runs the guest's audio and display: with a game playing sound the
byte reached the hub 8–11 ms after the guest wrote it in about 1 request in
50). The guest's `WriteFile` through vioser costs 20–50 µs. Both go with a
different doorbell, which needs the VM to restart and is proposed, not done:

* **An ivshmem doorbell** (`ivshmem-doorbell` with an `ivshmem-server`, or
  `ioeventfd`/`irqfd` registered for the arena device): the guest rings by
  one MMIO write (the driver's `IOCTL_IVSHMEM_RING_DOORBELL`), KVM signals an
  eventfd the hub (or the waiter itself) reads, and the host rings back by
  writing an eventfd KVM turns into the guest's MSI-X, with no QEMU thread
  and no virtio-serial queue on either way. Expected saving per isolated
  request: QEMU's wake and work (~35 µs, and the main loop's tail on a busy
  guest), the hub's socket hop (~12 µs) and most of `WriteFile` (~20–40 µs).
  It needs the guest's ivshmem driver to bind interrupts (the virtio-win
  driver does), nix-config's VM definition to add the server and the
  device's `vectors`, and a VM restart at a time the family does not use it.

**Host power, measured and not taken.** The host's cores clock down when
idle (`powersave`, EPP `balance_performance`); a wake runs the first
microseconds slowly. `energy_performance_preference = performance` on every
core cut the 1 s-gap mean from 536 to 262 µs before the software changes,
and costs ~10 W more package power on this laptop (turbostat, 30 s each:
15.2 W as it is, 27.2 W with it). Scoped to the host's two user cores
(14–15, where the hub and the proxy run) it cost 17.0 W, within this
machine's run-to-run noise (17.3 W after restoring), and its latency gain
after the software changes was lost in the guest's own load. Neither is
proposed: the software changes are, and a host-wide power setting for a
family laptop is the user's call.

**The teardown bug** (found on wcl-12128, 18:00 on 2026-10-19). A NixOS
switch re-executed the user's service manager while a session ended.
`systemctl --user is-active` failed during the re-execution, the service
read the failure as "the proxy's unit is gone" and ran `down`; every
`systemctl --user stop` in `down` failed the same way and was silenced;
`down` removed the session's directory, said "down ok", and the service
forgot the session. Its PulseAudio and GPU units ran on with nobody left who
knew their names. Now:

* the service asks `is-active` for the state and ends a session only when
  the manager says `inactive` or `failed`; no answer is no decision
  (`sessiond::classify_is_active`);
* `down` stops each unit and then asks for its state, retrying while the
  manager does not answer (`WC_LAUNCH_STOP_TRIES` tenths of a second, 10 s),
  and fails, keeping the directory and naming the units, if any is still
  running;
* the service forgets a session only after a `down` that worked, and on the
  macOS front end releases nothing to the guest before that, since the units
  may still write into its RAM (§103.15).

Tests: `down_stops_every_unit_even_while_the_manager_re_executes` and
`down_that_cannot_stop_the_units_fails_and_keeps_the_session` (the real
script against a stand-in `systemctl` that refuses like a re-executing
manager), `a_session_is_forgotten_only_after_a_down_that_worked`.

**The cold start.**

* **`up` in the service's own process** (`sessiond_ivshmem::up_inline`,
  called from `agent::start_session`): the header page read and checked,
  `arena.run`, `transport` and `session.index` written, the same words
  back, 0.2–0.5 ms where the script took 58–75 ms. It steps aside to the
  script whenever a broker hands out the arena (§111) or no hub is
  running, and `WC_SESSIOND_BASH_UP=1` forces the script.
  `up_in_process_matches_the_script` runs both on one header and compares
  their output and files, for a plain and an indexed session.
* **The `proxy` verb before its unit starts: 74–78 ms to 17 ms.** It
  scanned the store for PipeWire's node binary in a session whose sound is
  PulseAudio (25–35 ms), asked systemd for the doorbell twice, and forked
  some twenty `cat`, `grep`, `id` and `date`. The verb now stamps its
  stages into `proxy.timing`, which the service puts in its log line.
* **Tried and put back: not waiting for the session's PulseAudio.** With
  `proxy` returning before the server listened, the guest's sound ring
  announced its device first and the proxy made no sink for it
  (`scripts/wc-no-ssh.sh`, leg 1b). The guest numbers below were measured
  in that state; the wait is back, and its cost is whatever PulseAudio's
  start takes beyond the proxy's own (both start together). They are to be
  measured again.

Measured on the guest (test installation `wcil`, whose application is
`foot`, so the window's own start is shorter than Firefox's):

| stage | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| the service's `up` | 58–75 ms | 0.19–0.34 ms |
| the service's `proxy` | 163–260 ms | 107–147 ms (script 21–30, unit started 49–78, socket bound 68–109, rings 84–122) |
| the service's `gpu`, beside `proxy` | 124–217 ms | 112–132 ms |
| the host's answer, from the record | 226–338 ms | 123–150 ms |
| the launcher's session up, nothing running | 409–498 ms | 290–321 ms |
| the launcher's session up, the shared compositor running | — | 137–159 ms |
| click to window, nothing running | ~850 ms (Firefox) | 435 ms (897 the first time after a deploy, cold disk caches) |
| click to window, a new session in a running compositor | — | 286–376 ms |
| click to window, the session up | 532–659 ms (Firefox, 105.9) | 129–165 ms |

What is left is `systemd-run` (~35 ms) and the proxy's own start to its
socket (~35 ms). Units started ahead of the click, or socket-activated,
would take both out of the path; that changes how sessions own their
units, and is not done here.

## 106. Host integration: every host audio device in Linux, and links and files opened across the boundary, both ways

2026-10-19, branch `host-integration`, crate `wc-hostint`. The model is the
one the real-Mac prototype proved over vsock (`nix-darwin-subsystem-linux`,
`agent/`). Its pure functions and tests were adopted where they still fit
(the URL check, the rate limiter, the slugs and their deduplication). What
differs is the transport. Nothing here crosses
the boundary except through the session's shared memory: one ring slot for
messages, the sound ring for samples, and a file share that the VM already
has.

### 106.1 What it does

* **Audio per device.** Every host output (speakers, headphones, a display's
  audio) is its own PipeWire sink in Linux, and every host input (a
  microphone) its own source, named after the host device ("Speakers
  (Realtek(R) Audio)", "WH-1000XM5"). Plugging a device in or out adds or
  removes its node. When the host's default output or input changes, Linux's
  configured default follows within about a second.
* **Linux to host, links.** A Linux application's `xdg-open https://…`, and
  anything that honours `BROWSER` or the session's `mimeapps.list` for
  http, https and text/html, opens the link in the host's browser: Firefox
  by default on macOS (configurable), and the user's default browser on
  Windows unless one is configured.
* **Host to Linux, by type.** A Linux application whose desktop entry lists
  types (`MimeType=`) is registered for them on the host. On Windows that is
  a per-user ProgID, `OpenWithProgids` and Capabilities. On macOS it is the
  generated bundle's `CFBundleDocumentTypes` and `CFBundleURLTypes`. So
  Explorer's and Finder's "Open with", a double-click on a type whose default
  the user made the Linux application, and `open -a`, all start the Linux
  application with the file.
* **Linux to host, by type.** Each host application that opens some of the
  table's types appears in Linux as an application, "Notepad (Windows)" or
  "TextEdit (macOS)", in every "Open with" dialog. The host's default for a
  type is Linux's default for it.

### 106.2 The channel: one ring slot, either side asks

The control channel (§103.14, §103.15) is a request from the host and a
reply from Linux. Opening a link is the reverse, and the handler
lists are pushes. So host integration has a service slot of its own,
`OWNER_HOSTINT = SERVICE_TAG | 3` (sv-transport `wlbytes`). Like control
and sound, the proxy claims it. On macOS the main process opens it; on
Windows the compositor does (`sv-guest.exe`, the only process that can map
the ivshmem device). Each serves it on a thread of its own
(`wc_compositor::hostint::spawn`), never on the Wayland thread, and the
thread ends when the ring reaches EOF.

The wire format is `wc_hostint::wire`, one ASCII line per message. Free text
crosses only as base64 inside one word:

| direction | message | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| both | `hello 1 [PLATFORM]` | (re)start; the host answers with everything again |
| Linux → host | `req N url B64` | open a URL in the host's browser |
| Linux → host | `req N path B64` | open a host file with its default application |
| Linux → host | `req N with TOKEN B64` | open a URL or host file with one host application |
| host → Linux | `rep N ok` / `rep N err B64` | the result, with the host's reason |
| host → Linux | `handlers B64` | host applications: token, name, types, defaults, schemes |
| host → Linux | `paths B64` | the share map, and the drop directory for copies |

A host application crosses only as an opaque token
(`[a-z0-9]{1,32}`). Its executable path or bundle id stays on the host,
so Linux names an application and never sends a command (§94's rule, the
other way round). The host's checks are in `docs/security-model.md` R38.

### 106.3 Audio

**The transport is §103.16's sound ring.** The first plan pushed the device
list on this channel and gave Linux a child `pipewire` hosting one
pipe-tunnel node per device. The sound ring landed while this was being
built, and it already carries every device as a stream (`Device`, `Gone`,
`Default`, credit, capture `Start`/`Stop`) on `OWNER_AUDIO`. So that is the
one path, and the `audio` message is gone from this channel. What host
integration adds is:

* **The Windows device side** (`wc_compositor::sound_win`, in the
  compositor, which owns the rings). Endpoints are enumerated with
  `IMMDeviceEnumerator`. An `IMMNotificationClient`
  (`OnDefaultDeviceChanged`, state changes, added, removed) reports changes,
  debounced to at most 800 ms. Each active endpoint is a stream with its own
  mix rate and channel count. Each output stream is rendered by WASAPI in
  shared mode on that endpoint, from a 240 ms queue that is granted as
  credit and granted again exactly as WASAPI drains it. An output idle for
  3 s releases its endpoint. Each input is captured only between `Start`
  and `Stop`. Whatever the microphone records beyond the session's credit
  is counted as an overrun and never queued. Stream ids are never reused,
  and a format change makes a new stream. The macOS device side is
  `wc-launch/src/sound_mac.rs` (§103.16). Host integration makes it react
  to CoreAudio's property listeners instead of waiting for the next
  one-second poll, and refuses capture unless the process is the
  `org.waycompose.host` bundle (TCC, below).
* **Names.** A Linux sink or source is `<win|mac>.<sink|source>.<slug>`. The
  slug is the host's device name lowercased, with every run of other
  characters as one `_`. A second device with the same name gets `_2`, and a
  name already in use gets the next free number
  (`wc_hostint::audio::node_name`). The description is the host's name
  unchanged. So "Lautsprecher (2- High Definition Audio Device)" is
  `win.sink.lautsprecher_2-_high_definition_audio_device`, described as
  itself. §103.16's `wc_mac_out_<n>` names are replaced by these: a name
  that depends on a stream number is not stable from one session to the
  next.
* **Defaults** follow the host's within a second. The proxy sets the
  session's configured default (`pactl set-default-sink`/`-source`; under
  PipeWire that is `default.configured.audio.sink`/`.source` in the
  `default` metadata, the same key the prototype set with `pw-metadata`).
* **The session's server**, chosen by `wc-session` (`WC_LAUNCH_AUDIO`):
  `on` is §86's PulseAudio of the session's own (the default). `pipewire` is
  a private pipewire, WirePlumber and pipewire-pulse for the session under
  its run directory; WirePlumber's profile has no ALSA, Bluetooth, camera,
  D-Bus or logind, so it can never take real hardware. `system` is the
  user's own server (§103.16). `user-pipewire` is the same for a dedicated
  desktop user only: it is refused unless the session's user is
  `WC_LAUNCH_AUDIO_USER`, the `ConditionUser` of the prototype's units. The
  workstation that runs the macOS VM must never use `system` or
  `user-pipewire`: the VM's devices would become the desktop's.
* **Under PulseAudio** a stream is §103.16's `module-pipe-sink` or
  `module-pipe-source` on a FIFO the proxy serves, paced by its reader.
  **Under PipeWire that pacing does not exist.** pipewire-pulse's pipe sink
  runs on the graph's clock and drops what does not fit in the FIFO. With a
  1.5 s tone and the device side holding credit for 0.4 s, 4% of the samples
  were lost; at 1 s, 44%. So under PipeWire each stream is a node of its
  own, a graph driver that starts a cycle only when the ring's credit covers
  it (106.6).

**The microphone.** macOS: capture happens only in the long-lived main
process, started through Launch Services as the bundle
`org.waycompose.host` (`Waycompose Host.app`, written by `--install`, with
`LSUIElement` and `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`), so TCC asks once, for
that bundle, and never for a per-application face. Measured in the VM with
a virtio-sound input: the dialog named "Waycompose Host" with our usage
text. TCC's log named `org.waycompose.host` as responsible for itself.
After Allow, 368,640 bytes were captured in 2 s. A capture attempted from
any other process (an ssh shell) is refused by our own check before
CoreAudio is asked. Signing with a stable local certificate, so that TCC
does not ask again after a rebuild, is the Nix activation's job on the real
Mac (the prototype's `stable-codesign.nix`). In the VM the binary is
unsigned, and TCC logs "Failed to copy signing info". Windows has no
per-application microphone prompt for desktop applications beyond the
global privacy switch.

### 106.4 Links and files

**Linux side.** The session's applications get `wc-host-open` as a
high-priority `xdg-open` on `PATH` and `BROWSER=xdg-open`. Their
`XDG_DATA_DIRS` starts with the session's own applications directory, and
`XDG_CONFIG_DIRS` with a directory holding the session's `mimeapps.list`.
The proxy writes both from the host's `handlers`: `wc-host-browser.desktop`
for http, https and text/html, `wc-host-<token>.desktop` per host
application, and the host's defaults as Linux's defaults. Nothing is written
into the user's own `~/.config` or `~/.local`. `wc-host-open` sends one
request over a local socket in the session's run directory (0600, with the
peer's uid checked) to the proxy, which forwards it on the ring and prints
the host's refusal, if any. For `xdg-open` (no host application named), a
`file:` URL or local path is refused with a message, unless the file is in a
share both sides see. "Open with" a host application on a Linux-only file
copies it into the share's drop directory first, and the host opens the
copy.

**Paths.** Windows: the VM already shares the VM host's `/srv/winshare` with
the guest over virtio-fs, as `Z:`. That is the share, both ways, and
`Z:\waycompose-open` is the drop directory. A Windows file outside `Z:` that
is opened with a Linux application is copied there first, so the Linux
application edits the copy. macOS on a real Mac: the Linux VM mounts the
Mac user's home over virtio-fs at the same path, so the map is the identity.
The macOS VM is §106.6.

**Host side, Windows.** `wc-launch`'s deploy registers each application's
types under HKCU (`wc_hostint::assoc::windows_plan`). It writes a manifest,
and `--uninstall-assoc` removes exactly what the manifest lists. A file
opened through the registration runs `wc-launch --session-name S APP --file
"%1"`, which maps or copies the path and sends the existing `open` verb with
a `file:///` URL. The label in "Open with" is the shortcut's title, so two
installations stay apart. Opening for Linux uses `ShellExecuteW` with the
verb `open`, after `AssocIsDangerous` and the extension list, or the
handler's own executable through `CreateProcessW`. The configured browser
(`[hostint] browser`, with fixed `browser-arg`s before the URL, which is
always one argument of its own) replaces the default browser.

**On the compositor.** Only the compositor can map the ivshmem device, so it
serves both slots. `session_svc` opens `OWNER_HOSTINT` when the launcher
passed `--hostint` (with the share and browser from `[hostint]`), and runs
`sound_win` on `OWNER_AUDIO` in place of §105's single default-output
player.

**Host side, macOS.** The bundle's `Info.plist` lists the types at rank
`Alternate` (`wc_hostint::assoc::plist_types`). The face's
`application:openURLs:` hands each URL to the main process, which sends the
`open` verb. Opening for Linux uses `/usr/bin/open -a <browser> -- <url>`,
`/usr/bin/open -- <path>`, or `/usr/bin/open -b <bundle id> -- <target>`.

### 106.5 Under PipeWire, a node that drives its own graph

§103.16's pipe sink is paced by its reader under a real PulseAudio. Under
PipeWire's pulse server it is not. The module's stream is clocked by
whatever drives the graph, normally the dummy driver, and when the proxy
stops reading because the device side has granted no credit, the FIFO fills
and the module drops what does not fit. So under PipeWire each host device
is a node of `wc-pw-node`, a small C program (`crates/wc-proxy/pw-node`,
built by the flake as `.#wc-pw-node`; its RUNPATH is the store's
libpipewire, so the VM host needs its closure and not an installed
PipeWire). It hosts all of a session's devices. Each one is a `pw_stream`
with `PW_STREAM_FLAG_DRIVER`, as `Audio/Sink` or `Audio/Source`. A timer at
the quantum's period calls `pw_stream_trigger_process` only when the
output's credit covers a cycle, or when an input has a cycle of the
microphone's samples. While credit is held, no cycle runs, and the
application's stream waits as it would on a real device that is behind.
`sound.rs` starts it when `pactl info` names a PipeWire server and talks to
it on its stdin and stdout, in the sound ring's own frames. Start and Stop
of a microphone follow the node's state (streaming or paused). On a real
PulseAudio, `sound.rs` keeps §103.16's pipe modules.

Measured (scripts/wc-hostint-local.sh, a private PipeWire 1.6.9, a fake
device side that plays in real time from a 250 ms queue, a 1.5 s signal of
288,000 bytes with no zero frame, credit held in the middle):

| credit held | lost, pipe modules under PipeWire | lost, `wc-pw-node` | pacat longer than without a hold |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.1 s | 0 | 0 | +127 ms |
| 0.4 s | 45,056 B (15.6%) | 0 | +427 ms |
| 1 s | 159,744 B (55%) | 0 | +1024 ms |

With `wc-pw-node` the bytes that arrive are the bytes played, contiguous,
with nothing inserted. Under `on` (PulseAudio 17) nothing is lost either,
and pacat waits for the hold. PulseAudio inserts 12,288 bytes of silence
near the start of every stream (its own start-up underrun), so there the
check is that every frame arrives, in order.

Two bugs in shared code were found by these runs. PulseAudio 17's
`module-pipe-source` refuses a FIFO that exists, and `sound.rs` made it
first, so no microphone loaded under `on`. The session's PulseAudio also
reached the user's session bus through `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/bus`, even with
`DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` unset. A second session's PulseAudio then died
with "org.PulseAudio1 already taken", so `pulse.sh` now names a bus that
does not exist.

### 106.6 The macOS VM's share

On the real Mac the Linux VM mounts the Mac user's home at the same path
over libkrun's virtio-fs. In the macOS VM of role (a), Linux runs QEMU, so
the share goes the other way: a Linux directory
(`/mnt/datasets/macvm/shares/<instance>`) is exported to macOS by
`virtiofsd` (vhost-user-fs) and mounted at `~/LinuxShare`. §103.3 says that
Sonoma under QEMU binds only legacy virtio devices. That is wrong: modern
virtio-fs, 9p and virtio-sound all bind. What it takes:

* `virtiofsd --sandbox=namespace --uid-map :0:$UID:1: --gid-map :0:$GID:1:
  --translate-uid map:501:0:1 --translate-gid map:20:0:1`, unprivileged.
  `--inode-file-handles` needs a capability it does not have and is left off,
  with no problem seen.
* `mount_virtiofs -u 501 -g 20 <tag> ~/LinuxShare`. Without `-u`/`-g`, every
  create fails with EINVAL; with `--sandbox=none`, with EPERM.
* `--xattr --xattrmap ":prefix:all::user.virtiofs.::bad:all:::"`. Without
  xattrs, every Launch Services open of a file in the share fails with -4:
  its `Getxattr` is answered ENOSYS.
* macOS treats the mount as a network volume. TCC never lets a process of
  an ssh session in, and asks once for `org.waycompose.host`.
* `std::fs::copy` on macOS is `fcopyfile`, which the share does not support
  (ENOSYS), so the copy into the drop directory is a plain read and write.

9p mounts only as root (`/Volumes/...`), and its access fails.

### 106.7 What was run

**Linux, without a VM** (`scripts/wc-hostint-local.sh`, a private
PipeWire stack and a private PulseAudio, never the desktop's): a fake device
side announcing two outputs and a microphone with real names. 49 checks pass
under PipeWire and 44 under PulseAudio:
* the names are the slugs, and the descriptions the names (ö and ®
  included);
* a host default change is the session's default 25 ms later;
* hot-plug adds and removes nodes, and a second device of the same name gets
  `_2`;
* the credit holds above;
* a recorder on the source starts capture about 0.3 s later and stops it
  when it ends;
* `wc-host-open https://…` arrives as `req N url`, and the host's refusal is
  printed with exit 1;
* a Linux-only file is refused before anything is sent (exit 2);
* `--with` on a Linux-only file copies it into the drop directory and sends
  the host path.

Evidence: `/mnt/datasets/builds/evidence/host-integration/linux-local/`.

**The macOS VM** (Sonoma, 4 GiB, a real Linux session from the workstation,
with a temporary QEMU usb-audio, virtio-sound and virtio-fs). Each image was
judged by a fresh Sonnet agent; evidence is in
`/mnt/datasets/builds/evidence/host-integration/mac-e2e/`:
* **Audio.** Two sinks and a source,
  `mac.sink.apple_virtual_sound_device`, `mac.sink.audio_output_-_disabled`
  and `mac.source.apple_virtual_sound_device`, described by the Mac's
  names. When the Mac's default output changed, the session's default sink
  followed 66 ms later, and 106 ms later on the change back. A 3 s tone
  played. `parec` from the source started the Mac's recorder and got
  794,880 bytes in 5 s. TCC asked "“Waycompose Host” would like to access

* **Linux to Mac.** `xdg-open https://example.org` opened Safari (this VM

* **Mac to Linux.** A Mac file opened with the Linux Text Editor's bundle

* **Linux "Open with" a Mac application.** `wc-host-open --with <TextEdit's

* The generated bundle is in Finder's "Open With" for `.txt` and `.html`. It

**The macOS VM, second run** (an isolated session: `WC_LAUNCH_TEST_HOME`
gave the Linux applications a throwaway home, after the first run's Text

`…/mac-e2e2/`. Each click was made, and each image judged, by a fresh Sonnet

* **The browser comes to the front.** On macOS 14 an application started
  by a background process opens behind the active one (cooperative

* **Finder's "Open With" on a file Linux created in the share** opened it

* Audio, the refusals and "open with" TextEdit were as in the first run.

* **Found:** while TCC's dialog for "Waycompose Host" waits for an answer

**The Windows guest** (the test host's VM, while it was idle, under the lease,

**On one machine, before the guest** (`scripts/wc-hostint-win-local.sh`, on

of the merge itself: the proxy's socketless ring branch never claimed the

**The Mac's outputs and its microphone dialog.** While macOS asks the user
for the microphone, a CoreAudio start for the device that also has the
microphone waits in coreaudiod until the dialog is answered. The outputs are
therefore AUHAL units started on workers of their own, never on the sound

up: the output-only device played (a 3 s tone in 3.37 s), the Linux default
