  change; the proxy remaps the client's fd to the new size.
* **A buffer** is created upstream at once, under its id, as a **1x1 stub** on
  the stub pool (`width 1, height 1, stride 4`, the client's format). It holds
  no arena bytes.
* **The first attach backs it**: the stub buffer is destroyed, the pool
  **re-pointed** (destroyed and created again under the same id) at an extent
  of exactly the buffer's size (`stride * height`), and the buffer created
  again under its id at its real geometry at offset 0 of that extent; then the
  attach is forwarded. The commit copies from the client's pool at the
  buffer's offset into offset 0 of its extent. Every buffer is its own extent,
  so the pool's size never matters.
* The compositor frees an id at a destructor, so re-creating under the same id
  is legal at once; the `delete_id` that answers the proxy's own destroy is
  kept (a count per id, since one id may be destroyed by the proxy many
  times, and the answers come in order); the client's own destroys are
  answered to the client as always.
* **Reclaim**: when the arena has no room, buffers that are not attached to a
  surface (current or pending), released by the compositor, and older than
  250 ms lose their extent: the buffer is destroyed and re-created as a stub
  under its id, the extent freed at once (the compositor has released it and
  the destroy is ahead of any reuse in the same stream). The next attach backs
  it again with a full copy.
* **A buffer outlives its pool** (`weston-presentation-shm` destroys its pool
  at once). Re-pointing needs a live pool of the client, so when the client
  destroys its last live pool, its stub buffers are backed first.
  `wl_shm.release` is held until no live pool can need its `wl_shm`.
* **No room even after reclaiming**: `wl_display.error(no_memory)` on the
  buffer, with the arena's free bytes and largest run in the message; the
  client ends, and nothing more of it is forwarded, so the compositor's stream
  stays in step to its last byte.
* §104's failed dma-buf buffers are not `wl_buffer`s upstream (a placeholder);
  an attach of one is still held back, as §104 says.

What a pool costs now is one stub per session and the bytes of its attached
buffers. The pool-level machinery of stage 16 (deferral, `wanted`,
publication, pool reclaim, `--pool-headroom`) is gone; `--pool-headroom` is
accepted and unused.

### 109.4 Tested

* `a_pool_is_the_stub_at_once_and_every_resize_is_forwarded`: weston-terminal's
  nine doublings, each forwarded; no arena bytes until attach, then exactly
  800x600x4.
* `a_512_mib_pool_runs_in_a_32_mib_arena`: a 512 MiB pool, buffers created,
  attached, destroyed, the pool resized; the pixels arrive at offset 0 of the
  buffer's extent; ten 3 MiB buffers through a 32 MiB arena reclaim the cold
  ones (peak under 32 MiB, no `no_memory`), and a reclaimed buffer shown again
  is backed again.
* `a_buffer_bigger_than_the_arena_is_no_memory_naming_it`,
  `the_proxys_own_destroys_are_answered_to_it`, `buffers_outlive_their_pool`.
* Every one of them replays the compositor's object map over everything that
  crossed (`assert_in_step`): each message names a live object, every new id
  is the next slot or a freed one.
* `scripts/wc-lazy-pools.sh`: foot (512 MiB pool) and weston-terminal (nine
  doublings) through the whole no-ssh path in a **64 MiB** BAR: both map a
  window and keep running; foot's buffers held 2.7 MiB at peak, weston-
  terminal's 3.0 MiB; no `Invalid new_id`, no protocol error.

## 110. One pool: the Wayland arena and the GPU device

Written 2026-10-19, branch `windows-multi-install`, after §107 and §109. The
brief (user, through the coordinator): 128 MiB is not enough, because the GPU
must be usable properly; stop treating the 128 MiB arena as the Wayland
buffer space. Make the Wayland arena and the GPU pool **one** sub-allocated
pool, so Wayland buffers can lease from the 1 GiB GPU device too, with no
device-size change, and keep the pool and its regions open for regions that
are not BARs (§108).

### 110.1 Status in one paragraph

The shared compositor's arena is now a pool of **regions**: region 0 is its
own BAR (§107's `BarPool`, unchanged), and region 1 is the GPU device, leased
from the **same** allocator the GPU sessions lease from (`sv_arena::pool`,
§97), so a byte is a GPU session's or a Wayland buffer's and never both. A
session asks for memory as before (`grow N` on its arena slot); the BAR is
tried first, then the other regions in turn, and a grant from region K is
answered in §108.6's form, `ok ID region K OFFSET LEN`. The proxy maps it
from the file it was given for region K (`--arena-region 1=PATH`, the GPU
device's backing file, whose pool offsets are file offsets). Because the
ivshmem driver gives one mapping per device, only a process that maps the GPU
device can read a buffer there, so **the shared compositor runs the GPU pool
itself**: `sv-guest wayland … --with-gpu guest --pool …`, the GPU half on a
thread, the compositor on the main thread. Locally (`wc-multi-install.sh`
leg 7) three installations ran on a 32 MiB BAR whose own pool could not hold
one session's first region, every buffer leased from a 256 MiB file standing
in for the GPU device, three windows mapped, no two grants overlapping.
**Not run on the Windows guest** (110.6).

### 110.2 The pool, the regions, and who owns what

| region | memory | allocator | grants |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | the arena's BAR (device 0x1c), less the header page, the outbound window, the rings and the first MiB (kept for §108.2's table, 110.4) | the compositor's `BarPool` (§107): 1 MiB granules, ¾ cap per session | `ok ID OFFSET LEN`, arena offsets, as in §107 |
| 1 | the GPU device (0x1d, 1 GiB on the guest), region 0 of the GPU pool | the GPU pool's `sv_arena::pool` (§97): 64 KiB granules, a `Dedicated` lease on an account per Wayland session (`wayland <install> (session N)`), never the reserve kept for a GPU session's start, the pool's own ¾ cap | `ok ID region 1 OFFSET LEN`, device offsets |
| 2 … | §108's runtime regions (guest RAM, a Mac's chunks) | whoever announces them | `ok ID region K OFFSET LEN` |

Every grant, whatever its region, is one entry of the compositor's grant
table (`BarPool::adopt` for regions other than 0): one id space, ids never
reused in a run, the session's for `pool_check`, given back by `release ID`
or at the session's end, and then back to its own allocator
(`PoolRegion::release`). A region is two things and nothing more
(`session_svc::PoolRegion`): a mapping this process keeps, and an allocator
that leases ranges of it. `add_pool_region(K, ptr, len, src)` registers the
mapping as arena id `0xF000_0000 + K` (`wc_handle::arena::
register_borrowed_base`, no new mapping) so a grant is a window of it like
any BAR window. Nothing in the table says "BAR": a §108 region is another
`PoolRegion`.

### 110.3 Why the GPU pool runs in the compositor

The alternative was a guest-local protocol between the compositor and a
separate GPU process (the compositor asks it for a lease). It fails on the
reading side: the compositor has to read a Wayland buffer's pixels, and only
the process holding the GPU device's one mapping can. So both halves are one
process (`sv-guest` was always one binary with both). What that needed:

* **Two doorbell ports in one process.** The cross-VM wake was process-wide;
  the GPU rings ring `svbell` and the Wayland rings `wcbell`. A bell now looks
  its port up by the address of its lane (`park::cross_wake_at`): the GPU pool
  installs its port for its device's address range
  (`poolcold::attach_guest_bell_for`, `install_cross_wake_for`), and that
  install becomes the process-wide one only if there is none, so a separate
  GPU process behaves exactly as before.
* **A hook when the pool exists** (`pool_guest::set_pool_hook`): `sv-guest`
  makes the pool's region 0 the arena's region 1 (`one_pool::GpuRegion`).
* **The launcher** passes `--with-gpu` and the GPU half's arguments to the
  user's compositor and starts no GPU process of its own (`one-pool = on`, the
  default; `off` is §107's separate per-user GPU process).

What this costs: a GPU driver fault now ends the compositor too, and with it
every installation's windows, where before it ended the GPU sessions only.

### 110.4 The region table's place (§108.2), decided

§108.6 proposed the arena's region table in the first 64 KiB after the
header page, announced by a word in the header page. Accepted: a shared
compositor's `BarPool` starts at the arena's first MiB (`with_front`, the
granule above the table's 64 KiB), so no buffer ever lands there. The
announcement word is proposed at **byte 2048 of the header page** (after the
boot record's authenticator, which ends at 1872): `"WCRGNTB1"`, then the
table's arena offset (u64, 0) and its length (u32, 65536). It is not written
yet: the table itself is §108's to build.

### 110.5 Tested

* `barpool::another_regions_range_is_owned_like_a_bar_grant`,
  `the_front_is_never_granted`; `arena::a_borrowed_base_is_windowed_
  without_a_mapping_of_its_own`; `park::ranged_wake_tests`;
  `barwin::a_grant_parses…` (both answer forms).
* `sv-guest one_pool::wayland_and_gpu_leases_share_one_allocator`: a GPU
  session's leases and two Wayland sessions' through the real
  `PoolServer` interleave without a byte in common.
* `scripts/wc-multi-install.sh` leg 7: a 32 MiB BAR (rings 10, outbound 1,
  table 1: a 20 MiB pool, 15 MiB cap per session) beside a 256 MiB file as
  region 1 (`--pool-region-file`, a `FileRegion` over the same lease allocator,
  the harness's stand-in for the GPU pool). Three installations' sessions:
  every first region refused by the BAR's cap and granted from region 1, at 0,
  16 and 32 MiB; three windows mapped; every session answers; every region
  given back at `down`.

### 110.6 Not done, and on the guest

* **Not run on Windows.** On the guest, with `one-pool = on` (default) and
  `gpu-sessions` > 0: the compositor's log must say `pool region 1 (1024 MiB,
  the GPU device's pool…)`, a Firefox session must keep running when the
  arena's BAR is full (`granted region … of pool region 1`), the GPU sessions
  must still attach (the `svbell` port is now the GPU device range's, and the
  `wcbell` the process's), and the GPU pool's report must list `wayland …`
  accounts beside the GPU ones.
* **The BAR is not shrunk.** §108.6 says the arena's BAR can shrink to its
  bootstrap once regions grow; that is a device-size change, which this brief
  excludes.
* **§108's table** is reserved, not written (110.4); regions 2 and up come with
  it.
* **A Wayland grant in the GPU pool's region K > 0** (once §108 grows the GPU
  pool) is refused for now: this process maps only its region 0.

### 110.7 Gates

| gate | result |
|---|---|
| `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` | 114 binaries, **3250 passed, 0 failed**, 9 ignored |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` | exit 0; no warning in a file this section touched |
| `cargo check --workspace --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`; `-p wc-launch -p wc-compositor --target x86_64-apple-darwin` | exit 0 |
| `scripts/wc-xref.sh --list` | no missing citation |
| `scripts/wc-multi-install.sh` (legs 1–7), `scripts/wc-no-ssh.sh`, `scripts/wc-lazy-pools.sh` | OK, OK, OK |

## 111. One privileged component per machine: who may hold what, and what a dead process leaves behind

Written 2026-10-19, branch `broker` (from `session-fixes`, after §107.10).
The crate is `crates/wc-broker`; docs/security-model.md R44 is its argument.

### 111.1 Why

Three requests from the user, after the guest e2e of 2026-10-19:

1. **Liveness.** A process that holds a ring slot, a device, a region or a
   doorbell and dies must not leave it held. The kernel knows when a process
   exits; something privileged should be told and clean up, instead of idle
   timers guessing. (§107.10's stuck session was not a dead process, but the
   rule stands.)
2. **Isolation between users.** On a machine with several users, one user's
   processes must never get a mapping, handle, slot or lease of another's.
   The rule is the user's own: "just look at the user identification and not
   much more". A user is a uid or a SID. No keys, signatures or integrity
   levels beyond what §105 already has.
3. **No slowdown, and no duplication.** The data path stays as it is:
   zero-copy shared memory, doorbells, GPU pinning and address stability. And
   one crate does this for every platform and both roles, server (the
   compositor and GPU server: Windows, macOS, Linux) and client (the Linux
   side that runs the applications, `wc-proxy` and `sv-icd`).

Pieces that existed and fold into it: the Windows SYSTEM task that set the
ports' ACLs (`scripts/wc-port-access.ps1`, §91), the macOS keeper
(`wc-launch --keeper`, §103.15), and the Windows large-page keeper of §108.10.

### 111.2 The shape: a control plane that moves handles

The one fact that decides the design: on the Windows guest each ivshmem device
allows **one mapping** (the driver ties it to the handle that asked) and each
virtio-serial port **one opener**. A broker that relayed the data would be a
copy and a hop on every frame and every doorbell. So the broker never touches
data. It opens a device and **moves** the handle into the process that asked
(Windows: `DuplicateHandle` with `DUPLICATE_CLOSE_SOURCE`; Unix: the fd sent
with `SCM_RIGHTS`, the broker's copy closed). From then on the process maps the
BAR or reads the port exactly as when it opened it itself: the same code, the
same mapping, the same wake.

The handle is moved, not shared, for a reason beyond tidiness. If the broker
kept its own handle to the ivshmem device, the driver's cleanup would not run
when the holder's process died (the file object would still be open), and the
mapping it made into the dead process would be torn down later from another
process's context. Moving it leaves exactly today's lifetime: the device is
released when the holder's process exits.

A region (a guest-RAM section on Windows, a wired shm object on macOS, a memfd
on Linux, a dma-buf of guest RAM on the host) is different: the broker keeps a
handle and gives copies. That is the keeper rule: the memory outlives a
crashed owner until its pool has let go of it.

### 111.3 The rules, in one state machine (`core.rs`)

`Core` has no operating system in it. The platform halves tell it who
connected, what was asked and which process exited; it answers and returns
notices (destroy this object, push this line, this region is drained). So the
rules are one implementation, unit-tested without any platform.

1. **A user owns what its processes asked for.** Only that user's processes,
   and the broker's admins (root, SYSTEM, its own account), get a handle to it.
2. **A device has one holder.** Lent to one process at a time; a request from
   another user's process is refused while it is held ("one user at a time"),
   one from the same user's other process too (the device has one opener). It
   is free again when the holder's **process** exits. Its connection closing
   is not enough, because the handle lives in the process.
3. **A region outlives its owner until its pool has let go.** The owner is
   the connection that allocated it. When that connection or process ends,
   its regions become **orphans** of their pool, still held. The same user's
   next process that serves the pool adopts them (`adopt POOL`) and frees each
   once the host has unmapped it. A region is destroyed only by its owner's
   `free`, or by its release rule: `OwnerFree` (Windows, §108.10: never on a
   timeout) or `Probe` (macOS, §103.15: the host's release word, or a time).
4. **A lease is a holder's claim on one region's epoch** (the client role,
   §108.4). It ends by `close`, by the connection, or by the process. A
   retiring region pushes `!retiring ID EPOCH` to its holders and is
   **drained** when the last lease ends. That is the gate for `UNMAPPED`.
5. **Exits are told.** A subscribed connection of the same user (and admins)
   gets `!exited PID ROLE` and `!device-free NAME`.

### 111.4 The protocol (`proto.rs`)

One line each way on a local socket (Unix) or pipe (Windows), the same text
everywhere:

```text
hello ROLE                    -> ok hello RUN USER PID
device NAME                   -> ok device NAME HANDLE        (moved)
alloc POOL BYTES [large]      -> ok region ID POOL LEN EPOCH PIECES
open ID                       -> ok region ID POOL LEN EPOCH PIECES
find POOL                     -> ok region ...   (the live region of a published place, e.g. gpu.3)
close ID | free ID            -> ok
adopt POOL                    -> ok adopted [ID:LEN ...]
connect NAME                  -> ok connect NAME HANDLE       (a fresh connection to a local service)
sign INSTALL SESSION INDEX ARUN APAGES OUTBOUND RRUN RPAGES GPU SEQ
                              -> ok signed SEQ MAC IDENTITY...
subscribe                     -> ok, then !exited PID ROLE | !device-free NAME | !retiring ID EPOCH
stats                         -> ok stats K=V ...
refused                       -> err WHY
```

`HANDLE` is `fd` on Unix (the fds travel with the line, in order) and the
handle's value on Windows (the broker has already put it into the caller).
`PIECES` is `HANDLE@OFFSET+LEN,...`: one piece for a region the broker made,
several for a host region made of dma-bufs. A malformed line is refused by
name; words are `[A-Za-z0-9-_.:]{1,64}`, lines at most 4096 bytes.

### 111.5 The platforms (`sys/`)

| | identity | liveness | handles | regions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Linux | `SO_PEERCRED` uid | pidfd (`pidfd_open`), one epoll thread | `SCM_RIGHTS` | sealed memfd; on the host, dma-bufs of guest RAM (§108) |
| macOS | `getpeereid` + `LOCAL_PEERPID` | kqueue `EVFILT_PROC`/`NOTE_EXIT` | `SCM_RIGHTS` | POSIX shm, unlinked at once, mapped and wired by the broker |
| Windows | the pipe client's token user SID (`ImpersonateNamedPipeClient`), checked against the process's own token | a wait on the process handle | `DuplicateHandle` into the process | unnamed pagefile sections, large pages when asked (§108.7) |

Each platform half is a `server::Platform`: accept and identify, watch a pid,
open a device, make a region, send a line with handles, and (§111.6) say who
the caller is. Everything else is `server.rs`, one serving loop: a thread per
connection, one lock on the core, notices carried out under it. A session
asks a handful of questions when it starts; nothing per frame.

### 111.6 The boot record says who asked, and the broker signs it

The host must know which server-side user a session belongs to, to run its
Linux side as the Linux user mapped to them (111.10). A compositor cannot be
trusted to say: with the device handle moved into it, it maps the BAR
read-write and could write any bytes into the header page. So the existing
§105 HMAC moves to the broker. The installations' keys move from the user's
install directory into a directory only the broker's account can read, and
the boot record gains an identity area, covered by the MAC:

```text
  page 0, from macboot::OFF_IDENTITY (1920)
  0   "WCIDNT01"
  8   u16 length, then "os=windows user=NAME id=S-1-5-21-…" (at most 246 bytes)
```

`sign` takes the record's fields from the compositor and the identity from the
kernel (the token's SID and account name, or the uid and its name), never from
the request, and answers the MAC (`Auth::sign_identity`). The compositor
publishes record, identity and MAC (`publish_identity`). A user process that
rewrites the identity in the page it can write makes the MAC fail
(`the_identity_is_covered_by_the_mac_and_none_is_sections_107s`). With no
identity the message is §107's, byte for byte, so a host that has not been
updated reads today's records as before. It is the same HMAC, signed by the
trusted party; no new cryptography.

### 111.7 Tests of the shared parts

* `core::tests` (8): one holder and its return at the holder's exit; named
  users; a region is its user's only, root may open it; the keeper rule (an
  owner's death leaves orphans that only the same user's next provider of the
  pool adopts, never a timeout); the probe rule; leases and drain by close,
  connection and process; exits told only to the user's subscribers and
  admins; the budget.
* `proto::tests` (3): every request survives its own line; malformed lines
  are refused; a region reply with several pieces round-trips.
* `tests/unix.rs` (6), on a real socket with a second process (the test binary
  run again): a device moved into a child, refused to the parent while the
  child lives, `!exited` and `!device-free` pushed and the device lent again
  the moment the child exits; a device for another uid refused; a memfd region
  shared by two connections, its owner's connection closed, the orphan still
  mapped and readable, adopted by the right pool only and freed; `sign` with
  and without a key, the MAC verifying for the kernel's identity and not for
  another; `connect` handing out fresh connections to a local service.
* `macboot::identity_tests` (2).

### 111.8 Windows

Written 2026-10-20, branch `broker-win`. The code is
`crates/wc-broker/src/sys/windows/` (the platform half, the service, the
holder, the devices' security), the Windows `Client` in `client.rs`,
`sv-guest broker`, and `scripts/wc-broker-install.ps1` run by
`scripts/wc-launch.sh deploy`.

**The service.** `sv-guest broker` runs under the service control manager as
`waycompose-broker`, `LocalSystem`, automatic start, restarted 1 s, 5 s and
30 s after a failure. Its binary is `C:\Program Files\waycompose\sv-guest.exe`,
which users may read and run but not write: a SYSTEM service that ran a file
its user could replace would hand that user SYSTEM. `--console` runs the same
code in a console, for tests. Its log is `C:\ProgramData\waycompose\broker.log`.

**The pipe.** `\\.\pipe\waycompose-broker`, `PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS`, the
first instance made with `FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE` (so whoever made the
name first makes the broker fail to start, instead of sharing it). The
descriptor gives SYSTEM and Administrators everything and authenticated users
`0x12019b`: read, `FILE_WRITE_DATA`, attributes, but not
`FILE_APPEND_DATA`, which on a pipe is `FILE_CREATE_PIPE_INSTANCE` and would let
a user answer in the broker's place. A client therefore opens it with
`GENERIC_READ | FILE_WRITE_DATA` and identification-level impersonation only.
The first build granted `0x12008b` (no write at all) and its client asked for
`GENERIC_WRITE`; Wine enforced neither, the test VM refused every user. Every
authenticated user, not only `INTERACTIVE`, because a process the task
scheduler or a service starts for a user carries a batch or service logon and
is that user's all the same.

**Who asks.** Per connection: `GetNamedPipeClientProcessId`; the user SID of
the client's token by `ImpersonateNamedPipeClient`, `OpenThreadToken`
(as self) and `RevertToSelf` (a thread that cannot revert ends the process);
then `OpenProcess(PROCESS_DUP_HANDLE | SYNCHRONIZE |
PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION)` on that pid and the process's own token
must name the same SID, so a pid reused between the two is refused. The user
is `sid:S-1-5-21-…`. Only SYSTEM (`S-1-5-18`) is an admin: an administrator's
process is one more user here, and was refused the arena while u1 held it.

**Liveness.** The process handle opened at connect, waited on by the thread
pool (`RegisterWaitForSingleObject`, once). Every connection of one process
shares that handle; the exit is told to the core once per watch, and the wait
is unregistered outside its own callback.

**Handles.** `DuplicateHandle` into the client's process, values in the
reply. A device is moved (`DUPLICATE_SAME_ACCESS | DUPLICATE_CLOSE_SOURCE`):
the broker keeps no handle, so the ivshmem driver's release and vioser's
close run in the holder's process exactly as when it opened the device
itself. A region is copied (`DUPLICATE_SAME_ACCESS`). If the reply cannot be
written, the handles just put into the client are closed there again.

**Devices.** `arena` = ivshmem in PCI slot 0x1c, `gpu` = slot 0x1d,
`wcbell` and `svbell` = the virtio-serial ports by name (`--device
NAME=ivshmem:SLOT|port:NAME|path:PATH` changes them; `path:` is a stand-in
for tests). The open is the code the processes used before, split in two:
`wc_handle::open_ivshmem_slot` + `map_ivshmem_device` (what
`map_ivshmem_slot` now is), and `sv_transport::winpipe::open_virtio_port_handle`
+ `Pipe::from_port_handle` (what `open_virtio_port` now is). The broker
calls the first half, the compositor or GPU process the second, so the
mapping and the port I/O are the same code as before the broker.

**The devices' security, which replaces `wc-port-access.ps1` (§91).** At
every start the broker gives the four devices `D:P(A;;FA;;;SY)(A;;FA;;;BA)`,
as the PnP security property (applied at every device start, with nothing of
ours running) and on the live device object, finding the ports by name as the
script did. It re-enables a recorded port left disabled (§99.6). What each
device had before is kept in `C:\ProgramData\waycompose\devices.txt` for
`sv-guest broker revert-acl`. The baseline on the test VM is worth stating:
the Looking Glass B7 ivshmem driver leaves its devices
`(A;;0x1201bf;;;WD)`, read and write for Everyone, and an ordinary user's
process mapped the GPU device directly before the broker (`direct-opened`,
`bw ... 4.97 GiB/s` as u1). After it, the same open is access denied. A port
another process holds cannot be opened to change its descriptor (vioser is
exclusive). Startup refuses if the port's live or PnP protection cannot be
verified. Security reads retry access-denied opens for up to two seconds to
allow asynchronous driver closes to finish; unreadable protection still fails.

**Regions.** Unnamed pagefile sections (`CreateFileMappingW` with no name,
`SEC_COMMIT`), so no other process can open one by name; `large` adds
`SEC_LARGE_PAGES` when the broker holds `SeLockMemoryPrivilege` (SYSTEM does)
and the length is a whole number of large pages, and is refused otherwise.
The region-init hook (`Windows::with_region_init`) is where §108.8's stamp
plugs in: `Fn(&mut [u8], region id, page size) -> io::Result<Option<String>>`,
called once on each new region with the whole region mapped into the broker
for the call only; the word it returns ends the `ok region` reply (the
nonce), an error refuses the alloc. The windows-guest-ram keeper's protocol
maps onto the broker's: `hello POOL` is `hello` + `adopt POOL`, `alloc` and
`free` are the same, and pools are per SID by construction.

**The holder.** Proposed from the windows-guest-ram side and adopted: the
broker starts `sv-guest broker holder`, a second SYSTEM process that holds a
`DuplicateHandle` copy of every region and does nothing else (it never maps
one). Its pipe, `\\.\pipe\waycompose-broker-holder`, admits SYSTEM and its
owner; the broker checks that the holder's process runs as its own account.
`add`, `del`, `list` and `quit` are its protocol. A restarted broker lists
the holder's regions, duplicates each back out, and serves it as an orphan of
its user's pool under its old id (`Core::restore_orphan`). A holder that
died is started again and given every region. So a region the host still
maps is lost only if the broker, the holder and every provider die together;
before the holder, the broker's crash while the provider was down was enough.
An orderly stop of the service leaves the holder running (an upgrade keeps
the regions). `sv-guest broker holder-quit` atomically refuses while any
region remains. Normal region release permits holder exit. On refusal,
uninstall retains the binary, service, protections and recovery state, and
restarts a previously running service to adopt retained regions.

**Signing (§111.6).** `Platform::identity` is `os=windows
user=<LookupAccountSidW name, %XX-escaped to one word> id=<SID>`. The keys are
`C:\ProgramData\waycompose\keys\<install>.key`, SYSTEM and Administrators
only. The compositor's boot path asks the broker (`Client::sign`) and
publishes with `macboot::publish_identity`; without a broker it signs from
the installation's key file as before, with one log line. `wc-launch` no
longer refuses to start when the user's key file is gone (deploy moves it).
The host's sessiond verifies with `verifies_identity` when the identity area
is present, refuses one that does not parse, and hands the identity on in its
`Request` for 111.10.

**Integration.** The compositor asks for `arena` (its `--arena-ivshmem`
device 0) and `wcbell`, the GPU process for `gpu` (its `--ivshmem-slot`) and
`svbell`, each over one connection per process kept for the process's life
(`client::process_client`). A missing or refusing broker gives one line,
`[wc-broker] device NAME: not from the broker (WHY); opening it directly`,
and the open as before; `WC_BROKER=off` skips it. `wc-launch` needs no
device.

The following measurements describe the original broker. Its cross-SID raw
BAR regrant and unconditional uninstall behavior are superseded by the
ownership and checked-shutdown restrictions below.

**Measured**, on a local test VM (the deployment host's QEMU 10.2.2, 3 GiB, 4 vCPUs,
a 64 MiB ivshmem device at 0x1c and one at 0x1d, the Looking Glass B7
driver), two local non-admin users u1 and u2 run through the task scheduler;
evidence in `/mnt/datasets/builds/evidence/session-fixes/broker-win/`:

| what | result |
|---|---|
| u1 asks for `arena`, maps the 64 MiB BAR | lent in 1.2 ms (process start excluded), mapped 67108864 |
| u2 asks for `arena` while u1 holds it | `device arena is held by another user's process` |
| u2 opens the arena, or `wcbell`, directly | access denied (error 5) |
| u2 `OpenProcess(PROCESS_DUP_HANDLE)` on u1's region holder | access denied |
| u2 `open` of u1's region by id; `adopt gpu` | `region 1 is another user's`; 0 adopted |
| `taskkill /F` of u1's holder | arena lent again 69 ms after taskkill started (taskkill itself 47 ms; one attempt) |
| u2 after that | lent and mapped |
| `sign` as u1 and as u2 | `os=windows user=u1 id=…-1001` and `user=u2 id=…-1002`; MAC verifies for its own identity, not for a rewritten one, not with it removed |
| control RTT (`stats`, u1, 5000) | mean 101 µs, p50 70 µs, p99 911 µs |
| `alloc` of a 2 MiB region | 207 µs |
| `sign` | 0.4 to 0.6 ms (reads the key file) |
| write+read through the GPU BAR, 5 runs each | lent: median 14.1 GiB/s; opened directly: 13.2 GiB/s (the same mapping code; the spread, 9.9 to 17.6, is the VM's) |
| a port lent | ~101 ms, all of it vioser's: a raw `CreateFileW` on the port takes ~100 ms, and so does its `CloseHandle`, with no Rust code involved (`portopen.ps1`) |
| u1's process ends with a region of pool `keep`; the service process is killed (`taskkill /F`) | the service manager restarted it, serving 1.6 s after the kill; the holder had kept the region; u2 adopted 0, u1 adopted it and read back what it wrote |
| `wc-launch.sh broker-uninstall`'s script | service deleted, holder ended, the four devices' PnP property removed and live descriptors restored to the driver's |

So the broker adds one request per device per process start (well under the
0.2 ms bar of §105 at the median), nothing per frame, and the data path is
the same code and speed. Under Wine (`tests/windows.rs`, own `WINEPREFIX`, 8
tests): a stand-in device moved into a child, refused to the parent, free
0.14 ms after the child was killed; a section mapped in two processes; an
orphan adopted; `sign`; the holder restoring a region after the broker was
killed and again after the holder was killed; RTT mean 41 µs, p99 59 µs.

**Deploy.** `WC_LAUNCH_BROKER=install scripts/wc-launch.sh deploy`
runs `wc-broker-install.ps1 -Action install` over its administrator channel:
Program Files, the service, failure actions, the §91 task and its files
removed, the service started. Then `-Action key -Install NAME` with the
installation's key on stdin, and the user's `session.key` is deleted.
`WC_LAUNCH_BROKER=key` registers only this installation's key in an already
running broker. It never installs or restarts the service and is allowed for
tests. The key and its protected parent directories belong to Administrators
and grant access only to SYSTEM and Administrators. Provisioning replaces the
key object using a protected temporary file, then replaces the whole DACL.
An already-open handle to an old readable key cannot observe the rotated
bytes. Reparse directories and key paths are refused. The service executable
and recovery files also have privileged ownership. This matters because an
owner can change a DACL even without a grant in that DACL.
Installation does not trust SCM's transient Running state alone. The ready
command opens an overlapped pipe, checks its kernel server PID against the
current running SCM service and its token SID against SYSTEM, then checks
hello/stats. While the verified process remains pinned, it independently
checks both live and PnP protection for present BARs and doorbell ports, then
rechecks process liveness and SCM before success. Each exchange has a one-second I/O deadline; cancellation is
drained before its buffers disappear. Generic private/user broker clients
keep their existing connection behavior.

`WC_LAUNCH_BROKER=skip`, the default, is the pre-§111 deploy: the broker is guest-wide, so a deploy installs it only when asked for by name, and a test installation is refused it (2026-10-20: the default had been `install`, and a test installation's deploy put the broker under the deployment guest's production installations). `wc-launch.sh broker-show`
and `broker-uninstall` (service deleted, devices' descriptors restored,
holder ended, keys kept). A deploy with `skip` refuses if the broker already
exists, before stopping a session or copying any files. Use `key` there;
recreating a desktop-readable signing key would defeat the broker identity
check. Unknown service status also refuses the deploy.

**Rollback baseline and refusal.** The first broker start records each device's
live DACL and PnP descriptor before changing either. Binary `SPDRP_SECURITY`
includes the mandatory label. The five-column `devices.txt` and durable count
checkpoint are flushed before mutation. Missing, truncated, unreadable or
invalid installed history requires trusted recovery. A fresh install records
an explicit empty baseline; restart cannot invent lost history. Independent
startup verification requires both live and PnP descriptors on the BARs and
doorbell ports to remain protected, even when securing failed or rollback history was lost. Unknown or
permissive protection fails before the public pipe or signer is created.
Missing optional devices are skipped. Protected devices with missing history
can still recover retained holder sections; their uninstall stays refused.

Uninstall checks before stopping the service whether either original raw BAR
descriptor could expose old bytes. Anything beyond the exact protected SYSTEM
and Administrators DACL refuses restoration. Direct `revert-acl` enforces the
same check. Retaining the SID file cannot police direct opens through a
permissive DACL. Uninstall is therefore unavailable for ordinary pre-broker
permissive raw baselines and is not an application rollback procedure. The
installer retains the original port task/files and all recovery state on
refusal. Any saved legacy grant task, script or port map also refuses uninstall
before service mutation. Such unreviewed code could undo safe raw descriptors
later, so protected original ACLs alone do not make legacy task restoration safe. Only an empty holder and protected raw baseline permit removal.

Raw BAR ownership is bound to the canonical physical PnP instance and a
privileged reviewed SID policy. Process exit, holder or broker restart, and
protocol alias changes cannot reassign it. Missing or untrusted policy denies
access. There is no first-claim or reset API. This is a single-owner limitation
until host/GPU drain can be proved.

A private Windows clone proved old BAR bytes crossed SIDs before this policy.
The corrected binary refuses the other SID after process exit, holder
replacement and broker restart; the owner still reads its original bytes.
Both ordinary users are denied direct raw opens. An actual-section proof
retained `user1-secret` through refused uninstall and direct refused holder
quit, recovered the same holder, then adopted/read and normally released it.
Unsafe raw rollback and missing-baseline uninstall refuse before service
mutation. Evidence is
`/mnt/datasets/builds/evidence/session-fixes/broker-rollback/`, especially
`raw-policy-clone.txt`, `raw-policy-alias.txt`,
`uninstall-lifetime-proof.txt` and `uninstall-direct-open-denied.txt`.
The final real Windows unit run passed all 30 tests in
`uninstall-windows-units-final.txt`.

**What remains.** Running the compositor and the GPU process on the VM under
the broker end to end under the mapped Linux user (the probe exercises the
same calls, not the products), and a run on the deployment guest (not touched
here). The large-page stamping hook is implemented by `stamp_guest_ram`.

### 111.9 macOS

Branch `broker-mac`. Role (a), the macOS VM, is built and was run in the VM
(below). Role (b), the real Mac, is designed only (111.9.6).

#### 111.9.1 What the LaunchDaemon is

`wc-broker serve` runs as the LaunchDaemon `org.waycompose.broker`: root,
started at boot, restarted by launchd whenever it ends (`KeepAlive`). It is
the one privileged component of a macOS server and replaces three things:

| before | now |
|---|---|
| `wc-launch --keeper`, a child of each main process, mapping and wiring the session's windows by their shm names (§103.15) | the broker makes each window (`alloc POOL BYTES`, the pool is the session id), maps and wires it, and keeps it after the main process dies |
| the main process and the GPU server opening `/dev/cu.org.sirati.{wcbell,svbell}.0` themselves (the nodes were 0666) | the nodes are root's and 0600; the broker opens a port, sets raw mode and moves the fd in (`device wcbell`, `device svbell`) |
| role (a): an unsigned boot record; role (b): a record signed with `session.key` from the user's support directory | the broker signs (`sign`) with `/Library/Application Support/waycompose/keys/<install>.key` (0600, in a 0700 directory, both root's) over the identity it read with `getpeereid` (`os=macos user=NAME id=UID`) |

Its socket is `/var/run/waycompose/broker.sock`, mode 0666; every request is
decided by the caller's uid (111.3). The binary, the keys and the plist
(`/Library/LaunchDaemons/org.waycompose.broker.plist`, written by
`wc-broker plist BIN`, so it has one source) are root's and not writable by
any user. `scripts/mac-launch-install.sh` installs and bootstraps it; the
host keeps the installation's key in `$BASE/keys` and runs `mac-sessiond
--keys` with it.

#### 111.9.2 The main process and the GPU server

* **Windows.** `wc_handle::arena::set_region_keeper` now takes a function
  from a length to an fd. The main process installs one that asks the broker
  (`alloc <session> <len>`). `alloc_kept` maps the fd, wires it and stamps it.
  The broker wired the object before the stamps exist, so it holds the pages
  before the host can find them, which is a stronger order than the keeper's
  (it mapped after the stamps, before the hello). The objects are POSIX shm,
  unlinked by the broker the moment it made them: no name reaches them, only
  the fds the broker sends.
* **No broker, no session** (role (a)): the main process refuses to start,
  as it refused without a keeper (`NO BROKER, NO SESSION` in `main.log`).
  Role (b) maps a file and runs on without one, signing with the key file.
* **Doorbells.** The main process asks `device wcbell` and passes the fd to
  the compositor as `--wayland-rings fd:N`; the doorman and wake code are
  unchanged and run on that fd. If the broker refuses (another user's session
  holds the port), the port's own name is passed and its open fails on the
  root-only node, which the compositor logs, and the rings poll.
* **The GPU server** starts as `wc-launch --gpu-exec <session> svbell --
  sv-guest gpu guest ...`. Before `exec`, which keeps the pid, it says
  `hello gpu`, `tie <session>` and `device svbell`, and adds `--bell fd:N`.
  So the broker watches the GPU server's pid, the port is the GPU server's,
  and the server is ended when its session is released, as the keeper ended
  it.
* **The boot record.** `wc_compositor::set_boot_signer` takes the broker's
  `sign`; `ringlink` (role (a)) and `session_svc` (role (b)) publish the
  record with `publish_identity`. Without a signer, or when it refuses, the
  record goes out as before, with one log line.

#### 111.9.3 The release rule, per pool (the core and server changes)

The keeper's rule was "every window of the session goes when the release word
in the session's boot page is set". The release word is in one region, the
ring window's page 0, and decides for all of the session's regions; a
per-region probe would have released the arena on any page whose word at
offset 1728 happened to be nonzero. So, additively:

* `core.rs`, rule 6: `pool_released(id)` destroys every orphan of the region's
  (user, pool) and ends the pool's tied processes; `tie(conn, pool)` records
  that the caller's process ends with the pool (only itself); `tick` ends the
  ties of a pool whose last orphan went by time; `Notice::End(pid)`;
  `role(pid)` and `tied(pid)` for logs and tests.
* `proto.rs`: `tie POOL -> ok`. `client.rs`: `Client::tie`.
* `server.rs`: `Platform::released_pool(&obj)` (default no), asked before
  `released`; `Platform::end(pid)` (default nothing); `Broker::drain_orphans
  (limit)` for a shutdown; a log line per process exit with the orphans it
  left.
* `sys/unix.rs`: `Unix::mac_keeper()` (wire every region; the pool probe is
  `macboot::is_boot_page` and `load_released` on the region's page 0), `end`
  sends SIGKILL only to a pid the watcher still watches, and a port that is a
  tty is put in raw mode before it is moved.

The host's `mac-sessiond` writes `macboot::RELEASED` once the proxy's and
GPU units have ended. The daemon uses `Release::Probe { after: None }`.
Elapsed time cannot prove that the host stopped writing, so there is no
timeout release and `--release-after` is rejected. The original 600-second
fallback could free wired pages while the host still wrote into them.

**Shutdown**: SIGTERM first quiesces allocation under the broker's state
lock, then keeps serving and probing until **all** live and orphan regions
are released. It waits indefinitely if needed. The original ten-second
orphan-only wait could exit with live or orphan host mappings and was unsafe.
The plist now sets `ExitTimeOut` to zero, disabling launchd's automatic
shutdown SIGKILL deadline. The installer refuses to replace a loaded broker
or an existing broker socket before changing either end's installed files;
it no longer issues `launchctl bootout`. To upgrade, first end sessions and
verify their host release, SIGTERM the daemon, wait for its exit, and prevent
new sessions before unloading its job. Never force bootout of an old broker
that still holds regions.

**Independent retention after broker death.** Before any region grant, a
private retention process receives the already allocated shared-memory fd,
creates its own shared mapping, independently calls `mlock`, and acknowledges
success. It is another invocation of `wc-broker`, with no public socket,
allocator or authorization endpoint. The broker alone decides grants and
normal destruction. The holder uses a separate session/process group, and
launchd's `AbandonProcessGroup` preserves it when the broker exits.

Broker EOF never frees its mappings. The holder restores their metadata as
orphans in the same `Core` lifetime engine, uses `Release::Probe { after: None }`,
and frees only the matching user's pool when its boot page carries the host
release word. Other pools remain wired. No deadline, signal handler or channel
error unwinds existing holds. A missing or failed holder refuses new grants.
This covers a broker-process crash with a surviving holder. It does not cover
holder and broker failure together, VM termination, or the GPU server's own
extent. A region never stamped with a boot release page may remain held
indefinitely after broker death. New brokers do not yet re-adopt old holders;
those holders independently wait for host release rather than freeing on
restart.

#### 111.9.4 Tests

* `core::tests` (+2): a released boot region frees its whole pool and ends its
  tie, and nothing of another pool, another user's pool of the same name, or a
  live owner's; a pool that times out ends its ties once.
* `tests/unix.rs`, the keeper on a real socket, as Linux runs the same
  code but the watcher: a "main" process allocates the arena and the ring
  window and writes a boot page, a "GPU server" ties itself; the main process
  is killed with SIGKILL; the two regions stay held and readable for 2.5 s
  without the word; the test writes `RELEASED` into the boot page as the host
  does, and within a tick both regions are gone and the GPU process is
  SIGKILLed. This test uses no timeout release, matching the daemon. A
  separate generic core-policy test uses an explicit optional timeout; it
  does not select the policy used for host-visible wired RAM.
* `daemon::tests`: `serve` arguments reject timeout-release overrides; a
  simulated month without a host release retains both orphan regions; the
  release word frees the pool; the plist disables forced-kill deadlines.
* `daemon_shutdown_retains_live_regions_and_orphans_until_explicit_release`:
  a real daemon receives SIGTERM with a live region, remains alive beyond
  the old ten-second limit, then retains the orphan, rejects allocation and
  exits only after explicit adoption/free. Runs on Linux without a VM.
* `scripts/mac-broker-term-test.sh`: VM stubs cover a root daemon staying
  alive, actual exit plus a live replacement, probe/transport errors, an
  unchanged pid, invalid pid output and a dead replacement. Shutdown
  observation uses a monotonic 12-second deadline, comprising the expected
  ten-second released-pool case and a two-second scheduling/SSH margin.
  Every VM call is bounded by the remaining deadline; retained active
  regions correctly make this timing gate fail rather than force an exit.
* `wc-arena-host`: `who_asked_is_read_and_with_keys_verified` (the identity
  reported, verified with `--keys`, refused when another user's identity is
  written over it or the record is unsigned). `sessiond_ivshmem` verifies with
  `verifies_identity`, which is §107's check when there is no identity.

**In the VM** (wayland-host, 4096 MiB, 2026-10-20 11:06–11:20,
`scripts/mac-broker-test.sh` driven by a waiter; evidence in
`/mnt/datasets/builds/evidence/session-fixes/broker-mac/`, `broker-*.txt`,
`keeper-*.txt`, `broker-daemon.log`, `vmrun.log`):

* **The daemon and the ports.** launchd ran it (`keepalive | runatload`).
  The port nodes became `crw------- root wheel`, the socket
  `srw-rw-rw-`, the keys directory `drwx------` and the key `-rw-------`, all
  root's. The VM's user could not read the key. The daemon lent `wcbell` to
  every main process and `svbell` to the GPU server (`device ... lent to
  process N`), and logged each exit by kqueue (`process N (main) exited`).
* **SIGKILL of the main process under load, 5 times** (Console open, foot on
  this side scrolling `seq` into the session): every time the broker held
  the session's two windows (64 MiB arena, 6 MiB rings) as orphans after the
  exit, the host's session service took the session down and wrote the
  release word, and the broker freed the pool on it (`the release word of
  pool wcm-N is set; freeing the pool's orphans`). Kernel panic reports
  before 0, after 0; the guest stayed up.
* **The GPU server** was tied to its session (`ends with pool`), its exit
  seen, and its session's pool freed by the release word; 300 frames
  presented (PASS).
* **SIGTERM to the daemon** while it held 2 orphans: the daemon logged its
  shutdown wait, but exit and restart were not proved. The harness queried
  the root daemon with an unprivileged `kill -0`, which treats permission
  denial as process exit. It then reported the same pid before and after
  the signal. The 0.70 s measurement is invalid. The harness now requires a successful root probe and positive PID absence,
  enforces an elapsed observation deadline, and validates a different live
  replacement pid; the corrected safety rerun is recorded below.
* **A second macOS user** (`wctest2`, made with `sysadminctl`, deleted
  after): its `open` of user 1's regions, `find` of user 1's pool and
  `device wcbell` (held by user 1's main process) were refused by uid; it
  could not read the key; its own `alloc` worked; `sign` named it
  (`os=macos user=wctest2 id=503`). The host logged user 1's sessions as
  `asked by os=macos user=<user> id=501 (verified, installation wcm)`.
  `svbell`, free at that moment, was lent to user 2: a free device goes to
  any user, one at a time, by design.

**Not shown by this run, and why:**

* **Wayland round trip and present time, before and after.** The VM was
  slow throughout. The host's memory group for the macOS VMs was near its
  limit while another instance ran, and every number was far from §103.15's
  in both builds: the GPU present was 8.50 ms/frame with the keeper and
  23.35 ms/frame with the broker (§103.15: 0.56), and the broker's
  2000 round trips gave p50 3.52 ms, p99 179 ms (§103.15: 0.248, 0.322). The
  keeper's round-trip leg produced no number: its main process had already
  ended when the client connected. Nothing on the data path changed (the
  doorbell is the same port, now an inherited fd; the windows are the same
  wired pages), but "the same within noise" is **not measured**; it needs a
  rerun on a quiet host.
* **The second user's own session.** Its main process, started with
  `sudo -u` from ssh, wrote no log, so a second session side by side was not
  run.
* The harness's check that a user cannot open a port node itself used
  `head -c0`, which macOS rejects; the node modes above are the evidence.
  Fixed before the safety rerun below.

**Safety rerun, 3072 MiB VM, 2026-10-20 around 12:00-12:04.** Evidence is
in `evidence/session-fixes/broker-mac/safe-rerun/`, outside git. The new broker
was built after the no-timeout correction; no unsafe old baseline ran.

* The corrected direct port-open probe and root-key read were refused.
  The LaunchDaemon was root's, the ports 0600, the socket 0666 and the key
  directory/key 0700/0600.
* Five recorded main-process SIGKILL cycles each ended with host teardown,
  the host release word and pool reclamation. Recursive panic-file counts
  were four before and four after, and guest uptime continued throughout.
  The harness used default foot settings and throwaway Linux HOME/XDG
  state; Console ran on a private D-Bus session.
* The root daemon held two orphan regions when SIGTERM arrived. A successful
  root process-table snapshot observed its exit after 5210 ms, including SSH
  observation overhead, and launchd reported a different live pid, 581 to
  1265. Its log showed host release followed by `every region released;
  exiting`. This replaces the original run's invalid 0.70 s assertion.
* The 2000 Wayland round trips measured mean 3.240 ms, p50 1.231 ms,
  p99 12.646 ms and maximum 1470.707 ms. The runtime ctypes/libwayland
  fixture includes Python call overhead. This **fails** the 0.2 ms target;
  it proves neither acceptable latency nor broker overhead relative to the
  old unsafe baseline. Concurrent second-user sessions and fresh GPU timing
  remain unproved by this rerun.
* The successful VM run peaked at 4,423,475,200 bytes including QEMU/cache;
  an earlier cold-start attempt peaked at 5,089,390,592 bytes before tests.
  These observations include reclaimable cache, not only configured RAM. Cleanup
  restored guest support/apps, host files and original unit arguments,
  removed the test daemon/key, cleanly stopped the VM and restored its
  original 4096 MiB configuration. The peer's `work` VM was untouched.

**Restart ownership.** The restored older `mac-sessiond` exposed a separate
isolation bug: startup adopted every active `wc-launch-*` unit, including
unrelated `wcma-*`, `wcmb-*` and `wcmc-*` harness sessions with no known boot
page. It then ran `down` for them. Restart state is now scoped by configured
QMP path, VM hint, session script and key policy; each checkpoint carries that
full owner description. Recovery requires a matching boot page in that VM
and its configured MAC policy. A directory hash only names this state and is
not trusted as authorization. Every managed session has a boot record, and
ownership is checked again before teardown. Unowned/legacy global state is
left untouched; failed host release retains the checkpoint for retry.
Before upgrading the old service with live sessions, drain those sessions
through their actual owner. Old global checkpoints cannot prove installation
ownership and are not automatically migrated.

**Independent-holder macOS runtime proof, 2026-10-20.** The disposable
`wayland-host` VM ran at 3072 MiB under an exclusive run lease, using the
vmhost-built broker from `5ec8367`. A native fixture allocated two 64 KiB regions
in pool A and one in pool B, stamped them, closed every fd and mapping, and
exited before the broker was killed. No GUI or application workload was used.

The root LaunchDaemon broker PID 383 was SIGKILLed. Twelve seconds later its
separate holder PID 385 remained, reparented to launchd. Native
`mach_vm_region(..., VM_REGION_BASIC_INFO_64, ...)` inspection reported
`user_wired_count=1` for all three independent holder mappings, at the same
addresses observed before broker death. The host wrote sentinel values directly
through QEMU's shared guest-RAM backend both before and after the broker kill;
Mach reads of the holder's mappings verified both values.

The host then wrote pool A's release word exactly once, stopped accessing that
pool, and observed both A mappings disappear while B remained wired at the same
address with its sentinel intact. Pool B's release ended the holder. A successful
sudo process-table snapshot positively established its absence. Panic-file
counts stayed 4 before and 4 after. This proves broker-process SIGKILL retention
and per-pool host release in this macOS VM; it does not test simultaneous
holder/broker death, a full graphical session or the GPU server's own extent.

The VM was cleanly stopped, its exact prior 4096 MiB configuration restored, and
the temporary job, binaries and socket removed. Both existing host units kept
their PIDs and arguments throughout. Measured VM-unit MemoryPeak was
5,239,672,832 bytes including QEMU/cache. Evidence is in
`evidence/session-fixes/broker-mac/holder-vm/`. An earlier successful run is
retained as `holder-vm-first`; the final run strengthened holder-exit observation
with a successful full process-table query.

#### 111.9.5 Limits

* **One wcbell port.** The VM has one rings port, and a port has one holder.
  A second macOS user's session gets no doorbell: it polls its rings, and the
  host finds its record only by a periodic sweep (`--sweep-secs`). A port per
  user (`org.sirati.wcbell.N`, a chardev each on the hub) is the fix.
* **Independent holder limits.** A broker-process crash leaves its separate
  wired holder alive until host release. Simultaneous holder/broker death or
  VM termination still loses those wires. Restarted brokers do not re-adopt
  the old holders, so old allocations remain private to their original
  clients until host release; missing release pages retain memory indefinitely.
  The disposable macOS VM proof above verifies independent wiring and
  launchd survival for a broker-process SIGKILL. It does not establish safety
  against failure of the holder itself or a terminated VM.
* **The GPU server's own extent** is still its own superpages: kept by
  nothing if the GPU server itself crashes while `sv-hostd` serves it
  (§103.15's remaining case). Moving it into the broker would change its
  pinning from superpages to wired 4 KiB pages, which this work must not do.
* `end` checks that the pid is still watched, but the kqueue exit event and
  the release can race by microseconds; the pid would then have to be reused
  in that window.

#### 111.9.6 Role (b), the real Mac (designed, not built)

On the real Mac the Linux VM is a user's libkrun process. Its shared memory is
a file on a RAM-disk volume shared through virtio-fs DAX
(`/Volumes/linux-vm-shm/arena`); its doorbells are FIFO pairs the VM manager
makes (`~/.local/state/linux-vm/bells/<name>.{to-guest,from-guest}`). Both
belong to the VM, and the VM belongs to one Mac user.

What the same LaunchDaemon does there, with no code beyond what exists:

* **Signs.** `session_svc` asks the broker when the main process has one;
  `sessiond_ivshmem` in the guest verifies the identity. The peer moves
  `session.key` from the support directory into the daemon's keys directory
  and installs the daemon (`wc-broker plist`, the same plist).
* **Watches** the main process and logs its exit; nothing is held, because
  file pages are not freed when a process dies (the file holds them; only a
  truncate would, and nothing truncates a live arena). No keeper is needed in
  role (b).

The arena file and the bell FIFOs stay the user's, 0600 in the user's own
directories. With one VM per user that is already per-user isolation, and
routing them through the broker would add a hop for nothing.

If one Linux VM is to serve several Mac users (as the macOS VM in role (a)
serves its users), the peer would change:

1. The VM manager runs as a LaunchDaemon (or under the broker's account), and
   makes the arena file and the FIFOs root's, 0600, in a root directory
   (`/var/run/waycompose/vm/<vm>/`).
2. The broker lends a bell as **two descriptors** (`device wcbell` answering
   `fd fd`, a device of two paths): an additive change to the device reply
   and `Client::device`.
3. The broker opens the arena file and publishes each session's part of it
   as a region of that user's pool (`Broker::publish`, then `find <pool>`),
   and `WC_IVSHMEM_STANDIN` takes an inherited fd instead of a path.
4. `mac.rs` replaces `fifo_bell(prefix)` with `device wcbell` and the
   `arena-file` path with `find`.

### 111.10 The Linux host: sessions run as the mapped user

Written 2026-10-20, branch `broker-host`. Until now the doorbell hub (§99) and
the session service (§105) were user units of the VM host's admin account,
and every session's proxy, applications, sound and host integration ran as
that admin. So the guest's Windows user ran Linux programs with the admin's
files and keys. On the client role's host now:

* the hub and the session service are **system services** of their own
  account, `waycompose` (group `wc-arena`). Only they open the arena and GPU
  BAR files and QEMU's doorbell sockets; desktop users have neither the group
  nor an ACL;
* a root-owned table, `/etc/waycompose/users.conf`, maps the boot record's
  identity (111.6) to a Linux user. A record nobody is mapped for is refused,
  and the guest reads why in the boot page;
* a session runs **as that user, in that user's systemd manager**, with their
  home and groups. Its processes get the BAR files and the hub through the
  broker the session service embeds.

#### The table

```text
# SERVER   SERVER-USER    LINUX-USER      [installs=a,b] [id=SID-or-uid]
vm-guest   <guest-user>   <desktop-user>  installs=wcivs,wcmc,wclinux
vm-guest   <guest-user>   wctest          installs=wctest1
vm-guest   -              <desktop-user>  installs=wcivs        # transitional
```

`SERVER` is the VM a service serves (`--server`); it reads only those lines.
`SERVER-USER` is matched against the identity's account name, without regard
to ASCII case when the identity's os is `windows` (Windows' own rule) and
exactly otherwise; `id=` pins the account's SID or uid as well. `installs=`
narrows a line to those installations. The first matching line wins. A table
with one bad line fails whole, and the service does not start: a policy read
in part would map someone it should not (`wc_broker::usermap`, 5 tests).
`root` is never a target. The NixOS option `services.waycompose.mappings`
writes the file.

What the guest is told, verbatim from the tests:

* `<os> user <name> (<id>) is not mapped to any Linux user on this host`;
* `... may not start installation <name> on this host`: the user is mapped,
  for other installations;
* `the boot record of installation <name> carries no identity, and this host
  requires one`;
* `the boot record ... does not verify under its key with the identity it
  carries`: the identity was rewritten (111.6);
* `the boot record's identity area does not parse`: never read as "none".

**Transitional, and to be removed.** The guest's privileged service (111.8)
is not deployed yet, so today's records carry no identity. With
`--accept-unidentified`, a record without one maps through a `-` line, which
must name its installations, one Linux user per installation. A record that
has an identity never matches `-`. Remove the flag and the `-` lines
(`acceptUnidentified`, `unidentified` in the NixOS module) as soon as every
installation on the guest boots through its service; from then on an
unsigned record is refused.

#### Who starts the session: the user's own agent

The service runs as `waycompose` and must start processes in another user's
manager. Three ways were weighed:

* (a) `systemd-run --machine=<user>@.host --user` from the service. It needs a
  polkit rule letting `waycompose` manage units in other users' managers, and
  polkit's `manage-units` action cannot be scoped to one target user
  without matching on unit names it cannot see. Rejected: a rule that broad is
  more than a session start needs.
* (b) a socket-activated agent per user. Chosen. `wc-session-agent.socket` is a
  user unit (`Accept=yes`) at `/run/waycompose-agent/<user>/agent.sock`, in a
  directory only that user can write. The service connects and checks with
  `SO_PEERCRED` that the socket is the mapped uid's (the listener is that
  user's manager). The agent checks that the caller is `waycompose` or root.
  Then it runs the installation's `wc-session up/proxy/gpu` itself, as the
  user, so `systemd-run --user` lands in the user's manager as it always did.
  No polkit, no root helper. The agent stays connected until the session's
  proxy unit ends, runs `down`, and says `ended`; then the service unpublishes
  the session's regions.
* (c) a system service with `User=` per session: not the user's manager, no
  session environment, and every session a new system unit. Rejected.

The line on the agent's socket is `start INSTALL ID RUNID INDEX GPU
ARENA-REGION GPU-REGION`. It is parsed as untrusted input; `wc-session`
validates the words again (§94). The mapped users linger, so their agents
are there before anybody logs in.

One test, leg 5 of `scripts/wc-broker-host.sh`, maps a user to an account
whose agent socket is a link to another user's. The service refuses it:
`... is uid 1000's socket, not uid 65534's`.

#### The session service and the broker: one process

`wc-arena-host sessiond --broker /run/waycompose/broker.sock` serves
`wc_broker::server::Broker<Unix>` on a thread of its own. One process,
because:

* what the broker hands out per session is decided by the service. It
  publishes the BAR files for the uid users.conf just named, when the session
  starts (`publish(uid, "arena"|"gpu", …)`). It unpublishes them when the
  session ends. Two processes would need a protocol between them for exactly
  that, plus a story for when one restarts without the other;
* a restart of the service (a changed users.conf, `restartTriggers`) costs
  running sessions nothing they hold. Their fds and mappings are theirs, and
  the per-process broker connection reconnects lazily.

The hub stays a separate service. Its QEMU connections live in systemd's fd
store (§99.6), and it must not restart when the mapping changes.

A session's processes reach everything through specs the binaries take
wherever a path was taken before. `wc-session` writes them when the service
passes `WC_BROKER` and the region ids (`WC_LAUNCH_BROKER_ARENA`, `_GPU`).
Without them it writes the old paths, so nothing changes where no broker runs:

| before | through the broker | who |
|---|---|---|
| `/run/windows-vm/wc-arena/arena` | `broker:<id>` (`open`) | wc-proxy, `wc-arena-host broker-read` (the header `up` checks) |
| `/run/windows-vm/wc-arena/gpu` | `broker:<id>` | sv-hostd `--region`, and sv-icd, which opens the name sv-hostd sends it |
| `~/…/wc-bell/wl.sock`, `sv.sock` | `broker:wl-hub`, `broker:sv-hub` (`connect`) | wc-proxy, sv-hostd `--cold-bell`, sv-icd `SV_BELL` |

`sv_transport::brokered` holds two hooks, a service connector and a region
opener. `wc_broker::client::install_hooks` fills them with the process's one
broker connection. So `vdoorbell::PortHandle::open`, `poolcold::HubBell` and
`region::open_named` understand `broker:` with no broker client in
sv-transport. The connection is per process and kept for its life: the broker
watches the process through it, and the leases are its. For leases held for
one of several clients (the proxy's Wayland clients, §112),
`client::own_connection` gives a connection whose leases end when it is
dropped.

**Every fd of one region shares one file offset.** The broker's fd and every
copy it sends are one open file description. The first run of the harness
failed on exactly this: `up` read the header with `read`, which moved the
offset, and the proxy's own `read` then found zeros. Readers of a broker
region use `mmap` or positional I/O (`read_exact_at`). The header readers do
now, and `client::open_path`'s comment says so.

The guest-RAM substrate (§108) is embedded the same way.
`wc_broker::host::Embedded` (`attach(&Broker<Unix>, &SessionsView)` once,
`session_up`, `session_down`) is the interface. `SessionsView` answers whose
each live session is. `embedded(GuestRam)` in `sessiond_ivshmem.rs` is where a
component is constructed, from the `--guest-ram-*` flags: `-boot`, `-qemu-pid`
/ `-qemu-pidfile` / `--guest-ram`, `-bell`, and `-user UID|mapped`. `mapped` is
users.conf's mapping of the guest GPU process's user, `UserMap::resolve_any`.

#### Layout

| what | where | whose |
|---|---|---|
| the services' binaries (`wc-arena-host`, `sv-hostd`) | `/var/lib/waycompose/bin` | root, 0755 |
| an installation's definition (`wc-session`, `apps.ini`, `gpu.env`, `bin/`) | `/var/lib/waycompose/installs/<name>` | root, 0755 |
| its key | `…/<name>/session.key` | `waycompose`, 0600 (the service checks) |
| sequence numbers (§105) | `/var/lib/waycompose/sessiond` | `waycompose`, 0700 |
| broker, hub | `/run/waycompose/{broker.sock,hub/}` | `waycompose`; broker socket 0666 (access is per request, by uid), hub 0750 |
| agents | `/run/waycompose-agent/<user>/agent.sock` | a root tree (systemd-tmpfiles refuses a root directory under the service's), each directory the user's |
| a session's run directory | `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/wc-launch/<id>` of the mapped user | the user, 0700 |
| per-user state: Firefox profiles, Prism's data | the mapped user's home (`~/.wc-launch/<profile>`, `~/wc-mc`) | the user |

`apps.ini` spells per-user paths `~/…`, which `wc-session` expands to the
running user's home in `exec`, `profile`, every word of `args`, and `env`
values. So one definition serves whichever user its guest user is mapped to.
A definition holds nothing of a user's. Nothing writes into the installation
directory at run time (checked: every `$BASE` use in `wc-session` reads).

#### The existing installations (the Windows VM host)

`scripts/wc-users-migrate.sh plan|apply|verify|remove-old|rollback ADMIN
DESKTOP BIN-DIR INSTALL...` moves them, as root, after the switch to the
generation with `services.waycompose`. For each installation it does this:

* the base its admin link names is copied into `/var/lib/waycompose/installs`,
  with this branch's binaries over `bin/`, root's, and the key `waycompose`'s.
  GC roots of `bin/`'s store links are registered again;
* every path under the admin's home that `apps.ini` names is copied into the
  desktop user's home: the Firefox profile `wcivs` uses, the Prism data and
  launcher `wcmc` uses. The copy is chowned. Absolute paths in its text files
  are rewritten (Prism's config, the recorded launches, Firefox's prefs), and
  `apps.ini` says `~/`;
* the sequence numbers move, so an old record cannot be replayed;
* the admin's user units stop and are kept in a backup. The running VM's ACLs
  for the admin and the desktop user are dropped and one for `waycompose` is
  added; the VM is not restarted;
* `remove-old` deletes the admin's copies only after a session was seen
  working. `rollback` restores a previous protected installation snapshot
  beneath the system layout, with its current trusted key. It keeps the
  system services, user mapping and broker protection. It never restores
  admin user units, desktop raw-resource ACLs or an exposed old key. A
  missing confirmed snapshot refuses rollback. First migration preserves
  the original `wc-launch` profile renderer and `libsv_wlshim.so` presentation
  library while upgrading the broker-dependent launcher script, proxy, ICD
  and transport services. The pre-broker installation is kept under
  `legacy-original` as recovery history, not executable rollback.

  Run a real mapped-user product session successfully, end it, then invoke
  `wc-users-migrate.sh baseline-confirm ADMIN DESKTOP unused INSTALL`.
  This explicit operator confirmation snapshots that tested protected
  installation. It does not run the product test itself. Replacing an
  installation requires a confirmed baseline; deployments never overwrite it
  automatically. Confirm a later candidate only after its own successful
  product session. Root first installs the accepted stock-policy source hashes
  in `/var/lib/waycompose/policy/stock-session.sources`, owned by root with
  mode 0600 beneath a root-owned 0700 directory. Each line is
  `stock-defaults-v1 SHA256`, from the exact script accepted by the real
  mapped-user stock-policy proof. Deployment never creates this receipt.
  Confirmation records that source hash alongside the tested snapshot;
  deployment and rollback validate the actual script bytes against it.
  Old pre-stock snapshots or a newly added version label alone cannot pass.
  Adding a reviewed policy source requires its own successful product proof;
  preserve an older receipt entry only while that source remains approved.
  Rollback restores the accepted application's configuration
  and binaries, including its known-working broker-aware transport baseline,
  with the current trusted key. Shared services and user mapping stay in place.
  Both confirmation and rollback require idle admin and mapped-user sessions.

Before first-install SCM changes, the Windows installer creates a fresh
privileged Data directory object and empty signer tree under a validated
parent. It moves the entire old Data object into a newly protected recovery
container without traversing or normalizing retired descendants. A retained
old writable directory handle can change only that retired generation.
Directory creation uses native atomic create-new semantics and supplies its
owner/DACL at creation. Existing raw security history refuses fresh replacement
and requires trusted recovery.

Existing-service installs require protected directory-generation receipts
bound to current NTFS object IDs, plus per-install key enrollment receipts.
The key action requires a valid fresh Data generation and creates each new key
object with privileged security at creation. The executable directory similarly
requires fresh generation provenance; unknown, exposed or reparse binary
directories refuse before Data or SCM changes. Unknown keys and stale receipts
cannot bless replacement objects merely through owner/DACL normalization.

Actual Windows filesystem fixtures exercised writable old parent handles,
retired ACL edits and relative injected-directory/key creation. The active
Data/Keys object identities and ACLs remained unchanged. A retained writable
old key handle prevented old-directory rename; the installer failed closed
without publishing a new generation. Fixtures also verified native name
collision, raw-history and unsafe-anchor refusals and binary-directory
provenance/reparse checks. No actual family/service/device objects were touched.

Migration replaces the running raw-resource ACLs completely and makes their
owner/group root, with only the named service account allowed. It clears
inherited default ACLs on the directory and removes base group grants, so
processes retaining an old `wc-arena` supplementary group cannot reopen the
BARs. A bounded real-UID fixture verified both fresh opens fail for an already
running UID1000/GID982 process, while both retained shared mappings remain
writable and the designated service UID can still open the files. It used
isolated temporary files, not family BARs.

A bounded native fixture now proves the service and signer at uid 1000 map
an authenticated boot record to a real agent and application at uid 1001.
The named stock `wayland-info` application reads the live registry through
`wc-session`, the proxy and control rings. Its proxy holds the descriptor the
broker opened while direct opens of the service-owned synthetic BARs fail.
The private user manager and every application use synthetic HOME/XDG paths;
family VM, render-node and DRM paths are masked in both fixture namespaces.

The rollback fixture executes the actual installed original `wc-launch`
profile renderer, confirms a baseline only after that mapped-user product
session ends, deploys a broken renderer and changed preferences, then runs
`rollback`. The original renderer bytes and false preference return and the
real application runs again. Transport hashes, service/signer processes,
current protected key and an independent shared mapping/sentinel remain
unchanged. The original presentation shim is restored by hash; GPU presentation
is not exercised. This is a native synthetic-BAR fixture, separate from the
real Windows broker tests, and does not restore pre-broker transports.
Evidence is `distinct-uid-original-renderer-rollback.txt` beneath
`/mnt/datasets/builds/evidence/session-fixes/broker-rollback/`.
Family migration and deployment remain pending review.

**wclinux is the exception.** The nested "Windows 7 (Linux)" demo desktop
runs as the desktop user, like his applications. Its seat is still brought up
as root through win7-desktop.nix's sudo rule. That rule's users are now an
option, `seatUsers` (default: the owner, unchanged elsewhere). The seat still
asks for a password at its login screen. The seat now also accepts the GPU
words a brokered session passes: `SV_BELL=broker:<name>`, and `WC_BROKER`
only as `/run/waycompose/broker.sock`. So its KWin's sv-icd reaches the GPU
BAR through the broker as the desktop user, and the desktop user's ACL on the
GPU file is gone. The nested-session user lingers now. win7-desktop's
`linger = false` became a default, because the agent must be there before any
login.

**Test installations** of other agents run as the Linux user `wctest`: name
them in the host configuration's `wctestInstalls`, which adds
`<guest-user> -> wctest installs=…` to the table. Deploy them into
`/var/lib/waycompose/installs/<name>` as the migration script lays them out.

**Deploying onto the system layout.** Once a host runs the system services,
`scripts/wc-launch.sh deploy` in its old form would write the admin's hub and
session service units back beside them, and two session services would race
for every boot record. So it refuses on such a host (`/etc/waycompose/users.conf`
or a system `wc-sessiond.service` present), and `install_services` refuses too.
`WC_LAUNCH_HOST_LAYOUT=system` is the form for it:

* the installation is built as before, in a stage in the admin's home
  (`~/.cache/waycompose-stage/<name>`), GC roots included;
* `scripts/wc-users-migrate.sh install-staged ADMIN auto STAGE NAME`, as root
  (`WC_LAUNCH_HOST_ROOT`, default `sudo -n`; `sudokey run --` on the deployment
  host), replaces `/var/lib/waycompose/installs/<name>` by it. The stage's
  paths become the installation's, the admin's home becomes `~/` (the mapped
  user's), and the GC roots are registered at their new path. Only a
  root-generated, broker-confirmed key is installed. A legacy stage key is
  discarded;
* the deploy is refused unless `users.conf` maps the installation to a user. A
  test installation is named in the host's `wctestInstalls`, so it runs as
  `wctest`, with its profile in that user's home;
* no unit is written, and the system hub's and session service's binaries are
  left alone. `WC_LAUNCH_SYSTEM_BINS=install` replaces them and restarts both,
  which is a doorbell blip of about a second for every session;
* the debug ssh transport is not available with it.

Before the first privileged-identity migration, `key-prepare` stops both
legacy and system verifiers after refusing active sessions. It disables the
legacy admin units and removes retired verifier keys before provisioning,
so a restart or reboot cannot revive exposed trust. It generates a
fresh key beneath root-owned `/var/lib/waycompose/key-trust/<name>` with
0700 directories and 0600 files. `key-export` sends that candidate directly
to the deploy channel, never into the admin's staging tree. The Windows
broker's privileged key provisioning must succeed before `key-confirm`
records protected provenance. `apply` and `install-staged` refuse keys
without that provenance. They never infer historical secrecy from a key's
current owner or mode. Failure keeps the old verifier stopped; retry uses
the same protected candidate. Already protected deployments reuse their
key. Every script-managed shared-verifier restart first checks that all
installed directories have protected broker-confirmed provenance and match
their registry key; a partially migrated directory leaves services stopped. Privileged broker provisioning through the old user layout is refused.
Generation provenance is written only when the helper actually generates a
candidate. A preexisting key with root ownership and 0600 mode but no such
provenance is refused, not relabelled. A lost candidate cannot inherit an old
broker confirmation. A generated candidate interrupted before broker
confirmation can be retried unchanged. Generation is serialized.

The focused fixture reproduces a first migration whose candidate `wc-session`
exits 91, then runs the restored original executable after protected rollback.
It checks normalized system paths and the current trusted key. This is an
isolated filesystem fixture, not a live mapped-user application session.
The private Windows clone additionally passed real broker signing and host
boot-record verification with the replacement key while rejecting the retired
key. An already-open handle to the previously readable key retained only the
retired bytes after replacement. The replacement object allowed only SYSTEM
and Administrators. Evidence and the recipe are outside git in
`evidence/session-fixes/broker-rollback/key-rotation-proof.txt` and
`key-rotation-proof.ps1`; neither records key bytes or fingerprints.

The root helper and privileged deployment channel are trusted administration
interfaces, not interfaces exposed to desktop clients.

`scripts/wc-users-migrate-test.sh` runs `install-staged` in a dry tree
